=== dsacpp-01 | A vector of your own: raw memory and the rule of five
--- teach
In DSA I you built a dynamic array in Python: a list with spare room that doubles its capacity when it fills up. Python found the memory for you, and gave it back when nothing used it any more. C++ does neither. You ask for memory, and you give it back, exactly once. This course builds the DSA I structures again in C++, where the machine is visible. It starts with the structure you use most, a vector, and with the five special member functions that make a class that owns memory safe to copy, move and destroy.

### An array on the heap

`new double[n]` asks for room for `n` doubles, side by side, on the **[[heap|heap-array]]**: memory that stays until you give it back. It returns a `double*`, a pointer to the first one. `delete[] p` gives the whole array back.

```cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::size_t n = 4;
    double* temps = new double[n];   // room for 4 doubles; their values are not set yet
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) temps[i] = 20.0 + i;
    std::cout << temps[3] << "\n";   // 23
    delete[] temps;                  // give all 4 back
}
```

Four facts to keep:

- The values in a new array are **not set**: reading one before writing it is undefined behaviour. `new double[n]()`, with empty brackets after, sets them all to zero.
- `p[i]` on a pointer means "the item `i` places after the one `p` points at", exactly as on an array.
- An array made with `new[]` must be given back with `delete[]`, brackets included. Plain `delete` on it is undefined behaviour.
- `delete[] nullptr` is allowed and does nothing. So "no array yet" is easy to say: a null pointer.

### Size, capacity and the invariant

A vector needs three members:

```cpp fragment
int* data_ = nullptr;   // the array, or nullptr when there is none
std::size_t size_ = 0;  // how many slots hold values
std::size_t cap_ = 0;   // how many slots the array has
```

**Size** is how many values the vector holds. **Capacity** is how many fit before it must grow. `std::size_t` is the unsigned type C++ uses for sizes and indexes.

The class keeps an **invariant**, a set of facts that are true between any two calls of its member functions:

1. `size_ <= cap_`.
2. If `cap_` is 0, `data_` is `nullptr`. Otherwise `data_` points at an array of exactly `cap_` ints made by `new[]`.
3. The values are in slots `0` to `size_ - 1`, in order.
4. This object is the only one that will ever `delete[]` that array.

Rule 4 is the one Python never asked for. It is called **ownership**: the owner of a piece of memory is the one object responsible for giving it back. Most of this lesson is about keeping rule 4 true.

### Growing

When `size_ == cap_` there is no free slot. Growing takes four steps, in this order:

1. Allocate a bigger array: twice the capacity, or 1 when the capacity is 0.
2. Copy the values across.
3. `delete[]` the old array.
4. Point `data_` at the new array, and update `cap_`.

Deleting before copying would copy out of memory you no longer own. Here are steps 1 and 2 as a helper for an array of doubles:

```cpp fragment
double* copy_into_bigger(const double* old, std::size_t count, std::size_t new_cap) {
    double* fresh = new double[new_cap];
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) fresh[i] = old[i];
    return fresh;
}
```

The cost is the one you proved in DSA I. One growth copies every value, so it is O(n). But with doubling, n appends copy fewer than 2n values in total, so an append is **amortised O(1)**.

### A smaller class for the examples

The examples from here on use a simpler class than the vector, so that the task stays yours to write. A `Track` holds a fixed number of `double` readings in one heap array, with two members: `double* points_`, the array, and `std::size_t n_`, how many readings it holds. `Track t(3);` makes one with three readings. It never grows, but it owns memory exactly as a vector does, so it needs all the same special functions.

### Operator functions: `v[i]`

C++ lets a class say what an operator means for it. A member function named `operator[]` runs when you write `t[i]` on an object `t`. Returning a **reference** (`double&`) lets the caller write through it, as in `t[2] = 5.0`:

```cpp fragment
double& operator[](std::size_t i) { return points_[i]; }
const double& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return points_[i]; }
```

The second version is called on a `const` object. It returns a `const` reference, so a `const` object can be read but not changed. Two functions with the same name, one `const` and one not, are normal in C++.

### The destructor

A **destructor** runs automatically when an object's life ends: at the closing `}` of the block that made it, or when `delete` is used on it. Its name is the class name after a tilde, `~`. It takes nothing and returns nothing:

```cpp fragment
~Track() { delete[] points_; }
```

It runs exactly once per object, and nobody can forget to call it. That makes it the place to give memory back. Tying a resource to an object's lifetime like this is called **[[RAII|raii]]**: leaving the scope *is* the clean-up.

### The copy that is not a copy

Now the trap. If a class does not say how to copy itself, the compiler writes a copy constructor that copies each member. For a pointer, that copies the address, not the array:

```cpp fragment
Track a(3);    // a.points_ holds the address of an array
Track b = a;   // b.points_ holds the same address: one array, two owners
```

Rule 4 is broken: both objects believe they own the array. Writing `b[0] = 1.0` silently changes `a[0]` too. Then `b` dies and deletes the array, and `a` dies and deletes it again: a **[[double delete|double-delete]]**. This is called a **shallow copy**. You want a **deep copy**: a new array, with the values copied into it.

### The copy constructor

The **copy constructor** makes a new object as a copy of an existing one. It takes the original by `const` reference:

```cpp fragment
Track(const Track& other) : points_(other.n_ ? new double[other.n_] : nullptr), n_(other.n_) {
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) points_[i] = other.points_[i];
}
```

The new object gets its own array, so each array still has exactly one owner. An empty original needs no array at all: `nullptr`, by rule 2.

### Copy assignment

`a = b;`, between two objects that already exist, calls the **copy assignment operator**, `Track& operator=(const Track& other)`. It has two jobs the constructor did not have. `a` already owns an array, which must be given back. And `a = a` must still work: that is **self-assignment**.

The obvious version gets self-assignment wrong. It deletes its own array, then allocates a new one and copies from `other`. But when `other` *is* this object, it is copying out of the array it has just deleted.

The safe pattern is **[[copy and swap|copy-and-swap]]**, in three steps:

1. Make a full copy of `other` in a local variable. If `other` is this object, nothing has been changed yet, so the copy is right.
2. Swap this object's members with the copy's. Now this object owns the new array, and the copy owns the old one.
3. Return. The copy dies at the `}`, and its destructor frees the old array.

`std::swap(x, y)`, from `<utility>`, trades the values of two variables. A member function `swap` that trades every member makes step 2 one line. The operator ends with `return *this;`. `this` is a pointer to the object the member function was called on, so `*this` is that object itself. Returning it by reference lets `a = b = c` work, as it does for ints.

### Moving: take the array instead of copying it

Many copies are wasted. In `t = make_track();`, the function returns a temporary `Track`; copy assignment would copy its whole array into `t`, and then the temporary would be destroyed a moment later, array and all. It is far cheaper to *take* the array. C++ has a feature for exactly that, called **move semantics**.

An expression whose object nobody can use afterwards, like a temporary or a value being returned, is an **[[rvalue|rvalue]]**. A parameter of type `Track&&`, with two ampersands, is an **rvalue reference**: it binds only to such objects. A constructor that takes one is a **move constructor**:

```cpp fragment
Track(Track&& other) noexcept : points_(other.points_), n_(other.n_) {
    other.points_ = nullptr;   // the source gives the array up
    other.n_ = 0;
}
```

The two lines in the body are what matter. Without them both objects would own the array again, and the double delete would be back. After the move the source is **empty but valid**: it can still be destroyed, assigned to or reused. A move costs O(1), whatever the size.

`noexcept` promises that the function never throws an exception. Moves should say it; the next lesson shows why `std::vector` looks for it.

### std::move

A variable with a name is never an rvalue, even when you are finished with it. To say "you may take from this one", write `std::move(x)`, from `<utility>`:

```cpp fragment
Track a(1000);
Track b = std::move(a);   // the move constructor runs: b takes the array, a is left empty
```

`std::move` moves nothing by itself. It is a cast: it marks `a` as an rvalue, so the compiler picks the move constructor instead of the copy constructor. Afterwards, do not rely on what `a` holds; give it a new value or let it die.

### Move assignment, and the rule of five

The fifth special function is the **move assignment operator**, `Track& operator=(Track&& other) noexcept`. It gives back the array this object owns, takes `other`'s, and leaves `other` empty. `a = std::move(a)` must not destroy `a`'s values. The check `if (this != &other)` compares two addresses, and skips the work when they are the same object.

Destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment: together they are **[[the rule of five|rule-of-five]]**. If a class needs one of them written by hand, it almost always needs all five, because the reason is always the same: the class owns something that a member-by-member copy gets wrong.

Some types should never be copied. Writing `= delete` after a declaration forbids it, and any attempt becomes a compile error:

```cpp fragment
Track(const Track&) = delete;             // copying a Track will not compile
Track& operator=(const Track&) = delete;
```

### The memory ledger

How can a test know there is no leak and no double delete? C++ lets a program replace the global `operator new[]` and `operator delete[]`: the functions that every `new[]` and `delete[]` call to get and return memory. The starter of this lesson's task does that with a small **ledger**, and the checks read it:

- `ledger::made` counts every array made with `new[]`;
- `ledger::live` counts the arrays not given back yet;
- `ledger::bad` counts `delete[]` calls on an address that is not live: a double delete, caught before it can do harm.

So a check can say "after this block `ledger::live` is back where it started, so nothing leaked, and `ledger::bad` is 0, so nothing was deleted twice". Tools like [[AddressSanitizer and Valgrind|leak-tools]] work on the same idea. Leave the ledger as it is.

### Why it is correct

The claim: every array the vector makes is deleted exactly once, and never used after that. The proof checks rule 4, "each array has exactly one owner, and only its owner deletes it", in every function that touches `data_`:

1. **The default constructor** makes no array. Nothing to own.
2. **Growth** makes a new array, copies into it, deletes the old one and takes the new one. The old array's only owner was this object, and after step 4 nothing points at it. One array freed once, one array with one owner.
3. **The copy constructor** makes a *new* array for the new object. The original keeps its own. One owner each.
4. **Copy assignment** by copy and swap: the local copy owns a fresh array; the swap trades owners; the copy's destructor frees the old array once. One owner each.
5. **The move constructor** takes the array and sets the source's pointer to `nullptr`. The array changes owner; it never has two.
6. **Move assignment** frees this object's old array once, takes the source's, and empties the source. With `this == &other` it changes nothing.
7. **The destructor** deletes the array of the object that owns it. Each object's destructor runs once.

Every array has one owner from the moment it is made, and it is deleted only by that owner, either when growing (after which nothing points at it) or in the destructor. So it is deleted exactly once. And it is never used afterwards: growth points `data_` at the new array straight after deleting the old one, a moved-from object holds `nullptr`, and the destructor is the last thing that happens to an object. That is "no leak, no double delete, no use after delete" as an argument, not a hope.

### What it costs

| operation | time | why |
|---|---|---|
| `push_back` | amortised O(1), worst case O(n) | a growth copies n values, but n pushes copy fewer than 2n in total |
| `operator[]`, `size` | O(1) | one address calculation |
| `pop_back` | O(1) | the size drops by one; nothing is freed |
| copy | O(n) time and O(n) memory | every value goes into a new array |
| move | O(1) | three members copied, three reset |
| destructor | O(1) for ints | one `delete[]` |

After a growth the capacity is less than twice the size plus one, so at most about half of the array is spare.

### Where it is used

- `std::vector` is this design, plus templates (lesson 3), iterators (lesson 4) and a lot of care.
- Every C++ class that owns something follows the same five rules: files, network sockets, locks, GPU buffers, a telemetry frame's bytes.
- Flight software often allocates every buffer once at start-up, then never again, so that a mission can never run out of memory halfway through.

**Watch out:** the classic bugs, all of them rule 4 broken:

- No copy constructor: the compiler's shallow copy gives two owners, and a double delete when both die.
- A move that forgets to set the source's pointer to `nullptr`: two owners again.
- Copy assignment that deletes first and copies second: `a = a` copies from freed memory.
- `delete` instead of `delete[]` on an array made with `new[]`.
- Growing by deleting the old array before copying out of it.

::: context heap-array The heap, and why the values are not set
A function's ordinary variables live on the stack and vanish when it returns. Memory from `new` comes from the heap, a large pool the program manages, and stays until `delete` gives it back. C++ does not fill a new array of ints or doubles with zeros, because a program that is about to overwrite every slot would pay for nothing. The slots hold whatever bytes were there before. Reading one is undefined behaviour, which is why the vector only ever reads slots below `size_`.
:::

::: context raii Resource acquisition is initialisation
Bjarne Stroustrup, who created C++, named the idea in the 1980s: get the resource in the constructor, give it back in the destructor. The name is clumsy, but the effect is strong. Every path out of a block, a `return` in the middle, a `break`, the end of the block, runs the destructors of the objects made in it, in reverse order. So there is no separate clean-up step to forget. The same pattern closes files (`std::ifstream`) and releases locks (`std::lock_guard`), and the smart pointers of the next lesson are RAII for memory.
:::

::: context double-delete What a double delete does
The heap keeps its own records of which blocks are free, often inside the freed blocks themselves. Deleting a block twice puts it on the free list twice, so two later `new` calls can hand out the same memory to two different objects, which then overwrite each other. Sometimes the program crashes at once; sometimes it corrupts data much later, far from the bug. Attackers use double frees and use-after-free bugs to take control of programs, which is why browsers and operating systems treat them as serious security flaws.

:::

::: context copy-and-swap Why copy first
Copy and swap does all the work that might fail, making the new array, before it touches this object. If that step failed, for example because memory ran out, this object would still hold its old, valid contents. That promise is called the strong guarantee: an operation either succeeds completely or leaves everything as it was. The same shape shows up in databases, as "prepare, then commit", and in file saving, where a program writes a new file and only then renames it over the old one.
:::

::: context rvalue Left and right of the equals sign
The names come from C. An lvalue could stand on the left of `=`: a variable, something with a name and an address you can take. An rvalue could only stand on the right: `2 + 3`, or the result of a function that returns by value, a temporary that disappears at the end of the statement. An rvalue reference, `T&&`, catches exactly those temporaries, the objects nothing else will ever look at again, which is why taking their contents is safe.
:::

::: context rule-of-five From three to five, and zero
Before C++11 there was no moving, and the advice was the rule of three: destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment. Move semantics added the two move functions, and the rule became five. If you write a destructor or a copy function, the compiler stops writing the move functions for you, so copies quietly happen where moves were meant. The opposite advice, the rule of zero, says most classes should own nothing directly, and hold members that already manage themselves. The next lesson does exactly that.
:::

::: context leak-tools How leak checkers work
AddressSanitizer, built into clang and gcc, replaces the memory functions with its own. It surrounds every block with poisoned bytes and keeps freed memory out of use for a while, so a read past the end or after a delete stops the program at once and prints where the memory was made and where it was freed. Valgrind runs the program on a simulated processor and watches every memory access. At exit, both report blocks that nothing freed. The ledger here is the same idea in thirty lines.
:::
--- task
Write `class IntVector`, a growable array of `int`s that owns its memory. No `main`: the checker supplies it. Keep the memory ledger at the top of the starter exactly as it is; the checks use it to count arrays.

- `IntVector()`: an empty vector with size 0 and capacity 0. It allocates nothing.
- `void push_back(int x)` adds `x` at the end. When the vector is full it grows first: capacity 0 becomes 1, and any other capacity doubles. Use `new int[...]` and `delete[]`.
- `void pop_back()` removes the last value and keeps the capacity. On an empty vector it does nothing.
- `int& operator[](std::size_t i)` and `const int& operator[](std::size_t i) const` give the value at index `i`.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`, and `const int* data() const`, which returns the array (`nullptr` while the capacity is 0).
- The rule of five:
  - `~IntVector()` gives the array back.
  - `IntVector(const IntVector& other)` makes a deep copy whose capacity equals `other`'s size. Copying an empty vector allocates nothing.
  - `IntVector& operator=(const IntVector& other)` makes this vector a deep copy of `other`, and gives back the old array. `v = v` leaves `v` unchanged.
  - `IntVector(IntVector&& other) noexcept` takes `other`'s array without allocating, and leaves `other` empty: size 0, capacity 0, `data()` is `nullptr`.
  - `IntVector& operator=(IntVector&& other) noexcept` gives back the old array, takes `other`'s, and leaves `other` empty. `v = std::move(v)` leaves `v` unchanged.

No check may find a leak (`ledger::live` back where it started) or a double delete (`ledger::bad` stays 0).
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class IntVector {
public:
    IntVector() {}
    ~IntVector() {}
    IntVector(const IntVector& other) {}
    IntVector& operator=(const IntVector& other) { return *this; }
    IntVector(IntVector&& other) noexcept {}
    IntVector& operator=(IntVector&& other) noexcept { return *this; }

    void push_back(int x) {}
    void pop_back() {}
    int& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const int& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const int* data() const { return data_; }

private:
    int* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class IntVector {
public:
    IntVector() = default;

    ~IntVector() { delete[] data_; }

    IntVector(const IntVector& other)
        : data_(other.size_ ? new int[other.size_] : nullptr), size_(other.size_), cap_(other.size_) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) data_[i] = other.data_[i];
    }

    IntVector& operator=(const IntVector& other) {
        IntVector copy(other);   // all the work first; this object is untouched so far
        swap(copy);              // this object takes the new array, copy takes the old one
        return *this;            // copy's destructor frees the old array
    }

    IntVector(IntVector&& other) noexcept : data_(other.data_), size_(other.size_), cap_(other.cap_) {
        other.data_ = nullptr;
        other.size_ = 0;
        other.cap_ = 0;
    }

    IntVector& operator=(IntVector&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            delete[] data_;
            data_ = other.data_;
            size_ = other.size_;
            cap_ = other.cap_;
            other.data_ = nullptr;
            other.size_ = 0;
            other.cap_ = 0;
        }
        return *this;
    }

    void swap(IntVector& other) noexcept {
        std::swap(data_, other.data_);
        std::swap(size_, other.size_);
        std::swap(cap_, other.cap_);
    }

    void push_back(int x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) grow();
        data_[size_] = x;
        ++size_;
    }

    void pop_back() {
        if (size_ > 0) --size_;
    }

    int& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const int& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const int* data() const { return data_; }

private:
    void grow() {
        std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_;
        int* bigger = new int[new_cap];
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) bigger[i] = data_[i];
        delete[] data_;   // only after copying out of it
        data_ = bigger;
        cap_ = new_cap;
    }

    int* data_ = nullptr;   // nullptr exactly when cap_ == 0
    std::size_t size_ = 0;  // size_ <= cap_
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Start with `push_back`. When `size_ == cap_`, make a new array of the new capacity, copy the `size_` values into it, `delete[]` the old one, and point `data_` at the new one. Then write the value at index `size_` and add one to `size_`. The destructor is one line: `delete[] data_;`.
--- hint
The copy constructor allocates `other.size_` ints (or keeps `nullptr` when that is 0) and copies each value. Copy assignment is copy and swap: make a local copy of `other`, swap all three members with it using `std::swap`, and return `*this`.
--- hint
The move constructor copies the three members from `other`, then sets `other.data_` to `nullptr` and its size and capacity to 0. Move assignment does the same after `delete[] data_;`, all inside `if (this != &other)`.

+++ practice | A grid of readings that copies properly
--- task
A sensor panel reports a grid of temperatures. `class Grid` stores `rows × cols` doubles in **one** array made with `new double[...]()`, row after row: the cell at row `r`, column `c` is at index `r * cols + c`. The starter already has the constructor, the destructor and the accessors. Copying a `Grid` is broken: it copies the pointer, so two grids share one array and it is deleted twice.

Add the two copy functions:

- `Grid(const Grid& other)`: a deep copy with the same shape and values. When `other` has no cells (`rows * cols` is 0), allocate nothing.
- `Grid& operator=(const Grid& other)`: make this grid a deep copy of `other`, which may have a different shape, and give back the old array. `g = g` leaves `g` unchanged.

Keep the memory ledger as it is. After any check, `ledger::live` must be back where it started and `ledger::bad` must be 0.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class Grid {
public:
    Grid(std::size_t rows, std::size_t cols)
        : cells_(rows * cols ? new double[rows * cols]() : nullptr), rows_(rows), cols_(cols) {}
    ~Grid() { delete[] cells_; }

    double& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }
    const double& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) const { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }
    std::size_t rows() const { return rows_; }
    std::size_t cols() const { return cols_; }
    const double* data() const { return cells_; }

private:
    double* cells_;
    std::size_t rows_;
    std::size_t cols_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class Grid {
public:
    Grid(std::size_t rows, std::size_t cols)
        : cells_(rows * cols ? new double[rows * cols]() : nullptr), rows_(rows), cols_(cols) {}
    ~Grid() { delete[] cells_; }

    Grid(const Grid& other)
        : cells_(other.count() ? new double[other.count()] : nullptr), rows_(other.rows_), cols_(other.cols_) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count(); ++i) cells_[i] = other.cells_[i];
    }

    Grid& operator=(const Grid& other) {
        Grid copy(other);
        std::swap(cells_, copy.cells_);
        std::swap(rows_, copy.rows_);
        std::swap(cols_, copy.cols_);
        return *this;
    }

    double& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }
    const double& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) const { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }
    std::size_t rows() const { return rows_; }
    std::size_t cols() const { return cols_; }
    const double* data() const { return cells_; }

private:
    std::size_t count() const { return rows_ * cols_; }

    double* cells_;
    std::size_t rows_;
    std::size_t cols_;
};
--- hint
The copy constructor allocates `other.rows_ * other.cols_` doubles (or keeps `nullptr` when that is 0) and copies them one by one. A small private helper that returns `rows_ * cols_` keeps this tidy.
--- hint
For assignment, use copy and swap: build `Grid copy(other);`, then `std::swap` each of the three members with `copy`'s, and `return *this;`. The copy's destructor frees the old array, and `g = g` works with no special case.

--- check test | Copying and destroying gives every array back once
[] { int live = ledger::live; { Grid a(4, 4); Grid b(a); Grid c(b); c.at(3, 3) = 1.0; } return ledger::live == live && ledger::bad == 0; }()
?? Two grids sharing one array delete it twice. Give the copy a new array.
--- check test | Assignment can change the shape, and frees the old array

--- check test | g = g leaves g unchanged
[] { Grid a(2, 2); a.at(0, 1) = 4.0; Grid& same = a; a = same; return a.rows() == 2 && a.at(0, 1) == 4.0 && ledger::bad == 0; }()
--- check test | An empty grid copies without allocating

+++ practice | A frame that can move but never copy
--- task
A radio frame owns a block of bytes. Copying one by accident would double the memory traffic, so `class Frame` must be **move-only**: moving is allowed, copying does not compile.

- `explicit Frame(std::size_t n)` owns `n` bytes, all zero, made with `new unsigned char[n]()`. When `n` is 0 it allocates nothing.
- `~Frame()` gives the bytes back.
- The copy constructor and copy assignment are deleted with `= delete`.
- `Frame(Frame&& other) noexcept` and `Frame& operator=(Frame&& other) noexcept` take `other`'s bytes without allocating and leave `other` with size 0 and `data()` equal to `nullptr`. `f = std::move(f)` leaves `f` unchanged.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `unsigned char& operator[](std::size_t i)` and `const unsigned char* data() const`.

Also write `Frame make_frame(std::size_t n, unsigned char fill)`, a free function that returns a new frame of `n` bytes, each set to `fill`.
--- starter

    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;

#include <type_traits>

public:

    unsigned char* bytes_ = nullptr;

#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <type_traits>

class Frame {
public:
    explicit Frame(std::size_t n) : bytes_(n ? new unsigned char[n]() : nullptr), n_(n) {}
    ~Frame() { delete[] bytes_; }

    Frame(const Frame&) = delete;
    Frame& operator=(const Frame&) = delete;

    Frame(Frame&& other) noexcept : bytes_(other.bytes_), n_(other.n_) {
        other.bytes_ = nullptr;
        other.n_ = 0;
    }

    Frame& operator=(Frame&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            delete[] bytes_;
            bytes_ = other.bytes_;
            n_ = other.n_;
            other.bytes_ = nullptr;
            other.n_ = 0;
        }
        return *this;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return n_; }
    unsigned char& operator[](std::size_t i) { return bytes_[i]; }
    const unsigned char* data() const { return bytes_; }

private:
    unsigned char* bytes_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t n_ = 0;
};

Frame make_frame(std::size_t n, unsigned char fill) {
    Frame f(n);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) f[i] = fill;
    return f;
}
--- hint
Deleting the copy functions is two declarations ending in `= delete`. The move constructor copies the pointer and the size from `other`, then sets `other`'s pointer to `nullptr` and its size to 0.
--- hint
Move assignment: inside `if (this != &other)`, `delete[]` your own bytes first, then take `other`'s and empty `other`. In `make_frame`, fill a local `Frame` and `return` it: returning a local variable moves it, or builds it in place.
--- check test | Copying is forbidden, moving is noexcept
!std::is_copy_constructible_v<Frame> && !std::is_copy_assignable_v<Frame> && std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<Frame> && std::is_nothrow_move_assignable_v<Frame>
?? Declare Frame(const Frame&) = delete; and the same for copy assignment. Mark both moves noexcept.
--- check test | make_frame fills the bytes and makes one array
[] { int made = ledger::made; Frame f = make_frame(5, 7); return ledger::made - made == 1 && f.size() == 5 && f[0] == 7 && f[4] == 7; }()
--- check test | A move takes the bytes and empties the source
[] { Frame a(8); a[3] = 42; const unsigned char* p = a.data(); int made = ledger::made; Frame b(std::move(a)); return ledger::made == made && b.data() == p && b[3] == 42 && b.size() == 8 && a.size() == 0 && a.data() == nullptr; }()
--- check test | Move assignment frees the old bytes, and self-move changes nothing
[] { int live = ledger::live; { Frame a(3); Frame b(6); a = std::move(b); if (a.size() != 6 || b.size() != 0 || b.data() != nullptr) return false; Frame& same = a; a = std::move(same); if (a.size() != 6 || a.data() == nullptr) return false; } return ledger::live == live && ledger::bad == 0; }()
--- check test | A zero-byte frame allocates nothing
[] { int made = ledger::made; Frame f(0); Frame g = make_frame(0, 1); return ledger::made == made && f.data() == nullptr && g.size() == 0; }()

+++ practice | Reserve ahead, shrink after
--- task
A logger knows roughly how many readings a pass will bring, so it wants to allocate once instead of growing again and again. Write `class Readings`, a growable array of `int`s, with two extra controls. Copying is not needed: delete both copy functions.

- `Readings()` is empty with capacity 0 and allocates nothing. `~Readings()` gives the array back.
- `void push_back(int x)` grows like the lesson's vector when full: capacity 0 becomes 1, anything else doubles.
- `void reserve(std::size_t n)`: when `n` is more than the capacity, move to a new array of **exactly** `n` slots, keeping the values. Otherwise do nothing.
- `void shrink_to_fit()`: when the capacity is more than the size, move to a new array of **exactly** `size()` slots. When the size is 0, give the array back and keep `nullptr`. Otherwise do nothing.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`, `const int& operator[](std::size_t i) const`, `const int* data() const`.

Each reallocation makes one array and gives one back. Keep the memory ledger as it is.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class Readings {
public:
    Readings() {}
    Readings(const Readings&) = delete;
    Readings& operator=(const Readings&) = delete;

    void push_back(int x) {}
    void reserve(std::size_t n) {}
    void shrink_to_fit() {}
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const int& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    const int* data() const { return data_; }

private:
    int* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class Readings {
public:
    Readings() = default;
    ~Readings() { delete[] data_; }
    Readings(const Readings&) = delete;
    Readings& operator=(const Readings&) = delete;

    void push_back(int x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) reallocate(cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_);
        data_[size_] = x;
        ++size_;
    }

    void reserve(std::size_t n) {
        if (n > cap_) reallocate(n);
    }

    void shrink_to_fit() {
        if (cap_ > size_) reallocate(size_);
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const int& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    const int* data() const { return data_; }

private:
    // Moves the values to an array of exactly new_cap slots (none when new_cap is 0).
    void reallocate(std::size_t new_cap) {
        int* fresh = new_cap ? new int[new_cap] : nullptr;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) fresh[i] = data_[i];
        delete[] data_;
        data_ = fresh;
        cap_ = new_cap;
    }

    int* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
All three operations do the same thing with a different target capacity: make a new array of that size, copy the values over, `delete[]` the old one. Put that in one private helper, `reallocate(std::size_t new_cap)`.
--- hint
`push_back` calls it with the doubled capacity, `reserve(n)` only when `n > cap_`, and `shrink_to_fit()` only when `cap_ > size_`, with target `size_`. When the target is 0, the helper keeps `nullptr` instead of calling `new int[0]`.
--- check test | reserve(10000) then 10,000 pushes: exactly one array

?? After reserve, push_back should find room every time.
--- check test | reserve never shrinks and never reallocates for nothing
[] { Readings r; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) r.push_back(i); int made = ledger::made; r.reserve(8); r.reserve(3); r.reserve(0); return ledger::made == made && r.capacity() == 8 && r[4] == 4; }()
--- check test | shrink_to_fit keeps the values in an exact array
[] { int live = ledger::live; Readings r; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) r.push_back(i * i); int made = ledger::made; r.shrink_to_fit(); return ledger::made - made == 1 && ledger::live - live == 1 && r.capacity() == 5 && r[4] == 16 && r[0] == 0; }()
--- check test | shrink_to_fit on an empty array gives it back

--- check test | shrink_to_fit when already exact does nothing
[] { Readings r; r.reserve(2); r.push_back(1); r.push_back(2); int made = ledger::made; r.shrink_to_fit(); Readings e; e.shrink_to_fit(); return ledger::made == made && r.capacity() == 2 && e.data() == nullptr; }()

+++ practice | Insert and erase anywhere
--- task
Write `class Series`, a growable array of `int`s that can insert and erase at any position. Copying is not needed: delete both copy functions.

- `Series()` is empty with capacity 0; `~Series()` gives the array back.
- `bool insert(std::size_t pos, int x)` puts `x` at index `pos` and shifts the values from `pos` onwards one place right. `pos` may be anything from 0 to `size()`; `pos == size()` adds at the end. For any other `pos`, return `false` and change nothing. When the array is full, grow first: capacity 0 becomes 1, anything else doubles.
- `bool erase(std::size_t pos)` removes the value at index `pos` and shifts the rest one place left. `pos` must be below `size()`; otherwise return `false` and change nothing. The capacity stays the same.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const` and `int at(std::size_t i) const`.

Careful: `std::size_t` is unsigned, so a loop that counts down to 0 with `i >= 0` never ends.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class Series {
public:
    Series() {}
    Series(const Series&) = delete;
    Series& operator=(const Series&) = delete;

    bool insert(std::size_t pos, int x) { return false; }
    bool erase(std::size_t pos) { return false; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    int at(std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }

private:
    int* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class Series {
public:
    Series() = default;
    ~Series() { delete[] data_; }
    Series(const Series&) = delete;
    Series& operator=(const Series&) = delete;

    bool insert(std::size_t pos, int x) {
        if (pos > size_) return false;
        if (size_ == cap_) grow();
        for (std::size_t i = size_; i > pos; --i) data_[i] = data_[i - 1];
        data_[pos] = x;
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool erase(std::size_t pos) {
        if (pos >= size_) return false;
        for (std::size_t i = pos; i + 1 < size_; ++i) data_[i] = data_[i + 1];
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    int at(std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }

private:
    void grow() {
        std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_;
        int* bigger = new int[new_cap];
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) bigger[i] = data_[i];
        delete[] data_;
        data_ = bigger;
        cap_ = new_cap;
    }

    int* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Check the position first, before growing or moving anything, so a bad call changes nothing. For insert the valid positions are `0` to `size_` (both included); for erase they are `0` to `size_ - 1`.
--- hint
To shift right, start at the free slot and walk down: `for (std::size_t i = size_; i > pos; --i) data_[i] = data_[i - 1];`. The test `i > pos` stops before `i` would go below 0. To shift left, walk up from `pos` while `i + 1 < size_`.
--- check case | Inserting at the front, middle and end
[] { Series s; s.insert(0, 20); s.insert(0, 10); s.insert(2, 40); s.insert(2, 30); std::vector<int> out; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < s.size(); ++i) out.push_back(s.at(i)); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{10, 20, 30, 40}
--- check test | A position past the end is refused and changes nothing
[] { Series s; bool empty_refused = !s.insert(1, 5); s.insert(0, 5); bool refused = !s.insert(2, 6); return empty_refused && refused && s.size() == 1 && s.at(0) == 5; }()
--- check case | Erasing the first, a middle and the last value
[] { Series s; for (int i = 0; i < 6; ++i) s.insert(s.size(), i); s.erase(0); s.erase(2); s.erase(s.size() - 1); std::vector<int> out; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < s.size(); ++i) out.push_back(s.at(i)); out.push_back(static_cast<int>(s.capacity())); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{1, 2, 4, 8}
?? The last number is the capacity: erasing never shrinks it.
--- check test | Erase on an empty series, or past the end, is refused
[] { Series s; bool a = !s.erase(0); s.insert(0, 1); bool b = !s.erase(1); bool c = s.erase(0); bool d = !s.erase(0); return a && b && c && d && s.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Inserting at 0 over and over, through several growths
[] { int live = ledger::live; bool ok = true; { Series s; for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) s.insert(0, i); ok = s.size() == 100 && s.capacity() == 128 && s.at(0) == 99 && s.at(99) == 0 && s.at(50) == 49; } return ok && ledger::live == live && ledger::bad == 0; }()
?? A countdown loop over std::size_t must stop with i > pos, never i >= 0.

+++ practice | Debug: the packet that is freed twice
--- task
`class Packet` owns a payload of `int`s. Moving a packet should hand the payload over: the new packet owns it, and the old one is left empty, with size 0 and `data()` equal to `nullptr`.

It does not. After `Packet b(std::move(a));` both packets still point at the same array, `a.size()` is not 0, and when both die the array is deleted twice (the memory ledger counts it in `ledger::bad`). Find the bug in the move constructor and fix it. Everything else is correct.

class Packet {

    explicit Packet(std::size_t n) : data_(n ? new int[n]() : nullptr), n_(n) {}

+++ practice | Adding sensor traces without extra copies
--- task
A ground station adds up traces from several antennas, sample by sample. Each trace is a `Signal`: a fixed number of `double` samples in one array made with `new double[...]`. Arrays are large, so every allocation counts.

Write `class Signal` with the rule of five:

- `explicit Signal(std::size_t n, double fill)` holds `n` samples, each equal to `fill`. When `n` is 0 it allocates nothing.
- `~Signal()`, a deep copy constructor, copy assignment (deep; `s = s` changes nothing), and `noexcept` move constructor and move assignment that take the array without allocating and leave the source with size 0.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `double& operator[](std::size_t i)` and `const double& operator[](std::size_t i) const`.

Then write the free function `Signal plus(Signal a, const Signal& b)`. It returns the sample-by-sample sum (both have the same size). It must allocate **only** when it has to: `a` is taken **by value**, so a caller who passes a temporary or a `std::move`d signal has it moved in for free, and a caller who passes a named signal gets exactly one copy. Add `b` into `a` and return `a`.

So with three named signals, `plus(plus(x, y), z)` makes exactly one array, and `total = plus(std::move(total), s)` makes none.
--- starter

    ++ledger::made;

class Signal {
public:
    explicit Signal(std::size_t n, double fill) {}
    std::size_t size() const { return n_; }
    double& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const double& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }

private:
    double* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t n_ = 0;

Signal plus(Signal a, const Signal& b) {

--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }

class Signal {
public:
    explicit Signal(std::size_t n, double fill) : data_(n ? new double[n] : nullptr), n_(n) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) data_[i] = fill;
    }

    ~Signal() { delete[] data_; }

    Signal(const Signal& other) : data_(other.n_ ? new double[other.n_] : nullptr), n_(other.n_) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n_; ++i) data_[i] = other.data_[i];
    }

    Signal& operator=(const Signal& other) {
        Signal copy(other);
        std::swap(data_, copy.data_);
        std::swap(n_, copy.n_);
        return *this;
    }

    Signal(Signal&& other) noexcept : data_(other.data_), n_(other.n_) {
        other.data_ = nullptr;
        other.n_ = 0;
    }

    Signal& operator=(Signal&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            delete[] data_;
            data_ = other.data_;
            n_ = other.n_;
            other.data_ = nullptr;
            other.n_ = 0;
        }
        return *this;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return n_; }
    double& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const double& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }

private:
    double* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t n_ = 0;
};

// a is a copy only if the caller passed a named signal; a temporary is moved in.
Signal plus(Signal a, const Signal& b) {
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i) a[i] += b[i];
    return a;   // returning a parameter moves it out
}
--- hint
Write the five special functions exactly as in the lesson: the copy constructor allocates and copies, copy assignment is copy and swap, the moves steal the pointer and empty the source.
--- hint
In `plus`, the parameter `a` is already your own signal: the caller's copy or the caller's moved-in array. Add `b[i]` into `a[i]` for each sample, and `return a;`. Returning a parameter uses the move constructor, so no new array is made.
--- check test | The sum is right, and b is unchanged
[] { Signal x(4, 1.5); Signal y(4, 2.0); y[3] = 10.0; Signal s = plus(x, y); return s.size() == 4 && s[0] == 3.5 && s[3] == 11.5 && x[0] == 1.5 && y[0] == 2.0; }()
--- check test | plus(plus(x, y), z) makes exactly one array
[] { Signal x(1000, 1.0); Signal y(1000, 2.0); Signal z(1000, 3.0); int made = ledger::made; Signal s = plus(plus(x, y), z); return ledger::made - made == 1 && s[999] == 6.0 && x[0] == 1.0; }()
?? Take a by value and return it: a temporary argument is then moved in, not copied.
--- check test | Accumulating with std::move makes no arrays at all
[] { Signal total(500, 0.0); Signal s(500, 0.25); int made = ledger::made; for (int k = 0; k < 100; ++k) total = plus(std::move(total), s); return ledger::made == made && total.size() == 500 && total[0] == 25.0 && total[499] == 25.0; }()
--- check test | Copy assignment and self-assignment
[] { Signal a(3, 1.0); Signal b(5, 4.0); a = b; b[0] = 0.0; Signal& same = a; a = same; return a.size() == 5 && a[0] == 4.0 && a[4] == 4.0 && ledger::bad == 0; }()
--- check test | Moves leave the source empty, and nothing leaks
[] { int live = ledger::live; { Signal a(8, 2.0); Signal b(std::move(a)); if (a.size() != 0 || b.size() != 8) return false; Signal c(0, 1.0); c = std::move(b); if (b.size() != 0 || c[7] != 2.0) return false; Signal d = plus(Signal(8, 1.0), c); if (d[0] != 3.0) return false; } return ledger::live == live && ledger::bad == 0; }()

+++ question | Which step keeps one owner
--- ask
In the proof that every array is deleted exactly once, which fact about the **move constructor** is the one the argument depends on?
--- choice
It is marked `noexcept`, so it cannot fail halfway.
--- choice correct
It sets the source's pointer to `nullptr`, so the array moves to a new owner instead of gaining a second one.
--- choice
It runs in O(1) time, so no values are copied.
--- choice
It takes its argument by rvalue reference, so the source is a temporary that is never destroyed.
--- why
The claim is "each array has exactly one owner, and only its owner deletes it". After the move the new object points at the array; if the source still pointed at it too, both destructors would `delete[]` it. Setting the source's pointer to `nullptr` is what keeps the owner count at one. `noexcept` and O(1) are good properties, but the proof does not rest on them, and a moved-from source is still destroyed later, which is exactly why it must be left empty.

+++ question | What std::move does
--- ask
After `IntVector b = std::move(a);`, what did the call `std::move(a)` itself do?
--- choice
It copied `a`'s array into `b`.
--- choice
It emptied `a` and gave its array to `b`.
--- choice correct
Nothing at run time: it only cast `a` to an rvalue, so the compiler chose the move constructor, and that did the work.
--- choice
It destroyed `a`, so using `a` afterwards is an error.
--- why
`std::move` is only a cast to an rvalue reference. It lets overload resolution pick `IntVector(IntVector&&)` instead of the copy constructor. All the taking and emptying happens inside the move constructor you wrote. `a` still exists afterwards, empty but valid: you can assign to it, reuse it, or let it be destroyed.

+++ question | The copy assignment that deletes first
--- ask
This copy assignment gives back the old array first, then copies:

```cpp fragment
IntVector& operator=(const IntVector& other) {
    delete[] data_;
    data_ = new int[other.size_];
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < other.size_; ++i) data_[i] = other.data_[i];
    size_ = cap_ = other.size_;
    return *this;
}
```

What goes wrong with `v = v`?
--- choice
Nothing: the values are copied onto themselves.
--- choice correct
`other` is `v` itself, so `other.data_` is the array just deleted; the loop reads freed memory into the new array.
--- choice
The array is deleted twice, once here and once in the destructor.
--- choice
It leaks the old array.
--- why
With self-assignment, `other.data_` and `data_` are the same pointer. After `delete[] data_`, that pointer refers to freed memory, and then `data_` is replaced by the new array, so the loop copies from freed memory into itself. Copy and swap avoids this by making the copy while nothing has been changed.

=== dsacpp-02 | Growth without leaks: unique_ptr, moving elements, and invalidation
--- teach
Last lesson you kept one raw pointer safe by hand, with five special functions and a proof that each array is deleted exactly once. It works, but every line of it is a chance to break rule 4. This lesson hands the array to a member that owns it for you, `std::unique_ptr`, so the compiler enforces ownership. Then it deals with two things that matter once the elements are bigger than `int`s: growing by **moving** elements instead of copying them, and knowing exactly when a pointer into the vector stops being valid.

### A member that owns the array

You met `std::unique_ptr<T>` in the basics course: a pointer that owns one object and deletes it when it dies. `std::unique_ptr<T[]>`, with brackets, owns an **array** and calls `delete[]` on it. `std::make_unique<T[]>(n)`, from `<memory>`, makes one:

```cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

int main() {
    std::size_t n = 5;
    std::unique_ptr<double[]> volts = std::make_unique<double[]>(n);   // 5 doubles, all 0.0
    volts[2] = 3.3;                          // index it like an array
    double* raw = volts.get();               // a plain pointer to look through; it owns nothing
    std::cout << raw[2] << " " << volts[0] << "\n";   // 3.3 0
}   // volts dies here and runs delete[]: no leak, nothing to write
```

Three facts:

- `std::make_unique<T[]>(n)` **value-initialises** every slot: numbers become 0, and class types run their default constructor. So `T` needs a default constructor. (Next lesson removes that need.)
- A `unique_ptr` cannot be copied. `auto q = volts;` does not compile. It can be moved: `auto q = std::move(volts);` leaves `volts` holding `nullptr`.
- Assigning into a `unique_ptr` that already owns an array first takes the new pointer, then deletes the old array. So `data_ = std::move(fresh);` frees the old buffer for you.

### What the compiler writes for you now

Give the vector these members:

```cpp fragment
std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> data_;   // owns the array, or holds nullptr
std::size_t size_ = 0;
std::size_t cap_ = 0;
```

Now look at the five special functions the compiler writes when you write none:

- **The destructor** destroys each member, so `data_` runs `delete[]`. Correct, with no code.
- **Copying** is impossible for `data_`, so the compiler **deletes** the copy constructor and copy assignment. If the vector should be copyable, you write them.
- **Moving** moves each member. `data_` is moved properly: the source becomes `nullptr`. But `size_` and `cap_` are plain numbers, and "moving" a number copies it. The moved-from vector still says it has 5 values and room for 8, with no array at all. The invariant is broken, and the next `push_back` into it writes through a null pointer.

So even with a smart pointer, a class whose members must agree with each other writes its own moves. They are much shorter now.

### std::exchange

`std::exchange(x, v)`, from `<utility>`, stores `v` in `x` and returns the value `x` had before. It is "take the old value and leave a new one" in one expression, exactly what a move needs:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>

int main() {
    int fuel = 80;
    int taken = std::exchange(fuel, 0);
    std::cout << taken << " " << fuel << "\n";   // 80 0
}
```

In a move constructor's initializer list, `size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0))` takes the size and zeroes the source's in one step. `data_(std::move(other.data_))` does the same for the pointer.

### Elements that are expensive to copy

With `int`s, copying and moving are the same thing. Real elements often own memory themselves: a `std::string` label, a `std::vector` of samples. Copying a string with 1,000 characters copies 1,000 characters. Moving it takes its buffer, three pointer-sized values, whatever its length.

So when the vector grows, it should **move** each element into the new array:

```cpp fragment
fresh[i] = std::move(data_[i]);   // move assignment: take the element's contents
```

The old elements are left **moved-from**: valid, but with unspecified contents (a moved-from `std::string` is usually empty). That is fine, because the old array is about to be destroyed.

### Why std::vector wants noexcept

`std::vector` makes a promise, called the **[[strong guarantee|strong-guarantee]]**: if a `push_back` fails partway, for example because a copy runs out of memory and throws an exception, the vector is left exactly as it was. Copying the elements across keeps that promise, because the old array is untouched until the end. Moving does not: after moving half the elements, the old array is half moved-from, and there is no safe way back if the next move fails.

So `std::vector` moves elements only when their move constructor is marked `noexcept`, a promise it cannot fail. Otherwise it copies, and pays for it:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Loose {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    Loose() = default;
    Loose(const Loose&) { ++copies; }
    Loose(Loose&&) {}   // may throw, as far as the compiler knows
};

struct Tight {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    Tight() = default;
    Tight(const Tight&) { ++copies; }
    Tight(Tight&&) noexcept {}
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Loose> a;
    std::vector<Tight> b;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) {
        a.push_back(Loose());
        b.push_back(Tight());
    }
    std::cout << Loose::copies << " " << Tight::copies << "\n";   // 127 0
}
```

`static inline int copies = 0;` is one counter shared by the whole type, like the `static constexpr` constants you have used, but one that can change. The 127 copies are every element moved on every growth: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 64. Rule: always mark your move constructor and move assignment `noexcept`. This course compiles without exceptions, but the library still decides by what the type promises.

### Pointers into a vector, and when they die

Here is a bug that compiles cleanly:

```cpp fragment
std::vector<int> counts = {1, 2, 3};
int& first = counts[0];
counts.push_back(4);     // if this grows, the old array is freed
first = 10;              // may write into freed memory
```

`first` was a reference to a slot in the old array. The growth moved the values to a new array and deleted the old one, so `first` now refers to memory the vector gave back: a **[[dangling reference|dangling]]**. Using it is undefined behaviour. The same happens to pointers and iterators. When an operation makes them unusable, we say it **invalidates** them.

For `std::vector`, the rules follow from one fact: the elements move only when the array is replaced, or when the elements after a change are shifted.

| operation | what it invalidates |
|---|---|
| `push_back`, `emplace_back` | everything, if the capacity changed; otherwise only `end()` |
| `insert` | everything, if the capacity changed; otherwise everything at or after the insertion point |
| `erase` | everything at or after the erased element, and `end()` |
| `pop_back` | the last element and `end()` |
| `reserve(n)` | everything, if `n` is more than the capacity; otherwise nothing |
| `clear`, `shrink_to_fit` | everything (shrink only if it really reallocates) |
| move construction, `swap` | nothing but `end()`: pointers keep pointing at the same elements, which now belong to the other vector |
| reading: `[]`, `at`, `size` | nothing |

`reserve(n)` is how you make pointers safe on purpose: allocate room for `n` once, and the next pushes, up to `n` elements, move nothing.

### Pushing one of the vector's own elements

One more trap, inside the vector itself. `v.push_back(v[0])` passes a reference to an element of `v`. If the push has to grow, and moves the old elements before it copies the argument, the argument is by then a moved-from element, or even freed memory.

The fix is an order, not a special case. When growing:

1. make the new array;
2. put the new element into slot `size_` of the new array, **while the old array is still intact**;
3. move the old elements across;
4. switch `data_` to the new array.

`std::vector` guarantees that `v.push_back(v[0])` works, and implementations do exactly this.

### Why it is correct

Ownership, rule 4 of the last lesson, is now the compiler's job: a `unique_ptr` cannot be copied, and a move leaves the source holding `nullptr`. No array can have two owners, and the `unique_ptr` destructor deletes it once. What is left to prove is the size and capacity invariant, and that growth keeps every value:

- **Growth** builds the complete new array first: the new element in slot `size_`, then each old value moved once into the same slot number. Only then does `data_` switch, which frees the old array. The values are the old ones in the same order, plus the new one at the end, and `size_ + 1 <= new_cap`.
- **The move constructor** takes the array and exchanges the source's size and capacity for 0. The source ends as `nullptr`, 0, 0, which satisfies the invariant ("capacity 0 exactly when there is no array").
- **The copy constructor** makes a new array of `size_` slots and copies each value once.
- **Copy assignment** by copy and swap, as before.

And the order "build everything, then switch" is what gives the strong guarantee: until the last line, the vector itself has not changed.

### What it costs

| operation | cost |
|---|---|
| `push_back` | amortised O(1) element moves; a growth moves all n elements, each move O(1) |
| `reserve(n)` | one allocation and O(size) moves, once |
| copy | O(n) element copies |
| move | O(1), no element is touched |

One cost is hidden. `std::make_unique<Sample[]>(cap)` default-constructs **every** slot, including the spare ones: a vector of 513 elements with capacity 1,024 has built 511 elements that hold nothing. The next lesson separates allocating memory from constructing objects, and pays only for real elements.

### Where it is used

- `std::vector` itself: libstdc++, the standard library that ships with gcc, constructs the new element first when it grows, for exactly the reason above.
- Game engines and simulations store thousands of objects in vectors and hand out [[indexes instead of pointers|handles]], so that growth cannot leave anyone holding a dangling pointer.
- Use-after-free through a reallocated vector is one of the most common memory bugs in large C++ programs, browsers included.

**Watch out:**

- Holding a reference, pointer or iterator into a vector across a `push_back` or `insert`. Use an index, or `reserve` first.
- Letting the compiler write the moves for a class whose members must agree, like `data_` with `size_`. The moved-from object lies about its size.
- Growing by copying (`fresh[i] = data_[i]`) instead of moving: correct, but it copies every string on every growth.
- A move constructor without `noexcept`: `std::vector` then copies your type when it grows.
- `std::unique_ptr<T>` (no brackets) holding an array from `new T[n]`: it calls `delete` instead of `delete[]`. Use `std::unique_ptr<T[]>`.

::: context strong-guarantee Three levels of safety
In the late 1990s David Abrahams set out the guarantees the C++ standard library gives when an operation fails. The basic guarantee: nothing leaks and every object is still valid, though its value may have changed. The strong guarantee: the operation either succeeds completely or has no effect at all. The no-fail guarantee: it cannot fail, which is what `noexcept` states. `push_back` gives the strong guarantee, and it can only do so cheaply when moving an element is no-fail.
:::

::: context dangling A reference to something that is gone
A reference or pointer is just an address. Nothing in C++ tracks whether the memory at that address still belongs to what you meant, so a stale address keeps working until the memory is reused, and then it reads or overwrites someone else's data. That is why these bugs hide: a test can pass for years if nothing happens to reuse that block. Languages like Rust reject this program at compile time by tracking who may hold a reference while something might change the vector.
:::

::: context handles Indexes as handles
An index into a vector stays meaningful when the vector grows, because growth moves the values but keeps their order. So many systems store "entity 42" rather than a pointer to entity 42. The cost is one extra addition when you look the entity up. Game engines add a generation number to each slot, so that a handle to an entity that was removed and replaced is detected instead of silently reaching the newcomer. Telemetry systems do the same with sensor ids.
:::
--- task
Write `class SampleVector`, a growable array of `Sample`s stored in a `std::unique_ptr<Sample[]>`. No `main`. Keep the memory ledger and the `Sample` type exactly as they are in the starter: `Sample` counts how often it is copied and moved, in `Sample::copies` and `Sample::moves`, and the checks read those counters.

- `SampleVector()`: empty, capacity 0, allocates nothing.
- `void push_back(const Sample& s)` adds a copy of `s` (exactly one copy). `void push_back(Sample&& s)` adds `s` by moving it (no copy).
- When full, grow first: capacity 0 becomes 1, anything else doubles. Make the new array with `std::make_unique<Sample[]>`, and **move** the old elements into it; growing never copies.
- `v.push_back(v[0])` must work, even when that push has to grow.
- `void reserve(std::size_t n)`: when `n` is more than the capacity, move the elements to a new array of exactly `n` slots; otherwise do nothing.
- `Sample& operator[](std::size_t i)` and `const Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) const`; `std::size_t size() const`; `std::size_t capacity() const`; `const Sample* data() const`, the array (`nullptr` while the capacity is 0).
- `SampleVector(const SampleVector& other)`: a deep copy, with capacity equal to `other`'s size, copying each element once.
- `SampleVector& operator=(const SampleVector& other)`: a deep copy; `v = v` leaves `v` unchanged.
- `SampleVector(SampleVector&& other) noexcept` and `SampleVector& operator=(SampleVector&& other) noexcept`: take `other`'s array without copying or moving a single element, and leave `other` with size 0, capacity 0 and `data()` equal to `nullptr`.

You should not need to write a destructor.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>
#include <string>

// Given: a reading that counts its copies and moves. The checks use it. Leave it as it is.
struct Sample {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    std::string label;
    double value = 0.0;

    Sample() = default;
    Sample(std::string l, double v) : label(std::move(l)), value(v) {}
    Sample(const Sample& o) : label(o.label), value(o.value) { ++copies; }
    Sample(Sample&& o) noexcept : label(std::move(o.label)), value(o.value) { ++moves; }
    Sample& operator=(const Sample& o) { label = o.label; value = o.value; ++copies; return *this; }
    Sample& operator=(Sample&& o) noexcept { label = std::move(o.label); value = o.value; ++moves; return *this; }
};

class SampleVector {
public:
    SampleVector() {}

    void push_back(const Sample& s) {}
    void push_back(Sample&& s) {}
    void reserve(std::size_t n) {}

    Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const Sample* data() const { return data_.get(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
