--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>
#include <string>

// Given: a reading that counts its copies and moves. The checks use it. Leave it as it is.
struct Sample {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    std::string label;
    double value = 0.0;

    Sample() = default;
    Sample(std::string l, double v) : label(std::move(l)), value(v) {}
    Sample(const Sample& o) : label(o.label), value(o.value) { ++copies; }
    Sample(Sample&& o) noexcept : label(std::move(o.label)), value(o.value) { ++moves; }
    Sample& operator=(const Sample& o) { label = o.label; value = o.value; ++copies; return *this; }
    Sample& operator=(Sample&& o) noexcept { label = std::move(o.label); value = o.value; ++moves; return *this; }
};

class SampleVector {
public:
    SampleVector() = default;

    SampleVector(const SampleVector& other)
        : data_(other.size_ ? std::make_unique<Sample[]>(other.size_) : nullptr), size_(other.size_), cap_(other.size_) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) data_[i] = other.data_[i];
    }

    SampleVector& operator=(const SampleVector& other) {
        SampleVector copy(other);
        swap(copy);
        return *this;
    }

    SampleVector(SampleVector&& other) noexcept
        : data_(std::move(other.data_)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)), cap_(std::exchange(other.cap_, 0)) {}

    SampleVector& operator=(SampleVector&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            data_ = std::move(other.data_);   // frees our old array
            size_ = std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
            cap_ = std::exchange(other.cap_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    void swap(SampleVector& other) noexcept {
        std::swap(data_, other.data_);
        std::swap(size_, other.size_);
        std::swap(cap_, other.cap_);
    }

    void push_back(const Sample& s) {
        if (size_ < cap_) {
            data_[size_] = s;
        } else {
            std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> fresh = std::make_unique<Sample[]>(next_capacity());
            fresh[size_] = s;            // copy first: s may be one of our own elements
            adopt(std::move(fresh), next_capacity());
        }
        ++size_;
    }

    void push_back(Sample&& s) {
        if (size_ < cap_) {
            data_[size_] = std::move(s);
        } else {
            std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> fresh = std::make_unique<Sample[]>(next_capacity());
            fresh[size_] = std::move(s);
            adopt(std::move(fresh), next_capacity());
        }
        ++size_;
    }

    void reserve(std::size_t n) {
        if (n > cap_) adopt(std::make_unique<Sample[]>(n), n);
    }

    Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const Sample* data() const { return data_.get(); }

private:
    std::size_t next_capacity() const { return cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_; }

    // Moves the current elements into fresh (new_cap slots) and makes it the array.
    void adopt(std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> fresh, std::size_t new_cap) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) fresh[i] = std::move(data_[i]);
        data_ = std::move(fresh);   // the old array is deleted here
        cap_ = new_cap;
    }

    std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> data_;   // nullptr exactly when cap_ == 0
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Write one private helper that takes a new `std::unique_ptr<Sample[]>` and its capacity, moves each old element into it with `fresh[i] = std::move(data_[i])`, then does `data_ = std::move(fresh)`. That last line deletes the old array. `reserve` and both `push_back`s use it.
--- hint
In `push_back`, when there is room, assign into slot `size_` (copy for the `const Sample&` version, `std::move(s)` for the `Sample&&` one). When there is no room, make the new array, put the new element into its slot `size_` **first**, and only then move the old elements across.
--- hint
The moves use `std::exchange`: the move constructor's initializer list is `data_(std::move(other.data_)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)), cap_(std::exchange(other.cap_, 0))`. The copy constructor makes an array of `other.size_` slots (or `nullptr`) and assigns each element.

--- check test | A moved-from vector can be pushed into again

+++ practice | A frame buffer that only moves
--- task
A camera on a rover fills a frame buffer of `width × height` pixels, each a `std::uint16_t` (a 16-bit unsigned number, from `<cstdint>`). Buffers are big, so a `FrameBuffer` is **move-only**. Store the pixels in a `std::unique_ptr<std::uint16_t[]>`, row after row: pixel `(x, y)` is at index `y * width + x`.

- `FrameBuffer(std::size_t width, std::size_t height)`: every pixel 0, made with `std::make_unique<std::uint16_t[]>`. When `width * height` is 0, hold `nullptr` and allocate nothing.
- `std::uint16_t& at(std::size_t x, std::size_t y)`, `std::size_t width() const`, `std::size_t height() const`, `const std::uint16_t* data() const`.
- `FrameBuffer(FrameBuffer&& other) noexcept` and `FrameBuffer& operator=(FrameBuffer&& other) noexcept` take the pixels and leave `other` as a 0 × 0 buffer with `data()` equal to `nullptr`.
- Copying must not compile. (With a `unique_ptr` member, the compiler already deletes the copy functions. Do not write them.)

Keep the memory ledger as it is: `std::make_unique<T[]>` calls `new[]`, so the ledger counts these arrays too.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <cstdint>
#include <memory>
#include <type_traits>

class FrameBuffer {
public:
    FrameBuffer(std::size_t width, std::size_t height) {}

    std::uint16_t& at(std::size_t x, std::size_t y) { return pixels_[y * width_ + x]; }
    std::size_t width() const { return width_; }
    std::size_t height() const { return height_; }
    const std::uint16_t* data() const { return pixels_.get(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<std::uint16_t[]> pixels_;
    std::size_t width_ = 0;
    std::size_t height_ = 0;

#include <cstdint>
#include <memory>
#include <type_traits>

class FrameBuffer {
public:
    FrameBuffer(std::size_t width, std::size_t height)
        : pixels_(width * height ? std::make_unique<std::uint16_t[]>(width * height) : nullptr),
          width_(width), height_(height) {}

    FrameBuffer(FrameBuffer&& other) noexcept
        : pixels_(std::move(other.pixels_)),
          width_(std::exchange(other.width_, 0)),
          height_(std::exchange(other.height_, 0)) {}

    FrameBuffer& operator=(FrameBuffer&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            pixels_ = std::move(other.pixels_);
            width_ = std::exchange(other.width_, 0);
            height_ = std::exchange(other.height_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    std::uint16_t& at(std::size_t x, std::size_t y) { return pixels_[y * width_ + x]; }
    std::size_t width() const { return width_; }
    std::size_t height() const { return height_; }
    const std::uint16_t* data() const { return pixels_.get(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<std::uint16_t[]> pixels_;
    std::size_t width_ = 0;
    std::size_t height_ = 0;
};
--- hint
In the constructor's initializer list, make the array with `std::make_unique<std::uint16_t[]>(width * height)` when that product is not 0, and `nullptr` otherwise. `make_unique` sets every pixel to 0 for you.
--- hint
The moves take `std::move(other.pixels_)` and `std::exchange(other.width_, 0)` (and the same for the height). Move assignment does the same inside `if (this != &other)`; assigning into `pixels_` frees the old array.

+++ practice | Insert and erase by moving
--- task
`class SampleList` keeps up to a fixed number of `Sample`s in order, in a `std::unique_ptr<Sample[]>` made once by the constructor. It never grows. Shifting elements to make or close a gap must **move** them; copying a `Sample` is not allowed anywhere. Keep the `Sample` type as it is: it counts copies and moves.

- `explicit SampleList(std::size_t capacity)`: empty, with room for `capacity` samples (make the array with `std::make_unique<Sample[]>(capacity)`).
- `bool insert(std::size_t pos, Sample s)` puts `s` at index `pos`, shifting the samples from `pos` onwards one place right. `pos` may be anything from 0 to `size()`. Return `false`, changing nothing, when `pos` is too big or the list is full.
- `bool erase(std::size_t pos)` removes the sample at `pos`, shifting the rest one place left, and resets the slot that falls out of use to `Sample()`. Return `false` when `pos >= size()`.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`, `const Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) const`.

`s` is taken by value, so a caller who passes a temporary has it built right in the parameter; move it from there into its slot.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// Given: a reading that counts its copies and moves. Leave it as it is.
struct Sample {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    std::string label;
    double value = 0.0;

    Sample() = default;
    Sample(std::string l, double v) : label(std::move(l)), value(v) {}
    Sample(const Sample& o) : label(o.label), value(o.value) { ++copies; }
    Sample(Sample&& o) noexcept : label(std::move(o.label)), value(o.value) { ++moves; }
    Sample& operator=(const Sample& o) { label = o.label; value = o.value; ++copies; return *this; }
    Sample& operator=(Sample&& o) noexcept { label = std::move(o.label); value = o.value; ++moves; return *this; }
};

class SampleList {
public:
    explicit SampleList(std::size_t capacity) : data_(std::make_unique<Sample[]>(capacity)), cap_(capacity) {}

    bool insert(std::size_t pos, Sample s) { return false; }
    bool erase(std::size_t pos) { return false; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// Given: a reading that counts its copies and moves. Leave it as it is.
struct Sample {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    std::string label;
    double value = 0.0;

    Sample() = default;
    Sample(std::string l, double v) : label(std::move(l)), value(v) {}
    Sample(const Sample& o) : label(o.label), value(o.value) { ++copies; }
    Sample(Sample&& o) noexcept : label(std::move(o.label)), value(o.value) { ++moves; }
    Sample& operator=(const Sample& o) { label = o.label; value = o.value; ++copies; return *this; }
    Sample& operator=(Sample&& o) noexcept { label = std::move(o.label); value = o.value; ++moves; return *this; }
};

class SampleList {
public:
    explicit SampleList(std::size_t capacity) : data_(std::make_unique<Sample[]>(capacity)), cap_(capacity) {}

    bool insert(std::size_t pos, Sample s) {
        if (pos > size_ || size_ == cap_) return false;
        for (std::size_t i = size_; i > pos; --i) data_[i] = std::move(data_[i - 1]);
        data_[pos] = std::move(s);
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool erase(std::size_t pos) {
        if (pos >= size_) return false;
        for (std::size_t i = pos; i + 1 < size_; ++i) data_[i] = std::move(data_[i + 1]);
        --size_;
        data_[size_] = Sample();
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    const Sample& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_;
};
--- hint
Shifting right starts at the free slot and walks down to `pos`, moving each sample one place: `data_[i] = std::move(data_[i - 1]);`. Then move `s` into `data_[pos]`.
--- hint
For `erase`, walk up from `pos`, moving `data_[i + 1]` into `data_[i]`. After the loop and `--size_`, the slot at the new `size_` is a moved-from leftover: assign `Sample()` to it. Assigning a temporary is a move, not a copy.
--- check case | Inserting at the front, the end and the middle

=> std::string("abcd")
--- check test | Inserting temporaries never copies
[] { SampleList l(100); Sample::copies = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) l.insert(0, Sample("n" + std::to_string(i), i)); return Sample::copies == 0 && l.size() == 100 && l[0].label == "n99" && l[99].label == "n0"; }()
?? Shift with std::move, and move s into its slot.
--- check test | Inserting at 0 into 5 samples takes 6 moves
[] { SampleList l(10); for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) l.insert(l.size(), Sample("x", i)); Sample::moves = 0; Sample::copies = 0; l.insert(0, Sample("front", -1)); return Sample::moves == 6 && Sample::copies == 0 && l[0].label == "front" && l[5].value == 4; }()
--- check test | A full list or a bad position is refused

--- check test | erase shifts left, clears the old last slot, and refuses bad positions
[] { SampleList l(4); for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) l.insert(l.size(), Sample("e" + std::to_string(i), i)); Sample::copies = 0; bool ok = l.erase(1) && l.erase(2) && !l.erase(2); return ok && Sample::copies == 0 && l.size() == 2 && l[0].label == "e0" && l[1].label == "e2" && l[2].label.empty() && l[3].label.empty(); }()
--- check test | A capacity-0 list refuses everything
[] { SampleList l(0); return !l.insert(0, Sample("a", 1)) && !l.erase(0) && l.size() == 0; }()

+++ practice | Drop bad readings in one pass
--- task
A telemetry pass arrives as a `std::vector<Sample>`. Readings whose `value` is below a threshold are noise. Write `void drop_below(std::vector<Sample>& v, double min)` that removes every sample with `value < min`, keeps the others in their original order, and runs in O(n).

Erasing each bad sample with `v.erase` inside a loop is O(n²): every erase shifts everything after it, and it invalidates the iterator you are standing on. Instead use two indexes. Walk a read index over every sample, and keep a write index for the next place a kept sample goes. Move each kept sample from the read index to the write index (skip the move when they are the same), then cut the vector down to the write index with `v.resize(w)`.

A check counts the moves: removing half of 20,000 samples must take at most 20,000 moves and no copies. Keep the `Sample` type as it is.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// Given: a reading that counts its copies and moves. Leave it as it is.
struct Sample {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    std::string label;
    double value = 0.0;

    Sample() = default;
    Sample(std::string l, double v) : label(std::move(l)), value(v) {}
    Sample(const Sample& o) : label(o.label), value(o.value) { ++copies; }
    Sample(Sample&& o) noexcept : label(std::move(o.label)), value(o.value) { ++moves; }
    Sample& operator=(const Sample& o) { label = o.label; value = o.value; ++copies; return *this; }
    Sample& operator=(Sample&& o) noexcept { label = std::move(o.label); value = o.value; ++moves; return *this; }
};

void drop_below(std::vector<Sample>& v, double min) {
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        if (v[i].value < min) v.erase(v.begin() + i);
    }
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// Given: a reading that counts its copies and moves. Leave it as it is.
struct Sample {
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    std::string label;
    double value = 0.0;

    Sample() = default;
    Sample(std::string l, double v) : label(std::move(l)), value(v) {}
    Sample(const Sample& o) : label(o.label), value(o.value) { ++copies; }
    Sample(Sample&& o) noexcept : label(std::move(o.label)), value(o.value) { ++moves; }
    Sample& operator=(const Sample& o) { label = o.label; value = o.value; ++copies; return *this; }
    Sample& operator=(Sample&& o) noexcept { label = std::move(o.label); value = o.value; ++moves; return *this; }
};

void drop_below(std::vector<Sample>& v, double min) {
    std::size_t w = 0;   // v[0..w) holds the kept samples, in order
    for (std::size_t r = 0; r < v.size(); ++r) {
        if (v[r].value < min) continue;
        if (w != r) v[w] = std::move(v[r]);
        ++w;
    }
    v.resize(w);
}
--- hint
The starter has two problems. It is O(n²), because each `erase` shifts every later element. And after an erase, `i` moves on past the sample that just slid into position `i`, so two bad samples in a row leave one behind.
--- hint
Keep `w`, the number of samples kept so far. For each `r` from 0 to the end: if `v[r]` is kept, move it to `v[w]` (only when `w != r`) and add one to `w`. At the end, `v.resize(w)` drops the leftovers from the back, which moves nothing.
--- check case | Two bad readings in a row are both removed
[] { std::vector<Sample> v; v.emplace_back("a", 5); v.emplace_back("b", -1); v.emplace_back("c", -2); v.emplace_back("d", 7); v.emplace_back("e", 0); drop_below(v, 0.0); std::string out; for (const Sample& s : v) out += s.label; return out; }()
=> std::string("ade")
?? The starter skips the sample that slides into the erased position.
--- check test | Nothing to drop, everything to drop, and an empty vector
[] { std::vector<Sample> a; a.emplace_back("x", 1); a.emplace_back("y", 2); drop_below(a, -10); std::vector<Sample> b = a; drop_below(b, 100); std::vector<Sample> c; drop_below(c, 0); return a.size() == 2 && a[1].label == "y" && b.empty() && c.empty(); }()
--- check test | A value equal to min is kept
[] { std::vector<Sample> v; v.emplace_back("edge", 3.0); v.emplace_back("below", 2.999); drop_below(v, 3.0); return v.size() == 1 && v[0].label == "edge"; }()
--- check test | Half of 20,000 samples dropped in at most 20,000 moves, no copies
[] { std::vector<Sample> v; v.reserve(20000); for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) v.emplace_back("s", i % 2 ? 1.0 : -1.0); Sample::moves = 0; Sample::copies = 0; drop_below(v, 0.0); return v.size() == 10000 && Sample::copies == 0 && Sample::moves <= 20000 && v[9999].value == 1.0; }()
?? Erasing one at a time shifts about 50 million samples here. Move each kept sample once, then resize.
--- check test | The order of the kept samples does not change
[] { std::vector<Sample> v; for (int i = 0; i < 50; ++i) v.emplace_back(std::to_string(i), i % 3 == 0 ? -1.0 : double(i)); drop_below(v, 0.0); bool ordered = v.size() == 33; for (std::size_t i = 1; i < v.size(); ++i) ordered = ordered && v[i - 1].value < v[i].value; return ordered && v[0].label == "1" && v[32].label == "49"; }()

+++ practice | Resize, with every edge case
--- task
Write `class Levels`, a growable array of `int`s in a `std::unique_ptr<int[]>`, with `resize` and `reserve`. Copying is not needed.

- `Levels()`: empty, capacity 0, nothing allocated.
- `void reserve(std::size_t n)`: when `n` is more than the capacity, move to a new array of exactly `n` slots, keeping the values; otherwise do nothing.
- `void resize(std::size_t n, int fill)`: make the size `n`.
  - If `n` is more than the capacity, reallocate to exactly `n` slots first.
  - Every slot from the old size up to `n` gets `fill`. This includes slots that held values before a shrink: after `resize(2, 0)` and `resize(4, 9)`, slots 2 and 3 are 9, not the old values.
  - If `n` is smaller than the size, only the size drops; the capacity stays.
- `void clear()`: size 0, capacity unchanged.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`, `int operator[](std::size_t i) const`, `const int* data() const`.

Keep the memory ledger as it is.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>

class Levels {
public:
    void reserve(std::size_t n) {}
    void resize(std::size_t n, int fill) { size_ = n; }
    void clear() {}
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    int operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    const int* data() const { return data_.get(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<int[]> data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>

class Levels {
public:
    void reserve(std::size_t n) {
        if (n <= cap_) return;
        std::unique_ptr<int[]> fresh = std::make_unique<int[]>(n);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) fresh[i] = data_[i];
        data_ = std::move(fresh);
        cap_ = n;
    }

    void resize(std::size_t n, int fill) {
        reserve(n);
        for (std::size_t i = size_; i < n; ++i) data_[i] = fill;
        size_ = n;
    }

    void clear() { size_ = 0; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    int operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    const int* data() const { return data_.get(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<int[]> data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
`resize` can start by calling `reserve(n)`: that does nothing unless `n` is more than the capacity. After it, there is room for `n` values.
--- hint
Then fill the slots from the old size up to `n` with `fill`, and set the size to `n`. When `n` is smaller than the old size, that loop runs zero times, which is exactly right. The stale values left in slots past the size are overwritten the next time the size grows past them.
--- check case | Growing from empty fills every new slot
[] { Levels l; l.resize(3, 7); std::vector<int> out; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < l.size(); ++i) out.push_back(l[i]); out.push_back(static_cast<int>(l.capacity())); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{7, 7, 7, 3}
?? The last number is the capacity: exactly n when resize has to reallocate.
--- check test | Shrinking keeps the capacity and does not reallocate
[] { Levels l; l.resize(6, 1); int made = ledger::made; l.resize(2, 0); return ledger::made == made && l.size() == 2 && l.capacity() == 6 && l[1] == 1; }()
--- check case | Growing back after a shrink overwrites the old slots
[] { Levels l; l.resize(5, 3); l.resize(2, 0); l.resize(4, 9); std::vector<int> out; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < l.size(); ++i) out.push_back(l[i]); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{3, 3, 9, 9}
?? Slots past the old size may hold stale values. Write fill into every one of them.
--- check test | resize to the same size, and to 0
[] { Levels l; l.resize(3, 4); int made = ledger::made; l.resize(3, 8); bool same = l.size() == 3 && l[2] == 4; l.resize(0, 5); return same && ledger::made == made && l.size() == 0 && l.capacity() == 3; }()
--- check test | reserve then resize within it allocates once
[] { int live = ledger::live; bool ok; { Levels l; l.reserve(100); int made = ledger::made; l.resize(60, 2); l.resize(100, 3); ok = ledger::made == made && l.capacity() == 100 && l[59] == 2 && l[60] == 3; } return ok && ledger::live == live && ledger::bad == 0; }()
--- check test | clear keeps the capacity, and the values survive growth
[] { Levels l; l.resize(2, 1); l.clear(); bool cleared = l.size() == 0 && l.capacity() == 2; l.resize(1, 5); l.resize(10, 6); return cleared && l[0] == 5 && l[1] == 6 && l[9] == 6 && l.capacity() == 10; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the moved-from log that lies about its size
--- task
`class SensorLog` stores `double` readings in a `std::unique_ptr<double[]>`, with a size and a capacity. Its author let the compiler write both move functions with `= default`.

After `SensorLog b(std::move(a));`, `b` is fine, but `a` still reports its old size and capacity while holding no array. Pushing into `a` afterwards writes through a null pointer. A moved-from log must report size 0 and capacity 0, and work normally when used again.

Fix the two move functions. Everything else is correct.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>

class SensorLog {
public:
    SensorLog() = default;
    SensorLog(SensorLog&&) noexcept = default;
    SensorLog& operator=(SensorLog&&) noexcept = default;

    void push_back(double x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) {
            std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_;
            std::unique_ptr<double[]> fresh = std::make_unique<double[]>(new_cap);
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) fresh[i] = data_[i];
            data_ = std::move(fresh);
            cap_ = new_cap;
        }
        data_[size_] = x;
        ++size_;
    }

    double operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<double[]> data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>

class SensorLog {
public:
    SensorLog() = default;

    SensorLog(SensorLog&& other) noexcept
        : data_(std::move(other.data_)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)), cap_(std::exchange(other.cap_, 0)) {}

    SensorLog& operator=(SensorLog&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            data_ = std::move(other.data_);
            size_ = std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
            cap_ = std::exchange(other.cap_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    void push_back(double x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) {
            std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_;
            std::unique_ptr<double[]> fresh = std::make_unique<double[]>(new_cap);
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) fresh[i] = data_[i];
            data_ = std::move(fresh);
            cap_ = new_cap;
        }
        data_[size_] = x;
        ++size_;
    }

    double operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<double[]> data_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
The compiler's move moves each member. What does "moving" a `std::size_t` do to the source?
--- hint
Write both moves yourself. Move the `unique_ptr`, and take the size and capacity with `std::exchange(other.size_, 0)` and `std::exchange(other.cap_, 0)`, so the source is left with 0 for both.
--- check test | The moved-from log reports size 0 and capacity 0
[] { SensorLog a; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) a.push_back(i); SensorLog b(std::move(a)); return a.size() == 0 && a.capacity() == 0 && b.size() == 5 && b[4] == 4; }()
?? A moved std::size_t is only copied. Leave 0 behind with std::exchange.
--- check test | Move assignment empties the source too
[] { SensorLog a; SensorLog b; a.push_back(1.5); b.push_back(2.5); b.push_back(3.5); a = std::move(b); return b.size() == 0 && b.capacity() == 0 && a.size() == 2 && a[1] == 3.5; }()
--- check test | A moved-from log works when used again
[] { SensorLog a; a.push_back(9); SensorLog b(std::move(a)); if (a.size() != 0) return false; a.push_back(1); a.push_back(2); return a.size() == 2 && a[1] == 2 && a.capacity() == 2 && b[0] == 9; }()
--- check test | Nothing leaks, nothing is freed twice
[] { int live = ledger::live; { SensorLog a; for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) a.push_back(i); SensorLog b(std::move(a)); SensorLog c; c = std::move(b); if (c.size() != 20 || b.size() != 0) return false; } return ledger::live == live && ledger::bad == 0; }()

+++ practice | A log whose entries never move
--- task
A flight recorder hands out a reference to each entry it stores, and other parts of the system keep those references for the whole mission. A vector cannot promise that: growing moves every entry. So `class ChunkedLog` stores entries in **chunks** of 64, and never moves a chunk's entries:

- `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Entry[]>> chunks_` holds the chunks. When every chunk is full, add a new one with `std::make_unique<Entry[]>(kChunk)`. The vector of chunk pointers may grow and move the *pointers*, but the entries stay where they are.
- `Entry& push_back(int time, double value)` stores a new entry and returns a reference to it. That reference must stay valid, pointing at the same entry, however many entries come later.
- `Entry& operator[](std::size_t i)`: entry `i` is in chunk `i / kChunk`, at slot `i % kChunk`.
- `std::size_t size() const` and `std::size_t chunks() const`.

`struct Entry` and `kChunk = 64` are given. Keep the memory ledger: the checks count the chunks with it.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Entry {
    int time = 0;
    double value = 0.0;
};

class ChunkedLog {
public:
    static constexpr std::size_t kChunk = 64;

    Entry& push_back(int time, double value) {
        entries_.push_back(Entry{time, value});
        return entries_.back();
    }
    Entry& operator[](std::size_t i) { return entries_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return entries_.size(); }
    std::size_t chunks() const { return 0; }

private:
    std::vector<Entry> entries_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <utility>

// The memory ledger: it counts every new[] and delete[]. The checks read it. Leave it as it is.
namespace ledger {
inline void* blocks[1 << 12];
inline int live = 0;   // arrays made with new[] and not given back yet
inline int made = 0;   // arrays made with new[], ever
inline int bad = 0;    // delete[] of an address that is not live: a double delete
}
void* operator new[](std::size_t bytes) {
    void* p = std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1);
    if (ledger::live < (1 << 12)) ledger::blocks[ledger::live++] = p;
    ++ledger::made;
    return p;
}
void operator delete[](void* p) noexcept {
    if (!p) return;
    for (int i = 0; i < ledger::live; ++i) {
        if (ledger::blocks[i] == p) {
            ledger::blocks[i] = ledger::blocks[--ledger::live];
            std::free(p);
            return;
        }
    }
    ++ledger::bad;
}
void operator delete[](void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete[](p); }
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

struct Entry {
    int time = 0;
    double value = 0.0;
};

class ChunkedLog {
public:
    static constexpr std::size_t kChunk = 64;

    Entry& push_back(int time, double value) {
        if (size_ == chunks_.size() * kChunk) chunks_.push_back(std::make_unique<Entry[]>(kChunk));
        Entry& e = (*this)[size_];
        e.time = time;
        e.value = value;
        ++size_;
        return e;
    }

    Entry& operator[](std::size_t i) { return chunks_[i / kChunk][i % kChunk]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t chunks() const { return chunks_.size(); }

private:
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Entry[]>> chunks_;   // each chunk holds kChunk entries and never moves
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
The starter keeps entries in a `std::vector<Entry>`, so a growth moves them all and every reference handed out so far dangles. Keep a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Entry[]>>` of chunks and a count of entries instead.
--- hint
Every chunk is full exactly when `size_ == chunks_.size() * kChunk`; then push a new chunk. Entry `i` lives at `chunks_[i / kChunk][i % kChunk]`. Write the new entry there, add one to the count, and return a reference to that slot.
--- check test | A reference to the first entry survives 10,000 more pushes
[] { ChunkedLog log; Entry& first = log.push_back(1, 0.5); Entry* where = &first; for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) log.push_back(i + 2, i); return &log[0] == where && where->time == 1 && where->value == 0.5 && log.size() == 10001; }()
?? A std::vector<Entry> moves its entries when it grows. Chunks that never move keep every address valid.
--- check test | Every returned reference still points at its own entry
[] { ChunkedLog log; std::vector<Entry*> seen; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) seen.push_back(&log.push_back(i, i * 2.0)); bool ok = true; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) ok = ok && seen[i] == &log[i] && seen[i]->time == i; return ok; }()
--- check case | Chunks used for 0, 1, 64, 65 and 200 entries
[] { std::vector<std::size_t> out; for (int n : {0, 1, 64, 65, 200}) { ChunkedLog log; for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) log.push_back(i, 0); out.push_back(log.chunks()); } return out; }()
=> std::vector<std::size_t>{0, 1, 1, 2, 4}
--- check test | Each chunk is one array of 64, and all are freed

+++ question | Which pointer is still good
--- ask
```cpp fragment
std::vector<int> v;
v.reserve(100);
for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) v.push_back(i);
int* a = &v[3];
v.push_back(10);                   // (1)
int* b = &v[5];
v.erase(v.begin() + 4);            // (2)
```

After line (2), which of `a` and `b` still point at a valid element holding the value they held when they were taken?
--- choice
Neither: every change to a vector invalidates all pointers into it.
--- choice correct
Only `a`: line (1) did not reallocate, and line (2) only moves elements from index 4 on.
--- choice
Only `b`: it was taken after the push, so it is newer.
--- choice
Both: the capacity never changed, so nothing moved.
--- why
`reserve(100)` means eleven pushes never reallocate, so (1) keeps `a` valid. `erase` at index 4 shifts every later element one place left, so the slot `b` points at (index 5) now holds what was at index 6: it still points into the array, but at a different element. The rule is "invalidates everything at or after the erased point", and index 3 is before it.

+++ question | The type without noexcept
--- ask
A `Track` type has a correct move constructor, but it is not marked `noexcept`. A `std::vector<Track>` grows from 512 to 1,024 elements. What happens to the 512 existing elements?
--- choice
They are moved, because a move constructor exists.
--- choice correct
They are copied, because `std::vector` only moves during growth when moving cannot throw.
--- choice
The program does not compile.
--- choice
Half are moved and half are copied.
--- why
To keep the strong guarantee, growth must be able to undo itself if an element operation fails. Copying leaves the old array intact, so failure is recoverable; a move that throws halfway is not. The library checks `std::is_nothrow_move_constructible` and falls back to the copy constructor when the move might throw. Marking the move `noexcept` turns 512 copies into 512 moves.

=== dsacpp-03 | Templates: Vector<T>, and elements with no default constructor
--- teach
You have now written the same vector twice: `IntVector` for `int`s and `SampleVector` for `Sample`s. Apart from the element type, the code was identical. This lesson writes it once, as a **template**, so that `Vector<int>`, `Vector<std::string>` and `Vector<Sample>` all come from one piece of code. It also fixes the hidden cost from last lesson: `std::make_unique<T[]>(n)` built `n` objects you did not ask for, and refused types with no default constructor. A real vector separates *getting memory* from *building objects in it*.

### One definition, many types

Think of a template as a stencil. The stencil is not a drawing; you get a drawing when you trace it with a colour. A template is not code yet; the compiler makes real code when you use it with a type.

A **function template** starts with `template <typename T>`, which reads "for any type `T`":

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

template <typename T>
const T& larger(const T& a, const T& b) {
    return b < a ? a : b;
}

int main() {
    std::cout << larger(3, 9) << "\n";                                   // 9
    std::cout << larger(std::string("deneb"), std::string("altair")) << "\n";   // deneb
    std::cout << larger<double>(2, 7.5) << "\n";                         // 7.5
}
```

The compiler **deduces** `T` from the arguments: `int` in the first call, `std::string` in the second. In the third, the arguments have different types, so the call names `T` itself in angle brackets. Each different `T` makes a separate function. That step is called **instantiation**.

### A class template

A **class template** puts the same line before a class. Inside, `T` is used like any type:

```cpp fragment
template <typename T>
class Latest {
public:
    void record(const T& v) { value_ = v; ++count_; }
    const T& value() const { return value_; }
    int count() const { return count_; }
private:
    T value_{};
    int count_ = 0;
};
```

`Latest<double> gauge;` makes a class where every `T` is `double`. `Latest<std::string> status;` makes a second, separate class. `T value_{};` with empty braces **value-initialises** the member: 0 for numbers, the default constructor for classes.

### Members defined outside the class

A long member function can be declared in the class and defined below it. Outside the class, it needs the template line again, and the class name with its parameter, `Latest<T>::`:

```cpp fragment
template <typename T>
class Latest {
public:
    void record(const T& v);   // only declared here
    // ...
};

template <typename T>
void Latest<T>::record(const T& v) {
    value_ = v;
    ++count_;
}
```

Read `Latest<T>::record` as "the `record` that belongs to `Latest<T>`".

### Why the whole template goes in the header

In a normal project, a class is declared in a header (`vector.h`) and its functions are defined in a source file (`vector.cpp`) that is compiled once. That fails for a template. The compiler makes `Vector<int>::push_back` at the moment it sees `Vector<int>` used, and it can only do that if it can see the body of `push_back` right there. A file that includes only the declarations gets a **[[linker error|linker]]**: the function was declared but never made. So a template's member functions are defined in the header too, inside the class or below it. That is why the standard library's `<vector>` is a header full of code.

### Only what is used is made

A member function of a class template is instantiated only if something calls it. This is not a detail; it is what lets one template serve very different types. `std::unique_ptr<int>` cannot be copied, but `Vector<std::unique_ptr<int>>` still compiles, because as long as nobody copies the vector, its copy constructor is never made. Try to copy it, and only then does the compiler report an error.

### What T must provide

A template asks of `T` exactly what its code does with `T`, though C++20 lets it [[say so out loud|concepts]]. `std::make_unique<T[]>(n)` builds `n` objects with no arguments, so it demands a **default constructor**. Many useful types have none. A reading that makes no sense without its sensor id should not be constructible without one:

```cpp error
#include <memory>

struct Reading {
    explicit Reading(int sensor) : sensor_id(sensor) {}
    int sensor_id;
};

int main() {
    auto slots = std::make_unique<Reading[]>(8);   // error: Reading has no default constructor
}
```

A vector should need no such thing. `std::vector<Reading>` with `reserve(8)` works fine. The trick is to get memory without building objects in it.

### Room first, objects later

Four tools, all from `<memory>`, split the job in two. The first is an **[[allocator|allocator]]**, an object whose job is to hand out raw memory:

- `std::allocator<T>().allocate(n)` returns a `T*` to raw memory with room for `n` objects of type `T`. No object is built.
- `std::construct_at(p, args)` builds one `T` at address `p`, passing `args` to its constructor.
- `std::destroy_at(p)` runs the destructor of the object at `p`. The memory stays; the object is gone.
- `std::allocator<T>().deallocate(p, n)` gives the memory back. `n` must be the same number that was allocated.

`std::allocator<T>()` makes a temporary allocator object; it holds no state, so making one each time costs nothing. Here the constructor and destructor print, so you can see that only two objects ever exist in room for three:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

struct Beacon {
    explicit Beacon(int id) : id(id) { std::cout << "build " << id << "\n"; }
    ~Beacon() { std::cout << "destroy " << id << "\n"; }
    int id;
};

int main() {
    Beacon* room = std::allocator<Beacon>().allocate(3);   // raw memory; nothing printed
    std::construct_at(room, 7);                             // build 7
    std::construct_at(room + 1, 8);                         // build 8
    std::cout << room[1].id << "\n";                        // 8
    std::destroy_at(room + 1);                              // destroy 8
    std::destroy_at(room);                                  // destroy 7
    std::allocator<Beacon>().deallocate(room, 3);
}
```

### An object's lifetime

Every object has a **[[lifetime|lifetime]]**: it starts when its constructor finishes and ends when its destructor starts. Only in between may you use it. Before `construct_at` and after `destroy_at`, the memory is just bytes.

This is why `room[2] = Beacon(9);` would be wrong: assignment is a member function of an object that already exists, and slot 2 holds no object. Assigning into raw memory is undefined behaviour. To put a first value into a raw slot, you **construct** it there; to replace the value of a living object, you **assign** to it.

### The new invariant

The vector keeps `T* data_`, `size_` and `cap_`, and this invariant:

1. `data_` is `nullptr` when `cap_` is 0, and otherwise raw memory from `allocate(cap_)`.
2. Slots `0` to `size_ - 1` hold **living** objects.
3. Slots `size_` to `cap_ - 1` are **raw**: no object lives there.

Every operation is now a statement about lifetimes:

- **push_back** constructs a new object in slot `size_` (raw), then adds one to `size_`.
- **pop_back** subtracts one from `size_`, then destroys the object in slot `size_`, which becomes raw again.
- **clear** destroys every living object and sets `size_` to 0. The memory stays, all raw.
- **The destructor** destroys the living objects, then deallocates. It must not destroy the raw slots: they hold no objects.

### Growing with raw memory

Growth now has more steps, and the order matters:

1. Allocate raw memory for the new capacity.
2. Construct the new element in its slot `size_`, while the old array is still intact (the argument may be one of the old elements, as last lesson showed).
3. For each old element, **move-construct** a new one in the same slot of the new memory: `std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]))`. It is construction, not assignment, because the new slots are raw.
4. Destroy every old element, then deallocate the old memory.
5. Switch `data_` and `cap_`.

### Why it is correct

The claim has three parts: every object the vector builds is destroyed exactly once, no object is used outside its lifetime, and no `T` is ever built without arguments.

- **Every operation keeps the invariant.** push_back turns raw slot `size_` into a living one and moves the boundary up by one. pop_back moves the boundary down by one and ends that object's life. clear ends every life and puts the boundary at 0. Growth builds exactly `size_ + 1` living objects in new memory (slots `0` to `size_`), ends exactly the `size_` lives in the old memory, and frees it.
- **So each object is destroyed exactly once.** Objects are only ever destroyed at the moment they leave the living range `[0, size_)`, and each object leaves it once. The destructor destroys exactly the living range. Raw slots are never destroyed.
- **No object is used outside its lifetime.** `operator[]` is only valid for `i < size_`, a living slot. New values go into raw slots by construction, never by assignment.
- **No default construction.** Every `construct_at` call passes a value: a copy, a moved object or the pushed element. Nothing calls `T()`.

### What it costs

The big-O costs are last lesson's: push_back is amortised O(1), a growth moves every element once, a copy is O(n). What changes is the constant work: the vector now builds exactly `size()` objects, never `capacity()`. A `Vector<std::string>` with capacity 1,024 and 513 strings has built 513 strings, not 1,024.

### Where it is used

- `std::vector<T>` works exactly this way, through an allocator. So do `std::deque` and `std::optional<T>`, which keeps raw room for one `T` and builds it only when a value arrives.
- Game engines and flight software use **pools**: one block of raw memory allocated at start-up, with objects built in it and destroyed as the mission runs, so memory never runs out halfway through.
- Since C++20, `std::construct_at` and `std::destroy_at` can even run at compile time, which is how `std::vector` became usable inside `constexpr` functions.

**Watch out:**

- Assigning into a raw slot (`data_[size_] = x`) instead of constructing there. It may seem to work for `int`, and crash for `std::string`, whose assignment reads the garbage it thinks is its old buffer.
- Destroying the whole capacity in the destructor instead of the living range: that runs destructors on raw memory.
- Forgetting to destroy on `pop_back` or `clear`: the objects' own resources, like a string's buffer, leak.
- Deallocating with a different count than you allocated, or with `delete[]`. Memory from `allocate` goes back through `deallocate`.
- Moving the old elements by assignment during growth. The new slots are raw, so it must be `construct_at` with `std::move`.

::: context linker Declared but never made
Building a C++ program has two stages. The compiler turns each source file into an object file on its own, and then the linker joins the object files, matching each use of a function with the one place it was made. If `vector.cpp` never used `Vector<int>::push_back`, the compiler never instantiated it there, and `main.cpp` only saw a declaration. The linker then reports an undefined reference to `Vector<int>::push_back`. Putting the definitions in the header lets every file make what it uses; the linker keeps one copy of each.
:::

::: context concepts Saying what T needs
Before C++20, what a template needed from `T` was only written in comments, and a wrong type produced pages of errors from deep inside the template. C++20 added concepts: a template can say `template <std::movable T>` or add a `requires` clause, and a wrong type is rejected at the call, with a short message naming the missing ability. The standard library's own requirements, such as "the element type must be move-constructible for this operation", are written this way.
:::

::: context allocator Why a class for allocating
`std::allocator` looks like needless ceremony around `operator new`. It exists so that containers can take other allocators: one that hands out memory from a fixed buffer, one that counts bytes, one that uses shared memory between processes. `std::vector<T, Alloc>` has a second template parameter for exactly that, which defaults to `std::allocator<T>`. Flight and game software often plug in an arena allocator that never returns memory to the system until the end of a frame or a mission phase.
:::

::: context lifetime Objects and the bytes under them
The C++ standard describes memory and objects separately. Memory is bytes with addresses. An object is a typed thing that lives in some of those bytes for a while. Constructing starts the object's life and destroying ends it, whatever happens to the bytes. Compilers use these rules to optimise, assuming, for example, that a destroyed object is never read again. That is why using an object outside its lifetime is undefined behaviour even when the bytes are still there and look right.
:::
--- task
Write `template <typename T> class Vector`, a growable array that never builds an element it was not given. No `main`. Keep the given `Probe` type and the heap ledger exactly as they are: `Probe` has **no default constructor** and counts itself in `Probe::live`, `Probe::copies` and `Probe::moves`, and `heap::live` counts the memory blocks not yet given back.

Store the elements in raw memory from `std::allocator<T>().allocate(n)`, and build and destroy them with `std::construct_at` and `std::destroy_at`. `std::make_unique<T[]>` will not compile with `Probe`.

- `Vector()`: empty, capacity 0, no memory.
- `void push_back(const T& x)` (one copy of `x`) and `void push_back(T&& x)` (moved in, no copy). When full, grow first: capacity 0 becomes 1, anything else doubles. Growth **moves** the old elements into the new memory, never copies them. `v.push_back(v[0])` must work, even when that push grows.
- `void pop_back()` destroys the last element at once. On an empty vector it does nothing.
- `void clear()` destroys every element and keeps the capacity.
- `void reserve(std::size_t n)`: when `n` is more than the capacity, move the elements into new memory of exactly `n` slots; otherwise do nothing.
- `T& operator[](std::size_t i)`, `const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const`, `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`.
- The rule of five. `~Vector()` destroys the living elements and gives the memory back. The copy constructor builds a copy of each element (capacity equal to the size). Copy assignment: a deep copy; `v = v` changes nothing. The two moves are `noexcept`, take the memory without touching any element, and leave the source with size 0 and capacity 0.

Define both `push_back`s and `reserve` **outside** the class body, below it, as a header would.
--- starter

// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.

void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }

--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Vector {
public:
    Vector() = default;

    ~Vector() {
        clear();
        release(data_, cap_);
    }

    Vector(const Vector& other) : data_(acquire(other.size_)), cap_(other.size_) {
        for (; size_ < other.size_; ++size_) std::construct_at(data_ + size_, other.data_[size_]);
    }

    Vector& operator=(const Vector& other) {
        Vector copy(other);
        swap(copy);
        return *this;
    }

    Vector(Vector&& other) noexcept
        : data_(std::exchange(other.data_, nullptr)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)), cap_(std::exchange(other.cap_, 0)) {}

    Vector& operator=(Vector&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            clear();
            release(data_, cap_);
            data_ = std::exchange(other.data_, nullptr);
            size_ = std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
            cap_ = std::exchange(other.cap_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    void swap(Vector& other) noexcept {
        std::swap(data_, other.data_);
        std::swap(size_, other.size_);
        std::swap(cap_, other.cap_);
    }

    void push_back(const T& x);
    void push_back(T&& x);

    void pop_back() {
        if (size_ == 0) return;
        --size_;
        std::destroy_at(data_ + size_);
    }

    void clear() {
        while (size_ > 0) pop_back();
    }

    void reserve(std::size_t n);

    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }

private:
    static T* acquire(std::size_t n) { return n ? std::allocator<T>().allocate(n) : nullptr; }
    static void release(T* p, std::size_t n) {
        if (p) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(p, n);
    }
    std::size_t next_capacity() const { return cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_; }

    // Moves the living elements into fresh (raw memory for new_cap), then frees the old memory.
    void adopt(T* fresh, std::size_t new_cap) {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) {
            std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]));
            std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
        }
        release(data_, cap_);
        data_ = fresh;
        cap_ = new_cap;
    }

    T* data_ = nullptr;     // slots [0, size_) are alive, [size_, cap_) are raw
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};

template <typename T>
void Vector<T>::push_back(const T& x) {
    if (size_ < cap_) {
        std::construct_at(data_ + size_, x);
    } else {
        std::size_t new_cap = next_capacity();
        T* fresh = acquire(new_cap);
        std::construct_at(fresh + size_, x);   // x may live in the old memory: build it first
        adopt(fresh, new_cap);
    }
    ++size_;
}

template <typename T>
void Vector<T>::push_back(T&& x) {
    if (size_ < cap_) {
        std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(x));
    } else {
        std::size_t new_cap = next_capacity();
        T* fresh = acquire(new_cap);
        std::construct_at(fresh + size_, std::move(x));
        adopt(fresh, new_cap);
    }
    ++size_;
}

template <typename T>
void Vector<T>::reserve(std::size_t n) {
    if (n > cap_) adopt(acquire(n), n);
}
--- hint
Keep the invariant in mind: slots below `size_` hold living objects, slots from `size_` up to `cap_` are raw. push_back constructs into slot `size_` with `std::construct_at(data_ + size_, x)` and then adds one; pop_back subtracts one and calls `std::destroy_at(data_ + size_)`. `clear` can call pop_back until the size is 0.
--- hint
Write a private helper that takes new raw memory: for each living slot `i`, `std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]))` and then `std::destroy_at(data_ + i)`; then deallocate the old memory with the old capacity and switch `data_` and `cap_`. In push_back, when full, allocate the new memory and construct the new element in `fresh + size_` **before** calling that helper.
--- hint
The destructor is `clear()` followed by deallocating `data_` (when it is not `nullptr`) with `cap_`. The copy constructor allocates `other.size_` slots and constructs a copy of each element. The moves use `std::exchange` on all three members; move assignment clears and frees its own memory first.

+++ practice | The highest reading, for any type
--- task
Write two templates. Both may compare items **only with `<`**, and must work for types that have no default constructor.

- `template <typename T> std::size_t count_above(const std::vector<T>& items, const T& limit)` returns how many items are greater than `limit` (that is, `limit < item`).
- `template <typename T> class RunningMax` keeps the largest item seen so far, in a `std::optional<T>`:
  - `void add(const T& x)` records `x`. When `x` ties the current best (neither is less than the other), keep the earlier one.
  - `bool empty() const` is `true` until the first `add`.
  - `const T& best() const` returns the largest item (only called when not empty).
  - `std::size_t count() const` returns how many items were added.

For example, after adding 4, 9 and 2 to a `RunningMax<int>`, `best()` is 9 and `count()` is 3. `count_above(std::vector<int>{3, 8, 5, 8}, 5)` is 2.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
std::size_t count_above(const std::vector<T>& items, const T& limit) {
    return 0;
}

template <typename T>
class RunningMax {
public:
    void add(const T& x) {}
    bool empty() const { return true; }
    const T& best() const { return *best_; }
    std::size_t count() const { return 0; }

private:
    std::optional<T> best_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
std::size_t count_above(const std::vector<T>& items, const T& limit) {
    std::size_t n = 0;
    for (const T& item : items) {
        if (limit < item) ++n;
    }
    return n;
}

template <typename T>
class RunningMax {
public:
    void add(const T& x) {
        if (!best_ || *best_ < x) best_ = x;   // a tie is not "less", so the earlier item stays
        ++count_;
    }
    bool empty() const { return !best_.has_value(); }
    const T& best() const { return *best_; }
    std::size_t count() const { return count_; }

private:
    std::optional<T> best_;
    std::size_t count_ = 0;
};
--- hint
`count_above` is a loop over the items that adds one whenever `limit < item`. Write the comparison that way round, so that only `<` is used.
--- hint
In `add`, replace the best when there is none yet (`!best_`) or when `*best_ < x`. A tie makes `*best_ < x` false, so the earlier item stays. Keep a separate count member for `count()`.
