+++ practice | A slot for one object
--- task
`std::optional<T>` keeps raw room for one `T` and builds the object only when a value arrives. Build a smaller version, `template <typename T> class Slot`:

- `Slot()` allocates raw room for **one** `T` with `std::allocator<T>().allocate(1)`. It holds no value yet.
- `~Slot()` destroys the value if there is one, then gives the room back.
- `void put(const T& x)` and `void put(T&& x)`: when the slot is empty, **construct** the value in the room (a copy of `x`, or `x` moved in). When it already holds a value, **assign** to that value instead. `s.put(s.get())` must work.
- `void reset()` destroys the value, if there is one; the slot is then empty.
- `bool has_value() const`, and `T& get()`, `const T& get() const` (only called when there is a value).
- Copying is deleted.

Keep the heap ledger and the `Probe` type as they are. `Probe` has no default constructor, and `Probe::live` says how many exist.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Slot {
public:
    Slot() {}
    Slot(const Slot&) = delete;
    Slot& operator=(const Slot&) = delete;

    void put(const T& x) {}
    void put(T&& x) {}
    void reset() {}
    bool has_value() const { return false; }
    T& get() { return *room_; }
    const T& get() const { return *room_; }

private:
    T* room_ = nullptr;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Slot {
public:
    Slot() : room_(std::allocator<T>().allocate(1)) {}

    ~Slot() {
        reset();
        std::allocator<T>().deallocate(room_, 1);
    }

    Slot(const Slot&) = delete;
    Slot& operator=(const Slot&) = delete;

    void put(const T& x) {
        if (full_) {
            *room_ = x;   // a living object: assign
        } else {
            std::construct_at(room_, x);   // raw room: construct
            full_ = true;
        }
    }

    void put(T&& x) {
        if (full_) {
            *room_ = std::move(x);
        } else {
            std::construct_at(room_, std::move(x));
            full_ = true;
        }
    }

    void reset() {
        if (full_) {
            std::destroy_at(room_);
            full_ = false;
        }
    }

    bool has_value() const { return full_; }
    T& get() { return *room_; }
    const T& get() const { return *room_; }

private:
    T* room_;
    bool full_ = false;
};
--- hint
Keep a `bool` that says whether the room holds a living object. `put` constructs with `std::construct_at(room_, x)` when it does not, and assigns with `*room_ = x` when it does. Assigning to yourself is safe, which is why `s.put(s.get())` works.
--- hint
`reset` calls `std::destroy_at(room_)` only when there is a value, and clears the flag. The destructor calls `reset()` and then `std::allocator<T>().deallocate(room_, 1)`.
--- check test | put builds one object; reset destroys it
[] { Probe::live = 0; Slot<Probe> s; bool empty = !s.has_value() && Probe::live == 0; s.put(Probe(5)); bool one = s.has_value() && s.get().id == 5 && Probe::live == 1; s.reset(); return empty && one && !s.has_value() && Probe::live == 0; }()
?? The constructor allocates room only; the object is built by put, with std::construct_at.
--- check test | A second put assigns instead of rebuilding
[] { Probe::live = 0; Slot<Probe> s; Probe a(1); Probe b(2); s.put(a); Probe::copies = 0; s.put(b); return Probe::live == 3 && Probe::copies == 1 && s.get().id == 2; }()
--- check test | s.put(s.get()) keeps the value
[] { Slot<std::string> s; s.put(std::string("telemetry frame header, long enough to be on the heap")); s.put(s.get()); return s.has_value() && s.get() == "telemetry frame header, long enough to be on the heap"; }()
--- check test | Moving in, and reset on an empty slot
[] { Slot<std::unique_ptr<int>> s; s.reset(); s.put(std::make_unique<int>(8)); s.put(std::make_unique<int>(9)); return s.has_value() && *s.get() == 9; }()
--- check test | The destructor destroys the value and frees the room
[] { Probe::live = 0; long long blocks = heap::live; { Slot<Probe> a; a.put(Probe(3)); Slot<Probe> b; Slot<std::string> c; c.put(std::string(100, 'z')); } return Probe::live == 0 && heap::live == blocks; }()

+++ practice | A sorted list that only needs <
--- task
A catalogue keeps star magnitudes, names and timestamps in sorted order. Write `template <typename T> class SortedList`, holding a `std::vector<T>` in ascending order, that compares items **only with `<`**, using binary search from DSA I:

- `std::size_t count_less(const T& x) const` returns how many items are less than `x`: the lower bound, the first index `i` where `items[i] < x` is false. At most about log₂ n + 1 comparisons.
- `void insert(const T& x)` puts `x` in its sorted place, **after** any items equal to it. Find the place by binary search (the first index `i` where `x < items[i]`), then use the vector's `insert`.
- `bool contains(const T& x) const` is `true` when some item is equal to `x`, meaning neither is less than the other. It uses `count_less` and then at most one more comparison.
- `const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const` and `std::size_t size() const`.

A check counts the comparisons: `contains` on 100,000 items may use at most 20.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
class SortedList {
public:
    std::size_t count_less(const T& x) const {
        std::size_t n = 0;
        for (const T& item : items_) {
            if (item < x) ++n;
        }
        return n;
    }
    void insert(const T& x) { items_.push_back(x); }
    bool contains(const T& x) const { return false; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return items_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return items_.size(); }

private:
    std::vector<T> items_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
class SortedList {
public:
    // The first index whose item is not less than x.
    std::size_t count_less(const T& x) const {
        std::size_t lo = 0;
        std::size_t hi = items_.size();
        while (lo < hi) {
            std::size_t mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            if (items_[mid] < x) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid;
        }
        return lo;
    }

    void insert(const T& x) {
        std::size_t lo = 0;
        std::size_t hi = items_.size();
        while (lo < hi) {   // the first index whose item is greater than x
            std::size_t mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            if (x < items_[mid]) hi = mid;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        }
        items_.insert(items_.begin() + lo, x);
    }

    bool contains(const T& x) const {
        std::size_t i = count_less(x);
        return i < items_.size() && !(x < items_[i]);   // items_[i] < x is already false
    }

    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return items_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return items_.size(); }

private:
    std::vector<T> items_;   // ascending
};
--- hint
`count_less` is DSA I's lower bound: keep `lo` and `hi` with the answer in `[lo, hi]`; look at `mid`; if `items_[mid] < x` the answer is after `mid`, otherwise it is `mid` or before. The upper bound for `insert` is the same loop with the test `x < items_[mid]`.
--- hint
At the lower bound `i`, you already know `items_[i] < x` is false. So `x` is there exactly when `i` is inside the vector and `x < items_[i]` is also false: one more comparison. Insert with `items_.insert(items_.begin() + i, x)`.
--- check case | Inserting out of order gives sorted order
[] { SortedList<int> s; for (int x : {5, 1, 4, 1, 9, 2}) s.insert(x); std::vector<int> out; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < s.size(); ++i) out.push_back(s[i]); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 9}
--- check test | count_less and contains, at the ends and in the middle
[] { SortedList<int> s; for (int x : {10, 20, 20, 30}) s.insert(x); return s.count_less(5) == 0 && s.count_less(20) == 1 && s.count_less(25) == 3 && s.count_less(99) == 4 && s.contains(20) && s.contains(10) && s.contains(30) && !s.contains(15) && !s.contains(40) && !s.contains(0); }()
--- check test | An empty list
[] { SortedList<std::string> s; return s.count_less("vega") == 0 && !s.contains("vega") && s.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Equal items: a new one goes after the old ones
[] { struct Obs { explicit Obs(int m, char t) : mag(m), tag(t) {} int mag; char tag; bool operator<(const Obs& o) const { return mag < o.mag; } }; SortedList<Obs> s; s.insert(Obs(3, 'a')); s.insert(Obs(1, 'b')); s.insert(Obs(3, 'c')); s.insert(Obs(3, 'd')); s.insert(Obs(2, 'e')); return s[0].tag == 'b' && s[1].tag == 'e' && s[2].tag == 'a' && s[3].tag == 'c' && s[4].tag == 'd'; }()
?? Insert at the first index whose item is greater than x, so equal items stay in arrival order.
--- check test | contains on 100,000 items uses at most 20 comparisons
[] { static long long cmp = 0; struct Key { int v; bool operator<(const Key& o) const { ++cmp; return v < o.v; } }; SortedList<Key> s; for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) s.insert(Key{2 * i}); cmp = 0; bool hit = s.contains(Key{123456}); long long c1 = cmp; cmp = 0; bool miss = s.contains(Key{123457}); return hit && !miss && c1 <= 20 && cmp <= 20; }()
?? A loop over every item makes 100,000 comparisons. Halve the range each step.

+++ practice | Insert and erase in raw memory
--- task
`template <typename T> class Deck` holds up to a fixed number of elements, in order, in raw memory allocated once by the constructor. The hard part is the boundary between living and raw slots: when a new element pushes the others right, the last one moves into a **raw** slot, which needs construction, while the others move into **living** slots, which need assignment.

- `explicit Deck(std::size_t capacity)`: raw room for `capacity` elements from `std::allocator<T>().allocate` (none when `capacity` is 0).
- `~Deck()` destroys the living elements and gives the room back. Copying is deleted.
- `bool insert(std::size_t pos, T x)` puts `x` at index `pos` (from 0 to `size()`), moving the elements from `pos` onwards one place right. Return `false`, changing nothing, when `pos` is too big or the deck is full.
- `bool erase(std::size_t pos)` removes the element at `pos` (below `size()`), moving the rest left, and destroys the element in the slot that becomes raw. Return `false` for a bad `pos`.
- `T& operator[](std::size_t i)`, `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`.

At every moment `Probe::live` must equal the number of `Probe`s really in the deck, plus any the check itself holds. Keep the heap ledger and `Probe` as they are.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Deck {
public:
    explicit Deck(std::size_t capacity) : cap_(capacity) {}
    Deck(const Deck&) = delete;
    Deck& operator=(const Deck&) = delete;

    bool insert(std::size_t pos, T x) { return false; }
    bool erase(std::size_t pos) { return false; }
    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }

private:
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Deck {
public:
    explicit Deck(std::size_t capacity)
        : data_(capacity ? std::allocator<T>().allocate(capacity) : nullptr), cap_(capacity) {}

    ~Deck() {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
        if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
    }

    Deck(const Deck&) = delete;
    Deck& operator=(const Deck&) = delete;

    bool insert(std::size_t pos, T x) {
        if (pos > size_ || size_ == cap_) return false;
        if (pos == size_) {
            std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(x));   // straight into the raw slot
        } else {
            std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(data_[size_ - 1]));   // raw slot: construct
            for (std::size_t i = size_ - 1; i > pos; --i) data_[i] = std::move(data_[i - 1]);   // living: assign
            data_[pos] = std::move(x);
        }
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool erase(std::size_t pos) {
        if (pos >= size_) return false;
        for (std::size_t i = pos; i + 1 < size_; ++i) data_[i] = std::move(data_[i + 1]);
        --size_;
        std::destroy_at(data_ + size_);   // this slot is raw again
        return true;
    }

    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }

private:
    T* data_;               // [0, size_) alive, [size_, cap_) raw
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_;
};
--- hint
Inserting at `pos == size()` is the easy case: construct `x` straight into the raw slot `size_`. Otherwise, first move-**construct** the last element into the raw slot: `std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(data_[size_ - 1]))`.
--- hint
Then move-**assign** the others one place right, walking down from `size_ - 1` to `pos + 1`, and move-assign `x` into `data_[pos]`. For `erase`, move-assign left from `pos`, then `--size_` and `std::destroy_at(data_ + size_)`.
--- check case | Insert at the end, the front and the middle

=> std::vector<int>{10, 20, 30, 40}
--- check test | The number of living Probes always matches
[] { Probe::live = 0; Deck<Probe> d(10); for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) d.insert(0, Probe(i)); bool a = Probe::live == 5; d.insert(2, Probe(99)); bool b = Probe::live == 6 && d[2].id == 99; d.erase(0); d.erase(4); bool c = Probe::live == 4 && d.size() == 4; return a && b && c; }()
?? The slot at size() is raw: move the last element there with std::construct_at, not with =.
--- check test | A full deck and a bad position are refused
[] { Probe::live = 0; Deck<Probe> d(2); bool a = !d.insert(1, Probe(1)); d.insert(0, Probe(1)); d.insert(0, Probe(2)); bool b = !d.insert(1, Probe(3)); bool c = !d.erase(2); return a && b && c && d.size() == 2 && Probe::live == 2 && d[0].id == 2; }()
--- check test | Erasing everything, then a capacity-0 deck
[] { Probe::live = 0; Deck<Probe> d(3); for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) d.insert(d.size(), Probe(i)); d.erase(1); d.erase(0); d.erase(0); Deck<Probe> z(0); bool refused = !z.insert(0, Probe(1)); return d.size() == 0 && Probe::live == 0 && !d.erase(0) && refused; }()
--- check test | Strings: the destructor frees everything
[] { long long blocks = heap::live; { Deck<std::string> d(6); d.insert(0, std::string(50, 'a')); d.insert(0, std::string(50, 'b')); d.insert(1, std::string(50, 'c')); d.erase(2); if (d[0][0] != 'b' || d[1][0] != 'c' || d.size() != 2) return false; } return heap::live == blocks; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the stack that never lets go
--- task
`template <typename T> class Stack` keeps its elements in raw memory, with `push`, `pop`, `top` and `size`. Pushing and reading work, and the memory is always given back. But objects that have been popped are never destroyed: after pushing three `Probe`s and popping two, `Probe::live` is still 3, and a stack of strings leaks every popped string's buffer.

Find the bug and fix it. It is one missing line.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Stack {
public:
    Stack() = default;
    ~Stack() {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
        if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
    }
    Stack(const Stack&) = delete;
    Stack& operator=(const Stack&) = delete;

    void push(T x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) {
            std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 4 : 2 * cap_;
            T* fresh = std::allocator<T>().allocate(new_cap);
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) {
                std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]));
                std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
            }
            if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
            data_ = fresh;
            cap_ = new_cap;
        }
        std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(x));
        ++size_;
    }

    void pop() {
        if (size_ == 0) return;
        --size_;
    }

    T& top() { return data_[size_ - 1]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Stack {
public:
    Stack() = default;
    ~Stack() {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
        if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
    }
    Stack(const Stack&) = delete;
    Stack& operator=(const Stack&) = delete;

    void push(T x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) {
            std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 4 : 2 * cap_;
            T* fresh = std::allocator<T>().allocate(new_cap);
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) {
                std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]));
                std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
            }
            if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
            data_ = fresh;
            cap_ = new_cap;
        }
        std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(x));
        ++size_;
    }

    void pop() {
        if (size_ == 0) return;
        --size_;
        std::destroy_at(data_ + size_);
    }

    T& top() { return data_[size_ - 1]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
The destructor only destroys the slots below `size_`. After `pop` lowers `size_`, who will ever destroy the object that was on top?
--- hint
`pop` must end the popped object's life at once: after `--size_`, call `std::destroy_at(data_ + size_)`.
--- check test | Popping destroys at once
[] { Probe::live = 0; Stack<Probe> s; s.push(Probe(1)); s.push(Probe(2)); s.push(Probe(3)); s.pop(); s.pop(); return Probe::live == 1 && s.size() == 1 && s.top().id == 1; }()
?? When a slot leaves the living range, its object must be destroyed.
--- check test | Pop on an empty stack does nothing
[] { Probe::live = 0; Stack<Probe> s; s.pop(); s.push(Probe(4)); s.pop(); s.pop(); return Probe::live == 0 && s.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Popped strings do not leak
[] { long long blocks = heap::live; { Stack<std::string> s; for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) s.push(std::string(64, 'q')); for (int i = 0; i < 15; ++i) s.pop(); if (s.size() != 5) return false; } return heap::live == blocks; }()
--- check test | Push after pop reuses the slot
[] { Probe::live = 0; Stack<Probe> s; for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) s.push(Probe(i)); s.pop(); s.push(Probe(40)); return Probe::live == 4 && s.top().id == 40 && s.size() == 4; }()

+++ practice | An object pool for telemetry packets
--- task
Flight software often forbids allocating memory once the mission is running. Instead, a **pool** allocates raw room for a fixed number of objects at start-up, and builds and destroys objects in those slots as they come and go.

Write `template <typename T> class Pool`:

- `explicit Pool(std::size_t capacity)`: raw room for `capacity` objects from `std::allocator<T>().allocate` (none when 0), with every slot free. Copying is deleted.
- `int acquire(const T& x)` builds a copy of `x` in a free slot and returns the slot's number, or returns `-1` when no slot is free. Free slots are reused **last freed, first used**; at the start, slots come out as 0, 1, 2, …
- `bool release(int slot)` destroys the object in that slot and frees it. Return `false`, changing nothing, when the slot number is out of range or the slot is already free.
- `T& get(int slot)`, `bool in_use(int slot) const` (`false` for any out-of-range number), `std::size_t used() const`.
- `~Pool()` destroys the objects still in use, and only those, then gives the room back.

Keep the free slot numbers in a `std::vector<int>` used as a stack, and which slots are in use in a `std::vector<bool>`. Keep the heap ledger and `Probe` as they are.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Pool {
public:
    explicit Pool(std::size_t capacity) {}
    Pool(const Pool&) = delete;
    Pool& operator=(const Pool&) = delete;

    int acquire(const T& x) { return -1; }
    bool release(int slot) { return false; }
    T& get(int slot) { return room_[slot]; }
    bool in_use(int slot) const { return false; }
    std::size_t used() const { return 0; }

private:
    T* room_ = nullptr;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// Given: an element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T>
class Pool {
public:
    explicit Pool(std::size_t capacity)
        : room_(capacity ? std::allocator<T>().allocate(capacity) : nullptr), cap_(capacity), in_use_(capacity, false) {
        for (std::size_t i = capacity; i > 0; --i) free_.push_back(static_cast<int>(i - 1));   // slot 0 on top
    }

    ~Pool() {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < cap_; ++i) {
            if (in_use_[i]) std::destroy_at(room_ + i);
        }
        if (room_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(room_, cap_);
    }

    Pool(const Pool&) = delete;
    Pool& operator=(const Pool&) = delete;

    int acquire(const T& x) {
        if (free_.empty()) return -1;
        int slot = free_.back();
        free_.pop_back();
        std::construct_at(room_ + slot, x);
        in_use_[slot] = true;
        return slot;
    }

    bool release(int slot) {
        if (!in_use(slot)) return false;
        std::destroy_at(room_ + slot);
        in_use_[slot] = false;
        free_.push_back(slot);
        return true;
    }

    T& get(int slot) { return room_[slot]; }

    bool in_use(int slot) const {
        return slot >= 0 && static_cast<std::size_t>(slot) < cap_ && in_use_[slot];
    }

    std::size_t used() const { return cap_ - free_.size(); }

private:
    T* room_;
    std::size_t cap_;
    std::vector<bool> in_use_;
    std::vector<int> free_;   // free slot numbers; the back is used next
};
--- hint
Fill the free stack in the constructor so that slot 0 is on top: push `capacity - 1`, then `capacity - 2`, down to 0. `acquire` takes the back of the stack, constructs the copy in that slot, and marks it in use; `release` destroys, unmarks, and pushes the slot number back.
--- hint
`in_use` must check the range first (`slot >= 0` and below the capacity) before it looks in the `std::vector<bool>`, so that `release(-1)` or `release(100)` returns `false` safely. The destructor walks every slot and destroys only the ones marked in use.
--- check case | Slots come out 0, 1, 2, and the last freed is reused first
[] { Pool<Probe> p(4); std::vector<int> got; got.push_back(p.acquire(Probe(10))); got.push_back(p.acquire(Probe(11))); got.push_back(p.acquire(Probe(12))); p.release(0); p.release(2); got.push_back(p.acquire(Probe(13))); got.push_back(p.acquire(Probe(14))); got.push_back(p.acquire(Probe(15))); got.push_back(p.acquire(Probe(16))); return got; }()
=> std::vector<int>{0, 1, 2, 2, 0, 3, -1}
--- check test | Objects are built on acquire and destroyed on release
[] { Probe::live = 0; Pool<Probe> p(3); int a = p.acquire(Probe(1)); int b = p.acquire(Probe(2)); bool two = Probe::live == 2 && p.used() == 2 && p.get(b).id == 2; p.release(a); return two && Probe::live == 1 && p.used() == 1 && !p.in_use(a) && p.in_use(b); }()
?? The pool's constructor allocates raw room only. Construct on acquire, destroy on release.
--- check test | Bad and double releases are refused
[] { Probe::live = 0; Pool<Probe> p(2); int a = p.acquire(Probe(5)); bool first = p.release(a); bool again = !p.release(a); bool neg = !p.release(-1); bool big = !p.release(2); return first && again && neg && big && Probe::live == 0 && p.used() == 0 && !p.in_use(7) && !p.in_use(-3); }()
--- check test | The destructor destroys only the objects still in use
[] { Probe::live = 0; long long blocks = heap::live; { Pool<Probe> p(5); for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) p.acquire(Probe(i)); p.release(1); p.release(3); if (Probe::live != 3) return false; } return Probe::live == 0 && heap::live == blocks; }()
--- check test | A capacity-0 pool, and strings
[] { long long blocks = heap::live; bool ok; { Pool<int> z(0); Pool<std::string> s(2); int a = s.acquire(std::string(80, 'k')); int b = s.acquire(std::string(80, 'm')); s.release(a); int c = s.acquire(std::string(80, 'n')); ok = z.acquire(1) == -1 && c == a && s.get(b)[0] == 'm' && s.get(c)[0] == 'n'; } return ok && heap::live == blocks; }()

+++ question | Why the template lives in the header
--- ask
A team puts `template <typename T> class Vector { void push_back(const T& x); … };` in `vector.h`, and the body of `push_back` in `vector.cpp`. `main.cpp` includes `vector.h` and calls `push_back` on a `Vector<int>`. What happens?
--- choice
It works: the linker finds `push_back` in `vector.o`.
--- choice correct
The linker reports an undefined reference: `vector.cpp` never used `Vector<int>`, so no `Vector<int>::push_back` was ever made, and `main.cpp` could not make it without the body.
--- choice
The compiler rejects `vector.h`, because templates cannot declare member functions without bodies.
--- choice
It works, but more slowly, because the template is instantiated at run time.
--- why
Templates are instantiated at compile time, in the file that uses them, and only if the full definition is visible there. `main.cpp` sees only a declaration, so it emits a call and expects someone else to provide `Vector<int>::push_back`. `vector.cpp` has the body but never uses `Vector<int>`, so it makes nothing. Putting the definitions in the header fixes it.

+++ question | Assigning into raw memory
--- ask
Growth in a vector of strings allocates `fresh` with `std::allocator<std::string>().allocate(new_cap)` and then runs `fresh[i] = std::move(data_[i]);` for each element. Why is that wrong?
--- choice
It copies instead of moving.
--- choice
It leaks the old strings.
--- choice correct
`fresh[i]` is raw memory, not a string. Assignment is a member function of a living object, so it reads garbage as if it were a string's old buffer; the slot needs `std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]))`.
--- choice
Nothing: for strings, assigning and constructing do the same thing.
--- why
Construction starts an object's lifetime in raw memory. Assignment replaces the value of an object that is already alive, and a string's move assignment first frees its old buffer, which here is a garbage pointer. Raw slots get `construct_at`; living slots get `=`.

+++ question | A vector of unique_ptr
--- ask
`Vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> v;` compiles, and `push_back(std::make_unique<int>(3))` works, even though your `Vector` has a copy constructor that copies every element, and a `unique_ptr` cannot be copied. Why?
--- choice
The compiler quietly turns the copy constructor into a move constructor for move-only types.
--- choice correct
A member function of a class template is only instantiated if it is used. As long as nobody copies the vector, its copy constructor is never compiled for `std::unique_ptr<int>`.
--- choice
`std::unique_ptr` has a hidden copy constructor that the vector can use.
--- choice
Templates are checked only at run time, when the copy actually happens.
--- why
Instantiation is lazy: the compiler generates `Vector<std::unique_ptr<int>>::Vector(const Vector&)` only when some code needs it. Write `auto w = v;` and compilation fails at that line. This is what lets one container template serve both copyable and move-only element types.

=== dsacpp-04 | Iterators: making Vector<T> work with range-for and <algorithm>
--- teach
Your `Vector<T>` now stores anything, and gets every lifetime right. But try to use it like a standard container and it falls flat: `for (int x : v)` does not compile, and neither does `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())`. The missing piece is the **iterator**, the small type that lets any algorithm walk any container. This lesson explains what the library expects from an iterator, then gives `Vector<T>` iterators good enough for `std::sort`.

### Positions, not indexes

An index only means something to a container that has positions 0, 1, 2… A linked list has none. An **iterator** is a more general idea: an object that marks a position in a sequence. Three operations are enough to walk one:

- `*it` is the element at that position;
- `++it` moves to the next position;
- `it != last` asks whether two positions differ.

A pointer into an array does all three, which is no accident: iterators were designed as a generalisation of pointers.

A sequence is given as two iterators, `[first, last)`: `first` marks the first element, and `last` marks the position **one past** the last element. You met this [[half-open range|half-open]] in the intermediate course. It makes the empty sequence simply `first == last`, the length `last - first`, and every loop the same shape: keep going while `it != last`.

### What range-for really does

The compiler turns `for (auto x : v) { … }` into roughly this:

```cpp fragment
{
    auto first = v.begin();
    auto last = v.end();
    for (; first != last; ++first) {
        auto x = *first;
        // … the loop body …
    }
}
```

So a type works with range-for as soon as it has `begin()` and `end()` member functions returning something with `!=`, prefix `++` and `*`. Nothing more.

### A pointer is already an iterator

For elements stored side by side, a plain pointer does the job. Here a fixed shelf of four readings hands out pointers, and both range-for and `std::sort` accept them:

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>

class Shelf {
public:
    double* begin() { return slots_; }
    double* end() { return slots_ + 4; }   // one past the last slot
private:
    double slots_[4] = {7.5, 2.0, 9.25, 4.0};
};

int main() {
    Shelf s;
    std::sort(s.begin(), s.end());
    for (double x : s) std::cout << x << " ";   // 2 4 7.5 9.25
    std::cout << "\n";
}
```

The standard library's own vector iterators are usually a small class wrapped around a pointer instead. A class is a distinct type, so a vector's iterator cannot be mixed up with some unrelated pointer, and debug builds can add checks inside its operators. Writing that class is this lesson's job, and it teaches what every iterator must provide.

### Five categories

Not every sequence can do everything a pointer can. A singly linked list can step forward but not back; a stream of packets from a radio can be read only once. So iterators come in **categories**, each adding operations to the one before:

| category | adds | example | an algorithm that needs it |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | `*it` to read, `++it`, `==`; one pass only | reading from `std::cin` | `std::find`, `std::accumulate` |
| forward | several passes over the same data | singly linked list | `std::replace`, `std::adjacent_find` |
| bidirectional | `--it` | doubly linked list, `std::map` | `std::reverse` |
| random access | `it + n`, `it - n`, `it[n]`, `b - a`, `<`, all in O(1) | `std::deque` | `std::sort`, `std::nth_element` |
| contiguous | the elements are side by side in memory | `std::vector`, arrays | anything that hands the data to C code |

An algorithm states the weakest category it needs, and that decides which containers it works with. `std::sort` needs random access, because it jumps to the middle of a range in O(1); that is why it cannot sort a `std::list`, which has its own `sort` member instead.

### How an algorithm learns the category

An iterator class announces its category, and some facts about itself, with five member types. `std::iterator_traits<It>` reads them, and the algorithms read `std::iterator_traits`:

```cpp fragment
using iterator_category = std::random_access_iterator_tag;   // which category
using value_type = double;                // the element type, without const
using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;   // what b - a returns: a signed count
using pointer = double*;                  // what operator-> returns
using reference = double&;                // what operator* returns
```

The category is a **[[tag|tags]]**: an empty struct whose only job is to be a distinct type. `std::ptrdiff_t`, from `<cstddef>`, is the signed type for the distance between two positions. C++20 also names each category as a **concept** in `<iterator>`, so you can ask the compiler directly:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <list>

int main() {
    std::cout << std::random_access_iterator<int*> << "\n";                     // 1
    std::cout << std::random_access_iterator<std::list<int>::iterator> << "\n"; // 0
    std::cout << std::bidirectional_iterator<std::list<int>::iterator> << "\n"; // 1
}
```

### The operators, one by one

An iterator class overloads operators, the same way `operator[]` did in the first lesson. Here they are for a different iterator: one that walks every `k`-th element of an array, such as one channel out of interleaved sensor data.

- `operator*` returns a reference to the element, so `*it = 5` writes through it. `operator->` returns a pointer, so `it->label` reaches a member.

```cpp fragment
double& operator*() const { return *p_; }
double* operator->() const { return p_; }
```

- **Prefix** `++it` moves on and returns the iterator itself, by reference. **Postfix** `it++` returns a copy of the *old* position. C++ tells the two apart by a dummy `int` parameter that the postfix version takes and never uses:

```cpp fragment
Stride& operator++() { p_ += k_; return *this; }                    // ++it
Stride operator++(int) { Stride old = *this; p_ += k_; return old; }  // it++
```

Postfix makes a copy, which is why loops in C++ are usually written with `++it`.

- **Comparisons.** In C++20, one defaulted line gives `==` and `!=`, and another gives `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Both compare the members in order:

```cpp fragment
bool operator==(const Stride&) const = default;
auto operator<=>(const Stride&) const = default;
```

`<=>` is the **[[three-way comparison|spaceship]]** operator. The compiler rewrites `a < b` as `(a <=> b) < 0`.

- **Arithmetic** for random access: `it += n` returns the iterator by reference, `it + n` and `it - n` return new iterators, and `b - a` returns the `difference_type` between them. `n + it` has an `int` on the left, so it cannot be a member function; it is written inside the class as a `friend`, a free function that can see the private members:

```cpp fragment
friend Stride operator+(std::ptrdiff_t n, Stride it) { return it += n; }
```

### const_iterator

Walking a `const Vector` must not allow writing to it. So a container has two iterator types: `iterator`, whose `*` returns `T&`, and `const_iterator`, whose `*` returns `const T&`. The container gives `begin()` and `end()` a `const` overload returning `const_iterator`, and `cbegin()` and `cend()` always return one.

The two classes are identical apart from that `const`. So write the class once, as a template over the element type it points at, and use it twice:

```cpp fragment
template <typename U>        // U is T, or const T
class Iter { /* … U* p_; … */ };

using iterator = Iter<T>;
using const_iterator = Iter<const T>;
```

Inside, `value_type` must be the element type *without* `const`: `std::remove_const_t<U>`, from `<type_traits>`, removes it.

An `iterator` should convert to a `const_iterator` (you may always look where you could write), but never the other way (that would let a `const` container be changed). A **conversion operator**, a member function named `operator Iter<const U>()`, says how to turn one type into another. Only the one direction is written, so only that one works.

### Why it is correct

An algorithm like `std::sort` is proved correct once, in terms of what iterators promise, not of any particular container. The promises for a random-access iterator into a range `[first, last)` are:

1. `++it` moves to the next element, and `last` is reached from `first` after exactly `last - first` steps.
2. `it + n` is the position `n` steps of `++` away, and `(it + n) - it == n`.
3. `a < b` exactly when `b` can be reached from `a` by steps of `++`.
4. `*it` is the element at that position, and `it[n]` is `*(it + n)`.

`Iter` holds a pointer into the vector's array, where slots `0` to `size() - 1` hold the elements, and `end()` points one past the last. Each operator does the matching thing to the pointer: `++` adds one, `+ n` adds `n`, `-` subtracts, `<=>` compares addresses. Pointer arithmetic within one array satisfies all four promises, so `Iter` does too, and every proof that assumes them, `std::sort`'s included, applies to `Vector<T>`.

Two limits come with it. The promises only hold between iterators into the same vector, so comparing iterators from two different containers is undefined behaviour. And an iterator holds a raw address, so it is invalidated exactly as lesson 2 described: a push_back that grows frees the array it points into.

### What it costs

Every operation is one pointer operation: O(1). Compiled with optimisation, the class produces the same machine code as a raw pointer. C++ calls this a **[[zero-cost abstraction|zero-cost]]**: you pay nothing at run time for the safety and the clear types. With these iterators, `std::sort` on a `Vector<T>` is O(n log n), and `std::lower_bound` O(log n).

### Where it is used

- Every algorithm in `<algorithm>` and `<numeric>` takes iterators, which is why about a hundred algorithms work with every container: the design Alexander Stepanov set out for the [[Standard Template Library|stepanov]].
- C++20 ranges and views, such as `std::views::filter`, are built on the same iterator concepts.
- `std::istream_iterator` reads numbers from a stream one by one, as an input iterator, so `std::accumulate` can sum a file of telemetry without loading it all.

**Watch out:**

- `end()` is one **past** the last element. `*v.end()` is undefined behaviour, and an `end()` that returns the last element makes every loop skip it.
- Postfix `++` must return the **old** position. Returning the new one breaks `*it++`, a pattern the library itself uses.
- Forgetting the `const` overloads of `begin()` and `end()`: then a `const Vector&` cannot be looped over at all.
- Missing member types. `std::sort` then fails with a long error from inside `<algorithm>`, far from your code.
- Keeping an iterator across a `push_back` that may grow the vector.

::: context half-open Why one past the end
In 1982 Edsger Dijkstra wrote a short note arguing that a range of numbers is best written as "first included, last excluded": the length is `last - first`, two ranges that meet share the boundary with no gap and no overlap, and the empty range needs no special value. C++ iterators follow the same rule. The one-past-the-end position is always a valid address to compute and compare in C++, even though nothing lives there, precisely so that `end()` can exist.
:::

::: context tags Types used as labels
`std::random_access_iterator_tag` is an empty struct that inherits from `std::bidirectional_iterator_tag`, which inherits from `std::forward_iterator_tag`, and so on down to input. Before concepts, algorithms chose their fastest version by overloading on the tag. `std::advance(it, n)` calls one helper for random-access tags, which does `it += n` in O(1), and another for the rest, which loops `n` times. Inheritance makes a random-access iterator acceptable wherever a weaker one is.
:::

::: context spaceship Three answers in one
`a <=> b` answers less, equal or greater in one call, instead of making each of `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` a separate function to write and keep consistent. Its result is compared with 0: `(a <=> b) < 0` means `a` is less. When it is defaulted, the compiler compares the members one after another, like words in a dictionary, stopping at the first difference. The operator arrived in C++20, and was nicknamed after its shape.
:::

::: context zero-cost What you do not use, you do not pay for
Bjarne Stroustrup puts it this way: what you do not use, you do not pay for, and what you do use, you could not hand-code any better. A tiny class whose members are all inline disappears when the compiler optimises: `++it` on an iterator wrapping a pointer becomes the same single add instruction as `++p`. That is why C++ can offer safe types and clear names without slowing down the inner loops that flight software and games depend on.
:::

::: context stepanov One algorithm for every container
Before the STL, a library with 10 algorithms and 5 containers needed 50 functions. Alexander Stepanov's idea, developed with Meng Lee at Hewlett-Packard and accepted into C++ in 1994, was to write each algorithm once, against iterators, and to give each container iterators: 10 plus 5 pieces instead of 10 times 5. He also insisted that each algorithm's cost be part of its specification, which is why the standard promises complexities such as O(n log n) comparisons for `std::sort`.
:::
--- task
The starter holds a working `Vector<T>` from the last lesson (growth and lifetimes are done). Give it iterators. No `main`.

- Inside `Vector<T>`, write a class template `template <typename U> class Iter` that wraps a `U*`. It is used twice: `using iterator = Iter<T>;` and `using const_iterator = Iter<const T>;`.
- `Iter` is a **random-access** iterator. It has the five member types (`iterator_category` is `std::random_access_iterator_tag`, `value_type` is `std::remove_const_t<U>`, `difference_type` is `std::ptrdiff_t`, `pointer` is `U*`, `reference` is `U&`), a default constructor, and these operators: `*`, `->`, `[]`, prefix and postfix `++` and `--`, `+=`, `-=`, `it + n`, `n + it`, `it - n`, `it - it`, and all six comparisons.
- An `iterator` converts to a `const_iterator`; a `const_iterator` must not convert to an `iterator`.
- `Vector<T>` gets `iterator begin()`, `iterator end()`, `const_iterator begin() const`, `const_iterator end() const`, `const_iterator cbegin() const` and `const_iterator cend() const`. `end()` is one past the last element.

The checks use range-for, `std::find`, `std::sort`, `std::reverse`, `std::lower_bound` and the C++20 concept `std::random_access_iterator`.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <typename T>
class Vector {
public:
    Vector() = default;
    ~Vector() {
        clear();
        if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
    }
    Vector(const Vector&) = delete;
    Vector& operator=(const Vector&) = delete;

    void push_back(const T& x) { T copy(x); push_back(std::move(copy)); }
    void push_back(T&& x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) {
            std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_;
            T* fresh = std::allocator<T>().allocate(new_cap);
            std::construct_at(fresh + size_, std::move(x));
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) {
                std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]));
                std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
            }
            if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
            data_ = fresh;
            cap_ = new_cap;
        } else {
            std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(x));
        }
        ++size_;
    }
    void clear() {
        while (size_ > 0) std::destroy_at(data_ + --size_);
    }

    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    // Write Iter, iterator, const_iterator, begin, end, cbegin and cend.

private:
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>
#include <utility>

template <typename T>
class Vector {
public:
    Vector() = default;
    ~Vector() {
        clear();
        if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
    }
    Vector(const Vector&) = delete;
    Vector& operator=(const Vector&) = delete;

    void push_back(const T& x) { T copy(x); push_back(std::move(copy)); }
    void push_back(T&& x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) {
            std::size_t new_cap = cap_ == 0 ? 1 : 2 * cap_;
            T* fresh = std::allocator<T>().allocate(new_cap);
            std::construct_at(fresh + size_, std::move(x));
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) {
                std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]));
                std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
            }
            if (data_) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
            data_ = fresh;
            cap_ = new_cap;
        } else {
            std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(x));
        }
        ++size_;
    }
    void clear() {
        while (size_ > 0) std::destroy_at(data_ + --size_);
    }

    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    template <typename U>   // U is T or const T
    class Iter {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::random_access_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = std::remove_const_t<U>;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = U*;
        using reference = U&;

        Iter() = default;
        explicit Iter(U* p) : p_(p) {}

        // iterator -> const_iterator; no conversion is written for the other way
        operator Iter<const U>() const { return Iter<const U>(p_); }

        reference operator*() const { return *p_; }
        pointer operator->() const { return p_; }
        reference operator[](difference_type n) const { return p_[n]; }

        Iter& operator++() { ++p_; return *this; }
        Iter operator++(int) { Iter old = *this; ++p_; return old; }
        Iter& operator--() { --p_; return *this; }
        Iter operator--(int) { Iter old = *this; --p_; return old; }

        Iter& operator+=(difference_type n) { p_ += n; return *this; }
        Iter& operator-=(difference_type n) { p_ -= n; return *this; }
        Iter operator+(difference_type n) const { return Iter(p_ + n); }
        Iter operator-(difference_type n) const { return Iter(p_ - n); }
        difference_type operator-(const Iter& other) const { return p_ - other.p_; }
        friend Iter operator+(difference_type n, const Iter& it) { return it + n; }

        bool operator==(const Iter&) const = default;
        auto operator<=>(const Iter&) const = default;

    private:
        U* p_ = nullptr;
    };

    using iterator = Iter<T>;
    using const_iterator = Iter<const T>;

    iterator begin() { return iterator(data_); }
    iterator end() { return iterator(data_ + size_); }
    const_iterator begin() const { return const_iterator(data_); }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(data_ + size_); }
    const_iterator cbegin() const { return begin(); }
    const_iterator cend() const { return end(); }

private:
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Start with what range-for needs: in `Iter`, a constructor from `U*`, `operator*`, prefix `operator++` and `operator==` (defaulted). Then `begin()` returns `iterator(data_)` and `end()` returns `iterator(data_ + size_)`. Add the five member types next; `std::sort` reads them.
--- hint
Each remaining operator is one pointer operation: `+=` adds to the pointer and returns `*this`; `it + n` returns `Iter(p_ + n)`; `it - it` returns the difference of the two pointers. `n + it` goes inside the class as `friend Iter operator+(difference_type n, const Iter& it)`. Postfix `++` copies `*this`, increments, and returns the copy. `auto operator<=>(const Iter&) const = default;` gives the four ordering comparisons.
--- hint
The conversion to `const_iterator` is a member `operator Iter<const U>() const { return Iter<const U>(p_); }`. The `const` overloads `begin() const` and `end() const` return `const_iterator`, and `cbegin` and `cend` call them.

+++ practice | A range of numbers you can loop over
--- task
Python's `range(first, last, step)` produces numbers without storing them. Write `class IntRange` that does the same in C++, with a **forward iterator** that computes each value as it goes. Use `long long` for every value.

- `IntRange(long long first, long long last, long long step)`: the numbers `first`, `first + step`, `first + 2·step`, … that are below `last`. `step` is always positive. When `last <= first`, the range is empty.
- `long long size() const`: how many numbers there are. For example `IntRange(0, 10, 3)` holds 0, 3, 6, 9, so its size is 4. It must be computed, not counted, because ranges can hold billions of numbers.
- A nested `class iterator` with the member types (`iterator_category` is `std::forward_iterator_tag`, `value_type` is `long long`, `difference_type` is `std::ptrdiff_t`, `pointer` is `const long long*`, and `reference` is `long long`, because values are computed and returned by value), a default constructor, `operator*`, prefix and postfix `++`, and `==`.
- `iterator begin() const` and `iterator end() const`. `end()` must be exactly the position the iterator reaches after `size()` steps, so that loops stop even when `step` does not divide `last - first`.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>

class IntRange {
public:
    class iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = long long;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const long long*;
        using reference = long long;

        iterator() = default;
        iterator(long long value, long long step) : value_(value), step_(step) {}
        long long operator*() const { return 0; }
        iterator& operator++() { return *this; }
        iterator operator++(int) { return *this; }
        bool operator==(const iterator&) const = default;

    private:
        long long value_ = 0;
        long long step_ = 1;
    };

    IntRange(long long first, long long last, long long step) : first_(first), last_(last), step_(step) {}
    long long size() const { return 0; }
    iterator begin() const { return iterator(first_, step_); }
    iterator end() const { return iterator(first_, step_); }

private:
    long long first_;
    long long last_;
    long long step_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>

class IntRange {
public:
    class iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = long long;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const long long*;
        using reference = long long;

        iterator() = default;
        iterator(long long value, long long step) : value_(value), step_(step) {}
        long long operator*() const { return value_; }
        iterator& operator++() { value_ += step_; return *this; }
        iterator operator++(int) { iterator old = *this; value_ += step_; return old; }
        bool operator==(const iterator&) const = default;

    private:
        long long value_ = 0;
        long long step_ = 1;
    };

    IntRange(long long first, long long last, long long step) : first_(first), last_(last), step_(step) {}

    long long size() const {
        if (last_ <= first_) return 0;
        return (last_ - first_ + step_ - 1) / step_;   // rounded up
    }

    iterator begin() const { return iterator(first_, step_); }
    iterator end() const { return iterator(first_ + size() * step_, step_); }   // after size() steps

private:
    long long first_;
    long long last_;
    long long step_;
};
--- hint
The iterator holds the current value and the step. `*` returns the value, prefix `++` adds the step and returns `*this`, and postfix `++` copies `*this` first and returns the copy.
--- hint
The size is the number of steps that stay below `last`: `(last - first + step - 1) / step`, which rounds up, or 0 when `last <= first`. Then `end()` is the iterator at `first + size() * step`. Using `last` itself would never be reached when the step does not divide the gap, and the loop would never stop.
--- check case | IntRange(0, 10, 3) holds 0, 3, 6, 9
[] { std::vector<long long> out; for (long long x : IntRange(0, 10, 3)) out.push_back(x); return out; }()
=> std::vector<long long>{0, 3, 6, 9}
?? end() must be where the iterator lands after size() steps: 12 here, not 10.

--- check test | Postfix returns the old value
[] { IntRange r(100, 200, 25); auto it = r.begin(); long long a = *it++; long long b = *it; long long c = *++it; return a == 100 && b == 125 && c == 150; }()
--- check test | It is a forward iterator, and std::distance agrees with size()

+++ practice | Walking backwards
--- task
`std::reverse_iterator` turns any bidirectional iterator around. Build your own, `template <typename It> class Reverse`, to see the trick it uses.

A reverse iterator stores a normal iterator called its **base**, and always stands one place *after* the element it refers to. So `Reverse(v.end())` refers to the last element, and `Reverse(v.begin())` is the end of the reversed range. That offset keeps everything half-open, with no position before the first element needed.

- `explicit Reverse(It base)`, a default constructor, and `It base() const`.
- `operator*` returns the element just before the base: copy the base, step the copy back once with `--`, and return `*copy`.
- Prefix and postfix `++` step the base **back**; prefix and postfix `--` step it **forward**.
- `==` compares the bases.
- The member types: `iterator_category` is `std::bidirectional_iterator_tag`, and the other four come from the base iterator's traits, for example `using value_type = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::value_type;`. Inside a template, a type name that depends on a template parameter needs the word `typename` in front, as there.

Also write `template <typename It> Reverse<It> make_reverse(It it)`, which returns `Reverse<It>(it)`, so callers need not spell out the type.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <list>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename It>
class Reverse {
public:
    using iterator_category = std::bidirectional_iterator_tag;
    using value_type = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::value_type;
    using difference_type = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::difference_type;
    using pointer = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::pointer;
    using reference = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::reference;

    Reverse() = default;
    explicit Reverse(It base) : base_(base) {}
    It base() const { return base_; }

    // Write *, prefix and postfix ++ and --, and ==.

private:
    It base_{};
};

// Write make_reverse.
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <list>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename It>
class Reverse {
public:
    using iterator_category = std::bidirectional_iterator_tag;
    using value_type = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::value_type;
    using difference_type = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::difference_type;
    using pointer = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::pointer;
    using reference = typename std::iterator_traits<It>::reference;

    Reverse() = default;
    explicit Reverse(It base) : base_(base) {}
    It base() const { return base_; }

    reference operator*() const {
        It before = base_;
        --before;   // a reverse iterator refers to the element just before its base
        return *before;
    }

    Reverse& operator++() { --base_; return *this; }
    Reverse operator++(int) { Reverse old = *this; --base_; return old; }
    Reverse& operator--() { ++base_; return *this; }
    Reverse operator--(int) { Reverse old = *this; ++base_; return old; }
    bool operator==(const Reverse&) const = default;

private:
    It base_{};
};

template <typename It>
Reverse<It> make_reverse(It it) {
    return Reverse<It>(it);
}
--- hint
Every operator is one step on the base, in the opposite direction: `++` on a reverse iterator is `--base_`, and `--` is `++base_`. Postfix versions copy `*this` first and return the copy. `bool operator==(const Reverse&) const = default;` compares the bases.
--- hint
`operator*` must not change the iterator, so work on a copy: `It before = base_; --before; return *before;`. The reference it returns points into the container, not into the copy, so it stays valid after the function returns.
--- check case | A vector, read backwards

=> std::vector<int>{5, 4, 3, 2, 1}
--- check test | Reverse(v.end()) refers to the last element
[] { std::vector<std::string> v{"alpha", "beta", "gamma"}; auto r = make_reverse(v.end()); return *r == "gamma" && r.base() == v.end() && *++r == "beta"; }()
?? Read the element just before the base, not the base itself.
--- check test | A std::list, and postfix and -- in both forms

--- check test | An empty container: begin and end of the reversed range are equal
[] { std::vector<double> v; std::list<char> l; return make_reverse(v.end()) == make_reverse(v.begin()) && make_reverse(l.end()) == make_reverse(l.begin()); }()
--- check test | It is a bidirectional iterator, and std::find finds the last match
[] { std::vector<int> v{7, 1, 7, 2}; auto hit = std::find(make_reverse(v.end()), make_reverse(v.begin()), 7); return std::bidirectional_iterator<Reverse<std::vector<int>::iterator>> && std::bidirectional_iterator<Reverse<std::list<int>::iterator>> && hit.base() - v.begin() == 3; }()

+++ practice | Binary search on any forward iterator
--- task
DSA I's lower bound works on a list with indexes. Write it once for **any** forward iterator, as the standard library does:

`template <typename It, typename T> It first_not_less(It first, It last, const T& x)` returns the first position in the sorted range `[first, last)` whose element is **not** less than `x`, or `last` if there is none. Compare only with `*it < x`.

It must make at most about log₂ n + 1 comparisons, even on a `std::list`, which has no indexes and no `it + n`. Two helpers from `<iterator>` make that possible:

- `std::distance(first, last)` counts the steps from `first` to `last` (O(1) for random access, O(n) for a list);
- `std::advance(it, n)` moves `it` forward `n` steps (O(1) or O(n) in the same way).

Keep a count of the elements still in play. Look at the middle one: if it is less than `x`, the answer is after it; otherwise the answer is it, or before it. A check counts the comparisons on 1,000 elements.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <list>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename It, typename T>
It first_not_less(It first, It last, const T& x) {
    while (first != last && *first < x) ++first;
    return first;
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <list>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

template <typename It, typename T>
It first_not_less(It first, It last, const T& x) {
    auto count = std::distance(first, last);   // the answer is in [first, first + count]
    while (count > 0) {
        auto half = count / 2;
        It mid = first;
        std::advance(mid, half);
        if (*mid < x) {
            first = ++mid;          // the answer is after mid
            count -= half + 1;
        } else {
            count = half;           // the answer is mid or before it
        }
    }
    return first;
}
--- hint
The starter is correct but walks the whole range: up to n comparisons. Keep `count = std::distance(first, last)` instead, the number of elements still in play, starting at `first`.
--- hint
While `count > 0`: let `half = count / 2`, copy `first` into `mid` and `std::advance(mid, half)`. If `*mid < x`, set `first` to the position after `mid` and take `half + 1` off `count`; otherwise set `count = half`. When `count` reaches 0, `first` is the answer.
--- check test | On a vector: the middle, the ends, and duplicates

--- check test | An empty range and a one-element range
[] { std::vector<int> e; std::list<int> one{5}; return first_not_less(e.begin(), e.end(), 3) == e.end() && first_not_less(one.begin(), one.end(), 5) == one.begin() && first_not_less(one.begin(), one.end(), 6) == one.end(); }()
--- check test | On a std::list of strings
[] { std::list<std::string> l{"ceres", "eris", "haumea", "makemake", "pluto"}; auto it = first_not_less(l.begin(), l.end(), std::string("m")); return it != l.end() && *it == "makemake"; }()
--- check test | 1,000 elements on a list: at most 11 comparisons
[] { static int cmp = 0; struct Mag { int v; bool operator<(const Mag& o) const { ++cmp; return v < o.v; } }; std::list<Mag> l; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) l.push_back(Mag{2 * i}); cmp = 0; auto it = first_not_less(l.begin(), l.end(), Mag{1501}); int c1 = cmp; cmp = 0; auto end = first_not_less(l.begin(), l.end(), Mag{5000}); return it->v == 1502 && end == l.end() && c1 <= 11 && cmp <= 11; }()
?? A walk from the front compares up to 1,000 times. Halve the number of elements in play each step.

+++ practice | Skip the empty slots
--- task
A rack has a fixed number of slots, and each slot holds a sensor reading or nothing. `class Rack` stores them as a `std::vector<std::optional<int>>`. Looping over a rack should visit only the filled slots, in order, so it needs an iterator that **skips** the empty ones.

- `explicit Rack(std::size_t slots)`: that many slots, all empty. `void set(std::size_t i, int value)` fills slot `i`, and `void clear(std::size_t i)` empties it.
- A nested forward `class iterator` holding a pointer to the slots and an index, with the member types (`std::forward_iterator_tag`, `int`, `std::ptrdiff_t`, `const int*`, `const int&`), a default constructor, `*` (returns the reading as `const int&`), prefix and postfix `++`, and `==`.
- `iterator begin() const` is the first **filled** slot, or `end()` when there is none. `iterator end() const` is the index equal to the number of slots.
- `++` moves to the next filled slot, or to `end()` when there are no more.

Every edge case counts: no slots at all, all slots empty, empty slots at the start, in a row, or at the end.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <optional>
#include <vector>

class Rack {
public:
    explicit Rack(std::size_t slots) : slots_(slots) {}
    void set(std::size_t i, int value) { slots_[i] = value; }
    void clear(std::size_t i) { slots_[i].reset(); }

    class iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        iterator() = default;
        iterator(const std::vector<std::optional<int>>* slots, std::size_t i) : slots_(slots), i_(i) {}
        const int& operator*() const { return *(*slots_)[i_]; }
        iterator& operator++() { ++i_; return *this; }
        iterator operator++(int) { iterator old = *this; ++i_; return old; }
        bool operator==(const iterator&) const = default;

    private:
        const std::vector<std::optional<int>>* slots_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t i_ = 0;
    };

    iterator begin() const { return end(); }
    iterator end() const { return iterator(&slots_, slots_.size()); }

private:
    std::vector<std::optional<int>> slots_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <optional>
#include <vector>

class Rack {
public:
    explicit Rack(std::size_t slots) : slots_(slots) {}
    void set(std::size_t i, int value) { slots_[i] = value; }
    void clear(std::size_t i) { slots_[i].reset(); }

    class iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        iterator() = default;
        iterator(const std::vector<std::optional<int>>* slots, std::size_t i) : slots_(slots), i_(i) { skip(); }
        const int& operator*() const { return *(*slots_)[i_]; }
        iterator& operator++() { ++i_; skip(); return *this; }
        iterator operator++(int) { iterator old = *this; ++*this; return old; }
        bool operator==(const iterator&) const = default;

    private:
        // Moves forward to the next filled slot, or to the end.
        void skip() {
            while (i_ < slots_->size() && !(*slots_)[i_].has_value()) ++i_;
        }

        const std::vector<std::optional<int>>* slots_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t i_ = 0;
    };

    iterator begin() const { return iterator(&slots_, 0); }
    iterator end() const { return iterator(&slots_, slots_.size()); }

private:
    std::vector<std::optional<int>> slots_;
};
--- hint
Give the iterator a private helper, `skip()`, that moves the index forward while it is inside the slots and the slot there is empty. The invariant: an iterator always stands on a filled slot, or at the end.
--- hint
Call `skip()` in the constructor that takes a position (so `begin()` can simply be position 0), and after moving the index on in prefix `++`. The loop condition checks `i_ < slots_->size()` first, so it never looks past the last slot.
--- check case | Only the filled slots, in order
[] { Rack r(6); r.set(1, 10); r.set(2, 20); r.set(5, 50); std::vector<int> out; for (int x : r) out.push_back(x); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{10, 20, 50}
--- check test | No slots, and all slots empty
[] { Rack none(0); Rack blank(4); int n = 0; for (int x : blank) n += x + 1; return none.begin() == none.end() && blank.begin() == blank.end() && n == 0; }()
?? begin() must skip empty slots too, all the way to end() if they are all empty.
--- check case | Empty slots at the start, in a row and at the end
[] { Rack r(9); r.set(3, 3); r.set(4, 4); r.set(7, 7); std::vector<int> out; for (int x : r) out.push_back(x); r.clear(4); for (int x : r) out.push_back(x); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{3, 4, 7, 3, 7}
--- check test | Every slot filled, and postfix ++
[] { Rack r(3); for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) r.set(i, i * 11); auto it = r.begin(); int a = *it++; int b = *it; return a == 0 && b == 11 && *++it == 22 && ++it == r.end(); }()
--- check test | It is a forward iterator, and std::distance counts filled slots
[] { Rack r(100); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i += 7) r.set(i, i); return std::forward_iterator<Rack::iterator> && std::distance(r.begin(), r.end()) == 15; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the cursor that runs ahead
--- task
`class Track` stores `double` readings side by side, and its iterator, `Cursor`, wraps a pointer. Range-for and prefix `++` work. But `it++` is supposed to hand back the position **before** the step, and it does not: code that reads `*it++` gets the next reading instead, and a loop that copies with `*out++ = *in++` skips readings.

Find the bug and fix it. Only the postfix operator is wrong.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>

class Track {
public:
    class Cursor {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = double;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = double*;
        using reference = double&;

        Cursor() = default;
        explicit Cursor(double* p) : p_(p) {}
        double& operator*() const { return *p_; }
        Cursor& operator++() { ++p_; return *this; }
        Cursor operator++(int) { ++p_; return *this; }
        bool operator==(const Cursor&) const = default;

    private:
        double* p_ = nullptr;
    };

    void add(double x) { if (n_ < 8) slots_[n_++] = x; }
    Cursor begin() { return Cursor(slots_); }
    Cursor end() { return Cursor(slots_ + n_); }

private:
    double slots_[8] = {};
    std::size_t n_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>

class Track {
public:
    class Cursor {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = double;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = double*;
        using reference = double&;

        Cursor() = default;
        explicit Cursor(double* p) : p_(p) {}
        double& operator*() const { return *p_; }
        Cursor& operator++() { ++p_; return *this; }
        Cursor operator++(int) {
            Cursor old = *this;
            ++p_;
            return old;
        }
        bool operator==(const Cursor&) const = default;

    private:
        double* p_ = nullptr;
    };

    void add(double x) { if (n_ < 8) slots_[n_++] = x; }
    Cursor begin() { return Cursor(slots_); }
    Cursor end() { return Cursor(slots_ + n_); }

private:
    double slots_[8] = {};
    std::size_t n_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Postfix `it++` has two jobs: move the iterator on, and give back where it *was*. Which of the two does the starter's version do?
--- hint
Save a copy of `*this` before incrementing, and return that copy.
--- check test | *it++ reads the current reading, then moves on
[] { Track t; t.add(1.5); t.add(2.5); t.add(3.5); auto it = t.begin(); double a = *it++; double b = *it++; return a == 1.5 && b == 2.5 && *it == 3.5; }()
?? Return a copy made before the increment.
--- check test | Copying with *out++ = *in++ keeps every reading
[] { Track t; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) t.add(i * 1.0); double out[5] = {}; double* o = out; auto in = t.begin(); while (in != t.end()) *o++ = *in++; return out[0] == 0.0 && out[1] == 1.0 && out[4] == 4.0; }()
--- check test | Prefix ++ and range-for still work
[] { Track t; t.add(2); t.add(4); double sum = 0; for (double x : t) sum += x; auto it = t.begin(); ++it; return sum == 6 && *it == 4; }()
--- check test | Postfix on the last reading gives the last reading and reaches end
