+++ practice | The hottest patch of a thermal image
--- task
A thermal camera produces a grid of temperatures, stored row after row in one `std::vector<int>`. Analysts look at rectangular **windows** of it: find the hottest cell in a patch, or average a region. Copying the window out would waste time, so write a **view** with its own iterator that walks the window in place, row by row.

`class Grid` is given. Write `class Window`:

- `Window(const Grid& g, std::size_t row, std::size_t col, std::size_t height, std::size_t width)`: the cells in rows `row` to `row + height - 1` and columns `col` to `col + width - 1`. The window always fits inside the grid. `height` or `width` may be 0, and then the window is empty.
- A nested forward `class iterator` (member types `std::forward_iterator_tag`, `int`, `std::ptrdiff_t`, `const int*`, `const int&`; a default constructor; `*`; prefix and postfix `++`; `==`). It walks along a row of the window, and after the last column of the window it jumps to the first column of the next row.
- `iterator begin() const` and `iterator end() const`. For an empty window, `begin() == end()`.

Store the iterator's position as a row and a column **inside the window**. Then the end is simply row `height`, column 0.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <vector>

class Grid {
public:
    Grid(std::size_t rows, std::size_t cols) : cols_(cols), cells_(rows * cols, 0) {}
    int& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }
    const int& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) const { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }

private:
    std::size_t cols_;
    std::vector<int> cells_;
};

class Window {
public:
    class iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        iterator() = default;
        const int& operator*() const { return *cell_; }
        iterator& operator++() { return *this; }
        iterator operator++(int) { return *this; }
        bool operator==(const iterator&) const = default;

    private:
        const int* cell_ = nullptr;
    };

    Window(const Grid& g, std::size_t row, std::size_t col, std::size_t height, std::size_t width) {}
    iterator begin() const { return iterator(); }
    iterator end() const { return iterator(); }
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <vector>

class Grid {
public:
    Grid(std::size_t rows, std::size_t cols) : cols_(cols), cells_(rows * cols, 0) {}
    int& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }
    const int& at(std::size_t r, std::size_t c) const { return cells_[r * cols_ + c]; }

private:
    std::size_t cols_;
    std::vector<int> cells_;
};

class Window {
public:
    class iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        iterator() = default;
        iterator(const Window* w, std::size_t r, std::size_t c) : w_(w), r_(r), c_(c) {}

        const int& operator*() const { return w_->grid_->at(w_->row_ + r_, w_->col_ + c_); }

        iterator& operator++() {
            ++c_;
            if (c_ == w_->width_) {   // past the window's last column: start the next row
                c_ = 0;
                ++r_;
            }
            return *this;
        }

        iterator operator++(int) { iterator old = *this; ++*this; return old; }
        bool operator==(const iterator&) const = default;

    private:
        const Window* w_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t r_ = 0;   // row inside the window
        std::size_t c_ = 0;   // column inside the window
    };

    Window(const Grid& g, std::size_t row, std::size_t col, std::size_t height, std::size_t width)
        : grid_(&g), row_(row), col_(col), height_(height), width_(width) {}

    iterator begin() const { return height_ == 0 || width_ == 0 ? end() : iterator(this, 0, 0); }
    iterator end() const { return iterator(this, height_, 0); }

private:
    const Grid* grid_;
    std::size_t row_;
    std::size_t col_;
    std::size_t height_;
    std::size_t width_;
};
--- hint
The window stores a pointer to the grid, its top-left corner and its size. The iterator stores a pointer to the window and its position inside it, `r` and `c`. `*` reads `grid->at(row + r, col + c)`.
--- hint
`++` adds one to `c`; when `c` reaches the window's width, set `c` back to 0 and add one to `r`. Then the end is `(height, 0)`. An empty window needs care: with width 0, `c` would never equal the width after an increment, so let `begin()` return `end()` whenever the height or the width is 0.
--- check case | A 2 by 3 window, row by row

=> std::vector<int>{12, 13, 14, 22, 23, 24}
--- check test | The hottest cell with std::max_element
[] { Grid g(6, 6); g.at(4, 4) = 90; g.at(1, 1) = 70; g.at(2, 3) = 55; Window w(g, 1, 1, 3, 3); auto hot = std::max_element(w.begin(), w.end()); return *hot == 70 && std::forward_iterator<Window::iterator>; }()
--- check test | Empty windows: height 0 or width 0
[] { Grid g(3, 3); g.at(0, 0) = 1; Window a(g, 0, 0, 0, 3); Window b(g, 0, 0, 3, 0); int n = 0; for (int t : b) n += t + 1; return a.begin() == a.end() && b.begin() == b.end() && n == 0; }()
?? With width 0 the column never equals the width after ++. Make begin() return end() for an empty window.

--- check test | The whole grid, and std::distance

+++ question | What std::sort needs
--- ask
`std::sort(l.begin(), l.end())` does not compile when `l` is a `std::list<int>`. Why?
--- choice
A list's elements are not stored in order, so they cannot be sorted.
--- choice correct
`std::sort` needs random-access iterators, to jump to the middle of a range in O(1), and a list only offers bidirectional ones.
--- choice
`std::list` has no `begin()` and `end()`.
--- choice
Lists hold their elements on the heap, and `std::sort` only works on the stack.
--- why
Each algorithm names the weakest iterator category it needs. `std::sort`'s partitioning and its insertion-sort phase compute positions like `first + (last - first) / 2`, which only random-access iterators provide in O(1). `std::list` has its own `sort()` member, a merge sort that relinks nodes and needs only forward steps.

+++ question | The end that is one too early
--- ask
A container's `end()` returns an iterator to its **last** element instead of one past it. What does `for (int x : c)` do on a container holding 3, 5, 8?
--- choice
It crashes, because `end()` must not point at an element.
--- choice
It visits 3, 5 and 8, because range-for includes the end.
--- choice correct
It visits 3 and 5 only: the loop stops as soon as the iterator equals `end()`, before reading that element.
--- choice
It never stops.
--- why
Range-for keeps going while `first != last`, and reads `*first` only inside the loop. With `last` on the 8, the loop stops when it reaches the 8, so the 8 is never read. An empty container is worse: it cannot even say where its last element is. One past the end makes `[begin, end)` hold every element, and makes the empty range simply `begin == end`.

=== dsacpp-05 | A singly linked list with unique_ptr: ownership down the chain
--- teach
In DSA I you built a singly linked list in Python: nodes that each hold a value and a link to the next node. Python's garbage collector freed a node once nothing linked to it. In C++ the question is sharper: **who owns each node?** This lesson answers it with `std::unique_ptr`, so that the list frees itself. Then it meets a failure Python never showed you: with a long enough list, the automatic clean-up crashes the program. You will see why, and fix it with a one-line loop.

### Ownership down the chain

Give each node a `std::unique_ptr` to the next one:

```cpp fragment
struct Waypoint {
    explicit Waypoint(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
    std::string name;
    std::unique_ptr<Waypoint> next;   // owns the rest of the route
};
```

The list holds a `std::unique_ptr<Waypoint> head_` that owns the first node. The first node owns the second, the second owns the third, and so on. Every node has exactly one owner: the `head_`, or the `next` of the node before it. That is the whole ownership design, and `unique_ptr` enforces it: a node cannot accidentally get two owners, because a `unique_ptr` cannot be copied.

When `head_` is destroyed it deletes the first node; that node's destructor destroys its `next`, which deletes the second node, and so on down the chain. No destructor to write, no leak possible. At least, that is the theory.

### Looking without owning

To walk the list you need to point at nodes without taking them over. A raw pointer does exactly that: it **[[observes|observing]]**. `get()` gives the raw pointer inside a `unique_ptr`:

```cpp fragment
for (const Waypoint* p = head_.get(); p != nullptr; p = p->next.get()) {
    std::cout << p->name << "\n";
}
```

The rule from the basics course applies: a raw pointer looks, a `unique_ptr` owns. The walk changes no ownership, so it can never free anything by accident.

### Adding at the front

To add a node at the front, the new node must take over the old first node, and then `head_` must take over the new node. Each step is a move:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

struct Waypoint {
    explicit Waypoint(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
    std::string name;
    std::unique_ptr<Waypoint> next;
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Waypoint> head;
    for (std::string name : {"landing", "orbit", "launch"}) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Waypoint>(name);
        fresh->next = std::move(head);   // 1. the new node takes the old chain
        head = std::move(fresh);         // 2. head takes the new node
    }
    for (const Waypoint* p = head.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) std::cout << p->name << " ";
    std::cout << "\n";   // launch orbit landing
}
```

The order matters. Doing step 2 first would make `head` take the new node and destroy the whole old chain, because assigning into a `unique_ptr` deletes what it owned.

### Removing from the front

`head_ = std::move(head_->next);` removes the first node, in one line. It looks dangerous: the right side reaches into the very node the assignment is about to delete. It is safe because of the exact order in which a `unique_ptr` move assignment works:

1. It first **releases** the right side: it takes the pointer out of `head_->next`, leaving that `next` holding `nullptr`.
2. Then it stores that pointer in `head_`.
3. Only then does it delete the node `head_` used to own. That node's `next` is already `nullptr`, so deleting it deletes only that one node.

The same shape removes the node after any node `p`: `p->next = std::move(p->next->next);`.

### Links to links

Some jobs, like removing every node that matches, would need a special case for the first node, which is owned by `head_` rather than by a node. The special case disappears if you walk the **owning links** themselves: a pointer to the `unique_ptr` that owns the current node.

```cpp fragment
std::unique_ptr<Waypoint>* link = &head_;   // first the head, later some node's next
while (*link) {
    // (*link) is the unique_ptr that owns the current node
    link = &(*link)->next;
}
// now *link is the empty unique_ptr at the very end: a place to attach a new node
```

`link` points at `head_` first, then at the first node's `next`, then at the second node's `next`… Whatever you do through `*link` works the same for every position, the first included. Here it walks to the end of the chain; attaching `*link = std::make_unique<Waypoint>("dock");` there appends a node.

### The destructor that crashes

Here is the problem. Destroying `head_` deletes node 1. Node 1's destructor destroys its `next`, which deletes node 2, whose destructor destroys its `next`… and none of those calls has returned yet. Destroying a list of n nodes runs n destructors **nested inside each other**, each one waiting on the [[call stack|call-stack]] for the next.

The call stack is small: typically 8 MB for a desktop program, and far less in a browser or on a flight computer. Each nested call uses some of it. A list of a few hundred thousand nodes runs out: a **stack overflow**, and the program crashes in the middle of freeing memory. The list works perfectly for every test with ten nodes, and dies in production with a million.

This is a real and well-known failure of `unique_ptr` chains. Herb Sutter used it as an example in his 2016 CppCon talk on [[leak-freedom|sutter]].

### The loop that fixes it

Take the nodes apart one at a time, from the front, so that each one is deleted with an empty `next`:

```cpp fragment
while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
```

Each pass is exactly the "remove from the front" step above: it releases the second node out of the first, then deletes the first, whose `next` is now `nullptr`, so that deletion runs one destructor and returns. The stack never holds more than one node's destructor. Put this loop in the list's destructor, and in every other place that throws a whole chain away.

### The five special functions, again

Writing a destructor has a side effect: the compiler **stops writing the move operations** for you. With the `unique_ptr` member, copying is deleted too, so the list could neither be copied nor moved. You write them:

- **Move constructor:** take `other.head_`, take its size with `std::exchange`. O(1).
- **Move assignment:** `= default` is a trap here. The defaulted version assigns into `head_`, which deletes this list's old chain the recursive way, and the crash is back. Clear this list with the loop first, then take `other`'s chain.
- **Copy constructor:** walk `other` and append a copy of each value, using a link-to-link pointer that always points at the empty `next` at the end, so that each append is O(1). A recursive copy would overflow the stack just like the destructor.
- **Copy assignment:** copy and swap.

### Why it is correct

The ownership invariant: every node is owned by exactly one `unique_ptr`, which is either `head_` or the `next` of the node before it, and following `next` from `head_` reaches every node once and ends at `nullptr`. `size_` is the number of nodes.

- **push_front** gives the new node the old chain, then gives `head_` the new node: every old node keeps its single owner, and the new node has one.
- **pop_front** releases node 2 from node 1, gives it to `head_`, and deletes node 1, which owns nothing any more. Every other node keeps its owner.
- **The destructor loop** keeps the invariant after every pass, removes one node per pass, and stops when `head_` is empty, so it runs exactly n times. The stack depth of each pass is constant, whatever n is.
- **The copy constructor** makes one new node per node of `other`, in order, each owned by the empty link at the end of the copy, so the copy satisfies the invariant after every step and shares no node with `other`.
- **The moves** hand the whole chain from one `head_` to another: each node keeps its owner inside the chain, and only the first node changes owner, from `other.head_` to `head_`.
- **Reversal** (the task) moves each node from the front of the old chain to the front of a new one. Each move takes the node from its single owner and gives it to one new owner, so the invariant holds after each step, and no node is created or destroyed.

### What it costs

| operation | time | extra stack |
|---|---|---|
| push_front, pop_front, front | O(1) | O(1) |
| size (kept in a member) | O(1) | O(1) |
| find, contains | O(n) | O(1) |
| copy | O(n) | O(1) with the loop, O(n) if recursive |
| destruction | O(n) | O(1) with the loop, O(n) if left to the compiler |
| reverse | O(n) | O(1) |

A node costs more memory than you might think: 4 bytes of `int`, 8 of pointer (on a 64-bit machine), padding, and the heap's own bookkeeping for each separate allocation, often 16 bytes more. A million `int`s take 4 MB in a vector and about 32 MB as a list, scattered across memory. Lesson 18 measures what that scattering costs.

### Where it is used

- `std::forward_list` is exactly this structure, minus the stored size.
- Memory allocators keep **[[free lists|free-list]]**: freed blocks linked through their own first bytes.
- A hash map with chaining (lesson 8) keeps each bucket as a short list.
- Undo histories, and a mission's command queue where commands are only ever added and taken at the front.

**Watch out:**

- Leaving destruction to the compiler. It works for short lists and crashes with a stack overflow on long ones.
- `= default` for the move assignment of a list with a hand-written destructor: it frees the old chain recursively.
- Writing `head_ = std::move(fresh);` before `fresh->next = std::move(head_);` in push_front: the old chain is deleted.
- Using a `unique_ptr` after moving from it. After `a = std::move(b);`, `b` holds `nullptr`, and `b->next` crashes.
- Reaching for `release()` to get around "cannot copy a `unique_ptr`". It hands out a raw pointer that owns the node, and the node leaks unless someone remembers to delete it.

::: context observing Owning and observing pointers
The C++ Core Guidelines, a set of rules edited by Bjarne Stroustrup and Herb Sutter, say that a raw pointer (`T*`) never owns what it points at. Ownership is shown in the type instead: `std::unique_ptr` for one owner, `std::shared_ptr` for shared ownership. A raw pointer is then only ever a way to look. That makes code easy to check: if you see `delete` applied to a raw pointer, something is wrong. An observer must never outlive what it observes, which in a list is guaranteed while you do not remove nodes during the walk.
:::

::: context call-stack Where nested calls wait
Each function call gets a frame on the call stack: room for its local variables and the address to return to. A call nested inside another adds a frame on top, and the frame goes away when the call returns. The stack has a fixed size, set when the program starts. Recursion that goes a million calls deep needs a million frames at once. In DSA I, Python stopped you at about a thousand with `RecursionError`. C++ does not check: it simply runs off the end of the stack and the operating system kills the program.
:::

::: context sutter Leak-freedom by construction
Herb Sutter chaired the C++ standards committee for many years. His 2016 talk "Leak-Freedom in C++... By Default" showed how choosing the right owning pointer for each link makes leaks impossible by construction, and then where that approach bites: destroying a long chain of owning pointers nests one destructor call per node, and a long enough chain overflows the stack. The cure is to take the chain apart one node at a time, as here. The general lesson: RAII frees resources automatically, but you still decide the order, and a recursive order costs stack space.
:::

::: context free-list Lists inside freed memory
When a program frees a small block, the allocator does not hand it back to the operating system. It keeps it for the next request of the same size, on a free list. The trick is that the link to the next free block is stored inside the freed block itself, since nobody else is using those bytes. Asking for a block is then a pop from the front of a singly linked list, and freeing one is a push: both O(1). It is also why a double free is so harmful: the same block ends up in the list twice.
:::
--- task
Write `class IntList`, a singly linked list of `int`s where every node is owned by a `std::unique_ptr`. No `main`. Keep the heap ledger at the top of the starter as it is: `heap::live` counts memory blocks not yet given back, and each node is one block.

The node type is given: `struct Node { explicit Node(int v); int value; std::unique_ptr<Node> next; };`, nested in the class. Write:

- `void push_front(int x)`; `bool pop_front()`, which removes the first value and returns `true`, or returns `false` on an empty list; `int& front()` and `const int& front() const` (only called on a non-empty list).
- `std::size_t size() const` in O(1), and `bool empty() const`.
- `bool contains(int x) const`.
- `std::vector<int> to_vector() const`: the values from front to back.
- `void reverse()`: reverse the list in place by relinking the nodes. It must not create or destroy a single node, so every value stays at the same address.
- `~IntList()`: frees every node with a loop, so a list of 1,000,000 nodes does not overflow the stack.
- `IntList(const IntList& other)`: a deep copy, same order, in O(n) and without recursion. `IntList& operator=(const IntList& other)`: a deep copy; `l = l` changes nothing.
- `IntList(IntList&& other) noexcept` and `IntList& operator=(IntList&& other) noexcept`: take `other`'s nodes in O(1) and leave `other` empty. Move assignment must free this list's old nodes with the loop too.

The checks build lists of 1,000,000 nodes.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class IntList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    IntList() = default;

    void push_front(int x) {}
    bool pop_front() { return false; }
    int& front() { return head_->value; }
    const int& front() const { return head_->value; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    bool empty() const { return size_ == 0; }
    bool contains(int x) const { return false; }
    std::vector<int> to_vector() const { return {}; }
    void reverse() {}

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class IntList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    IntList() = default;

    ~IntList() { clear(); }

    IntList(const IntList& other) : size_(other.size_) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;   // always the empty link at the end of the copy
        for (const Node* p = other.head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) {
            *link = std::make_unique<Node>(p->value);
            link = &(*link)->next;
        }
    }

    IntList& operator=(const IntList& other) {
        IntList copy(other);
        std::swap(head_, copy.head_);
        std::swap(size_, copy.size_);
        return *this;   // copy's destructor frees our old nodes, with the loop
    }

    IntList(IntList&& other) noexcept : head_(std::move(other.head_)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)) {}

    IntList& operator=(IntList&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            clear();   // not head_ = ...: that would free the old chain recursively
            head_ = std::move(other.head_);
            size_ = std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }

    bool pop_front() {
        if (!head_) return false;
        head_ = std::move(head_->next);   // releases node 2, then deletes node 1 alone
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    int& front() { return head_->value; }
    const int& front() const { return head_->value; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    bool empty() const { return size_ == 0; }

    bool contains(int x) const {
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) {
            if (p->value == x) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    std::vector<int> to_vector() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        out.reserve(size_);
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    void reverse() {
        std::unique_ptr<Node> done;   // the reversed part, built at its front
        while (head_) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> rest = std::move(head_->next);
            head_->next = std::move(done);
            done = std::move(head_);
            head_ = std::move(rest);
        }
        head_ = std::move(done);
    }

private:
    void clear() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);   // one node at a time: constant stack depth
        size_ = 0;
    }

    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
push_front is two moves in this order: the new node's `next` takes `head_`, then `head_` takes the new node. pop_front is `head_ = std::move(head_->next);`. Write a private `clear()` with the loop `while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);` and call it from the destructor.
--- hint
To reverse, keep a second `std::unique_ptr<Node> done`, empty at first. While `head_` has a node: save `head_->next` in a local `rest`, give `done` to `head_->next`, give `head_` to `done`, and give `rest` to `head_`. At the end, `head_` takes `done`.
--- hint
The copy constructor keeps `std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;`. For each node of `other`, it sets `*link = std::make_unique<Node>(value)` and moves `link` to `&(*link)->next`. Move assignment calls `clear()` before `head_ = std::move(other.head_);`, and both moves take the size with `std::exchange(other.size_, 0)`.
--- check case | push_front puts values at the front
[] { IntList l; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; ++i) l.push_front(i * 10); return l.to_vector(); }()
=> std::vector<int>{40, 30, 20, 10}
--- check test | size, empty, front and contains
[] { IntList l; bool was_empty = l.empty() && l.size() == 0 && !l.contains(3); l.push_front(3); l.push_front(8); l.front() = 9; return was_empty && l.size() == 2 && !l.empty() && l.front() == 9 && l.contains(3) && l.contains(9) && !l.contains(8); }()
--- check test | pop_front removes from the front, and refuses when empty
[] { IntList l; bool refused = !l.pop_front(); l.push_front(1); l.push_front(2); bool popped = l.pop_front(); return refused && popped && l.size() == 1 && l.front() == 1 && l.pop_front() && l.empty() && !l.pop_front(); }()

--- check case | reverse turns the list around

?? Move the unique_ptrs around; never call make_unique in reverse.
--- check test | A copy is deep and in the same order

+++ practice | A route with a tail pointer
--- task
A flight plan is a list of stops, added at the **end** and flown from the front. `class Route` is a singly linked list whose nodes are owned by `std::unique_ptr`s, as in the lesson. Walking to the end for every append would make building a route of n stops O(n²), so the route also keeps a raw pointer to its last stop, `Stop* tail_`. The tail pointer only **observes**: the last stop is owned by the `next` of the stop before it (or by `head_`).

- `void push_back(std::string name)` appends in O(1).
- `bool pop_front()` removes the first stop, or returns `false` when the route is empty. When the last stop goes, `tail_` must become `nullptr`, or the next `push_back` would write through a pointer to a freed stop.
- `const std::string& back() const` is the last stop's name (only called on a non-empty route).
- `std::vector<std::string> names() const` lists the stops from first to last. `std::size_t size() const`.
- `~Route()` frees the stops with a loop. Copying and moving are deleted.

Keep the heap ledger as it is.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Route {
public:
    struct Stop {
        explicit Stop(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
        std::string name;
        std::unique_ptr<Stop> next;
    };

    Route() = default;
    Route(const Route&) = delete;
    Route& operator=(const Route&) = delete;

    void push_back(std::string name) {}
    bool pop_front() { return false; }
    const std::string& back() const { return tail_->name; }
    std::vector<std::string> names() const { return {}; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Stop> head_;
    Stop* tail_ = nullptr;   // observes the last stop; owns nothing
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Route {
public:
    struct Stop {
        explicit Stop(std::string n) : name(std::move(n)) {}
        std::string name;
        std::unique_ptr<Stop> next;
    };

    Route() = default;
    ~Route() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Route(const Route&) = delete;
    Route& operator=(const Route&) = delete;

    void push_back(std::string name) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Stop>(std::move(name));
        Stop* raw = fresh.get();
        if (tail_) tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        else head_ = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = raw;
        ++size_;
    }

    bool pop_front() {
        if (!head_) return false;
        head_ = std::move(head_->next);
        if (!head_) tail_ = nullptr;   // the last stop is gone
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    const std::string& back() const { return tail_->name; }

    std::vector<std::string> names() const {
        std::vector<std::string> out;
        for (const Stop* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->name);
        return out;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Stop> head_;
    Stop* tail_ = nullptr;   // observes the last stop; owns nothing
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
In `push_back`, make the new stop, keep its raw address with `get()` before you move the `unique_ptr` away, then attach it: to `tail_->next` when there is a last stop, or to `head_` when the route is empty. Finally point `tail_` at the new stop.
--- hint
`pop_front` is `head_ = std::move(head_->next);`. Afterwards, if `head_` is empty, the route is empty, so set `tail_` to `nullptr`. The destructor is the loop from the lesson.
--- check case | Stops come out in the order they were added
[] { Route r; r.push_back("launch"); r.push_back("orbit"); r.push_back("dock"); std::vector<std::string> n = r.names(); n.push_back(r.back()); return n; }()
=> std::vector<std::string>{"launch", "orbit", "dock", "dock"}
--- check test | Popping to empty, then adding again
[] { Route r; r.push_back("a"); r.push_back("b"); r.pop_front(); r.pop_front(); bool empty = r.size() == 0 && !r.pop_front(); r.push_back("c"); r.push_back("d"); return empty && r.names() == std::vector<std::string>{"c", "d"} && r.back() == "d" && r.size() == 2; }()
?? When pop_front removes the last stop, tail_ must be set to nullptr.
--- check test | back() after pops that leave one stop
[] { Route r; for (std::string s : {"x", "y", "z"}) r.push_back(s); r.pop_front(); r.pop_front(); return r.back() == "z" && r.size() == 1 && r.names().size() == 1; }()
--- check test | 200,000 appends are fast, and every stop is freed
[] { long long blocks = heap::live; bool ok; { Route r; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) r.push_back(std::to_string(i)); ok = r.size() == 200000 && r.back() == "199999"; } return ok && heap::live == blocks; }()
?? Walking to the end for every append is O(n²). Keep the tail pointer up to date.
--- check test | 1,000,000 stops are freed without overflowing the stack
[] { long long blocks = heap::live; { Route r; for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) r.push_back(""); } return heap::live == blocks; }()

+++ practice | Iterating a linked list
--- task
`class Log` is a singly linked list of `int`s with `push_front` and a safe destructor. Range-for and the standard algorithms cannot use it yet. Give it a **forward iterator** for reading:

- A nested `class const_iterator` holding a `const Node*` (the observed node; `nullptr` is the end). Member types: `iterator_category` is `std::forward_iterator_tag`, `value_type` is `int`, `difference_type` is `std::ptrdiff_t`, `pointer` is `const int*`, `reference` is `const int&`. It needs a default constructor, `*` (the node's value), prefix and postfix `++` (move to `next`), and `==`.
- `const_iterator begin() const` (the first node) and `const_iterator end() const` (a `nullptr` node).

The checks use range-for, `std::find`, `std::max_element` and `std::distance`.
--- starter

    }

    Log& operator=(const Log&) = delete;

--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

class Log {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    Log() = default;
    ~Log() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Log(const Log&) = delete;
    Log& operator=(const Log&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
    }

    class const_iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        const_iterator() = default;
        explicit const_iterator(const Node* n) : n_(n) {}
        const int& operator*() const { return n_->value; }
        const_iterator& operator++() { n_ = n_->next.get(); return *this; }
        const_iterator operator++(int) { const_iterator old = *this; n_ = n_->next.get(); return old; }
        bool operator==(const const_iterator&) const = default;

    private:
        const Node* n_ = nullptr;   // observes; nullptr is the end
    };

    const_iterator begin() const { return const_iterator(head_.get()); }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(nullptr); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
};
--- hint
The iterator only observes, so it holds a `const Node*`. `*` returns `n_->value`, and prefix `++` sets `n_ = n_->next.get()` and returns `*this`. The end of the list is where `next` is empty, so `end()` is an iterator holding `nullptr`.
--- hint
`begin()` wraps `head_.get()`. Postfix `++` copies `*this`, steps, and returns the copy. `bool operator==(const const_iterator&) const = default;` compares the node pointers.
--- check test | range-for visits every value, front to back
[] { Log l; for (int i = 1; i <= 5; ++i) l.push_front(i); int order = 0; for (int x : l) order = order * 10 + x; return order == 54321; }()
--- check test | An empty log: begin() == end()
[] { Log l; int n = 0; for (int x : l) n += x + 1; return l.begin() == l.end() && n == 0; }()
--- check test | std::find, std::max_element and std::distance
[] { Log l; for (int x : {4, 9, 1, 7}) l.push_front(x); auto hit = std::find(l.begin(), l.end(), 9); auto miss = std::find(l.begin(), l.end(), 5); return hit != l.end() && *hit == 9 && miss == l.end() && *std::max_element(l.begin(), l.end()) == 9 && std::distance(l.begin(), l.end()) == 4; }()
--- check test | Postfix returns the old position
[] { Log l; l.push_front(2); l.push_front(1); auto it = l.begin(); int a = *it++; int b = *it++; return a == 1 && b == 2 && it == l.end(); }()
--- check test | It is a forward iterator, and *it is const int&
std::forward_iterator<Log::const_iterator> && std::is_same_v<decltype(*std::declval<const Log&>().begin()), const int&>

+++ practice | Merging two sorted lists by relinking
--- task
Two ground stations each deliver readings as a sorted singly linked list. Merging them should not copy a single node: it should **relink** the nodes of both lists into one sorted chain, like the merge in DSA I's merge sort, but with pointers instead of indexes.

`class Chain` is given, with `push_front`, `front`, `size`, `to_vector` and a safe destructor. Write the member function `void merge_from(Chain& other)`:

- Both chains are sorted from smallest to largest. Afterwards, this chain holds every node of both, sorted, and `other` is empty (size 0).
- When two values are equal, this chain's node comes first, so the merge is stable.
- No node is created or destroyed. It must work with no recursion on chains of 200,000 nodes each.

Take both chains apart into two local `unique_ptr`s, and build the result through a link-to-link pointer that always points at the empty `next` at the end of the merged part.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Chain {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    Chain() = default;
    ~Chain() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Chain(const Chain&) = delete;
    Chain& operator=(const Chain&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }
    const int& front() const { return head_->value; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> to_vector() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    void merge_from(Chain& other) {}

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Chain {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    Chain() = default;
    ~Chain() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Chain(const Chain&) = delete;
    Chain& operator=(const Chain&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }
    const int& front() const { return head_->value; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> to_vector() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    void merge_from(Chain& other) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node> a = std::move(head_);
        std::unique_ptr<Node> b = std::move(other.head_);
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;   // the empty link at the end of the merged part
        while (a && b) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node>& take = b->value < a->value ? b : a;   // ties take from a
            *link = std::move(take);             // the merged chain owns the node now
            take = std::move((*link)->next);     // its old list moves on to the next node
            link = &(*link)->next;
        }
        *link = a ? std::move(a) : std::move(b);   // the leftovers are already sorted
        size_ += std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Start with `std::unique_ptr<Node> a = std::move(head_);` and the same for `b` from `other.head_`, and `std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;`. While both `a` and `b` hold nodes, pick the one to take: `b` only when `b->value < a->value`, so ties take from `a`.
--- hint
Taking a node is three moves. `*link = std::move(take);` hands the node to the merged chain. `take = std::move((*link)->next);` gives the rest of that list back to `take`. `link = &(*link)->next;` moves the link to the new end. After the loop, attach whichever of `a` and `b` still holds nodes, and move `other`'s size into this one.
--- check case | Two sorted chains become one
[] { Chain a; Chain b; for (int x : {9, 5, 3, 1}) a.push_front(x); for (int x : {8, 6, 4, 2}) b.push_front(x); a.merge_from(b); std::vector<int> v = a.to_vector(); v.push_back(int(a.size())); v.push_back(int(b.size())); return v; }()
=> std::vector<int>{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 8, 0}
--- check test | Merging with an empty chain, on either side
[] { Chain a; Chain b; Chain e1; Chain e2; for (int x : {3, 1}) a.push_front(x); a.merge_from(e1); e2.merge_from(a); Chain z1; Chain z2; z1.merge_from(z2); return e2.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{1, 3} && e2.size() == 2 && a.size() == 0 && z1.size() == 0 && b.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Ties: this chain's node comes first
[] { Chain a; Chain b; a.push_front(5); b.push_front(5); const int* mine = &a.front(); a.merge_from(b); return &a.front() == mine && a.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{5, 5}; }()
?? When the values are equal, take from this chain: test b->value < a->value, not <=.
--- check test | One chain entirely before the other
[] { Chain a; Chain b; for (int x : {30, 20}) a.push_front(x); for (int x : {2, 1}) b.push_front(x); a.merge_from(b); return a.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{1, 2, 20, 30}; }()
--- check test | 200,000 + 200,000 nodes, relinked without making or freeing any
[] { Chain a; Chain b; for (int i = 199999; i >= 0; --i) { a.push_front(2 * i); b.push_front(2 * i + 1); } long long blocks = heap::live; a.merge_from(b); long long after = heap::live; std::vector<int> v = a.to_vector(); bool sorted = v.size() == 400000; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size() && sorted; ++i) sorted = v[i] == int(i); return sorted && after == blocks && a.size() == 400000 && b.size() == 0; }()
?? Move the existing nodes; never call make_unique in merge_from.

+++ practice | Remove every match
--- task
Write the member function `std::size_t remove_all(int x)` for `class Readings`, a singly linked list of `int`s. It removes every node whose value equals `x`, frees those nodes, keeps the other nodes in order, updates the size, and returns how many nodes it removed.

Every position must work: matches at the front, several in a row, at the end, everywhere, or nowhere, and an empty list. The clean way has no special case for the front: walk a pointer to the owning link, `std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;`. When the node that `*link` owns matches, remove it with `*link = std::move((*link)->next);` and stay on the same link; otherwise step on to the node's `next`.

Keep the heap ledger as it is: each node is one block.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Readings {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    Readings() = default;
    ~Readings() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Readings(const Readings&) = delete;
    Readings& operator=(const Readings&) = delete;

        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }

    std::vector<int> to_vector() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    std::size_t remove_all(int x) { return 0; }

    std::size_t size_ = 0;

--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Readings {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    Readings() = default;
    ~Readings() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Readings(const Readings&) = delete;
    Readings& operator=(const Readings&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> to_vector() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    std::size_t remove_all(int x) {
        std::size_t removed = 0;
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;
        while (*link) {
            if ((*link)->value == x) {
                *link = std::move((*link)->next);   // frees the matching node; stay on this link
                ++removed;
            } else {
                link = &(*link)->next;
            }
        }
        size_ -= removed;
        return removed;
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Loop while `*link` holds a node. If `(*link)->value == x`, do `*link = std::move((*link)->next);`: the link now owns the node after the match, and the match is freed. Do not move `link` on in that case, because the new node it owns may match too.
--- hint
Only when the node does not match, step on with `link = &(*link)->next;`. Count the removals, and take the count off `size_` at the end.
--- check case | Matches at the front, in a row and at the end
[] { Readings r; for (int x : {7, 3, 7, 7, 2, 7}) r.push_front(x); std::size_t n = r.remove_all(7); std::vector<int> v = r.to_vector(); v.push_back(int(n)); v.push_back(int(r.size())); return v; }()
=> std::vector<int>{2, 3, 4, 2}
?? After removing a node, the link now owns the next node, which may match too: check it before stepping on.
--- check test | Every node matches, and no node matches
[] { Readings all; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) all.push_front(4); Readings none; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) none.push_front(i); std::size_t a = all.remove_all(4); std::size_t b = none.remove_all(9); return a == 5 && all.size() == 0 && all.to_vector().empty() && b == 0 && none.size() == 5 && none.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{4, 3, 2, 1, 0}; }()
--- check test | An empty list, and a single node
[] { Readings e; Readings one; one.push_front(1); std::size_t a = e.remove_all(1); std::size_t b = one.remove_all(2); std::size_t c = one.remove_all(1); return a == 0 && b == 0 && c == 1 && one.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Removed nodes are freed
[] { Readings r; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) r.push_front(i % 4); long long blocks = heap::live; std::size_t n = r.remove_all(0); return n == 250 && heap::live == blocks - 250 && r.size() == 750; }()
--- check test | 1,000,000 nodes, removing every other one
[] { Readings r; for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) r.push_front(i % 2); std::size_t n = r.remove_all(1); return n == 500000 && r.size() == 500000; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the move assignment that crashes
--- task
`class IntList` frees its nodes with a loop in its destructor, and its move constructor is correct. Its author wrote the move assignment as `= default`.

Two things go wrong. After `a = std::move(b);`, `b` still reports its old size although it holds no nodes. And moving a short list into a list of a million nodes crashes the program with a stack overflow. Fix the move assignment. Everything else is correct.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IntList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    IntList() = default;
    ~IntList() { clear(); }
    IntList(IntList&& other) noexcept : head_(std::move(other.head_)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)) {}
    IntList& operator=(IntList&&) noexcept = default;

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    int front() const { return head_->value; }

    void clear() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
        size_ = 0;
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IntList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    IntList() = default;
    ~IntList() { clear(); }
    IntList(IntList&& other) noexcept : head_(std::move(other.head_)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)) {}

    IntList& operator=(IntList&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            clear();   // free the old nodes one at a time first
            head_ = std::move(other.head_);
            size_ = std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    int front() const { return head_->value; }

    void clear() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
        size_ = 0;
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
The defaulted move assignment does `head_ = std::move(other.head_);` and `size_ = other.size_;`. What happens to this list's old nodes in the first step, and what is left in `other.size_` after the second?
--- hint
Write it yourself: inside `if (this != &other)`, call `clear()` first, so the old nodes go one at a time, then take `other.head_` and take its size with `std::exchange(other.size_, 0)`.
--- check test | The moved-from list reports size 0
[] { IntList a; IntList b; for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) b.push_front(i); a = std::move(b); return b.size() == 0 && a.size() == 3 && a.front() == 2; }()
?? A defaulted move copies size_ and leaves it in the source. Use std::exchange.
--- check test | Moving into a list that already has nodes replaces them
[] { IntList a; IntList b; a.push_front(1); a.push_front(2); b.push_front(9); a = std::move(b); return a.size() == 1 && a.front() == 9 && b.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | A moved-from list can be used again
[] { IntList a; IntList b; b.push_front(5); a = std::move(b); b.push_front(6); b.push_front(7); return b.size() == 2 && b.front() == 7 && a.front() == 5; }()
--- check test | Moving into a list of 1,000,000 nodes does not overflow the stack
[] { IntList big; for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) big.push_front(i); IntList small; small.push_front(1); big = std::move(small); return big.size() == 1 && big.front() == 1; }()
?? Assigning into head_ frees the old chain recursively. Call clear() first.

+++ practice | Restoring packets that arrive in reversed bursts
--- task
A radio link sends packets in bursts of `k`, and a hardware quirk delivers each full burst in reverse order. The receiver stores packet numbers in a singly linked list. Write the member function `void reverse_groups(std::size_t k)` for `class Packets` that reverses each consecutive group of `k` nodes in place:

- `1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8` with `k = 3` becomes `3 2 1 6 5 4 7 8`. A final group with fewer than `k` nodes stays as it is.
- `k` of 0 or 1 changes nothing. `k` equal to the size reverses the whole list; `k` bigger than the size changes nothing.
- Relink the nodes: no node is created or destroyed, and every value keeps its address. No recursion: a check uses 1,000,000 nodes.

Build the result through a link-to-link pointer. For each group, first count ahead to see whether `k` nodes remain; if so, reverse exactly `k` nodes the way the lesson's `reverse` does, attach the reversed group at the link, and move the link to the `next` of the group's new last node (the group's old first node).
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Packets {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    Packets() = default;
    ~Packets() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Packets(const Packets&) = delete;
    Packets& operator=(const Packets&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
    }
    int& front() { return head_->value; }
    std::vector<int> to_vector() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    void reverse_groups(std::size_t k) {}

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Packets {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

    Packets() = default;
    ~Packets() {
        while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);
    }
    Packets(const Packets&) = delete;
    Packets& operator=(const Packets&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        fresh->next = std::move(head_);
        head_ = std::move(fresh);
    }
    int& front() { return head_->value; }
    std::vector<int> to_vector() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    void reverse_groups(std::size_t k) {
        if (k <= 1) return;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> rest = std::move(head_);   // not yet processed
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;            // where the next group attaches
        while (rest) {
            std::size_t ahead = 0;
            for (const Node* p = rest.get(); p && ahead < k; p = p->next.get()) ++ahead;
            if (ahead < k) break;                         // a short last group stays as it is

            Node* group_last = rest.get();                // the group's first node ends up last
            std::unique_ptr<Node> group;
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < k; ++i) {
                std::unique_ptr<Node> after = std::move(rest->next);
                rest->next = std::move(group);
                group = std::move(rest);
                rest = std::move(after);
            }
            *link = std::move(group);
            link = &group_last->next;
        }
        *link = std::move(rest);
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> head_;
};
--- hint
Move the whole chain into a local `rest`, and keep `std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head_;` for where the next finished group goes. Each round, count up to `k` nodes ahead of `rest`; if there are fewer, stop and attach `rest` as it is.
--- hint
Before reversing a group, remember `Node* group_last = rest.get();`: that node will be last in the reversed group. Reverse `k` nodes off the front of `rest` into a local `group` (four moves per node, as in the lesson), then `*link = std::move(group);` and `link = &group_last->next;`. After the loop, `*link = std::move(rest);`.
--- check case | Bursts of 3, with a short last burst
[] { Packets p; for (int i = 8; i >= 1; --i) p.push_front(i); p.reverse_groups(3); return p.to_vector(); }()
=> std::vector<int>{3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4, 7, 8}
--- check test | k of 0 or 1 changes nothing
[] { Packets p; for (int i = 4; i >= 1; --i) p.push_front(i); p.reverse_groups(0); p.reverse_groups(1); return p.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{1, 2, 3, 4}; }()
--- check test | k equal to the size, and k bigger than the size
[] { Packets a; Packets b; for (int i = 4; i >= 1; --i) { a.push_front(i); b.push_front(i); } a.reverse_groups(4); b.reverse_groups(5); return a.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{4, 3, 2, 1} && b.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{1, 2, 3, 4}; }()
?? Count ahead first: a group with fewer than k nodes must not be reversed.
--- check test | An empty list, and groups that divide the list exactly
[] { Packets e; e.reverse_groups(3); Packets p; for (int i = 6; i >= 1; --i) p.push_front(i); p.reverse_groups(2); return e.to_vector().empty() && p.to_vector() == std::vector<int>{2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5}; }()
--- check test | Nodes are relinked, not copied: values keep their addresses
[] { Packets p; p.push_front(3); int* three = &p.front(); p.push_front(2); p.push_front(1); long long blocks = heap::live; p.reverse_groups(3); return heap::live == blocks && &p.front() == three && p.front() == 3; }()
--- check test | 1,000,000 packets in bursts of 4
[] { Packets p; for (int i = 999999; i >= 0; --i) p.push_front(i); p.reverse_groups(4); std::vector<int> v = p.to_vector(); return v.size() == 1000000 && v[0] == 3 && v[3] == 0 && v[4] == 7 && v[999999] == 999996; }()

+++ question | Why the default destruction crashes
--- ask
A list whose nodes own the next node through `std::unique_ptr`, with no destructor written, crashes when a list of a million nodes is destroyed. What is the cause?
--- choice
`unique_ptr` leaks nodes, and the program runs out of heap memory.
--- choice correct
Each node's destructor destroys its `next`, which runs the next node's destructor before the first one returns: a million nested calls overflow the call stack.
--- choice
The nodes are deleted twice, once by `head_` and once by the node before them.
--- choice
Destroying a million nodes takes longer than the time limit.
--- why
Destruction is recursive: `~unique_ptr` deletes the node, `~Node` destroys the node's `next`, which is another `~unique_ptr`, and so on. None of those calls returns until the end of the chain is reached, so the depth equals the length. The loop `while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_->next);` deletes one node at a time, each with an empty `next`, at constant stack depth.

+++ question | The one-line pop_front
--- ask
Why is `head_ = std::move(head_->next);` safe, even though the right side lives inside the node the assignment deletes?
--- choice
Because `std::move` copies `head_->next` somewhere safe before anything is deleted.
--- choice correct
A `unique_ptr` move assignment first releases the pointer out of `head_->next`, then stores it in `head_`, and only then deletes the old first node, whose `next` is by then empty.
--- choice
It is not safe; it only works by luck.
--- choice
Because `unique_ptr` never deletes anything during assignment.
--- why
`unique_ptr::operator=(unique_ptr&& r)` behaves like `reset(r.release())`. The argument is evaluated first: `release()` takes the second node's address out of the first node and leaves `nullptr` there. Then `reset` installs the new pointer and deletes the old node, which now owns nothing, so exactly one node is freed.

+++ question | The destructor that turned off moving
--- ask
A list class has a `std::unique_ptr<Node> head_`, a `std::size_t size_`, and a hand-written destructor, and nothing else special. What does `IntList b = std::move(a);` do?
--- choice
It moves `head_` and `size_`, because the compiler always writes the move constructor.
--- choice
It copies every node.
--- choice correct
It does not compile: declaring a destructor stops the compiler from writing the move operations, and the copy constructor is deleted because `unique_ptr` cannot be copied.
--- choice
It compiles, but leaves `a` pointing at the same nodes as `b`.
--- why
A user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor and move assignment. Normally a move would then fall back to copying, but the implicit copy constructor is deleted because the `unique_ptr` member cannot be copied. So there is no usable constructor, and you must declare the moves yourself, carefully, as the lesson showed.

=== dsacpp-06 | A doubly linked list: owning next, observing prev
--- teach
Last lesson each node owned the next one, and ownership ran in one direction, down the chain. A doubly linked list, which you built in DSA I, also links each node back to the one before it. Now there are two pointers between neighbours, and they cannot both own. This lesson settles which one owns and which one only **observes**, places a sentinel in a list where ownership only runs one way, and finds out what moving a list does to a sentinel that lives inside the list object.

### Two links, one owner

Each node gets two pointers:

```cpp fragment
struct Car {
    explicit Car(int n) : number(n) {}
    int number;
    std::unique_ptr<Car> next;   // owns the car behind it
    Car* prev = nullptr;         // observes the car in front of it
};
```

Why not make `prev` a `unique_ptr` too? Then each car would be owned twice, once by the car in front and once by the car behind, and deleted twice. A `unique_ptr` exists to rule that out.

Why not `std::shared_ptr` both ways? A `shared_ptr` counts its owners and deletes the object when the count reaches 0. Two neighbours that own each other keep each other's count above 0 forever, so when the list lets go of them, nothing ever frees them: a [[reference cycle|cycles]], and a leak.

The rule that settles it: **ownership must never form a loop.** Owning pointers form a chain (or a tree), and every pointer that goes back up the chain only observes. An observing pointer is safe as long as what it observes outlives it. Here that holds by construction: a node's `prev` points at the node that owns it, and an owner cannot be destroyed before what it owns is handed on.

### A sentinel inside the list

In DSA I you put a sentinel at each end, so that every real node always had a neighbour on both sides. With one-way ownership, a chain cannot loop back to its start, so the C++ version keeps **one** sentinel at the front, as an ordinary member of the list:

```cpp fragment
Car head_;             // the sentinel: part of the list object itself, never on the heap
Car* tail_ = &head_;   // observes the last real car, or the sentinel when there is none
```

The first real node is `head_.next`. Every real node now has a non-null `prev`: the node before it, or the sentinel. That removes every special case at the front. The back has no sentinel, so `tail_` observes the last node, and the list is empty exactly when `tail_ == &head_`. Writing `Car* tail_ = &head_;` in the class gives each new list that value; `&head_` is the address of the list's own member.

### Inserting after a node: four links, in order

To put a new node `n` after a node `a` (a real node or the sentinel), four links change. With `unique_ptr`s, the order is decided by ownership: nothing may be left without an owner, even for one line.

```cpp fragment
auto fresh = std::make_unique<Car>(42);
Car* n = fresh.get();              // keep the address: fresh is about to give the node away
n->prev = a;                       // 1. back link to a
n->next = std::move(a->next);      // 2. n takes over a's old successor (if any)
if (n->next) n->next->prev = n;    // 3. that successor now points back at n...
else tail_ = n;                    //    ...or n is the new last node
a->next = std::move(fresh);        // 4. a takes over n
```

Adding at the front is inserting after `&head_`. Adding at the back is inserting after `tail_`. Inserting before a real node `b` is inserting after `b->prev`, which is never null thanks to the sentinel. One piece of code, no special cases.

### Erasing a node: the last line frees it

To remove a real node `x`, let `a = x->prev`. Two links change, and the order matters even more:

1. Point the successor's `prev` back at `a`, or, if `x` is the last node, set `tail_ = a`.
2. `a->next = std::move(x->next);` The assignment first takes the successor out of `x`, then gives it to `a`, and only then deletes what `a->next` owned before, which is `x`.

After step 2, `x` is freed. Any use of `x` after that line, even reading `x->next`, is a use-after-free. So step 1 must come first, and step 2 must be the last line that touches `x`.

### Handles

`push_back` can return the new node's address, a `Node*`, as a **[[handle|handles]]**. Whoever holds it can later erase that node in O(1), with no search. Unlike a pointer into a vector, a handle survives every other change to the list: other nodes are inserted and erased around it, but this node never moves, because nodes are separate heap blocks. A handle becomes dangling only when its own node is erased. `std::list` makes the same promise for its iterators.

### Moving a list with a sentinel inside

Here is the trap that belongs to C++. The sentinel is a member, so it lives inside the list object. The first real node's `prev` holds the address of that member: `&other.head_`. Move the chain into another list, and that first node still points back at the *old* list's sentinel. Walking backwards from the new list runs into the other object.

So a move must **re-point** the first node's `prev` at the new sentinel, set `tail_` (which may have been `&other.head_`), and reset the source to an empty list: its `tail_` back to `&other.head_`, its size to 0. The compiler's default move does none of that; it copies `tail_` as a number and leaves `prev` alone. Any structure that stores addresses of its own members has this problem, and must write its moves.

### Why it is correct

Four invariants hold between any two calls:

1. **Ownership:** every real node is owned by exactly one `unique_ptr`: `head_.next`, or the `next` of the node before it. Following `next` from `head_` visits every node once and ends at `nullptr`.
2. **Back links:** for every node `x` with a successor, `x->next->prev == x`; the first real node's `prev` is `&head_`.
3. **Tail:** `tail_` is the last real node, or `&head_` when there is none.
4. **Size:** `size_` counts the real nodes.

**Inserting after `a`.** Step 2 moves `a`'s successor `b` into `n`, so `b` keeps exactly one owner; step 4 gives `n` its one owner, `a`. The back links become `n->prev == a` and `b->prev == n`, which is invariant 2 for the pairs (a, n) and (n, b). If there was no `b`, `n` is last, and step 3 sets `tail_`. Nothing else changes.

**Erasing `x`**, with `a = x->prev` and successor `b`. Step 1 makes `b->prev == a` (or `tail_ == a` when `x` was last). Step 2 gives `b` to `a` and frees `x`, which owns nothing by then. Now `a` and `b` are neighbours with both links right, and `x` is gone from both chains.

**Moving** takes the whole chain, then restores invariant 2 for the first node and invariant 3 for both lists.

### What it costs

| operation | time |
|---|---|
| push_front, push_back, pop_front, pop_back | O(1) |
| insert before or after a handle, erase a handle | O(1) |
| find by value | O(n) |
| walk forwards or backwards | O(n) |
| move | O(1) |
| copy, destruction | O(n), with O(1) stack if done with loops |

Each node carries two pointers, 16 bytes on a 64-bit machine, on top of its value and the allocator's bookkeeping. That is the price of O(1) erase from a handle.

### Where it is used

- An **LRU cache** keeps entries in a doubly linked list in order of use, with a hash map from key to node handle. A hit moves the node to the front in O(1); eviction erases the last node.
- The Linux kernel's `list_head` is a circular doubly linked list with a sentinel, embedded directly inside the structures it links: an [[intrusive list|intrusive]].
- Text editors, schedulers' queues of ready tasks, and `std::list`, whose `splice` moves a node from one list to another in O(1).

**Watch out:**

- Touching `x` after `a->next = std::move(x->next);`. That line freed it.
- Forgetting `tail_` when the last node is erased or a new last node is added. The next `push_back` then writes through a pointer to a freed node.
- Moving a list without re-pointing the first node's `prev`. The list works forwards and breaks backwards, which makes the bug easy to miss.
- Keeping a handle to a node after erasing it.
- Linking nodes both ways with `shared_ptr`: the cycle never frees.

::: context cycles Why counting owners fails on loops
Reference counting keeps, next to each object, the number of `shared_ptr`s that point at it, and deletes the object when the number falls to 0. It is simple and prompt, but blind to loops: two objects that point at each other each have a count of at least 1, even when nothing else in the program can reach them. Python uses reference counting too, and adds a separate cycle collector that looks for such islands. C++ has none, so its answer is `std::weak_ptr`, a pointer that observes without counting, or, as here, a plain raw pointer for the back direction.
:::

::: context handles Handles and iterator stability
The standard containers differ sharply in what survives a change. In a `std::vector`, an insert can invalidate every iterator. In a `std::list`, an insert invalidates nothing, and an erase invalidates only iterators to the erased element. That is why programs that must hold on to positions for a long time, like an LRU cache or a scheduler that cancels timers, use lists or node-based maps even though walking them is slower. The handle is only as good as the promise that its node still exists.
:::

::: context intrusive Links inside the data
An intrusive list stores the `next` and `prev` pointers inside the objects themselves, instead of wrapping each object in a separate node. The Linux kernel does this everywhere: a process structure contains several `list_head` members, so the same process can sit on several lists at once, such as its parent's list of children and the list of all tasks, without a single extra allocation. The price is that the object has to know about the lists it can be in. Flight software likes the idea for the same reason as the kernel: no allocation at run time.

--- task
Write `class DList`, a doubly linked list of `int`s. No `main`. The node type is given and public, because callers hold `Node*` handles:

```cpp fragment
struct Node {
    explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
    int value;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> next;   // owns the next node
    Node* prev = nullptr;         // observes the node before
};
```

The list keeps a sentinel `Node head_;` as a member, `Node* tail_` observing the last real node (or `&head_` when empty), and `std::size_t size_`. Keep the heap ledger as it is.

- `Node* push_front(int x)` and `Node* push_back(int x)` add a node and return its handle.
- `Node* insert_before(Node* pos, int x)` puts a new node just before the real node `pos`, and returns its handle.
- `void erase(Node* x)` removes the real node `x` in O(1).
- `bool pop_front()` and `bool pop_back()` remove the first or last node, or return `false` on an empty list.
- `std::size_t size() const`; `std::vector<int> forward() const` (first to last, following `next`); `std::vector<int> backward() const` (last to first, following `prev` from `tail_`).
- `~DList()` frees the nodes with a loop: a list of 1,000,000 nodes must not overflow the stack.
- `DList(const DList& other)` and `DList& operator=(const DList& other)`: deep copies; `l = l` changes nothing.
- `DList(DList&& other) noexcept` and `DList& operator=(DList&& other) noexcept`: take the nodes in O(1), re-point the first node's `prev` at this list's sentinel, set `tail_` correctly, and leave `other` a valid empty list that can be used again.

Handles must stay valid while other nodes are inserted and erased.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

public:

        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}

        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;   // owns the next node
        Node* prev = nullptr;         // observes the node before
    };

    DList() = default;

    Node* push_front(int x) { return nullptr; }
    Node* push_back(int x) { return nullptr; }

    bool pop_back() { return false; }
