--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;   // owns the next node
        Node* prev = nullptr;         // observes the node before
    };

    DList() = default;

    ~DList() { clear(); }

    DList(const DList& other) {
        for (const Node* p = other.head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) push_back(p->value);
    }

    DList& operator=(const DList& other) {
        DList copy(other);        // made first, so l = l is safe
        *this = std::move(copy);
        return *this;
    }

    DList(DList&& other) noexcept { take(other); }

    DList& operator=(DList&& other) noexcept {
        if (this != &other) {
            clear();
            take(other);
        }
        return *this;
    }

    Node* push_front(int x) { return insert_after(&head_, x); }
    Node* push_back(int x) { return insert_after(tail_, x); }
    Node* insert_before(Node* pos, int x) { return insert_after(pos->prev, x); }

    void erase(Node* x) {
        Node* a = x->prev;
        if (x->next) x->next->prev = a;
        else tail_ = a;
        --size_;
        a->next = std::move(x->next);   // frees x: nothing may touch x after this line
    }

    bool pop_front() {
        if (size_ == 0) return false;
        erase(head_.next.get());
        return true;
    }

    bool pop_back() {
        if (size_ == 0) return false;
        erase(tail_);
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    std::vector<int> backward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

private:
    // Puts a new node right after a (a real node or the sentinel) and returns it.
    Node* insert_after(Node* a, int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = a;
        n->next = std::move(a->next);
        if (n->next) n->next->prev = n;
        else tail_ = n;
        a->next = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
        return n;
    }

    void clear() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);   // one node at a time
        tail_ = &head_;
        size_ = 0;
    }

    // Takes other's nodes; this list must be empty.
    void take(DList& other) {
        head_.next = std::move(other.head_.next);
        if (head_.next) {
            head_.next->prev = &head_;   // it pointed back at other's sentinel
            tail_ = other.tail_;
        } else {
            tail_ = &head_;
        }
        size_ = std::exchange(other.size_, 0);
        other.tail_ = &other.head_;
    }

    Node head_;            // the sentinel
    Node* tail_ = &head_;  // the last real node, or &head_ when empty
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint

--- hint
`erase(x)`: let `a = x->prev`; if `x` has a successor, point its `prev` at `a`, otherwise set `tail_ = a`; lower the size; and end with `a->next = std::move(x->next);`, which frees `x`. The destructor loops `while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);`.
--- hint

Move assignment clears this list first. The copy constructor pushes back each value of `other`; copy assignment makes a copy and move-assigns it.

+++ practice | A deque built from owning and observing links
--- task
Write `class Deque`, a double-ended queue of `int`s built as a doubly linked list: each node's `next` is a `std::unique_ptr` that owns the following node, and each node's `prev` is a raw pointer that only observes. Use a sentinel member `Node head_;` and a raw `Node* tail_` that observes the last node (or `&head_` when empty), as in the lesson. Copying and moving are deleted.

- `void push_front(int x)` and `void push_back(int x)`.
- `std::optional<int> pop_front()` and `std::optional<int> pop_back()` remove and return the value at that end, or return `std::nullopt` (no value) when the deque is empty.
- `std::optional<int> front() const` and `std::optional<int> back() const` look without removing, with `std::nullopt` when empty.
- `std::size_t size() const`, and `std::vector<int> backward() const` (last to first, following `prev`).
- `~Deque()` frees the nodes with a loop.

Keep the heap ledger as it is.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Deque {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    Deque() = default;
    Deque(const Deque&) = delete;
    Deque& operator=(const Deque&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) {}
    void push_back(int x) {}
    std::optional<int> pop_front() { return std::nullopt; }
    std::optional<int> pop_back() { return std::nullopt; }
    std::optional<int> front() const { return std::nullopt; }
    std::optional<int> back() const { return std::nullopt; }
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> backward() const { return {}; }

private:
    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class Deque {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    Deque() = default;
    ~Deque() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    Deque(const Deque&) = delete;
    Deque& operator=(const Deque&) = delete;

    void push_front(int x) { insert_after(&head_, x); }
    void push_back(int x) { insert_after(tail_, x); }

    std::optional<int> pop_front() {
        if (size_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        int v = head_.next->value;
        erase(head_.next.get());
        return v;
    }

    std::optional<int> pop_back() {
        if (size_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        int v = tail_->value;
        erase(tail_);
        return v;
    }

    std::optional<int> front() const {
        if (size_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        return head_.next->value;
    }

    std::optional<int> back() const {
        if (size_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        return tail_->value;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    std::vector<int> backward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

private:
    void insert_after(Node* a, int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = a;
        n->next = std::move(a->next);
        if (n->next) n->next->prev = n;
        else tail_ = n;
        a->next = std::move(fresh);
        ++size_;
    }

    void erase(Node* x) {
        Node* a = x->prev;
        if (x->next) x->next->prev = a;
        else tail_ = a;
        --size_;
        a->next = std::move(x->next);   // frees x
    }

    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Two private helpers do all the work: `insert_after(Node* a, int x)` with the lesson's four links, and `erase(Node* x)` that fixes the successor's `prev` (or `tail_`) and ends with `a->next = std::move(x->next);`. `push_front` inserts after `&head_`, `push_back` after `tail_`.
--- hint
A pop must read the value **before** erasing, because erasing frees the node. An empty deque is `size_ == 0`; return `std::nullopt` then. Returning a plain `int` from a function whose type is `std::optional<int>` wraps it automatically.
--- check test | Both ends, both ways
[] { Deque d; d.push_back(2); d.push_front(1); d.push_back(3); return d.front() == 1 && d.back() == 3 && d.size() == 3 && d.backward() == std::vector<int>{3, 2, 1}; }()
--- check test | Pops return the values in order, then nothing
[] { Deque d; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; ++i) d.push_back(i); std::optional<int> a = d.pop_front(); std::optional<int> b = d.pop_back(); std::optional<int> c = d.pop_back(); std::optional<int> e = d.pop_front(); return a == 1 && b == 4 && c == 3 && e == 2 && !d.pop_front().has_value() && !d.pop_back().has_value() && d.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | An empty deque has no front or back, and can be refilled
[] { Deque d; bool none = !d.front() && !d.back() && d.backward().empty(); d.push_front(5); d.pop_back(); d.push_back(6); return none && d.front() == 6 && d.back() == 6 && d.backward() == std::vector<int>{6}; }()
?? When the last node goes, tail_ must return to &head_.
--- check test | 1,000,000 nodes, and every node is freed

+++ practice | Splicing a node from one list to another
--- task
`std::list::splice` moves a node from one list to another in O(1), without allocating: the node itself changes lists, so a handle to it stays valid. Write the member function `void splice_back(DList& from, Node* x)` for the given `class DList`:

- `x` is a real node of `from`, and `from` is a different list from this one.
- Take `x` out of `from` (fixing `from`'s links, its `tail_` and its size) and attach it at the end of this list (fixing this list's links, `tail_` and size).
- Never create or destroy a node: `x` keeps its address and its value.

The ownership move is the heart of it: `x` is owned by `x->prev->next`. Move that `unique_ptr` into a local first, so `x` always has an owner, then relink both lists around it.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    DList() = default;
    ~DList() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;

    Node* push_back(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = n;
        ++size_;
        return n;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }
    std::vector<int> backward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    void splice_back(DList& from, Node* x) {}

private:
    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    DList() = default;
    ~DList() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;

    Node* push_back(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = n;
        ++size_;
        return n;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }
    std::vector<int> backward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    void splice_back(DList& from, Node* x) {
        Node* a = x->prev;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> taken = std::move(a->next);   // x's owner is now this local
        a->next = std::move(x->next);                        // a takes x's successor
        if (a->next) a->next->prev = a;
        else from.tail_ = a;
        --from.size_;

        x->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(taken);
        tail_ = x;
        ++size_;
    }

private:
    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Let `a = x->prev`. First `std::unique_ptr<Node> taken = std::move(a->next);`: now a local owns `x`, and nothing is freed. Then `a->next = std::move(x->next);` closes the gap in `from`; point the successor's `prev` back at `a`, or set `from.tail_ = a` if `x` was last, and lower `from.size_`.
--- hint
To attach at this list's end: `x->prev = tail_;`, `tail_->next = std::move(taken);`, `tail_ = x;`, and raise `size_`. A member function can use the private members of another object of the same class, so `from.tail_` and `from.size_` are allowed.

?? Move x's owning unique_ptr into a local before relinking, so nothing frees x.

+++ practice | An LRU cache
--- task
A ground station caches the most recently used telemetry records and throws away the one used longest ago when the cache is full: a **least recently used** (LRU) cache. Every operation must be O(1).

Write `class LruCache`:

- `explicit LruCache(std::size_t capacity)`: the cache holds at most `capacity` entries (always at least 1).
- `std::optional<int> get(int key)`: the value stored for `key`, or `std::nullopt`. A hit makes that entry the most recently used.
- `void put(int key, int value)`: store the value. If the key is already there, update its value; either way the entry becomes the most recently used. If a new key makes the cache hold more than `capacity` entries, remove the least recently used entry.
- `std::size_t size() const`, and `std::vector<int> keys() const`: the keys from most to least recently used.

Keep the entries in a doubly linked list in order of use, most recent at the front, with owning `next`, observing `prev`, a sentinel and a tail pointer, as in the lesson. Keep a `std::unordered_map<int, Node*>` from each key to its node's handle, so that finding an entry and moving it to the front are both O(1). Free the nodes with a loop in the destructor.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class LruCache {
public:
    explicit LruCache(std::size_t capacity) : capacity_(capacity) {}
    std::optional<int> get(int key) { return std::nullopt; }
    void put(int key, int value) {}
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    std::vector<int> keys() const { return {}; }

private:
    std::size_t capacity_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class LruCache {
public:
    explicit LruCache(std::size_t capacity) : capacity_(capacity) {}

    ~LruCache() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    LruCache(const LruCache&) = delete;
    LruCache& operator=(const LruCache&) = delete;

    std::optional<int> get(int key) {
        auto it = where_.find(key);
        if (it == where_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        Node* n = it->second;
        to_front(n);
        return n->value;
    }

    void put(int key, int value) {
        auto it = where_.find(key);
        if (it != where_.end()) {
            it->second->value = value;
            to_front(it->second);
            return;
        }
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(key, value);
        where_[key] = fresh.get();
        link_after(&head_, std::move(fresh));
        if (where_.size() > capacity_) {
            Node* old = tail_;
            where_.erase(old->key);
            unlink(old);   // the returned owner dies here, freeing the node
        }
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return where_.size(); }

    std::vector<int> keys() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->key);
        return out;
    }

private:
    struct Node {
        Node() = default;
        Node(int k, int v) : key(k), value(v) {}
        int key = 0;
        int value = 0;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    // Takes n out of the list and hands back the unique_ptr that owned it.
    std::unique_ptr<Node> unlink(Node* n) {
        Node* a = n->prev;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> owned = std::move(a->next);
        a->next = std::move(n->next);
        if (a->next) a->next->prev = a;
        else tail_ = a;
        return owned;
    }

    void link_after(Node* a, std::unique_ptr<Node> fresh) {
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = a;
        n->next = std::move(a->next);
        if (n->next) n->next->prev = n;
        else tail_ = n;
        a->next = std::move(fresh);
    }

    void to_front(Node* n) {
        if (head_.next.get() != n) link_after(&head_, unlink(n));
    }

    std::size_t capacity_;
    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::unordered_map<int, Node*> where_;   // key -> handle of its node
};
--- hint
Give the node a key and a value. Write two list helpers: `unlink(Node* n)`, which takes `n` out and returns the `unique_ptr` that owned it (so the node survives), and `link_after(Node* a, std::unique_ptr<Node> n)`, which puts it back after `a`. Moving to the front is `link_after(&head_, unlink(n))`.
--- hint
`get`: look the key up in the map; on a hit, move its node to the front and return the value. `put`: on a hit, update and move to the front. On a miss, make a node at the front and record its handle in the map; then, if the map holds more than `capacity_` entries, the least recently used entry is `tail_`: erase its key from the map, then unlink it and let the returned `unique_ptr` free it.
--- check case | The classic sequence
[] { LruCache c(2); c.put(1, 10); c.put(2, 20); std::vector<int> out; out.push_back(c.get(1).value_or(-1)); c.put(3, 30); out.push_back(c.get(2).value_or(-1)); out.push_back(c.get(3).value_or(-1)); c.put(4, 40); out.push_back(c.get(1).value_or(-1)); out.push_back(c.get(3).value_or(-1)); out.push_back(c.get(4).value_or(-1)); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{10, -1, 30, -1, 30, 40}
?? A get must move the entry to the front, so that the eviction takes the entry used longest ago.
--- check test | Updating a key moves it to the front without growing
[] { LruCache c(3); c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2); c.put(3, 3); c.put(1, 100); c.put(4, 4); return c.size() == 3 && c.get(1) == 100 && !c.get(2).has_value() && c.keys() == std::vector<int>{1, 4, 3}; }()
--- check test | Capacity 1, and a miss changes nothing
[] { LruCache c(1); bool miss = !c.get(5).has_value() && c.size() == 0; c.put(5, 50); c.put(6, 60); return miss && c.size() == 1 && !c.get(5).has_value() && c.get(6) == 60 && c.keys() == std::vector<int>{6}; }()
--- check test | 200,000 operations on a cache of 50,000 entries
[] { LruCache c(50000); unsigned x = 7; long long hits = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { x = x * 1103515245u + 12345u; int key = int((x >> 8) % 80000); if (i % 3 == 0) { if (c.get(key)) ++hits; } else { c.put(key, i); } } std::vector<int> k = c.keys(); return c.size() == 50000 && k.size() == 50000 && hits > 0; }()
?? Every step must be O(1): find nodes through the map, never by walking the list.

+++ practice | Erasing a range of nodes
--- task
Write the member function `std::size_t erase_range(Node* first, Node* last)` for the given `class DList`. It removes the nodes in the half-open range `[first, last)`: from `first` up to, but not including, `last`. It returns how many nodes it removed.

- `first` is a real node of the list, or `nullptr`, meaning the end.
- `last` is a real node at or after `first`, or `nullptr`, meaning "to the end of the list".
- When `first == last`, the range is empty: nothing happens, and the result is 0.

Every case must leave the links right in both directions: a range at the front, in the middle, at the end (`last` is `nullptr`, so `tail_` changes), the whole list, and an empty range. The removed nodes must be freed without recursion: a check erases 1,000,000 nodes at once.

A clean way: let `a = first->prev`. Move `a->next` (the owner of `first`) into a local `doomed`. If `last` is a real node, the node just before it owns it: move that `next` into `a->next` and point `last->prev` at `a`. Otherwise `a` is the new last node. Then free `doomed` with the loop, counting as you go.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    DList() = default;
    ~DList() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;

    Node* push_back(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = n;
        ++size_;
        return n;

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);

        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    std::size_t erase_range(Node* first, Node* last) { return 0; }

    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;

--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    DList() = default;
    ~DList() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;

    Node* push_back(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = n;
        ++size_;
        return n;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }
    std::vector<int> backward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

    std::size_t erase_range(Node* first, Node* last) {
        if (first == last) return 0;
        Node* a = first->prev;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> doomed = std::move(a->next);   // first and everything after it
        if (last) {
            a->next = std::move(last->prev->next);           // cut the doomed chain just before last
            last->prev = a;
        } else {
            tail_ = a;
        }
        std::size_t removed = 0;
        while (doomed) {
            doomed = std::move(doomed->next);                // one node at a time
            ++removed;
        }
        size_ -= removed;
        return removed;
    }

private:
    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Handle `first == last` first: return 0. Otherwise `a = first->prev` is never null, thanks to the sentinel. `std::unique_ptr<Node> doomed = std::move(a->next);` detaches `first` and everything after it in one move.
--- hint
If `last` is a real node, `last->prev->next` owns it, and `last->prev` is inside the doomed chain: `a->next = std::move(last->prev->next);` takes `last` back and ends the doomed chain there; then `last->prev = a;`. If `last` is `nullptr`, set `tail_ = a`. Free `doomed` with `while (doomed) doomed = std::move(doomed->next);`, counting, and take the count off the size.

[] { DList l; std::vector<DList::Node*> h; for (int i = 0; i < 6; ++i) h.push_back(l.push_back(i)); std::size_t n = l.erase_range(h[1], h[4]); return n == 3 && l.forward() == std::vector<int>{0, 4, 5} && l.backward() == std::vector<int>{5, 4, 0} && l.size() == 3; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the moved list that points back at its old home
--- task
`class DList` keeps its sentinel `head_` as a member. Its move constructor takes the other list's nodes and fixes `tail_`, but moving still breaks the list: after `DList b(std::move(a));`, removing `b`'s first node leaves that node in `b` and hands the rest of the chain to `a`, and walking `b` backwards runs off into `a`.

Find the bug in the move constructor and fix it. It is one missing line.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    DList() = default;
    ~DList() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;

    DList(DList&& other) noexcept : size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)) {
        head_.next = std::move(other.head_.next);
        tail_ = head_.next ? other.tail_ : &head_;
        other.tail_ = &other.head_;
    }

    void push_back(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = n;
        ++size_;
    }

    bool pop_front() {
        if (size_ == 0) return false;
        Node* x = head_.next.get();
        Node* a = x->prev;
        if (x->next) x->next->prev = a;
        else tail_ = a;
        --size_;
        a->next = std::move(x->next);
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }
    std::vector<int> backward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

private:
    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    DList() = default;
    ~DList() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;

    DList(DList&& other) noexcept : size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)) {
        head_.next = std::move(other.head_.next);
        if (head_.next) head_.next->prev = &head_;   // it still pointed at other's sentinel
        tail_ = head_.next ? other.tail_ : &head_;
        other.tail_ = &other.head_;
    }

    void push_back(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = n;
        ++size_;
    }

    bool pop_front() {
        if (size_ == 0) return false;
        Node* x = head_.next.get();
        Node* a = x->prev;
        if (x->next) x->next->prev = a;
        else tail_ = a;
        --size_;
        a->next = std::move(x->next);
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);

        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }

private:
    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Before the move, the first real node's `prev` held `&other.head_`, the address of a member of the *other* object. What does it hold after the move constructor finishes?
--- hint
When there is a first node, point its `prev` at this list's own sentinel: `head_.next->prev = &head_;`.

+++ practice | Sorting a doubly linked list by relinking
--- task
Merge sort is the natural sort for linked lists: it needs no jumping to positions, only walking and relinking. Write the member function `void sort()` for the given `class DList`. It sorts the values from smallest to largest by **relinking nodes**, never creating or destroying one, so every handle still points at the same value afterwards. It must be **stable** (nodes with equal values keep their order) and O(n log n): a check sorts 200,000 nodes.

A clean plan:

1. Move the whole chain out of `head_.next` into a local `std::unique_ptr<Node>`.
2. Sort it as a **singly** linked chain, following only `next`: a recursive merge sort that splits a chain of `n` nodes after `n / 2` of them, sorts both halves, and merges them with a link-to-link pointer. Recursion depth is only about log₂ n. On ties, take from the left half.
3. Put the sorted chain back in `head_.next`, then walk it once to set every `prev` (the first node's `prev` is `&head_`) and `tail_`.

`nodes()` returns the node addresses from first to last; the checks use it to test stability.
--- starter

#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>

void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;

        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p);

--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: counts memory blocks from operator new that are not yet given back.
// std::allocator uses operator new. The checks read heap::live. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class DList {
public:
    struct Node {
        explicit Node(int v = 0) : value(v) {}
        int value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
        Node* prev = nullptr;
    };

    DList() = default;
    ~DList() {
        while (head_.next) head_.next = std::move(head_.next->next);
    }
    DList(const DList&) = delete;
    DList& operator=(const DList&) = delete;

    Node* push_back(int x) {
        auto fresh = std::make_unique<Node>(x);
        Node* n = fresh.get();
        n->prev = tail_;
        tail_->next = std::move(fresh);
        tail_ = n;
        ++size_;
        return n;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::vector<int> forward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }
    std::vector<int> backward() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        for (const Node* p = tail_; p != &head_; p = p->prev) out.push_back(p->value);
        return out;
    }
    std::vector<const Node*> nodes() const {
        std::vector<const Node*> out;
        for (const Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out.push_back(p);
        return out;
    }

    void sort() {
        head_.next = merge_sort(std::move(head_.next), size_);
        Node* before = &head_;   // re-thread the back links in one pass
        for (Node* p = head_.next.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) {
            p->prev = before;
            before = p;
        }
        tail_ = before;
    }

private:
    // Sorts a singly linked chain of n nodes, following next only.
    static std::unique_ptr<Node> merge_sort(std::unique_ptr<Node> chain, std::size_t n) {
        if (n <= 1) return chain;
        std::size_t half = n / 2;
        Node* cut = chain.get();
        for (std::size_t i = 1; i < half; ++i) cut = cut->next.get();
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right = std::move(cut->next);
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left = merge_sort(std::move(chain), half);
        right = merge_sort(std::move(right), n - half);

        std::unique_ptr<Node> out;
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &out;
        while (left && right) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node>& take = right->value < left->value ? right : left;   // ties from the left
            *link = std::move(take);
            take = std::move((*link)->next);
            link = &(*link)->next;
        }
        *link = left ? std::move(left) : std::move(right);
        return out;
    }

    Node head_;
    Node* tail_ = &head_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Write a private static helper `std::unique_ptr<Node> merge_sort(std::unique_ptr<Node> chain, std::size_t n)`. With `n <= 1` it returns the chain as it is. Otherwise walk `n / 2 - 1` steps to the node where the left half ends, move its `next` into `right`, and sort both halves recursively.
--- hint
Merge with `std::unique_ptr<Node> out;` and `std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &out;`: take from `right` only when `right->value < left->value`, move the taken node to `*link`, give its `next` back to the list it came from, and step `link` on. Attach the leftovers. In `sort()`, store the result in `head_.next`, then walk it setting `prev` and finally `tail_`.
--- check case | A small list sorts
[] { DList l; for (int x : {5, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6}) l.push_back(x); l.sort(); std::vector<int> v = l.forward(); for (int x : l.backward()) v.push_back(x); return v; }()
=> std::vector<int>{1, 2, 5, 5, 6, 9, 9, 6, 5, 5, 2, 1}
?? After sorting by next, walk the chain once to set every prev and tail_.
--- check test | Stable: equal values keep their order, and handles keep their values
[] { DList l; auto* a = l.push_back(2); auto* b = l.push_back(1); auto* c = l.push_back(2); auto* d = l.push_back(1); l.sort(); std::vector<const DList::Node*> n = l.nodes(); return n == std::vector<const DList::Node*>{b, d, a, c} && a->value == 2 && d->value == 1; }()
--- check test | Empty, one node, sorted and reversed input
[] { DList e; e.sort(); DList one; one.push_back(4); one.sort(); DList up; DList down; for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) { up.push_back(i); down.push_back(19 - i); } up.sort(); down.sort(); one.push_back(1); return e.size() == 0 && e.backward().empty() && one.forward() == std::vector<int>{4, 1} && up.forward() == down.forward() && down.backward()[0] == 19 && down.backward()[19] == 0; }()
--- check test | 200,000 nodes, relinked without making or freeing any
[] { DList l; unsigned x = 99; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { x = x * 1103515245u + 12345u; l.push_back(int((x >> 8) % 1000000)); } long long blocks = heap::live; l.sort(); long long after = heap::live; std::vector<int> f = l.forward(); std::vector<int> b = l.backward(); bool sorted = f.size() == 200000 && b.size() == 200000; for (std::size_t i = 1; i < f.size() && sorted; ++i) sorted = f[i - 1] <= f[i]; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < f.size() && sorted; ++i) sorted = f[i] == b[f.size() - 1 - i]; return sorted && after == blocks; }()
?? An O(n²) sort takes far too long here. Merge sort the chain by next, then fix prev.

+++ question | Which pointer may own
--- ask
In a doubly linked list, why is `next` a `std::unique_ptr` and `prev` a raw pointer, rather than both being `std::shared_ptr`?
--- choice
`shared_ptr` is slower, and that is the only difference.
--- choice correct
Two neighbours holding `shared_ptr`s to each other form a cycle: each keeps the other's count above zero, so neither is ever freed. Ownership must run one way; the back pointer only observes.
--- choice
A raw pointer is needed because `prev` can be null, and `shared_ptr` cannot.
--- choice
`unique_ptr` cannot point backwards.
--- why
Reference counting frees an object when its count reaches 0, and a cycle never reaches 0 on its own. Making ownership a chain (each node owned only by the one before it) and every back link an observing raw pointer keeps the ownership graph free of loops, so destroying the head frees everything. `std::weak_ptr` is the library's other answer: it observes a `shared_ptr` without counting.

+++ question | The order inside erase
--- ask
A student writes `erase(Node* x)` with the freeing move first:

```cpp fragment
Node* a = x->prev;
a->next = std::move(x->next);
if (x->next) x->next->prev = a;
else tail_ = a;
```

What goes wrong?
--- choice
Nothing: the order of the lines does not matter.
--- choice
It leaks `x`, because nothing deletes it.
--- choice correct
The second line frees `x`, so the third line reads freed memory. Even if those bytes were still intact, `x->next` has just been emptied by the move, so the code would always set `tail_ = a` and never fix the successor's `prev`.
--- choice
It deletes the successor together with `x`.
--- why
`a->next = std::move(x->next);` first releases the successor out of `x`, leaving `x->next` empty, then hands the successor to `a` and deletes `x`. Everything after that line that mentions `x` is a use-after-free, and its logic is wrong too. The lesson's order fixes the successor's `prev` (or `tail_`) first, so that the line that frees `x` is the last line that mentions it.

+++ question | Moving a list that holds its own sentinel
--- ask
`DList` keeps its sentinel as a member, `Node head_;`. Its move constructor takes `other.head_.next` and sets `tail_`, but nothing else. Which structure is left broken?
--- choice
The source list, which still owns the nodes.
--- choice correct
The first node's `prev`, which still holds `&other.head_`, the address of the old list's sentinel.
--- choice
The last node's `next`, which now points at the old list.
--- choice
Nothing: moving a `unique_ptr` moves everything it owns.
--- why
Moving the `unique_ptr` moves ownership of the chain, but the chain stores one address of the *old* object: the first node's back link to its sentinel. A walk backwards, or an erase of the first node, then reaches into the other list. Any object that stores addresses of its own members must fix them up when it is moved.

=== dsacpp-07 | A ring buffer: a fixed-capacity queue in an array
--- teach
Last lesson's doubly linked list asked the heap for a new node on every insert. In DSA I you built a circular buffer in Python: a queue that reuses a list's slots by wrapping round to the start. This lesson builds it again in C++, the way device drivers and flight software do. The capacity is fixed when the program is compiled, the slots live inside the object itself, and no operation ever asks for memory. So every operation is O(1) in the **worst case**, not just on average.

### The picture: a carousel with numbered places

A baggage carousel has a fixed number of places, and the belt goes round. Bags go on at one point and come off at another. Nobody builds a longer belt on a busy day: when every place is taken, the next bag has to wait. A **ring buffer** is that belt, in memory.

### The definition

A **ring buffer** of capacity N is a first-in, first-out queue that holds at most N items in an array of exactly N slots, and treats slot N − 1 as if slot 0 came right after it. It keeps two numbers:

- `head`: the slot of the front item, the oldest one;
- `count`: how many items it holds, from 0 to N.

The **invariant** is the one from DSA I: *the items, from front to back, are in slots (head + i) mod N for i = 0, 1, …, count − 1, and 0 ≤ count ≤ N.* Here "mod" is the remainder after dividing. Push writes into slot (head + count) mod N and adds one to count. Pop reads slot head, moves head one slot on, and takes one from count.

In everyday words: the items sit in a row that may run off the end of the array and carry on at the start, and the two numbers say where the row begins and how long it is.

DSA I proved that this invariant gives first-in, first-out order: push puts the new item at position count, just behind the back, and pop removes position 0, after which every other item's position drops by one, so items leave in exactly the order they arrived. What C++ adds is everything around it: what kind of thing N is, where the slots live, what happens to an item after it leaves, how `%` behaves, and how to say "full" when exceptions are turned off.

### The capacity as a template parameter

Your templates so far took types, like `Vector<T>`. A template can also take a value. A **non-type template parameter** is a template parameter that is a constant value, such as a `std::size_t`, instead of a type:

```cpp fragment
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Carousel {
    // N can be used here like any constant
};

Carousel<double, 16> belt;   // T is double, N is 16
```

N must be a [[compile-time constant|compile-time]]: a value the compiler knows while it compiles, such as `16` or a `constexpr` variable, never a number read while the program runs. `Carousel<double, 16>` and `Carousel<double, 32>` are two different types, and in each one the number is built into the machine code.

### std::array: the slots live inside the object

`std::array<T, N>` from `<array>` is a fixed-size array of N elements of type T. It is a thin wrapper round a plain C array: it stores nothing but the elements, and it never touches the heap. Its size is a template parameter too, so it fits a ring buffer exactly.

```cpp
#include <array>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::array<int, 5> bays{};    // five ints, all zero
    bays[2] = 7;
    std::cout << bays.size() << " " << bays[2] << "\n";   // 5 7
    std::cout << sizeof(bays) << "\n";                     // 20
}
```

The `{}` after the name sets every element to zero. Leave it out, and a local `std::array<int, 5>` holds whatever bytes happened to be in that memory. `sizeof` gives the size of an object in bytes: here 5 elements of 4 bytes each, and nothing else.

Because the slots are part of the object, a ring buffer declared inside a function lives entirely on the [[stack|stack-size]], and one that is a member of a class lives inside that class. Nothing is allocated when it is made, and nothing is freed when it goes away.

That choice has two costs:

- The array constructs all N elements up front, so T needs a default constructor. (Lesson 3's `Vector<T>` coped with a T that has no default constructor; this lesson keeps T default-constructible, to stay on the ring itself.)
- A big N makes a big object. A ring of a million `double`s is 8 MB, too big for a stack.

### Full and empty are answers, not errors

This course compiles with exceptions turned off, and so does most flight software. So "the buffer is full" and "the buffer is empty" must be ordinary return values:

- `push` returns `bool`: `true` if it stored the item, `false` if the buffer was full and nothing changed.
- `pop` returns `std::optional<T>`: the front item, or `std::nullopt` when the buffer is empty.

A caller who ignores push's `bool` silently loses data. C++ can warn about that. Mark the function with the attribute `[[nodiscard]]`, and the compiler [[complains whenever its result is thrown away|nodiscard]].

```cpp fragment
[[nodiscard]] bool send(const Frame& f);   // a warning if the caller ignores the bool
```

### Moving items in, and letting go of them on the way out

A queue of strings or `unique_ptr`s should move what it can, as in lesson 2. So push comes in two versions, called **overloads**: `push(const T&)` copies an item the caller keeps, and `push(T&&)` moves from an item the caller is giving away. With only the first, a ring of `std::unique_ptr<int>` would not even compile, because a `unique_ptr` cannot be copied.

Pop has a quieter job. Once an item has left the queue, the buffer must not keep any part of it alive. Moving out of the slot usually empties it, but not for every type: a type that has no move operations is copied instead, and the copy left in the slot keeps holding its memory, file or shared object until the slot happens to be reused. So after moving the item out, pop puts a fresh `T{}` into the slot.

You can watch a slot let go. A `std::shared_ptr` is a smart pointer that may have several owners at once; `use_count()` says how many there are right now.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

int main() {
    auto frame = std::make_shared<int>(42);
    std::shared_ptr<int> parked = frame;         // a second owner, like a copy left in a slot
    std::cout << frame.use_count() << "\n";      // 2
    parked = std::shared_ptr<int>{};             // overwrite it with an empty one
    std::cout << frame.use_count() << "\n";      // 1
}
```

### C++'s `%` is not Python's `%`

Stepping forward is easy: `(head + 1) % N` is the next slot. Stepping *back* bites twice in C++.

With `int`, C++ `%` [[rounds toward zero|round-to-zero]]: the answer takes the sign of the left side. So `-1 % 8` is `-1`, not 7 as in Python, and `-1` is not a slot.

With `std::size_t` there are no negative numbers at all. `0 - 1` wraps round to the largest `std::size_t`: 2⁶⁴ − 1 on a 64-bit machine, or 2³² − 1 where `std::size_t` has 32 bits, as in ORBIT's in-browser compiler. Take that `% 8` and you get 7, which looks right, but only by luck: 2⁶⁴ and 2³² are both multiples of 8. Take it `% 6` and you get 3, not 5, with either size.

```cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int s = -1;
    std::size_t u = 0;
    std::cout << s % 8 << "\n";            // -1
    std::cout << (u - 1) % 8 << "\n";      // 7, by luck
    std::cout << (u - 1) % 6 << "\n";      // 3, not 5
    std::cout << (u + 6 - 1) % 6 << "\n";  // 5
}
```

The safe rule: **never subtract before `%`**. To step back one slot, add N − 1 instead. That works because adding N never changes a remainder mod N, so (head + N − 1) mod N is the same as (head − 1) mod N, done without going below zero. And since head < N, the sum is below 2N, so it cannot overflow either.

### Full versus empty: three designs

If a ring kept only a head index and a tail index (the next free slot), a full buffer and an empty one would look the same: in both, head equals tail. Real code settles this in one of three ways.

1. **Head and count.** This lesson's choice. Full is count == N, empty is count == 0.
2. **Head and tail, one slot kept empty.** Full is (tail + 1) mod N == head, so a ring of N slots holds only N − 1 items. It wastes a slot, but each index is written by only one side, which helps when two threads share the ring.
3. **Free-running counters.** Keep two unsigned counters that are never reduced mod N, say of type `std::uint64_t` (exactly 64 bits on every machine): `pushes` counts every push ever, `pops` every pop. The item count is `pushes - pops`, and the slot for the next push is `pushes % N`.

Design 3 looks broken, because the counters overflow. It is not, and the reason is worth knowing. Arithmetic on `std::uint64_t` is done mod 2⁶⁴: every result is the true result's remainder after dividing by 2⁶⁴. (Every unsigned type works this way, mod 2 to the power of its number of bits.)

- **The count is right.** `pushes - pops` is the true count mod 2⁶⁴. The true count is between 0 and N, and N is far below 2⁶⁴, so taking the remainder changes nothing.
- **The slot is right only when N is a power of two.** When a counter wraps from 2⁶⁴ − 1 to 0, the slot must go on to the next one. (2⁶⁴ − 1) mod N is N − 1 exactly when N divides 2⁶⁴, which means N is a power of two. For N = 6 the slot would jump from 3 to 0 and skip slots 4 and 5.

A power-of-two N has a second reward. For such an N, `i % N` equals `i & (N - 1)`, a single [[bitwise AND|power-of-two]] that keeps the low bits of `i`. Because N is a template parameter, the compiler sees that N is a power of two and makes that swap for you.

### Why the C++ version is correct

DSA I proved the invariant gives first-in, first-out order. Three more facts make the C++ version safe:

1. **Every slot index is in range.** Every index is a remainder mod N, so it is between 0 and N − 1. The sums before `%` are at most (N − 1) + N, far from overflow.
2. **A live item is never overwritten.** Push writes slot (head + count) mod N only when count < N. That slot is position count in the row, one past the back, so it holds no live item.
3. **No left-over item stays alive.** Every slot outside the row holds `T{}`: true at the start, because the array is built with `{}`, and kept true because pop resets the slot it frees.

### What it costs

| Operation | Ring buffer | `std::vector` used as a queue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| push at the back | O(1) worst case | O(1) amortised: now and then one push copies everything |
| pop at the front | O(1) worst case | O(n): every item shifts left |
| i-th item from the front | O(1) | O(1) |
| memory | N slots plus two counters, fixed | grows and shrinks, on the heap |

"Worst case" is the important word. A growing array is O(1) *amortised*: most pushes are cheap, and an occasional one copies every element. That is fine for a batch job and fatal for a loop that must finish in time, every time; see [[real-time code|real-time]]. A ring buffer never has a slow operation.

### Overwrite-oldest mode

For a recorder, refusing new data when full is the wrong rule. The newest readings matter most, so when the buffer is full, a push drops the oldest item to make room: pop, then push. Aircraft [[flight data recorders|black-box]] keep their last hours of data exactly this way. The practice problems use this mode.

### Where it is used

- **Serial and radio drivers.** An interrupt pushes each byte as it arrives; the main loop pops them when it has time.
- **Audio.** Sound cards play from a ring that the program keeps topped up.
- **Operating systems.** Linux's `kfifo`, the `io_uring` queues shared between a program and the kernel, and network cards' packet queues are all rings, and several use free-running counters.
- **Lock-free queues** between two threads, [[one writer and one reader|spsc]].
- **ORBIT's world:** a telemetry downlink queue that holds frames until the next ground-station pass, and the last N samples of a sensor for a rolling average.

**Watch out:** stepping back with `(i - 1) % N`. With an `int` it can give −1, and with a `std::size_t` it gives a wrong slot for any N that is not a power of two, while seeming to work for N = 8. Write `(i + N - 1) % N`. The second classic bug is the full/empty mix-up: if your ring keeps only `head` and `tail`, the test `head == tail` cannot tell a full buffer from an empty one.

::: context compile-time Known while compiling
A compile-time constant is a value the compiler can work out before the program ever runs: a literal like `16`, a `constexpr` variable, or `sizeof(double)`. A value read from input is not one. Each different N makes the compiler build a separate copy of the class, called an instantiation, with N built into the instructions. That makes the code fast: a loop bound or a `% N` with a known N is cheaper than one with a variable. The price is that each size used adds its own copy of the code to the program.
:::

::: context stack-size Why the stack has room for small rings only
Each thread's stack is a fixed block of memory, usually 8 MB on desktop Linux and far less on small embedded chips and in WebAssembly, where it can be a few hundred kilobytes. A local variable's bytes come out of that block. A `std::array<double, 1000>` is 8 KB and fine. A `std::array<double, 1000000>` is 8 MB and will crash the program on the spot, a stack overflow. Big fixed buffers are made `static`, put in a global, or kept as members of an object that itself lives on the heap.
:::

::: context nodiscard Results you must not ignore
An attribute is a note to the compiler written in double square brackets, and `[[nodiscard]]` says: calling this and ignoring the result is almost certainly a mistake. Clang and GCC then warn at every call that throws the result away. It was added in C++17. The standard library itself marks functions like `empty()` with it, because people write `v.empty();` meaning `v.clear();`. Safety-critical coding rules, such as MISRA C++ and NASA JPL's Power of Ten, require every returned error value to be checked.
:::

::: context round-to-zero Two rules for negative remainders
When a division is not exact, a language must decide which way to round the quotient, and the remainder follows from that. C and C++ round toward zero: −7 / 2 is −3, so −7 % 2 is −1. Python rounds down, toward minus infinity: −7 // 2 is −4, so −7 % 2 is 1. Both keep the rule (a / b) · b + a % b = a. Before C99 and C++11, the rounding direction for negative numbers was left to each compiler; now C and C++ fix it as toward zero, the way most processors divide.
:::

::: context power-of-two Why a power of two makes % cheap
A number written in binary ends in its low bits. Dividing by 2^k just shifts those k low bits off the end, and they are exactly the remainder. So for N = 8 (binary 1000), N − 1 is 0111, and i & 7 keeps the last three bits of i, which is i % 8. An AND takes one clock cycle. A real division takes about 20 to 40 cycles on a modern processor. That is why hash tables and rings in fast code are so often sized 64, 1024 or 4096.

:::

::: context real-time When "on average" is not good enough
Real-time code must finish each job before a deadline, every time: a flight controller that runs its loop 400 times a second has 2.5 ms per pass. An operation that is usually fast but occasionally copies a million elements breaks that promise, even though its average cost is tiny. Asking the heap for memory is also unpredictable: it may search free lists or ask the operating system. So real-time rules, such as NASA JPL's Power of Ten, forbid allocating memory after start-up. Fixed rings, sized in advance, are the standard answer.
:::

::: context black-box Recorders that keep only the end
A flight data recorder writes without stopping, and when its memory is full it overwrites the oldest data. After an incident, what matters is the last stretch before it, and that is exactly what an overwrite-oldest ring holds. Cockpit voice recorders historically kept the last two hours; newer rules ask for 25. Car dashcams, "last N log lines" crash reports, and oscilloscopes that show the signal just before a trigger all work the same way.
:::

::: context spsc One writer, one reader, no locks
When exactly one thread pushes and exactly one pops, a ring buffer needs no lock. The writer is the only one who changes the tail, and the reader is the only one who changes the head; each only reads the other's number. With atomic counters and the right memory ordering, this is one of the fastest ways for two threads to talk. You will build real threads in the Operating Systems and Parallel Computing courses. The LMAX Disruptor, a trading system that passed millions of messages a second between threads, made this design famous.
:::
--- task
Write `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class RingBuffer`: a first-in, first-out queue of at most N items, stored in a `std::array<T, N>` member. It must never use the heap. No `main`.

- `static constexpr std::size_t capacity()` returns N.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `bool empty() const` and `bool full() const`.
- `bool push(const T& item)` copies the item in at the back; `bool push(T&& item)` moves it in. Both return `false`, and change nothing, when the buffer is full.
- `std::optional<T> pop()` removes the front item and returns it, moved out of its slot, then puts `T{}` into that slot so the buffer holds no part of the item any more. It returns `std::nullopt` when the buffer is empty.
- `const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const` returns the item `i` places from the front (0 is the front), for `i < size()`.

You may assume T has a default constructor. The checks store `int`s, `std::string`s, `std::unique_ptr`s (which cannot be copied) and `std::shared_ptr`s, run ten thousand mixed operations, and use `sizeof` to confirm the slots live inside the object.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
public:
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    bool empty() const { return true; }
    bool full() const { return false; }
    bool push(const T& item) { return false; }
    bool push(T&& item) { return false; }
    std::optional<T> pop() { return std::nullopt; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return slots_[0]; }

private:
    std::array<T, N> slots_{};
};
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingBuffer {
    static_assert(N > 0, "a ring buffer needs at least one slot");

public:
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }
    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }
    bool empty() const { return count_ == 0; }
    bool full() const { return count_ == N; }

    bool push(const T& item) {
        if (full()) return false;
        slots_[(head_ + count_) % N] = item;
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }

    bool push(T&& item) {
        if (full()) return false;
        slots_[(head_ + count_) % N] = std::move(item);
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }

    std::optional<T> pop() {
        if (empty()) return std::nullopt;
        std::optional<T> out(std::move(slots_[head_]));
        slots_[head_] = T{};   // let go of anything the moved-from slot still holds
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        --count_;
        return out;
    }

    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return slots_[(head_ + i) % N]; }

private:
    std::array<T, N> slots_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;    // slot of the front item
    std::size_t count_ = 0;   // items held, 0..N
};
--- hint
Keep two `std::size_t` members next to the array: `head_`, the slot of the front item, and `count_`, the number of items. The next free slot is `(head_ + count_) % N`. Both push overloads check `full()` first and write there; the `T&&` one uses `std::move(item)`.
--- hint
In `pop`, build the answer first by moving the front slot into a `std::optional<T>`. Only then reset that slot with `T{}`, move `head_` one slot on with `% N`, and lower `count_`.
--- hint
`operator[]` turns a position in the queue into a slot the same way push does: position `i` from the front lives in slot `(head_ + i) % N`.
--- check case | Items come out in the order they went in
[] { RingBuffer<int, 4> r; r.push(1); r.push(2); r.push(3); std::vector<int> out; while (auto x = r.pop()) out.push_back(*x); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{1, 2, 3}
--- check test | A full buffer refuses a push and keeps its items
[] { RingBuffer<int, 3> r; bool stored = r.push(10) && r.push(20) && r.push(30); bool refused = !r.push(40); return stored && refused && r.full() && r.size() == 3 && r[0] == 10 && r[2] == 30; }()
?? When `count_ == N`, return false before writing anything.
--- check test | Popping an empty buffer gives nothing, then it still works
[] { RingBuffer<std::string, 2> r; bool none = !r.pop().has_value() && r.empty(); r.push(std::string("ping")); auto x = r.pop(); return none && x && *x == "ping" && !r.pop() && r.size() == 0; }()
--- check case | After wrapping round, operator[] reads front to back

=> std::vector<int>{3, 4, 5}
?? Position i from the front is slot (head_ + i) % N, not slot i.
--- check test | Ten thousand mixed operations match a simple queue

+++ practice | A rolling mean of the last N readings
--- task
A temperature sensor reports one reading at a time. Write `template <std::size_t N> class RollingMean` that remembers only the latest N readings. No `main`.

- `void add(double reading)`: store the reading. When N readings are already held, the oldest is dropped to make room (overwrite-oldest mode).
- `std::size_t count() const`: how many readings are held, at most N.
- `double mean() const`: the average of the readings held, or `0.0` when there are none.

Both `add` and `mean` must be O(1): keep a running total, adding each new reading and taking away each dropped one. A check adds 200,000 readings to a `RollingMean<50000>` and asks for the mean after every one, which is far too slow if `mean` adds up all N values each time.

For example, a `RollingMean<3>` given 1, 2, 3 and 10 holds 2, 3 and 10, so its mean is 5.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>

template <std::size_t N>
class RollingMean {
public:
    void add(double reading) {}
    std::size_t count() const { return 0; }
    double mean() const { return 0.0; }
};
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>

template <std::size_t N>
class RollingMean {
public:
    void add(double reading) {
        if (count_ == N) {
            total_ -= slots_[head_];          // drop the oldest
            slots_[head_] = reading;          // its slot becomes the newest
            head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        } else {
            slots_[(head_ + count_) % N] = reading;
            ++count_;
        }
        total_ += reading;
    }

    std::size_t count() const { return count_; }
    double mean() const { return count_ == 0 ? 0.0 : total_ / count_; }

private:
    std::array<double, N> slots_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;
    std::size_t count_ = 0;
    double total_ = 0.0;
};
--- hint
This is a ring buffer in overwrite-oldest mode. When it is full, the newest reading goes into the oldest reading's slot, and the head moves one slot on.
--- hint
Keep a `double total_` beside the ring. Add every new reading to it, and subtract the reading that falls out. `mean()` is then one division, with a separate answer for zero readings.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { RollingMean<3> m; m.add(1); m.add(2); m.add(3); bool full = m.count() == 3 && m.mean() == 2.0; m.add(10); return full && m.count() == 3 && m.mean() == 5.0; }()
--- check test | No readings: mean 0 and count 0
[] { RollingMean<4> m; return m.count() == 0 && m.mean() == 0.0; }()
--- check test | Fewer readings than N: the mean of those held
[] { RollingMean<10> m; m.add(4); m.add(-2); return m.count() == 2 && m.mean() == 1.0; }()
--- check test | N = 1 keeps only the latest reading
[] { RollingMean<1> m; m.add(7); m.add(-3.5); return m.count() == 1 && m.mean() == -3.5; }()
--- check test | 200,000 readings, a mean after each one
[] { static RollingMean<50000> m; std::vector<double> prefix(200001, 0.0); for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + (i * 37 % 101); for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { m.add(i * 37 % 101); int lo = i + 1 > 50000 ? i + 1 - 50000 : 0; double want = (prefix[i + 1] - prefix[lo]) / (i + 1 - lo); if (m.mean() - want > 1e-9 || want - m.mean() > 1e-9) return false; } return m.count() == 50000; }()
?? Adding up all N readings on every call is 10 billion additions here. Keep a running total instead.

+++ practice | The last lines of a log
--- task
A crash report shows only the end of a log. Write `std::vector<std::string> last_lines(const std::string& text)` that returns the last 5 lines of `text`, oldest first. No `main`.

- Lines are separated by `'\n'`. A final `'\n'` at the very end does not start another line, and empty text has no lines. `std::getline` on a `std::istringstream` splits text exactly this way.
- If there are fewer than 5 lines, return all of them.
- Keep at most 5 lines at a time, in a `std::array<std::string, 5>` used as a ring buffer in overwrite-oldest mode: never store every line.

For example, the text `"a\nb\nc\nd\ne\nf\ng\n"` gives `{"c", "d", "e", "f", "g"}`.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <sstream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

std::vector<std::string> last_lines(const std::string& text) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <sstream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<std::string> last_lines(const std::string& text) {
    constexpr std::size_t kKeep = 5;
    std::array<std::string, kKeep> ring;
    std::size_t head = 0;
    std::size_t count = 0;
    std::istringstream in(text);
    std::string line;
    while (std::getline(in, line)) {
        if (count == kKeep) {
            ring[head] = std::move(line);    // overwrite the oldest line
            head = (head + 1) % kKeep;
        } else {
            ring[(head + count) % kKeep] = std::move(line);
            ++count;
        }
    }
    std::vector<std::string> out;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) out.push_back(ring[(head + i) % kKeep]);
    return out;
}
--- hint
Read line by line with `while (std::getline(in, line))`. Each line goes into a ring of 5 strings: into the next free slot while there is room, and over the oldest line once all 5 are taken.
--- hint
At the end, the oldest kept line is in slot `head`. Copy the kept lines out in queue order, `(head + i) % 5` for `i` from 0 up to the count.
--- check case | The example from the task
last_lines("a\nb\nc\nd\ne\nf\ng\n")
=> std::vector<std::string>{"c", "d", "e", "f", "g"}
--- check case | Fewer than five lines, no final newline
last_lines("boot\nlink up")
=> std::vector<std::string>{"boot", "link up"}
--- check case | Empty text has no lines
last_lines("")
=> std::vector<std::string>{}
--- check case | Exactly five lines
last_lines("1\n2\n3\n4\n5\n")
=> std::vector<std::string>{"1", "2", "3", "4", "5"}
--- check case | Blank lines count as lines
last_lines("x\n\n\ny\n\nz")
=> std::vector<std::string>{"", "", "y", "", "z"}
--- check test | Twelve thousand lines
[] { std::string t; for (int i = 0; i < 12000; ++i) t += "line " + std::to_string(i) + "\n"; auto v = last_lines(t); return v.size() == 5 && v[0] == "line 11995" && v[4] == "line 11999"; }()
--- check source | Keeps the lines in a std::array of five strings
std::array<\s*std::string\s*,\s*(5|kKeep|k\w+)\s*>

+++ practice | Range-for over a ring buffer
--- task
The starter has `Ring8`, a ring buffer of up to 8 `int`s, already working. Make it work with range-for and with `<algorithm>`, as you did for `Vector<T>`. No `main`.

1. Inside `Ring8`, write a class `const_iterator` that visits the items **front to back**. It holds a `const Ring8*` and a position counted from the front (0 is the front item). It needs:
   - the member types `using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;`, `using value_type = int;`, `using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;`, `using pointer = const int*;` and `using reference = const int&;`;
   - `const int& operator*() const`, which returns the item at its position (use `at`);
   - `const_iterator& operator++()` and `const_iterator operator++(int)`;
   - `bool operator==(const const_iterator&) const`.
2. `begin()` is position 0 and `end()` is position `size()`.
3. Outside the class, write `int total(const Ring8& r)`, the sum of the items using range-for, and `std::optional<int> largest(const Ring8& r)`, which uses `std::max_element` and returns `std::nullopt` for an empty ring.

Count positions from the front, not slots in the array. When the ring is full, its head slot and its next free slot are the same slot, so an `end()` built from a slot number would equal `begin()`, and a full ring would look empty.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <optional>

class Ring8 {
public:
    bool push(int x) {
        if (count_ == 8) return false;
        slots_[(head_ + count_) % 8] = x;
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }
    std::optional<int> pop() {
        if (count_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        int x = slots_[head_];
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % 8;
        --count_;
        return x;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }
    const int& at(std::size_t i) const { return slots_[(head_ + i) % 8]; }

    // Write class const_iterator here, then begin() and end().

private:
    std::array<int, 8> slots_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;
    std::size_t count_ = 0;
};

int total(const Ring8& r) { return 0; }
std::optional<int> largest(const Ring8& r) { return std::nullopt; }
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <optional>

class Ring8 {
public:
    bool push(int x) {
        if (count_ == 8) return false;
        slots_[(head_ + count_) % 8] = x;
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }
    std::optional<int> pop() {
        if (count_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        int x = slots_[head_];
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % 8;
        --count_;
        return x;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }
    const int& at(std::size_t i) const { return slots_[(head_ + i) % 8]; }

    class const_iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        const_iterator() = default;
        const_iterator(const Ring8* ring, std::size_t pos) : ring_(ring), pos_(pos) {}

        const int& operator*() const { return ring_->at(pos_); }
        const_iterator& operator++() {
            ++pos_;
            return *this;
        }
        const_iterator operator++(int) {
            const_iterator before = *this;
            ++pos_;
            return before;
        }
        bool operator==(const const_iterator& other) const { return ring_ == other.ring_ && pos_ == other.pos_; }

    private:
        const Ring8* ring_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t pos_ = 0;   // counted from the front, not a slot number
    };

    const_iterator begin() const { return const_iterator(this, 0); }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(this, count_); }

private:
    std::array<int, 8> slots_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;
    std::size_t count_ = 0;
};

int total(const Ring8& r) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int x : r) sum += x;
    return sum;
}

std::optional<int> largest(const Ring8& r) {
    auto it = std::max_element(r.begin(), r.end());
    if (it == r.end()) return std::nullopt;
    return *it;
}
--- hint
The iterator stores two things: a pointer to the ring and a position from the front. `*it` is `ring_->at(pos_)`, `++it` adds one to the position, and two iterators are equal when both parts are equal.
--- hint
`end()` is the position one past the back, which is `size()`. Because positions are counted from the front, a full ring has `begin()` at 0 and `end()` at 8, so they differ.
--- hint
For `largest`, `std::max_element(r.begin(), r.end())` returns `r.end()` when the ring is empty; check that before you dereference.

+++ practice | Counters that wrap: a ring with one-byte indexes
--- task
Write the free-running-counter design with counters small enough to watch them wrap. No `main`.

`template <typename T, std::size_t N> class TinyRing` holds at most N items. The starter gives its data members; keep exactly these and add no others:

- `std::array<T, N> slots_{};`
- `std::uint8_t pushes_ = 0;` counts every successful push, never reduced mod N;
- `std::uint8_t pops_ = 0;` counts every successful pop, the same way.

A `std::uint8_t` holds 0 to 255, and adding 1 to 255 gives 0. The `static_assert` in the starter allows only N that is a power of two from 1 to 128. Write:

- `std::size_t size() const`, `bool empty() const`, `bool full() const`;
- `bool push(const T& item)`, which returns `false` when full;
- `std::optional<T> pop()`, which returns `std::nullopt` when empty.

The next push goes to slot `pushes_ % N` and the front item is in slot `pops_ % N`. Watch out: in C++, `pushes_ - pops_` is computed as an `int`, because small integer types are promoted to `int` before arithmetic. After `pushes_` wraps past 255, that `int` is negative. The count you want is the difference taken mod 256.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <optional>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class TinyRing {
    static_assert(N >= 1 && N <= 128 && (N & (N - 1)) == 0, "N must be a power of two from 1 to 128");

public:
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    bool empty() const { return true; }
    bool full() const { return true; }
    bool push(const T& item) { return false; }
    std::optional<T> pop() { return std::nullopt; }

private:
    std::array<T, N> slots_{};
    std::uint8_t pushes_ = 0;
    std::uint8_t pops_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <optional>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class TinyRing {
    static_assert(N >= 1 && N <= 128 && (N & (N - 1)) == 0, "N must be a power of two from 1 to 128");

public:
    // Both counters are promoted to int before "-"; converting back to uint8_t takes the result mod 256.
    std::size_t size() const { return static_cast<std::uint8_t>(pushes_ - pops_); }
    bool empty() const { return size() == 0; }
    bool full() const { return size() == N; }

    bool push(const T& item) {
        if (full()) return false;
        slots_[pushes_ % N] = item;
        ++pushes_;   // wraps from 255 to 0, and pushes_ % N still moves on by one slot
        return true;
    }

    std::optional<T> pop() {
        if (empty()) return std::nullopt;
        std::optional<T> out(slots_[pops_ % N]);
        slots_[pops_ % N] = T{};
        ++pops_;
        return out;
    }

private:
    std::array<T, N> slots_{};
    std::uint8_t pushes_ = 0;
    std::uint8_t pops_ = 0;
};
--- hint
The true count is between 0 and N, and N is at most 128, so it is the difference of the two counters mod 256. Converting an `int` to `std::uint8_t` takes it mod 256.
--- hint
Write `size()` as the difference converted back with `static_cast<std::uint8_t>(...)`. Then `empty()` and `full()` compare `size()` with 0 and N.
--- hint
Slots come straight from the counters: push writes `slots_[pushes_ % N]` and then adds one to `pushes_`; pop reads `slots_[pops_ % N]` and then adds one to `pops_`. Because N divides 256, the slot keeps moving on by one even when a counter wraps.
--- check test | First in, first out

--- check test | Full after N pushes, even after the counters wrap
[] { TinyRing<int, 128> r; for (int i = 0; i < 200; ++i) { r.push(i); r.pop(); } for (int i = 0; i < 128; ++i) if (!r.push(i)) return false; bool full = r.full() && r.size() == 128 && !r.push(999); for (int i = 0; i < 128; ++i) { auto x = r.pop(); if (!x || *x != i) return false; } return full && r.empty() && !r.pop(); }()
?? After wrapping, pushes_ is smaller than pops_. The int difference is negative; take it mod 256.
--- check test | A thousand mixed operations with N = 4
