+++ practice | Debug: the deque that breaks at capacity 6
--- task
`RingDeque<T, N>` is a ring buffer that can add and remove at both ends:

- `push_back` and `push_front` add an item and return `false`, changing nothing, when full;
- `pop_front` and `pop_back` return the item, or `std::nullopt` when empty;
- `size()` returns the count.

With N = 8 every test passes. With N = 6, `push_front` on an empty deque writes the item into the wrong slot, and later pushes at the back overwrite it. For example, with N = 6, `push_front(1)` then `push_back(2)` then `push_back(3)` then popping from the front should give 1, 2, 3.

Find the bug and fix it. It is one line.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingDeque {
public:
    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }

    bool push_back(const T& item) {
        if (count_ == N) return false;
        slots_[(head_ + count_) % N] = item;
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }

    bool push_front(const T& item) {
        if (count_ == N) return false;
        head_ = (head_ - 1) % N;
        slots_[head_] = item;
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }

    std::optional<T> pop_front() {
        if (count_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        T item = slots_[head_];
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        --count_;
        return item;
    }

    std::optional<T> pop_back() {
        if (count_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        --count_;
        return slots_[(head_ + count_) % N];
    }

private:
    std::array<T, N> slots_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;
    std::size_t count_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class RingDeque {
public:
    std::size_t size() const { return count_; }

    bool push_back(const T& item) {
        if (count_ == N) return false;
        slots_[(head_ + count_) % N] = item;
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }

    bool push_front(const T& item) {
        if (count_ == N) return false;
        head_ = (head_ + N - 1) % N;
        slots_[head_] = item;
        ++count_;
        return true;
    }

    std::optional<T> pop_front() {
        if (count_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        T item = slots_[head_];
        head_ = (head_ + 1) % N;
        --count_;
        return item;
    }

    std::optional<T> pop_back() {
        if (count_ == 0) return std::nullopt;
        --count_;
        return slots_[(head_ + count_) % N];
    }

private:
    std::array<T, N> slots_{};
    std::size_t head_ = 0;
    std::size_t count_ = 0;
};
--- hint

--- hint
Never subtract before `%` with an unsigned number. Step back one slot by adding N − 1 instead.

+++ practice | A trigger capture, like an oscilloscope
--- task
An oscilloscope in "trigger" mode shows what happened just before and just after a signal crossed a line. Write `std::vector<int> capture(std::istream& in, int threshold)`. No `main`.

It reads whole numbers from `in` one at a time. The **trigger** is the first reading strictly greater than `threshold`. Return, in order:

- the up to 4 readings just before the trigger (fewer if the stream had fewer before it);
- the trigger itself;
- the up to 3 readings just after it (fewer if the stream ends sooner).

After the third reading following the trigger, stop: read nothing more from `in`, so whatever comes next is still there for the caller. If no reading is above the threshold, return the last 4 readings of the stream (fewer if it had fewer), like a recorder that never fired.

Keep at most 4 earlier readings at any moment, in a ring buffer: the stream may be far too long to store. For example, `"1 2 3 4 5 6 99 7 8 9 10"` with threshold 50 gives `{3, 4, 5, 6, 99, 7, 8, 9}`, and the 10 is still unread.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <istream>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> capture(std::istream& in, int threshold) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <istream>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> capture(std::istream& in, int threshold) {
    constexpr std::size_t kBefore = 4;
    constexpr int kAfter = 3;
    std::array<int, kBefore> ring{};
    std::size_t head = 0;
    std::size_t count = 0;
    std::vector<int> out;
    int x = 0;
    while (in >> x) {
        if (x > threshold) {
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) out.push_back(ring[(head + i) % kBefore]);
            out.push_back(x);
            for (int k = 0; k < kAfter && in >> x; ++k) out.push_back(x);
            return out;
        }
        if (count == kBefore) {
            ring[head] = x;                 // overwrite the oldest earlier reading
            head = (head + 1) % kBefore;
        } else {
            ring[(head + count) % kBefore] = x;
            ++count;
        }
    }
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) out.push_back(ring[(head + i) % kBefore]);
    return out;
}
--- hint
Until the trigger, every reading goes into a ring of 4 in overwrite-oldest mode. When the trigger arrives, copy the ring out front to back, add the trigger, then read at most 3 more.
--- hint
Stop reading as soon as you have the 3 readings after the trigger: a loop that counts to 3 and also stops when `in >> x` fails. Return straight away.
--- hint
If the loop ends without a trigger, the answer is the ring's contents in queue order: slot `(head + i) % 4` for `i` from 0 up to the count.
--- check case | The example from the task
[] { std::istringstream in("1 2 3 4 5 6 99 7 8 9 10"); return capture(in, 50); }()
=> std::vector<int>{3, 4, 5, 6, 99, 7, 8, 9}
--- check test | Stops reading after the third reading past the trigger
[] { std::istringstream in("1 2 3 4 5 6 99 7 8 9 10 11"); capture(in, 50); int next = 0; in >> next; return next == 10; }()
?? After the 3 readings that follow the trigger, return without reading again.
--- check case | Trigger first: nothing before it
[] { std::istringstream in("80 1 2 3 4"); return capture(in, 50); }()
=> std::vector<int>{80, 1, 2, 3}
--- check case | Stream ends soon after the trigger
[] { std::istringstream in("5 6 70 8"); return capture(in, 50); }()
=> std::vector<int>{5, 6, 70, 8}
--- check case | Equal to the threshold is not a trigger; no trigger gives the last four
[] { std::istringstream in("50 10 20 50 30 40"); return capture(in, 50); }()
=> std::vector<int>{20, 50, 30, 40}
--- check case | Empty stream
[] { std::istringstream in(""); return capture(in, 0); }()
=> std::vector<int>{}
--- check case | Negative readings and threshold
[] { std::istringstream in("-9 -8 -7 -6 -5 -4 -1 -3"); return capture(in, -2); }()
=> std::vector<int>{-7, -6, -5, -4, -1, -3}
--- check test | A long stream with a late trigger
[] { std::string s; for (int i = 0; i < 300000; ++i) s += std::to_string(i % 1000) + " "; s += "5000 1 2 3 4"; std::istringstream in(s); auto v = capture(in, 1000); return v == std::vector<int>{996, 997, 998, 999, 5000, 1, 2, 3}; }()

+++ question | Stepping back with an unsigned index
--- ask
A ring buffer has capacity 6, and its `head` is a `std::size_t` equal to 0. To step back one slot, the code runs `head = (head - 1) % 6;`. What is `head` afterwards?
--- answer
3
--- why
`head - 1` cannot be −1 in an unsigned type: it wraps to 2⁶⁴ − 1 (or 2³² − 1 where `std::size_t` has 32 bits). Both 2⁶⁴ and 2³² leave remainder 4 when divided by 6, so the wrapped value leaves remainder 3. The right slot is 5, which `(head + 6 - 1) % 6` gives. With capacity 8 the same bug gives 7, the right answer, because 8 divides 2⁶⁴ and 2³², which is why this bug hides in tests that use a power of two.

+++ question | Why free-running counters need a power of two
--- ask
A ring buffer keeps two unsigned 64-bit counters that are never reduced mod N, and uses `counter % N` as the slot. Why must N be a power of two?
--- choice
Because `%` is only allowed on powers of two for unsigned numbers.
--- choice correct
When a counter wraps from 2⁶⁴ − 1 to 0, the slot must move on by one; (2⁶⁴ − 1) mod N is N − 1 only when N divides 2⁶⁴.
--- choice
Because otherwise `pushes - pops` could be wrong when the counters wrap.
--- choice
Because the compiler refuses a non-type template parameter that is not a power of two.
--- why
The count is safe for any N: `pushes - pops` is the true count mod 2⁶⁴, and the true count is at most N. The slots are the problem. Before the wrap the slot is (2⁶⁴ − 1) mod N, after it the slot is 0. Those are neighbours only when (2⁶⁴ − 1) mod N = N − 1, that is when N divides 2⁶⁴, and the only divisors of 2⁶⁴ are powers of two.

=== dsacpp-08 | A hash map with chaining
--- teach
Last lesson's ring buffer found every item by its position. A hash map finds a value by its **key**, a name or number, in O(1) expected time. In DSA I you built one in Python as a list of lists, with Python's `hash` choosing the list. This lesson builds it in C++. Four things are new: where the hash function comes from (`std::hash`), how a class takes a function as a template parameter, what it costs to move every pair into bigger storage, and a question Python never made you ask: after an insert, which pointers into the map still point at the right thing?

### The picture: pigeonholes in a mail room

A mail room has a wall of numbered pigeonholes. A rule turns each surname into a hole number, say from its letters. To find a letter, you work out the number and look in that one hole, never the others. Two surnames can land in the same hole, so each hole holds a short pile, and you look through the pile. Too many letters, and every pile gets tall: then you build a wall with twice as many holes and re-sort all the mail.

### The definition

A **hash map with chaining** stores key-value pairs in B **buckets**. A **hash function** turns a key into a number, and the key's bucket is that number mod B. Each bucket holds a list, its **chain**, of the pairs whose keys land there.

This lesson's `HashMap<K, V, Hash>` keeps four facts true between operations, its invariant:

1. every pair (k, v) is in bucket hash(k) mod B;
2. no key appears twice;
3. `size_` is the number of pairs;
4. size_ ≤ B, so the **load factor** α = size_ / B is at most 1.

In everyday words: each key lives in the one bucket its hash picks, once, and there are never more keys than buckets.

### std::hash: a hash function for the standard types

`std::hash<K>` from `<functional>` is a class template with a version for every built-in type, `std::string`, pointers and more. It is a **function object**: an object you call like a function, because its class defines `operator()`. `std::hash<std::string>{}` makes one, and calling it gives a `std::size_t`.

```cpp
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::hash<std::string> h;
    std::cout << (h("vega") == h("vega")) << "\n";          // 1: equal keys, equal hashes
    std::cout << (h("vega") == h("deneb")) << "\n";         // 0 here, but a clash is allowed
    std::cout << std::hash<int>{}(1234) << "\n";            // 1234 with GCC's library
}
```

The standard promises one thing: equal keys give equal hashes, within one run of the program. It promises nothing about the actual numbers. They [[differ between standard libraries|hash-values]], and GCC's library hashes each integer to itself, which matters in a moment.

### A function object as a template parameter

The map takes its hash function as a type, with `std::hash<K>` as the default:

```cpp fragment
template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class HashMap {
    // ...
    Hash hash_{};     // an object of that type; call it as hash_(key)
};
```

Any class with a suitable `operator()` can stand in. Here is one that gives every key the same number, a terrible hash that is useful for testing, because it forces every key into one chain:

```cpp fragment
struct SameBucket {
    std::size_t operator()(int) const { return 0; }
};
HashMap<int, double, SameBucket> worst;   // every key collides
```

Why a type and not a plain function pointer? The compiler knows exactly which `operator()` will run, so it can [[paste its body in|inline]] at every call. A function object with no data members costs no memory either.

### A hash for your own type

To use your own struct as a key you need two things: `==` to say when two keys are the same, and a hash functor. In C++20, `= default` writes `==` for you, comparing member by member.

A hash for several members must mix them so that small differences change the result a lot. Adding or XOR-ing the members' hashes is the classic mistake: then (1, 2) and (2, 1) collide, and so do all the pairs with the same sum. A standard recipe folds each member in with a multiply-and-shift step, here for a radio callsign:

```cpp fragment
struct Callsign {
    std::string station;
    int channel;
    bool operator==(const Callsign&) const = default;
};

struct CallsignHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const Callsign& c) const {
        std::size_t h = std::hash<std::string>{}(c.station);
        h ^= std::hash<int>{}(c.channel) + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 + (h << 6) + (h >> 2);
        return h;
    }
};
```

The shifts `<<` and `>>` spread the bits of the hash so far over the whole number before the next member joins, so the order of the members matters. The long [[hexadecimal constant|golden-ratio]] is a fixed mixing number.

**The contract:** if `a == b`, then `hash(a) == hash(b)`. Break it, say by hashing a member that `==` ignores, and the map puts two equal keys in different buckets and finds neither reliably.

### The buckets: a vector of vectors of pairs

The storage is `std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<K, V>>>`: a vector of buckets, each bucket a vector of pairs. Looking in one bucket is a loop, and a structured binding names the two halves of each pair:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>> shelf = {{"lox", 3}, {"he", 9}};
    for (auto& [name, qty] : shelf) {
        if (name == "he") qty += 1;          // qty is the real .second, not a copy
    }
    std::cout << shelf[1].second << "\n";    // 10
}
```

### Finding: a pointer, or nothing

`find(key)` looks only in bucket hash(key) mod B, and returns a **pointer to the value**, or `nullptr` if the key is missing. A reference cannot say "missing", and returning `std::optional<V>` would hand back a copy that cannot change the value inside the map. The pointer is an **observing** pointer, as in lesson 6: the map owns the value, and the caller only looks at it. A `const` map needs a second `find` that returns `const V*`.

`operator[]` is find-or-insert: if the key is missing, it inserts the key with `V{}` and returns a reference to that new value. That is why `counts[word] += 1` works on a new word, and why `operator[]` needs V to have a default constructor.

### Erasing without shifting: swap and pop

The order of pairs inside a bucket means nothing. So erasing from the middle need not shift everything after it: move the last pair into the hole and drop the last place with `pop_back`.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> pile = {40, 11, 72, 5};
    std::size_t hole = 1;                    // erase the 11
    pile[hole] = std::move(pile.back());     // the 5 fills the hole
    pile.pop_back();
    for (int x : pile) std::cout << x << " ";   // 40 5 72
    std::cout << "\n";
}
```

Erasing the last pair itself needs no move at all: just `pop_back`. And moving an object onto itself is not safe for every type, so skip the move in that case.

### Rehashing: moving every pair

Before inserting a new key, if size_ + 1 would be more than B, the map **rehashes**: it makes a vector of 2B empty buckets, moves every pair into bucket hash(key) mod 2B, and swaps the new vector in. Use `std::move` on each pair, so a string key's characters are handed over, not copied. The hash of every key is computed again, because the bucket number depends on B.

A single rehash costs O(n + B). By the doubling argument from DSA I's amortised-analysis lesson, n inserts cause rehashes that move fewer than 2n pairs in total, so insert is **O(1) amortised**.

### Why it is correct

- **find:** by fact 1, a key can only be in bucket hash(key) mod B. So if the loop over that bucket does not find it, it is nowhere.
- **insert** first runs find, so it never adds a second copy (fact 2). It grows first when needed (fact 4), then appends to the key's bucket (fact 1), and adds one to size_ (fact 3).
- **erase** changes only the order inside one bucket and removes one pair, so facts 1, 2 and 3 still hold, and fact 4 only gets easier.
- **rehash** puts every pair into bucket hash(key) mod 2B, which is fact 1 for the new B. It moves pairs without copying or dropping any, so facts 2 and 3 are untouched.

### What it costs

Every operation costs O(1) to hash, plus a walk along one chain. How long is a chain? Suppose the hash sends each key to a bucket at random, evenly and independently of the others: the **[[simple uniform hashing|uniform-hashing]]** assumption. Take a stored key k. For every other stored key j, let X_j be 1 if j landed in k's bucket and 0 if not. The chance of that is 1/B, so the expected value of X_j is 1/B. By linearity of expectation, the expected number of other keys in k's bucket is the sum over the n − 1 other keys, (n − 1)/B, which is less than α. For a missing key the same argument gives n/B = α.

| Operation | Expected | Worst case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| find, erase | O(1 + α) = O(1) since α ≤ 1 | O(n): every key in one chain |
| insert, `operator[]` | O(1) amortised | O(n) |
| memory | O(n + B) | |

The worst case is real. If an attacker can choose your keys, and your hash is known, they can send keys that all collide and make every request O(n): a [[hash-flooding attack|hash-flooding]]. And a weak hash can do it by accident: GCC hashes integers to themselves, so with B = 16, keys 0, 16, 32, 48 all land in bucket 0. That is why GCC's own `std::unordered_map` uses [[a prime number of buckets|prime-buckets]] instead of a power of two.

### Which pointers survive?

`find` returns a pointer into a bucket's vector. Here is what later operations do to it:

- **Inserting another key into the same bucket** may make that vector full, so it moves its pairs to a bigger block of memory. The old pointer now points at freed memory.
- **A rehash** moves every pair into new vectors. Every pointer the map ever handed out now dangles.
- **Erasing** by swap-and-pop moves the bucket's last pair into the hole. A pointer to that last pair now points past the end of the bucket.

So in this design, **any insert of a new key or any erase may break every pointer from `find` or `operator[]`**. That includes the reference from `m[a]` when you then write `m[b]`. The rule: look a value up again after changing the map.

`std::unordered_map` makes the opposite choice. It keeps each pair in its own heap node, so pointers and references to an element survive inserts and rehashes. The price is one allocation per element, and a pointer to follow on every step along a chain. You will use it in depth later in the course.

### Where it is used

- **Compilers and interpreters**, for the symbol table: which name means which variable.
- **Caches**, from web servers to CPUs' branch predictors, map a key to a recent answer.
- **Databases** join two tables by hashing one of them on the join column.
- **ORBIT's world:** a ground station maps each telemetry channel's number to its handler and its last value, thousands of times a second.

**Watch out:** holding a reference or pointer from `find` or `operator[]` while you insert or erase. `int& total = m["total"]; m[word] += 1; total += 1;` compiles, runs, and sometimes writes into freed memory, whenever `m[word]` added a key that made a bucket or the whole table grow. The second trap is reading with `operator[]`: `if (m[key] > 0)` inserts every key it asks about.

::: context hash-values The numbers themselves are not promised
The standard fixes only the rule "equal keys, equal hashes". GCC's library returns each integer unchanged and hashes strings with an algorithm called MurmurHash; Clang's library uses different algorithms, so the same string gets a different number there. Some languages go further: Python and Rust mix a random seed into string hashes, so the numbers change from one run to the next. So never save hash values to a file, send them over a network, or write a test that expects a particular number.
:::

::: context inline Pasting a function's body in
Inlining means the compiler copies a function's body to the place where it is called, instead of jumping to the function and back. That saves the jump, and, more importantly, lets the compiler optimise the body together with the code around it. A call through a function pointer usually cannot be inlined, because the compiler cannot be sure which function it will reach. A template parameter names the exact type, so it can. This is also why `std::sort` with a lambda is usually faster than C's `qsort`, which calls its comparison through a pointer.
:::

::: context golden-ratio Where the magic number comes from
0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 is 2⁶⁴ divided by the golden ratio, about 1.618, rounded to a whole number. Its bits look random, with no pattern that lines up with common keys, so adding it scrambles well. This combining line comes from the Boost C++ libraries, where it is called `hash_combine`, and it is copied into countless codebases. Where `std::size_t` has only 32 bits, as in ORBIT's in-browser compiler, the long constant is cut down to its low 32 bits; code written for 32 bits uses 0x9e3779b9, the same ratio times 2³². It is fine for hash tables, but it is not a cryptographic hash: an attacker can still find collisions on purpose.
:::

::: context uniform-hashing The assumption behind O(1)
Simple uniform hashing says: each key is equally likely to land in any of the B buckets, whatever the other keys did. No fixed hash function truly does that for every possible set of keys. For any fixed function, some set of keys collides. The assumption describes a good hash on keys that were not chosen to attack it. A stronger guarantee comes from universal hashing, which picks the hash function at random from a family when the table is made, so no fixed set of keys is bad every time.
:::

::: context hash-flooding When an attacker picks the keys
In December 2011, at the 28C3 conference, two researchers showed that the web frameworks of PHP, Java, Python, Ruby and others could be frozen by one request. They sent a few megabytes of form fields whose names all hashed to the same bucket, so storing them took quadratic time and minutes of processor. The fix in most languages was a keyed hash: a random secret mixed into every hash, such as SipHash, so outsiders cannot predict collisions. Python and Rust use SipHash for strings for this reason.
:::

::: context prime-buckets Why some tables use a prime number of buckets
With B a power of two, hash mod B keeps only the low bits of the hash. If the hash is weak, like GCC's integer hash that returns the number itself, keys that share their low bits all collide: multiples of 16 in a table of 16 buckets all land in bucket 0. A prime B mixes every bit of the hash into the remainder, so GCC's `unordered_map` grows through primes such as 13, 29, 59 and 127. Tables that insist on powers of two instead scramble the hash first, as the next lesson shows.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Inter, Arial, sans-serif">
  <text x="90" y="20" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1f2a44">B = 8, keys 0, 8, 16, 24</text>
  <text x="270" y="20" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1f2a44">B = 7, same keys</text>
  <g font-size="11" fill="#1f2a44" text-anchor="middle">
    <rect x="20" y="30" width="140" height="14" fill="#f2b880" stroke="#1f2a44"/><text x="90" y="41">0: 0, 8, 16, 24</text>
    <rect x="20" y="46" width="140" height="14" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#6c7a93"/><text x="90" y="57">1: empty</text>
    <rect x="20" y="62" width="140" height="14" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#6c7a93"/><text x="90" y="73">2: empty</text>
    <rect x="20" y="78" width="140" height="14" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#6c7a93"/><text x="90" y="89">3 to 7: empty</text>
    <rect x="200" y="30" width="140" height="14" fill="#8fb8f0" stroke="#1d6fd1"/><text x="270" y="41">0: 0</text>
    <rect x="200" y="46" width="140" height="14" fill="#8fb8f0" stroke="#1d6fd1"/><text x="270" y="57">1: 8</text>
    <rect x="200" y="62" width="140" height="14" fill="#8fb8f0" stroke="#1d6fd1"/><text x="270" y="73">2: 16</text>
    <rect x="200" y="78" width="140" height="14" fill="#8fb8f0" stroke="#1d6fd1"/><text x="270" y="89">3: 24</text>
    <rect x="200" y="94" width="140" height="14" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#6c7a93"/><text x="270" y="105">4 to 6: empty</text>

```
:::
--- task
Write `template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>> class HashMap` with separate chaining. Store the buckets as `std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<K, V>>>` and keep a `Hash` object to call. No `main`.

- `HashMap()` starts with 8 empty buckets.
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t bucket_count() const`, and `double load_factor() const` (size divided by bucket count).
- `std::size_t bucket(const K& key) const` returns the key's bucket: its hash mod `bucket_count()`.
- `V* find(const K& key)` and `const V* find(const K& key) const` return a pointer to the key's value, or `nullptr`.
- `bool insert(const K& key, const V& value)` adds the pair and returns `true`. If the key is already there, it changes nothing and returns `false`.
- `V& operator[](const K& key)` returns the key's value, inserting `V{}` first if the key is missing.
- `bool erase(const K& key)` removes the key's pair by swap-and-pop and returns `true`, or returns `false` if the key is missing.
- **Growth:** before adding a new key, if `size() + 1` would be more than `bucket_count()`, move every pair (with `std::move`) into twice as many buckets. So the load factor never goes above 1.

The checks use `std::string` and `int` keys, a struct key with its own hash, a hash that sends every key to bucket 0, a hash that returns the key itself (so they can predict every bucket), twenty thousand random operations compared with `std::map`, and a count of key comparisons.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class HashMap {
public:
    HashMap() {}

    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t bucket_count() const { return 0; }
    double load_factor() const { return 0.0; }
    std::size_t bucket(const K& key) const { return 0; }

    V* find(const K& key) { return nullptr; }
    const V* find(const K& key) const { return nullptr; }
    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) { return false; }
    V& operator[](const K& key) { return unused_; }
    bool erase(const K& key) { return false; }

private:
    std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<K, V>>> buckets_;
    Hash hash_{};
    V unused_{};
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class HashMap {
public:
    HashMap() : buckets_(8) {}

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t bucket_count() const { return buckets_.size(); }
    double load_factor() const { return static_cast<double>(size_) / buckets_.size(); }
    std::size_t bucket(const K& key) const { return hash_(key) % buckets_.size(); }

    V* find(const K& key) {
        for (auto& [k, v] : buckets_[bucket(key)]) {
            if (k == key) return &v;
        }
        return nullptr;
    }

    const V* find(const K& key) const {
        for (const auto& [k, v] : buckets_[bucket(key)]) {
            if (k == key) return &v;
        }
        return nullptr;
    }

    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) {
        if (find(key) != nullptr) return false;
        grow_if_needed();
        buckets_[bucket(key)].emplace_back(key, value);
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    V& operator[](const K& key) {
        if (V* found = find(key)) return *found;
        grow_if_needed();
        auto& chain = buckets_[bucket(key)];
        chain.emplace_back(key, V{});
        ++size_;
        return chain.back().second;
    }

    bool erase(const K& key) {
        auto& chain = buckets_[bucket(key)];
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < chain.size(); ++i) {
            if (chain[i].first == key) {
                if (i + 1 != chain.size()) chain[i] = std::move(chain.back());
                chain.pop_back();
                --size_;
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

private:
    void grow_if_needed() {
        if (size_ + 1 <= buckets_.size()) return;
        std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<K, V>>> bigger(buckets_.size() * 2);
        for (auto& chain : buckets_) {
            for (auto& pair : chain) {
                bigger[hash_(pair.first) % bigger.size()].push_back(std::move(pair));
            }
        }
        buckets_.swap(bigger);
    }

    std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<K, V>>> buckets_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    Hash hash_{};
};
--- hint
Keep `buckets_`, a `std::size_t size_`, and a `Hash hash_{}`. Make 8 buckets in the constructor's initialiser list. `bucket(key)` is `hash_(key) % buckets_.size()`, and `find` loops over that one bucket only, returning `&v` for the matching pair.
--- hint
Write a private `grow_if_needed()` that returns straight away when `size_ + 1 <= buckets_.size()`. +++ practice | A hash for a 3D grid cell
--- task
A simulation divides space into cubes called voxels, and keeps the busy ones in a hash map. Write the key type and its hash. No `main`.

- `struct Voxel` with three `int` members `x`, `y` and `z` (in that order) and a defaulted `operator==`.
- `struct VoxelHash` whose `std::size_t operator()(const Voxel& v) const` mixes all three members.

The hash must obey the contract (equal voxels, equal hashes) and spread voxels well. The order of the members must matter, so (1, 2, 3), (3, 2, 1) and (2, 1, 3) should hash differently. A check puts the 8,000 voxels with coordinates 0 to 19 into 1,024 buckets by `hash % 1024`: no bucket may get more than 40. A hash that adds or XORs the three numbers fails that, because it only produces a few dozen different values.

For example, `std::unordered_map<Voxel, int, VoxelHash>` must then work as a map from voxels to counts.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <unordered_map>

struct Voxel {
    int x;
    int y;
    int z;
    bool operator==(const Voxel&) const = default;
};

struct VoxelHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const Voxel& v) const {
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(v.x ^ v.y ^ v.z);
    }
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <unordered_map>

struct Voxel {
    int x;
    int y;
    int z;
    bool operator==(const Voxel&) const = default;
};

struct VoxelHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const Voxel& v) const {
        std::size_t h = std::hash<int>{}(v.x);
        for (int part : {v.y, v.z}) {
            h ^= std::hash<int>{}(part) + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 + (h << 6) + (h >> 2);
        }
        return h;
    }
};
--- hint
XOR-ing or adding the three coordinates throws information away: every voxel whose coordinates XOR to the same number collides. Mix the members in one at a time, so each step changes all the bits of the running hash.
--- hint
Start from the hash of `x`, then fold in `y` and then `z` with the combining step from the lesson: XOR in the member's hash plus the mixing constant plus shifted copies of the hash so far.

+++ practice | Rehash by hand
--- task
Write the rehash step on its own. The table is `using Table = std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, std::string>>>;` (the starter has this line), and every key is 0 or more. No `main`.

Write `Table rehash(Table& old, std::size_t new_count)`. It returns a new table with `new_count` buckets holding every pair of `old`, with each pair in bucket `key % new_count`. Walk `old` bucket by bucket from bucket 0, and each bucket from front to back, appending each pair to the end of its new bucket; so pairs that land in the same new bucket keep that walking order.

**Move** each pair, never copy it: a check looks at a long string's character buffer before and after and expects the very same buffer (a moved `std::string` hands over its buffer; a copy makes a new one). After the call, `old` may hold moved-from pairs. `new_count` may be smaller than the old count, or 1; it is never 0.

For example, keys 3, 11, 4 in bucket order become, with 4 buckets, bucket 0 = {4} and bucket 3 = {3, 11}.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using Table = std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, std::string>>>;

Table rehash(Table& old, std::size_t new_count) {
    return Table(new_count);
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using Table = std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, std::string>>>;

Table rehash(Table& old, std::size_t new_count) {
    Table fresh(new_count);
    for (auto& chain : old) {
        for (auto& pair : chain) {
            std::size_t b = static_cast<std::size_t>(pair.first) % new_count;
            fresh[b].push_back(std::move(pair));
        }
    }
    return fresh;
}
--- hint
Make `Table fresh(new_count);`, which has `new_count` empty buckets. Loop over the old buckets in order, and over each bucket's pairs in order.
--- hint
Loop with `auto& pair` (a reference, so you can move from it) and `push_back(std::move(pair))` into bucket `pair.first % new_count`.

--- check test | Shrinking to one bucket keeps every pair in walking order

--- check test | An empty table stays empty

--- check test | Strings are moved, not copied

?? Loop with auto& and push_back(std::move(pair)). A copy allocates a new character buffer.

+++ practice | Chains of nodes: pointers that survive a rehash
--- task
The lesson's map moves pairs when it grows, so pointers from `find` break. Build the other design, the one `std::unordered_map` uses: every pair in its own heap node, so a rehash only relinks nodes and never moves a pair. No `main`.

`template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>> class NodeMap`. The starter gives the node type and the members: `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> heads_` holds each bucket's first node (or `nullptr`), and each node owns the next one through `next`, as in lesson 5's list. Write:

- `NodeMap()` with 8 buckets; `std::size_t size() const`; `std::size_t bucket_count() const`.
- `V* find(const K& key)`: a pointer to the value, or `nullptr`.
- `bool insert(const K& key, const V& value)`: adds a new node at the **front** of the key's chain and returns `true`, or returns `false` if the key is there.
- `bool erase(const K& key)`: unlinks and frees the key's node; `false` if missing.
- Growth: before adding a new key, if `size() + 1 > bucket_count()`, double the bucket count by **relinking**: take each node off its old chain and put it at the front of its new chain. Never create, copy or destroy a node while rehashing.

The checks keep a pointer from `find` across a thousand inserts and expect it to be unchanged.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class NodeMap {
    struct Node {
        K key;
        V value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

public:
    NodeMap() {}
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t bucket_count() const { return 0; }
    V* find(const K& key) { return nullptr; }
    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) { return false; }
    bool erase(const K& key) { return false; }

private:
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> heads_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    Hash hash_{};
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class NodeMap {
    struct Node {
        K key;
        V value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;
    };

public:
    NodeMap() : heads_(8) {}
    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t bucket_count() const { return heads_.size(); }

    V* find(const K& key) {
        for (Node* n = heads_[slot(key)].get(); n != nullptr; n = n->next.get()) {
            if (n->key == key) return &n->value;
        }
        return nullptr;
    }

    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) {
        if (find(key) != nullptr) return false;
        if (size_ + 1 > heads_.size()) grow();
        auto& head = heads_[slot(key)];
        auto node = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, value, nullptr});
        node->next = std::move(head);
        head = std::move(node);
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool erase(const K& key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &heads_[slot(key)];
        while (*link && !((*link)->key == key)) link = &(*link)->next;
        if (!*link) return false;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> rest = std::move((*link)->next);   // detach the rest of the chain first
        *link = std::move(rest);                                 // then free the old node
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

private:
    std::size_t slot(const K& key) const { return hash_(key) % heads_.size(); }

    void grow() {
        std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> bigger(heads_.size() * 2);
        for (auto& head : heads_) {
            while (head) {
                std::unique_ptr<Node> node = std::move(head);   // take the first node off
                head = std::move(node->next);                   // the rest of the chain stays
                auto& dest = bigger[hash_(node->key) % bigger.size()];
                node->next = std::move(dest);
                dest = std::move(node);
            }
        }
        heads_.swap(bigger);
    }

    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> heads_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    Hash hash_{};
};
--- hint
`find` walks one chain with a raw pointer: start at `heads_[b].get()` and step with `n = n->next.get()`. Inserting at the front is two moves: the new node's `next` takes the old head, then the head takes the new node.
--- hint
To erase, keep a pointer to the `std::unique_ptr` that points at the current node (start with `&heads_[b]`), and step it with `&(*link)->next`. When it points at the key's node, move that node's `next` into a local `std::unique_ptr` first, then move the local into `*link`: the old node is freed and the chain closes up.
--- hint
To rehash, repeatedly take the first node off an old chain (move the head into a local `std::unique_ptr`, then move its `next` back into the head), and push it onto the front of its new chain in the bigger vector.

+++ practice | Erase many from one bucket with swap-and-pop
--- task
The starter has `using Table = std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>>;`. Write `std::size_t erase_below(Table& t, int threshold)` that removes every pair whose value is less than `threshold`, from every bucket, and returns how many it removed. No `main`.

Use swap-and-pop inside each bucket: when the pair at position `i` must go, move the bucket's last pair into position `i` and `pop_back()`. Do not use `std::remove_if` or `erase`.

This is where the obvious loop breaks. After the last pair moves into position `i`, that pair has not been checked yet, so the loop must look at position `i` again instead of stepping on. The checks include buckets where several pairs in a row must go, where the last pair must go, where every pair must go, and empty buckets. The survivors may end up in a different order inside their bucket; the checks only look at which pairs are left in each bucket.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using Table = std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>>;

std::size_t erase_below(Table& t, int threshold) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using Table = std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>>;

std::size_t erase_below(Table& t, int threshold) {
    std::size_t removed = 0;
    for (auto& chain : t) {
        std::size_t i = 0;
        while (i < chain.size()) {
            if (chain[i].second < threshold) {
                if (i + 1 != chain.size()) chain[i] = std::move(chain.back());
                chain.pop_back();
                ++removed;          // do not step on: position i holds an unchecked pair now
            } else {
                ++i;
            }
        }
    }
    return removed;
}
--- hint
Use a `while` loop with your own index for each bucket, so you decide when to step on. Step on only when the pair at `i` stays.
--- hint
When the pair at `i` goes, move `chain.back()` into position `i` unless `i` is already the last position, then `pop_back()`, and stay at the same `i`.
--- check test | Several pairs in a row, and the last pair

?? After moving the last pair into position i, check position i again.
--- check test | Every pair goes, and empty buckets are fine
[] { Table t(3); t[1] = {{"x", 0}, {"y", -3}}; auto n = erase_below(t, 1); return n == 2 && t[0].empty() && t[1].empty() && t[2].empty(); }()
--- check test | No pair goes

--- check test | Survivors stay in their own buckets
[] { Table t(2); t[0] = {{"k1", 3}, {"k2", 8}, {"k3", 2}, {"k4", 7}}; t[1] = {{"m1", 9}, {"m2", 1}}; auto n = erase_below(t, 4); std::vector<std::string> b0, b1; for (auto& p : t[0]) b0.push_back(p.first); for (auto& p : t[1]) b1.push_back(p.first); std::sort(b0.begin(), b0.end()); return n == 3 && b0 == std::vector<std::string>{"k2", "k4"} && b1 == std::vector<std::string>{"m1"}; }()
--- check test | An empty table
[] { Table t; return erase_below(t, 100) == 0; }()
--- check test | 20,000 pairs in one bucket, half removed
[] { Table t(1); for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) t[0].push_back({std::to_string(i), i % 2 == 0 ? i : -i}); auto n = erase_below(t, 0); if (n != 10000 || t[0].size() != 10000) return false; for (auto& p : t[0]) if (p.second < 0) return false; return true; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the running total that went stale
--- task
`Counts` in the starter is a small chained hash map from words to counts, built like the lesson's: buckets are vectors of pairs, and it doubles its buckets when it would hold more keys than buckets.

`tally(words)` should count each word and also keep the total number of words under the key `"*total*"`. For example, `tally({"go", "stop", "go"})` should give `"go"` 2, `"stop"` 1 and `"*total*"` 3. With a few words it often works, but with many different words `"*total*"` comes out far too small (or the program crashes).

Find the bug in `tally` and fix it. Leave `Counts` as it is.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Counts {
public:
    Counts() : buckets_(8) {}

    int& operator[](const std::string& word) {
        auto& chain = buckets_[std::hash<std::string>{}(word) % buckets_.size()];
        for (auto& [w, n] : chain) {
            if (w == word) return n;
        }
        if (size_ + 1 > buckets_.size()) {
            grow();
            return (*this)[word];
        }
        chain.emplace_back(word, 0);
        ++size_;
        return chain.back().second;
    }

    int get(const std::string& word) const {
        for (const auto& [w, n] : buckets_[std::hash<std::string>{}(word) % buckets_.size()]) {
            if (w == word) return n;
        }
        return 0;
    }

private:
    void grow() {
        std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>> bigger(buckets_.size() * 2);
        for (auto& chain : buckets_) {
            for (auto& p : chain) bigger[std::hash<std::string>{}(p.first) % bigger.size()].push_back(std::move(p));
        }
        buckets_.swap(bigger);
    }

    std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>> buckets_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};

Counts tally(const std::vector<std::string>& words) {
    Counts c;
    int& total = c["*total*"];
    for (const auto& w : words) {
        c[w] += 1;
        total += 1;
    }
    return c;
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Counts {
public:
    Counts() : buckets_(8) {}

    int& operator[](const std::string& word) {
        auto& chain = buckets_[std::hash<std::string>{}(word) % buckets_.size()];
        for (auto& [w, n] : chain) {
            if (w == word) return n;
        }
        if (size_ + 1 > buckets_.size()) {
            grow();
            return (*this)[word];
        }
        chain.emplace_back(word, 0);
        ++size_;
        return chain.back().second;
    }

    int get(const std::string& word) const {
        for (const auto& [w, n] : buckets_[std::hash<std::string>{}(word) % buckets_.size()]) {
            if (w == word) return n;
        }
        return 0;
    }

private:
    void grow() {
        std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>> bigger(buckets_.size() * 2);
        for (auto& chain : buckets_) {
            for (auto& p : chain) bigger[std::hash<std::string>{}(p.first) % bigger.size()].push_back(std::move(p));
        }
        buckets_.swap(bigger);
    }

    std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>> buckets_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};

Counts tally(const std::vector<std::string>& words) {
    Counts c;
    c["*total*"] = 0;
    for (const auto& w : words) {
        c[w] += 1;
        c["*total*"] += 1;   // look it up again: c[w] may have moved every pair
    }
    return c;
}
--- hint
`total` is a reference to an `int` inside one of the bucket vectors. What happens to that vector when `c[w]` adds a new word and the map grows, or when the word lands in the same bucket and the vector needs more room?
--- hint
Do not keep a reference into the map across an insert. Look `"*total*"` up again each time you add to it.

+++ practice | Stretch: a least-recently-used cache of telemetry frames
--- task
A ground station keeps recently decoded telemetry frames in memory, up to a fixed number. When it is full and a new frame arrives, it throws away the frame that was used **least recently**. Write `class LruCache`. No `main`.

- `explicit LruCache(std::size_t capacity)`; the capacity is at least 1.
- `std::optional<std::string> get(int key)` returns the frame stored under `key`, or `std::nullopt`. A successful `get` makes that key the most recently used.
- `void put(int key, std::string frame)` stores the frame, replacing any old frame under that key, and makes the key the most recently used. If that leaves more than `capacity` keys, it removes the least recently used key.
- `std::size_t size() const` and `std::size_t evictions() const` (how many keys `put` has removed so far).

Both `get` and `put` must be O(1) on average: a check runs 400,000 operations on a cache of 50,000 frames, far too slow if you search a list. The standard design combines two containers:

- `std::list<std::pair<int, std::string>>`, the library's doubly linked list, in order from most to least recently used. `splice(begin(), list, it)` moves the node `it` to the front in O(1), and list iterators stay valid while other nodes are added, moved or erased.
- `std::unordered_map<int, std::list<std::pair<int, std::string>>::iterator>`, from each key to its node.

For example, with capacity 2: `put(1, "a")`, `put(2, "b")`, `get(1)`, `put(3, "c")` removes key 2, because key 1 was used more recently.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <list>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

class LruCache {
public:
    explicit LruCache(std::size_t capacity) : capacity_(capacity) {}
    std::optional<std::string> get(int key) { return std::nullopt; }
    void put(int key, std::string frame) {}
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t evictions() const { return 0; }

private:
    std::size_t capacity_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <list>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

class LruCache {
public:
    explicit LruCache(std::size_t capacity) : capacity_(capacity) {}

    std::optional<std::string> get(int key) {
        auto found = where_.find(key);
        if (found == where_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, found->second);   // now the most recent
        return found->second->second;
    }

    void put(int key, std::string frame) {
        auto found = where_.find(key);
        if (found != where_.end()) {
            found->second->second = std::move(frame);
            order_.splice(order_.begin(), order_, found->second);
            return;
        }
        order_.emplace_front(key, std::move(frame));
        where_[key] = order_.begin();
        if (where_.size() > capacity_) {
            where_.erase(order_.back().first);   // the least recently used key
            order_.pop_back();
            ++evictions_;
        }
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return where_.size(); }
    std::size_t evictions() const { return evictions_; }

private:
    std::size_t capacity_;
    std::size_t evictions_ = 0;
    std::list<std::pair<int, std::string>> order_;   // most recent first
    std::unordered_map<int, std::list<std::pair<int, std::string>>::iterator> where_;
};
--- hint
The list holds the frames in order of use, most recent at the front; the map finds a key's node without searching. Every successful `get` and every `put` moves that key's node to the front with `splice`.
--- hint
A new key goes in with `emplace_front`, and the map stores `order_.begin()`. If the cache is now over capacity, the least recently used key is `order_.back().first`: erase it from the map first, then `pop_back()` the list.
--- hint
When `put` finds the key already there, replace the frame through the stored iterator and move the node to the front; nothing is evicted.

+++ question | How long is the chain?
--- ask
A chained hash table has B buckets and holds n keys, and the hash obeys simple uniform hashing. For one stored key k, what is the expected number of **other** keys in k's bucket?
--- choice
n / B
--- choice correct
(n − 1) / B
--- choice
1
--- choice
log₂ n
--- why
For each of the n − 1 other keys j, let X_j be 1 if j landed in k's bucket. Each lands there with chance 1/B, so the expected value of X_j is 1/B. By linearity of expectation, the expected sum is (n − 1)/B. For a key that is not in the table there are n others, which gives n / B = α.

+++ question | Which operations break a pointer from find?
--- ask
In this lesson's `HashMap` (buckets are vectors of pairs, erase by swap-and-pop, doubling when full), you keep a `V*` returned by `find(k)`. Which later operations can leave it pointing at the wrong place?
--- choice
Only a rehash, because that is the only time pairs move.
--- choice
Only erasing k itself.
--- choice correct
Inserting any new key, and erasing any key.
--- choice
None: a pointer to a value always follows the value.
--- why
Inserting a new key can trigger a rehash, which moves every pair; even without one, it can make k's bucket vector reallocate. Erasing another key in k's bucket by swap-and-pop can move a pair into a different position of the same vector. `std::unordered_map` avoids all of this by giving every element its own node.

=== dsacpp-09 | Open addressing: linear probing, tombstones and the cache
--- teach
Last lesson's map kept each bucket in its own vector, and every bucket is a separate block of heap memory. **Open addressing** throws the buckets away: all the pairs live in one flat array, and a key that finds its slot taken tries the next slot. You built this in Python in DSA I, with linear probing and tombstones. In C++ you can see why it is so often the faster design, even though it looks at more slots: it is kind to the processor's cache. This lesson builds it with a power-of-two capacity, the tombstone bookkeeping a resize rule needs, and the numbers that say how full the table may get.

### The picture: parking on a street

Every house on a street has one parking spot in front of it. You drive to your own house; if the spot is taken, you take the next free spot along the street, and at the end of the street you carry on from the start. To find your car later, you walk from your house along the street until you see it, or until you reach an empty spot. An empty spot means your car is not parked anywhere further on, because you would have taken that spot.

### The definition

A **linear-probing** hash table is an array of `capacity` slots. Each slot is **empty**, **full** (holding a key and its value), or a **tombstone** (it held a pair that was erased). A key's **home** is hash(key) mod capacity. Its **probe sequence** is home, home + 1, home + 2, and so on, wrapping round mod capacity.

- **Search** walks the probe sequence and stops at the key (found) or at an empty slot (not there). It walks past tombstones.
- **Insert** of a key that is not there puts it into the first slot on its probe sequence that is not full: the first tombstone or the first empty slot, whichever comes first.
- **Erase** turns the key's slot into a tombstone.

The invariant that makes searching correct: *for every full slot holding key k, every slot from k's home up to the slot before k is full or a tombstone, never empty.* In everyday words: nothing empty sits between a key's home and the key. Two counts come with it: `size_` counts full slots, and `tombstones_` counts tombstones.

### Why a flat array wins in C++: the cache

The processor does not read memory one byte at a time. It fetches a whole **[[cache line|cache-line]]**, 64 bytes on most chips (128 on Apple's M-series), and keeps recently used lines in small, fast memories called caches. Reading something already in the cache takes about a nanosecond. Reading from main memory takes about [[a hundred times longer|latency]].

So what counts is how many *different lines* an operation touches, not how many slots it looks at:

- **Linear probing:** the next slot is right next to the last one, usually in the same cache line. Looking at three slots often costs one memory fetch.
- **Chaining with separate blocks:** the bucket's vector is somewhere else on the heap, and a chain of nodes (as in `std::unordered_map`) scatters every node. Each step along a chain can be a fresh fetch from main memory.

The flat array wins twice more: inserting never asks the heap for memory (only a resize does), and there is no pointer stored per pair.

### A slot in C++

Each slot holds a state, a key and a value. The state has three values, so an `enum class` with a one-byte underlying type fits:

```cpp fragment
enum class Mark : std::uint8_t { Vacant, Taken, Gone };
```

The `: std::uint8_t` after the name makes each `Mark` take one byte instead of an `int`'s four. How big is a whole slot? The compiler adds **padding**, unused bytes, so that each member starts at an address that is a multiple of its size. Here is a slot-like struct:

```cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

struct Bay {
    std::uint8_t state;
    int key;
    int value;
};

int main() {
    std::cout << sizeof(Bay) << "\n";         // 12: 1 byte, 3 bytes of padding, 4, 4
    std::cout << 64 / sizeof(Bay) << "\n";    // 5 bays fit in one 64-byte cache line
}
```

A slot stores a key and a value even when it is empty, so K and V need default constructors, and an erase should put `K{}` and `V{}` back, for the same reason a ring buffer's pop does: a tombstone must not keep a big string or a shared object alive.

### Power-of-two capacity, and why the hash must scramble

With capacity a power of two, the home is `hash & (capacity - 1)`, and stepping on is `i = (i + 1) & mask`, one AND each. That is why fast tables keep their capacity at 8, 16, 32 and so on.

The price: the mask keeps only the **low bits** of the hash. GCC's `std::hash<int>` returns the number itself, so keys that share their low bits all get the same home. Keys that are multiples of 64, such as addresses or sizes, are common, and in a table of 64 slots every one of them has home 0. Then the table is one long cluster and every operation is O(n).

The fix is to **[[scramble|mixing]]** the hash first, so that every input bit affects the low bits. Here is one standard scrambler, the last step of the MurmurHash3 algorithm, applied to keys that are multiples of 64:

```cpp
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

std::uint64_t scramble(std::uint64_t x) {
    x ^= x >> 33;
    x *= 0xff51afd7ed558ccdULL;
    x ^= x >> 33;
    x *= 0xc4ceb9fe1a85ec53ULL;
    x ^= x >> 33;
    return x;
}

int main() {
    for (std::uint64_t key = 0; key < 64 * 6; key += 64) {
        std::cout << (key & 63) << " " << (scramble(key) & 63) << "\n";
    }
}
```

The left column is always 0; the right column spreads over the table. Real flat tables either scramble every hash like this, or ask their users for a hash that already does.

### Tombstones and the resize rule

Why not just empty a slot on erase? Because it breaks the invariant. Say keys A and B share a home, A sits at the home and B one slot later. Empty A's slot, and a search for B stops at that empty slot and says "not there". A tombstone says "keep walking".

Tombstones are not free. A search walks past them, so for a *failed* search they are as bad as full slots. That is why the resize rule counts them: this lesson's table rebuilds before an insert whenever full slots plus tombstones would go above three quarters of the capacity. Rebuilding reinserts only the full slots into a fresh array, so it also clears every tombstone. If the table is mostly tombstones, the rebuild keeps the same capacity and only cleans; if it is really filling up, it doubles.

One more reason the rule matters: a search loop stops at an empty slot. If tombstones and full slots could fill the whole array, a search for a missing key would never meet an empty slot. The rule keeps at least a quarter of the slots empty, so every search ends. Code that must work on any table also caps the walk at `capacity` steps, as a second safety net.

### Why it is correct

- **Search.** Suppose key k is in the table. By the invariant, no empty slot lies between k's home and k, so the walk from home reaches k before any empty slot. So if the walk stops at an empty slot, k is not in the table.
- **Insert** first searches, so it never adds a second copy. It then places the key in the first non-full slot on its probe sequence. Every slot before that one is full, so the invariant holds for the new key; other keys' paths are unchanged, except that a tombstone or an empty slot became full, which never puts an empty slot into anyone's path.
- **Erase** turns a full slot into a tombstone. A tombstone is not empty, so no path gains an empty slot.
- **Rebuild** reinserts every key into an array with no tombstones, and each insert keeps the invariant.

### What it costs

Let α be the fraction of slots that are full (for failed searches, count tombstones too). In 1963 Donald [[Knuth|knuth]] worked out the expected number of slots a search examines, under uniform hashing:

- a successful search: about ½ (1 + 1 / (1 − α));
- an unsuccessful search, or an insert: about ½ (1 + 1 / (1 − α)²).

| α | successful | unsuccessful |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.50 | 1.5 | 2.5 |
| 0.75 | 2.5 | 8.5 |
| 0.90 | 5.5 | 50.5 |

The square in the second formula comes from **[[primary clustering|clustering]]**: full slots gather in long runs, a key that lands anywhere in a run joins its end, and so long runs grow faster than short ones. That is why flat tables stop at a load of about 0.75 or less, and why the tombstones must count.

- **find, insert, erase:** O(1) expected at a bounded load, O(n) in the worst case.
- **Rebuild:** O(capacity); doubling makes it O(1) amortised per insert, as for the dynamic array.
- **Memory:** capacity × sizeof(slot), in one block.

### Where it is used

- **Google's SwissTable**, published as Abseil's `flat_hash_map`, and **Rust's standard `HashMap`**, which copies its design, are open-addressing tables tuned for the cache; see [[how SwissTable probes|swiss-table]].
- **Python's `dict` and `set`** use open addressing with a scrambled probe order instead of steps of one.
- **Compilers:** LLVM's `DenseMap`, used all over the compiler that builds this course's C++, is a flat open-addressing table (it probes with growing steps rather than steps of one).
- **ORBIT's world:** flight software that may not allocate after start-up keeps a fixed-size flat table, for example of telemetry channel numbers, sized so its load stays below 0.5.

**Watch out:** erasing by marking a slot empty. The table still looks fine, and then a key further along the same cluster "disappears". The second trap is a search loop with no step limit: once tombstones and full slots fill every slot, a search for a missing key walks round the table forever.

::: context cache-line The unit the processor really reads
Main memory is read in blocks of 64 bytes called cache lines. When your code reads one slot, the processor fetches the whole line around it, so the neighbouring slots arrive for free. A linear-probing table with 12-byte slots gets five slots per line. A chain of heap nodes gets one useful node per line, with the rest of the line wasted on whatever happens to sit next to it.

    <rect x="138" y="26" width="64" height="34" fill="#8fb8f0" stroke="#1d6fd1"/><text x="170" y="47">slot 10</text>

::: context latency Latency numbers worth knowing
Rough figures for a modern desktop processor: a first-level cache hit takes about 1 ns, a second-level hit about 4 ns, a last-level hit about 15 ns, and a trip to main memory about 80 to 100 ns. In 100 ns the processor could have run several hundred instructions. The list known as "latency numbers every programmer should know", popularised by Jeff Dean at Google, makes the same point: most of the time a data structure spends is waiting for memory, so the layout often matters more than the instruction count.
:::

::: context mixing Scramblers, or finalisers
A scrambler, also called a mixer or a finaliser, is a function that makes every bit of its output depend on every bit of its input, so that nearby inputs give unrelated outputs. XOR with a shifted copy moves high bits down into low bits, and multiplying by a large odd number moves low bits up into high bits; alternating the two mixes thoroughly. Multiplying by an odd number and shifting can be undone, so a scrambler never makes two different keys collide. Abseil's tables mix every hash before using it for exactly this reason.
:::

::: context knuth The first analysis of an algorithm
Donald Knuth's analysis of linear probing, written up in 1963 while he was a graduate student, is often called the start of the analysis of algorithms as a subject. He later wrote that it was the first time he derived a non-trivial result about an algorithm's behaviour, and it led to his series of books, The Art of Computer Programming, whose volume 3 covers hashing. The formulas assume every probe sequence is equally likely, which a good scrambled hash comes close to.
:::

::: context clustering Why runs grow
Suppose the table has a run of 10 full slots in a row and, elsewhere, a lone full slot. A new key joins the long run if its home is any of those 10 slots or the empty slot just after them: 11 chances. It joins the lone slot's run with 2 chances. So long runs attract more keys and grow faster, which is called primary clustering. Probing with bigger or random-looking steps avoids it, at the cost of leaving the cache line; SwissTable and Python's dict make different trade-offs here.
:::

::: context swiss-table How SwissTable probes
SwissTable keeps, next to the slots, one control byte per slot: empty, deleted, or 7 bits of the key's hash. It checks 16 control bytes at once with a single SIMD instruction, which compares 16 bytes in parallel, and only looks at a real slot when those 7 bits match. So most failed comparisons never touch the keys at all. It was presented at CppCon 2017 by Matt Kulukundis, and Rust's `hashbrown`, which is Rust's standard `HashMap`, uses the same design.
:::
--- task
Write `template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>> class FlatMap`, a linear-probing table in one `std::vector` of slots. Each slot has a state (empty, full or tombstone), a key and a value. K and V have default constructors. No `main`.

- `FlatMap()` starts with 8 empty slots. The capacity is always a power of two, the home of a key is `hash(key) & (capacity() - 1)`, and each step goes to the next slot, wrapping round to slot 0.
- `std::size_t size() const` (full slots), `std::size_t capacity() const` (all slots), `std::size_t tombstones() const`.
- `V* find(const K& key)`: a pointer to the value, or `nullptr`. It walks past tombstones and stops at an empty slot, and never looks at more than `capacity()` slots.
- `std::size_t slot_of(const K& key) const`: the slot holding the key, or `capacity()` if it is not there.
- `std::size_t probes(const K& key) const`: how many slots a search for the key looks at, counting the slot where it stops (the key's slot, or the empty slot). At most `capacity()`.
- `bool erase(const K& key)`: turn the key's slot into a tombstone, put `K{}` and `V{}` into it, and return `true`; `false` if the key is missing.
- `bool insert(const K& key, const V& value)`: return `false` if the key is there. Otherwise, first, if `(size() + tombstones() + 1) * 4 > capacity() * 3`, rebuild: the new capacity is double the old one if `(size() + 1) * 2 > capacity()`, and the same otherwise; reinsert every full slot in slot order, leaving no tombstones. Then put the pair into the first slot on the key's probe sequence that is not full, and return `true`.

The checks use a hash that returns the key itself, so they know every home: for example, with 8 slots, keys 1, 9 and 17 sit in slots 1, 2 and 3.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <functional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class FlatMap {
public:
    FlatMap() {}
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t tombstones() const { return 0; }
    V* find(const K& key) { return nullptr; }
    std::size_t slot_of(const K& key) const { return 0; }
    std::size_t probes(const K& key) const { return 0; }
    bool erase(const K& key) { return false; }
    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) { return false; }
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <functional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V, typename Hash = std::hash<K>>
class FlatMap {
    enum class State : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };
    struct Slot {
        State state = State::Empty;
        K key{};
        V value{};
    };

public:
    FlatMap() : slots_(8) {}

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return slots_.size(); }
    std::size_t tombstones() const { return tombstones_; }

    V* find(const K& key) {
        std::size_t i = slot_of(key);
        return i == slots_.size() ? nullptr : &slots_[i].value;
    }

    std::size_t slot_of(const K& key) const {
        std::size_t mask = slots_.size() - 1;
        std::size_t i = hash_(key) & mask;
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < slots_.size(); ++step, i = (i + 1) & mask) {
            const Slot& s = slots_[i];
            if (s.state == State::Empty) break;
            if (s.state == State::Full && s.key == key) return i;
        }
        return slots_.size();
    }

    std::size_t probes(const K& key) const {
        std::size_t mask = slots_.size() - 1;
        std::size_t i = hash_(key) & mask;
        for (std::size_t looked = 1; looked <= slots_.size(); ++looked, i = (i + 1) & mask) {
            const Slot& s = slots_[i];
            if (s.state == State::Empty || (s.state == State::Full && s.key == key)) return looked;
        }
        return slots_.size();
    }

    bool erase(const K& key) {
        std::size_t i = slot_of(key);
        if (i == slots_.size()) return false;
        slots_[i].state = State::Tombstone;
        slots_[i].key = K{};
        slots_[i].value = V{};
        --size_;
        ++tombstones_;
        return true;
    }

    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) {
        if (slot_of(key) != slots_.size()) return false;
        if ((size_ + tombstones_ + 1) * 4 > slots_.size() * 3) {
            rebuild((size_ + 1) * 2 > slots_.size() ? slots_.size() * 2 : slots_.size());
        }
        std::size_t i = first_free(key);
        if (slots_[i].state == State::Tombstone) --tombstones_;
        slots_[i].state = State::Full;
        slots_[i].key = key;
        slots_[i].value = value;
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

private:
    // The first slot on the key's probe sequence that is not full. The load rule keeps one free.
    std::size_t first_free(const K& key) const {
        std::size_t mask = slots_.size() - 1;
        std::size_t i = hash_(key) & mask;
        while (slots_[i].state == State::Full) i = (i + 1) & mask;
        return i;
    }

    void rebuild(std::size_t new_capacity) {
        std::vector<Slot> old(new_capacity);
        old.swap(slots_);            // slots_ is now all empty, old holds the pairs
        tombstones_ = 0;
        for (Slot& s : old) {
            if (s.state != State::Full) continue;
            std::size_t i = first_free(s.key);
            slots_[i].state = State::Full;
            slots_[i].key = std::move(s.key);
            slots_[i].value = std::move(s.value);
        }
    }

    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t tombstones_ = 0;
    Hash hash_{};
};
--- hint
Give the class a private `enum class State : std::uint8_t` with three values and a `struct Slot` with a state, a key and a value, all with default member values. Store `std::vector<Slot> slots_` (8 of them to start), `size_` and `tombstones_`. The mask is `slots_.size() - 1`.
--- hint
`slot_of` walks from the home with `i = (i + 1) & mask` for at most `capacity()` steps: stop at an empty slot, skip tombstones, and return `i` at a full slot whose key matches. `find`, `erase` and `insert` can all start from it. `probes` is the same walk, counting.
--- hint
For `rebuild`, swap a fresh vector of the new capacity into `slots_`, set `tombstones_` to 0, and put each full slot of the old vector into the first non-full slot of its own probe sequence (no duplicate check is needed). In `insert`, after any rebuild, place the pair in the first non-full slot, and if that slot was a tombstone, take one off `tombstones_`.

+++ practice | Fibonacci hashing: multiply, keep the top bits
--- task
Another way to scramble a hash into a slot number: multiply by a fixed odd 64-bit constant and keep the **top** bits of the product, not the bottom ones. Multiplication carries every input bit upwards, so the top bits depend on all of them. With the constant 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 (2⁶⁴ divided by the golden ratio) this is called **Fibonacci hashing**. No `main`.

Write `std::uint64_t fib_slot(std::uint64_t key, unsigned bits)` that returns a slot in a table of 2^bits slots:

- multiply `key` by `0x9E3779B97F4A7C15` in `std::uint64_t` (the product wraps mod 2⁶⁴, which is what you want);
- shift the product right by `64 - bits`, keeping its top `bits` bits.

`bits` is from 0 to 64. When `bits` is 0 the table has one slot, so the answer is 0. Watch out: shifting a 64-bit number by 64 is undefined behaviour in C++, not 0, so that case needs its own line.

For example, `fib_slot(1, 10)` is 632 and `fib_slot(1024, 10)` is 887.
--- starter
#include <cstdint>

std::uint64_t fib_slot(std::uint64_t key, unsigned bits) {
    return key & ((1ULL << bits) - 1);
}
--- solution
#include <cstdint>

std::uint64_t fib_slot(std::uint64_t key, unsigned bits) {
    if (bits == 0) return 0;   // a shift by 64 would be undefined behaviour
    return (key * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15ULL) >> (64 - bits);
}
--- hint
Write the constant with the suffix `ULL` so it is an unsigned 64-bit literal, and multiply in `std::uint64_t`. The product wraps round, which keeps its low 64 bits.
--- hint
Shift right by `64 - bits`. Handle `bits == 0` first, returning 0, because a shift by the full width is undefined behaviour.

=> 632
--- check case | fib_slot(1024, 10)

=> 887
--- check test | More examples, including bits = 64 and the largest key

--- check test | One slot: always 0
fib_slot(0, 0) == 0 && fib_slot(123456789, 0) == 0 && fib_slot(18446744073709551615ULL, 0) == 0
?? A shift by 64 is undefined behaviour. Return 0 when bits is 0.
