+++ practice | Average probes of a table
--- task
Measure a linear-probing table instead of building one. A table is a `std::vector<int>` of slots: a value of 0 or more is a key, `-1` is an empty slot and `-2` is a tombstone. The home of key k is `k % table.size()`, and probing steps to the next slot, wrapping round. No `main`.

Write `struct ProbeStats { double hit; double miss; };` and `ProbeStats average_probes(const std::vector<int>& table)`:

- `hit` is the average, over all keys in the table, of the number of slots a search for that key looks at: from its home to its own slot, both counted. A key in its home slot takes 1. With no keys, `hit` is 0.
- `miss` is the average, over every slot used as a starting home, of the number of slots a search for a missing key looks at: from that home up to and including the first empty slot. Tombstones do not stop it. If the table has no empty slot, a miss looks at all `table.size()` slots. The table is never empty.

The distance from a home h to a slot i, going forward with wrap-around, is (i − h) mod size; with unsigned numbers, write it as `(i + size - h) % size`.

For example, `{-1, 1, 9, -2, 4, -1, -1, -1}` has keys 1 and 9 (home 1) and 4 (home 4). Hits take 1, 2 and 1, so `hit` is 4/3. Misses starting at slots 0 to 7 take 1, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, so `miss` is 18/8 = 2.25.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <vector>

struct ProbeStats {
    double hit;
    double miss;
};

ProbeStats average_probes(const std::vector<int>& table) {
    return {0.0, 0.0};
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <vector>

struct ProbeStats {
    double hit;
    double miss;
};

ProbeStats average_probes(const std::vector<int>& table) {
    const std::size_t n = table.size();
    double hit_total = 0;
    std::size_t keys = 0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (table[i] < 0) continue;
        std::size_t home = static_cast<std::size_t>(table[i]) % n;
        hit_total += static_cast<double>((i + n - home) % n + 1);
        ++keys;
    }
    double miss_total = 0;
    for (std::size_t home = 0; home < n; ++home) {
        std::size_t looked = 1;
        while (looked < n && table[(home + looked - 1) % n] != -1) ++looked;
        miss_total += static_cast<double>(looked);
    }
    return {keys == 0 ? 0.0 : hit_total / keys, miss_total / n};
}
--- hint
For `hit`, each key's count is its forward distance from its home plus one. Compute the distance as `(i + n - home) % n` so it never goes below zero.
--- hint
For `miss`, start at each home in turn and count slots until you reach a `-1`, counting that one too. Stop counting at `n` slots if there is no empty slot at all.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { auto s = average_probes({-1, 1, 9, -2, 4, -1, -1, -1}); return s.hit > 1.3333333 && s.hit < 1.3333334 && s.miss == 2.25; }()
--- check test | A cluster that wraps round the end
[] { auto s = average_probes({13, 20, -1, -1, -1, -1, 6}); return s.hit == 2.0 && s.miss > 13.0 / 7 - 1e-9 && s.miss < 13.0 / 7 + 1e-9; }()
?? Key 20 has home 6 and sits in slot 1: its distance is (1 + 7 - 6) % 7 = 2, so it takes 3 probes.
--- check test | No keys: hit is 0, and tombstones do not stop a miss
[] { auto s = average_probes({-2, -2, -1, -1}); return s.hit == 0.0 && s.miss == (3 + 2 + 1 + 1) / 4.0; }()
--- check test | No empty slot at all: every miss looks at the whole table
[] { auto s = average_probes({0, 1, -2}); return s.hit == 1.0 && s.miss == 3.0; }()
--- check test | One slot
[] { auto a = average_probes({-1}); auto b = average_probes({5}); return a.hit == 0.0 && a.miss == 1.0 && b.hit == 1.0 && b.miss == 1.0; }()

+++ practice | Range-for over a flat set
--- task
The starter has `FlatSet`, a working linear-probing set of `int` keys with tombstones and a fixed capacity. Iterating over a flat table means walking the slot array and skipping every slot that is not full. Make `FlatSet` work with range-for and `<algorithm>`. No `main`.

Inside `FlatSet`, write a class `const_iterator` that holds a `const FlatSet*` and a slot number, with:

- the member types `iterator_category` (`std::forward_iterator_tag`), `value_type` (`int`), `difference_type` (`std::ptrdiff_t`), `pointer` (`const int*`) and `reference` (`const int&`);
- `const int& operator*() const`, the key in its slot;
- `const_iterator& operator++()` and `const_iterator operator++(int)`, which move on to the next **full** slot, or to slot `capacity()` if there is none;
- `bool operator==(const const_iterator&) const`.

`begin()` is the first full slot (or `end()` if there is none), and `end()` is slot `capacity()`. The keys come out in slot order, which is not sorted order.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iterator>
#include <vector>

class FlatSet {
    enum class State : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };
    struct Slot {
        State state = State::Empty;
        int key = 0;
    };

public:
    explicit FlatSet(std::size_t capacity) : slots_(capacity) {}
    std::size_t capacity() const { return slots_.size(); }

    bool insert(int key) {
        if (contains(key)) return false;
        std::size_t i = home(key);
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < slots_.size(); ++step, i = (i + 1) % slots_.size()) {
            if (slots_[i].state != State::Full) {
                slots_[i] = Slot{State::Full, key};
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    bool contains(int key) const { return find_slot(key) != slots_.size(); }

    bool erase(int key) {
        std::size_t i = find_slot(key);
        if (i == slots_.size()) return false;
        slots_[i] = Slot{State::Tombstone, 0};
        return true;
    }

    // Write class const_iterator here, then begin() and end().

private:
    std::size_t home(int key) const { return static_cast<std::size_t>(key) % slots_.size(); }

    std::size_t find_slot(int key) const {
        std::size_t i = home(key);
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < slots_.size(); ++step, i = (i + 1) % slots_.size()) {
            if (slots_[i].state == State::Empty) break;
            if (slots_[i].state == State::Full && slots_[i].key == key) return i;
        }
        return slots_.size();
    }

    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iterator>
#include <vector>

class FlatSet {
    enum class State : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };
    struct Slot {
        State state = State::Empty;
        int key = 0;
    };

public:
    explicit FlatSet(std::size_t capacity) : slots_(capacity) {}
    std::size_t capacity() const { return slots_.size(); }

    bool insert(int key) {
        if (contains(key)) return false;
        std::size_t i = home(key);
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < slots_.size(); ++step, i = (i + 1) % slots_.size()) {
            if (slots_[i].state != State::Full) {
                slots_[i] = Slot{State::Full, key};
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    bool contains(int key) const { return find_slot(key) != slots_.size(); }

    bool erase(int key) {
        std::size_t i = find_slot(key);
        if (i == slots_.size()) return false;
        slots_[i] = Slot{State::Tombstone, 0};
        return true;
    }

    class const_iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        const_iterator() = default;
        const_iterator(const FlatSet* set, std::size_t slot) : set_(set), slot_(slot) { skip(); }

        const int& operator*() const { return set_->slots_[slot_].key; }
        const_iterator& operator++() {
            ++slot_;
            skip();
            return *this;
        }
        const_iterator operator++(int) {
            const_iterator before = *this;
            ++*this;
            return before;
        }
        bool operator==(const const_iterator& other) const { return set_ == other.set_ && slot_ == other.slot_; }

    private:
        // Move forward to the next full slot, or stop at capacity().
        void skip() {
            while (slot_ < set_->slots_.size() && set_->slots_[slot_].state != State::Full) ++slot_;
        }
        const FlatSet* set_ = nullptr;
        std::size_t slot_ = 0;
    };

    const_iterator begin() const { return const_iterator(this, 0); }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(this, slots_.size()); }

private:
    std::size_t home(int key) const { return static_cast<std::size_t>(key) % slots_.size(); }

    std::size_t find_slot(int key) const {
        std::size_t i = home(key);
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < slots_.size(); ++step, i = (i + 1) % slots_.size()) {
            if (slots_[i].state == State::Empty) break;
            if (slots_[i].state == State::Full && slots_[i].key == key) return i;
        }
        return slots_.size();
    }

    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
};
--- hint
Give the iterator a private helper that moves its slot number forward while the slot is not full and the number is below `capacity()`. Call it in the constructor (so `begin()` lands on the first full slot) and after every step in `operator++`.
--- hint
A nested class may read the private members of the class it sits in, so `*it` can return `set_->slots_[slot_].key` directly. `end()` is built at slot `capacity()`, where the helper does nothing.
--- check test | Range-for sees every key once, and skips tombstones

?? Skip slots that are empty or tombstones, both at the start and after every step.
--- check test | Keys come out in slot order

--- check test | An empty set, and a set of only tombstones
[] { FlatSet a(8); FlatSet b(4); b.insert(1); b.insert(2); b.erase(1); b.erase(2); return a.begin() == a.end() && b.begin() == b.end(); }()
--- check test | A full set, and std::count_if

+++ practice | A fixed table with no empty slot left
--- task
Flight software often uses a fixed-size table that never grows. Then nothing stops tombstones and keys from taking every slot, and any loop that waits for an empty slot runs forever. Write three functions on such a table. No `main`.

The starter defines `enum class Mark : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };` and `struct Cell { Mark mark = Mark::Empty; int key = 0; };`. A table is a `std::vector<Cell>` with at least one cell; its size need not be a power of two. Keys are 0 or more, the home of key k is `k % table.size()`, and probing steps forward with wrap-around.

- `bool contains(const std::vector<Cell>& table, int key)`: walk from the home, skip tombstones, stop at an empty cell or after looking at every cell once.
- `bool insert_into(std::vector<Cell>& table, int key)`: return `false` if the key is already there, or if there is no cell that is not full. Otherwise put the key into the first empty-or-tombstone cell on its path and return `true`.
- `bool erase_from(std::vector<Cell>& table, int key)`: turn the key's cell into a tombstone (with key 0) and return `true`, or return `false`.

The tricky case: a table with no empty cell at all, where the key is somewhere after a tombstone. `insert_into` must still notice it is already there, so it cannot stop at the first tombstone.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <vector>

enum class Mark : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };

struct Cell {
    Mark mark = Mark::Empty;
    int key = 0;
};

bool contains(const std::vector<Cell>& table, int key) { return false; }
bool insert_into(std::vector<Cell>& table, int key) { return false; }
bool erase_from(std::vector<Cell>& table, int key) { return false; }
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <vector>

enum class Mark : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };

struct Cell {
    Mark mark = Mark::Empty;
    int key = 0;
};

// The key's cell, or table.size() if it is not there. Looks at each cell at most once.
std::size_t locate(const std::vector<Cell>& table, int key) {
    const std::size_t n = table.size();
    std::size_t i = static_cast<std::size_t>(key) % n;
    for (std::size_t step = 0; step < n; ++step, i = (i + 1) % n) {
        if (table[i].mark == Mark::Empty) break;
        if (table[i].mark == Mark::Full && table[i].key == key) return i;
    }
    return n;
}

bool contains(const std::vector<Cell>& table, int key) { return locate(table, key) != table.size(); }

bool insert_into(std::vector<Cell>& table, int key) {
    if (contains(table, key)) return false;
    const std::size_t n = table.size();
    std::size_t i = static_cast<std::size_t>(key) % n;
    for (std::size_t step = 0; step < n; ++step, i = (i + 1) % n) {
        if (table[i].mark != Mark::Full) {
            table[i] = Cell{Mark::Full, key};
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;   // every cell is full
}

bool erase_from(std::vector<Cell>& table, int key) {
    std::size_t i = locate(table, key);
    if (i == table.size()) return false;
    table[i] = Cell{Mark::Tombstone, 0};
    return true;
}
--- hint
Every walk is a `for` loop that counts its steps and stops after `table.size()` of them, whatever it finds. Step with `i = (i + 1) % n`.
--- hint
Write one helper that returns the key's cell or `n`: it stops early only at an empty cell. `insert_into` calls it first; only when the key is missing does it walk again to the first cell that is not full.
--- check test | A table of only tombstones: nothing is found, and insert takes the home cell
[] { std::vector<Cell> t(4, Cell{Mark::Tombstone, 0}); bool none = !contains(t, 1) && !contains(t, 6); bool added = insert_into(t, 6); return none && added && t[2].mark == Mark::Full && t[2].key == 6 && contains(t, 6); }()
?? With no empty cell, a walk that only stops at an empty cell never stops. Count the steps.
--- check test | No empty cell, and the key sits after a tombstone
[] { std::vector<Cell> t = {Cell{Mark::Full, 3}, Cell{Mark::Tombstone, 0}, Cell{Mark::Full, 5}, Cell{Mark::Full, 9}}; bool twin = insert_into(t, 9); return !twin && contains(t, 9) && t[1].mark == Mark::Tombstone; }()
?? Key 9 has home 1, a tombstone. Check the whole path before you use that tombstone.
--- check test | A truly full table refuses a new key
[] { std::vector<Cell> t(3); bool a = insert_into(t, 0) && insert_into(t, 3) && insert_into(t, 6); bool refused = !insert_into(t, 9); return a && refused && contains(t, 6) && !contains(t, 9); }()
--- check test | Erase, then insert into the freed cell, with wrap-around
[] { std::vector<Cell> t(5); insert_into(t, 4); insert_into(t, 9); insert_into(t, 14); bool wrapped = t[0].key == 9 && t[1].key == 14; bool gone = erase_from(t, 9) && !erase_from(t, 9); bool found = contains(t, 14); insert_into(t, 19); return wrapped && gone && found && t[0].mark == Mark::Full && t[0].key == 19 && !contains(t, 9); }()
--- check test | One cell
[] { std::vector<Cell> t(1); bool a = insert_into(t, 7); bool b = !insert_into(t, 8); bool c = erase_from(t, 7); bool d = !contains(t, 7) && insert_into(t, 8); return a && b && c && d && contains(t, 8); }()

+++ practice | Debug: the insert that makes twins
--- task
`TagSet` is a linear-probing set of tag numbers (0 or more) in 16 fixed slots, with tombstones. `insert` should add a tag that is not already there and return `true`, or return `false` for a tag that is there. `size()` counts the tags.

It goes wrong after erasing. For example: insert 1, insert 17 (both have home 1, so 17 sits in slot 2), erase 1, then insert 17 again. That last insert should return `false`, and `size()` should stay 1. Instead it returns `true` and 17 is stored twice, so erasing 17 once leaves it still in the set.

Find the bug and fix it. The fix is one or two lines.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>

class TagSet {
    enum class Mark : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };
    struct Slot {
        Mark mark = Mark::Empty;
        int tag = 0;
    };

public:
    bool contains(int tag) const { return locate(tag) != 16; }

    bool insert(int tag) {
        std::size_t i = static_cast<std::size_t>(tag) % 16;
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < 16; ++step, i = (i + 1) % 16) {
            if (slots_[i].mark == Mark::Full && slots_[i].tag == tag) return false;
            if (slots_[i].mark != Mark::Full) {
                slots_[i] = Slot{Mark::Full, tag};
                ++size_;
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    bool erase(int tag) {
        std::size_t i = locate(tag);
        if (i == 16) return false;
        slots_[i] = Slot{Mark::Tombstone, 0};
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    std::size_t locate(int tag) const {
        std::size_t i = static_cast<std::size_t>(tag) % 16;
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < 16; ++step, i = (i + 1) % 16) {
            if (slots_[i].mark == Mark::Empty) break;
            if (slots_[i].mark == Mark::Full && slots_[i].tag == tag) return i;
        }
        return 16;
    }

    std::array<Slot, 16> slots_{};
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>

class TagSet {
    enum class Mark : std::uint8_t { Empty, Full, Tombstone };
    struct Slot {
        Mark mark = Mark::Empty;
        int tag = 0;
    };

public:
    bool contains(int tag) const { return locate(tag) != 16; }

    bool insert(int tag) {
        if (contains(tag)) return false;   // search the whole path first, past tombstones
        std::size_t i = static_cast<std::size_t>(tag) % 16;
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < 16; ++step, i = (i + 1) % 16) {
            if (slots_[i].mark != Mark::Full) {
                slots_[i] = Slot{Mark::Full, tag};
                ++size_;
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    bool erase(int tag) {
        std::size_t i = locate(tag);
        if (i == 16) return false;
        slots_[i] = Slot{Mark::Tombstone, 0};
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    std::size_t locate(int tag) const {
        std::size_t i = static_cast<std::size_t>(tag) % 16;
        for (std::size_t step = 0; step < 16; ++step, i = (i + 1) % 16) {
            if (slots_[i].mark == Mark::Empty) break;
            if (slots_[i].mark == Mark::Full && slots_[i].tag == tag) return i;
        }
        return 16;
    }

    std::array<Slot, 16> slots_{};
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Follow the example by hand. After erasing 1, slot 1 is a tombstone and 17 is still in slot 2. Where does the second `insert(17)` stop walking, and has it looked at slot 2 yet?
--- hint
Placing the tag at the first tombstone is right, but only once you know the tag is nowhere further along the path. Check for it with a full search first.

+++ practice | Stretch: Robin Hood hashing
--- task
Linear probing's worst keys can end up very far from home. **Robin Hood hashing** evens this out: while inserting, a key that has travelled further from its home than the key sitting in a slot takes that slot, and the displaced key carries on looking. It "takes from the rich" (keys close to home) "and gives to the poor". No `main`.

Write `class RobinHoodSet` for `int` keys (0 or more), with a fixed capacity and no erase. The home of key k is `k % capacity`, and a key's **distance** is how many steps forward (with wrap-around) its slot is from its home.

- `explicit RobinHoodSet(std::size_t capacity)`, at least 1 slot.
- `bool insert(int key)`: return `false` if the key is there or the set is full. Otherwise carry the key, with distance 0, from its home: at an empty slot, put the carried key there and stop; at a slot whose key has a **smaller** distance than the carried one, swap them (the carried key stays, the other key is now carried, keeping its own distance); then step on, adding 1 to the carried distance.
- `bool contains(int key) const`: walk from the home counting the distance d. Stop with `false` at an empty slot, **or** at a slot whose key's distance is smaller than d (our key would have taken that slot). Stop with `true` when the key matches.
- `std::size_t distance_of(int key) const`: the key's distance (the checks only ask about keys that are there).
- `std::size_t max_distance() const` and `std::size_t size() const`.

For example, with 8 slots, inserting 0, 8, 1, 16, 2, 9, 3 gives the distances 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3; plain linear probing would leave key 9 four steps from home. Robin Hood never changes the **total** distance of the keys, only how evenly it is shared.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class RobinHoodSet {
public:
    explicit RobinHoodSet(std::size_t capacity) {}
    bool insert(int key) { return false; }
    bool contains(int key) const { return false; }
    std::size_t distance_of(int key) const { return 0; }
    std::size_t max_distance() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class RobinHoodSet {
    struct Slot {
        bool full = false;
        int key = 0;
        std::size_t dist = 0;   // steps from the key's home
    };

public:
    explicit RobinHoodSet(std::size_t capacity) : slots_(capacity) {}

    bool insert(int key) {
        if (contains(key) || size_ == slots_.size()) return false;
        Slot carried{true, key, 0};
        std::size_t i = home(key);
        while (true) {
            Slot& s = slots_[i];
            if (!s.full) {
                s = carried;
                break;
            }
            if (s.dist < carried.dist) std::swap(s, carried);   // the poorer key takes the slot
            i = (i + 1) % slots_.size();
            ++carried.dist;
        }
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool contains(int key) const { return locate(key) != slots_.size(); }

    std::size_t distance_of(int key) const { return slots_[locate(key)].dist; }

    std::size_t max_distance() const {
        std::size_t most = 0;
        for (const Slot& s : slots_) {
            if (s.full && s.dist > most) most = s.dist;
        }
        return most;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

private:
    std::size_t home(int key) const { return static_cast<std::size_t>(key) % slots_.size(); }

    std::size_t locate(int key) const {
        std::size_t i = home(key);
        for (std::size_t d = 0; d < slots_.size(); ++d, i = (i + 1) % slots_.size()) {
            const Slot& s = slots_[i];
            if (!s.full || s.dist < d) break;   // our key would have stopped here
            if (s.key == key) return i;
        }
        return slots_.size();
    }

    std::vector<Slot> slots_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Store each key's distance in its slot, next to the key, so you never have to recompute it. The carried key during an insert is just a slot value (`full`, `key`, `dist`) that you swap with the resident one when the resident is closer to home.
--- hint
Check `contains` and fullness before you start moving keys, so an insert never stops half way. Inside the loop, the carried distance goes up by one with every step, whichever key is being carried.
--- hint
`contains` can stop early: as it walks, the resident keys' distances are compared with the distance it has walked so far. If a resident is closer to its home than that, the key you want would have displaced it, so it is not in the set.
--- check test | The example from the task

?? When the resident key's distance is smaller than the carried key's, swap them and keep walking with the displaced key.

+++ question | Why a tombstone and not an empty slot
--- ask
In a linear-probing table, keys A and B have the same home. A sits in its home slot and B in the next slot. You erase A by marking its slot **empty** instead of as a tombstone. What goes wrong?
--- choice
Nothing: B is still in the table, so searching finds it.
--- choice correct
A search for B starts at the home, sees an empty slot, and stops, so B is reported missing.
--- choice
The next insert of A goes into the wrong slot, but searches are unaffected.
--- choice
The table's size becomes wrong, but every search still works.
--- why
Searches stop at an empty slot because of the invariant: no empty slot lies between a key's home and the key. Emptying A's slot breaks that for B. A tombstone keeps the slot non-empty for searches while still letting an insert reuse it.

+++ question | Robin Hood and the total distance
--- ask
For the same keys inserted in the same order into tables of the same size, how does the total of all keys' distances from home compare between Robin Hood hashing and plain linear probing?
--- choice
Robin Hood's total is always smaller.
--- choice correct
The totals are equal; Robin Hood only shares the distance out more evenly, so the maximum drops.
--- choice
Robin Hood's total is larger, which is the price of a smaller maximum.
--- choice
It depends on the hash function.
--- why
Both methods fill exactly the same slots: an insert always ends at the first empty slot at or after the new key's home, whichever key finally lands there. Now take any slot i inside a run of full slots that starts at slot s. The keys that pass over i are those whose home is in s to i but whose slot is after i. Every slot from s to i holds a key whose home is in s to i, so the number passing over i is (the number of homes in s to i) − (i − s + 1): it depends only on the homes, not on which key sits where. The total distance is the sum, over all slots, of the keys passing over them, so it is the same for both methods. Only who travels how far changes.

=== dsacpp-10 | A binary heap, with the order as a template parameter
--- teach
The last two lessons answered "is this key here, and what goes with it?". A **priority queue** answers a different question: "of everything waiting, which comes first?". In DSA I you built its usual engine, the binary heap, on a Python list: sift up, sift down, and heapify in O(n), with the proof. This lesson builds it in C++ on a `std::vector`, and makes *what "first" means* a template parameter, called the **comparator**. That is exactly how `std::priority_queue` is built, and it explains the surprise that trips up almost everyone who first uses it: by default, it hands you the **largest** item.

### The picture: a chain of command

Picture an organisation chart where every manager outranks each of the people directly below them. Nobody promises anything about two people side by side, or about cousins in different branches. Yet the person at the very top outranks everyone, because every chain upwards only climbs in rank. That is a heap: a weak order, cheap to keep, that always knows its top.

### The definition, with a comparator

A **binary heap** stores n items in an array. The item at index i has its children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and for i > 0 its parent is at (i − 1) / 2, rounded down.

The order comes from a comparator `comp`: a function object where `comp(a, b)` is `true` when **a ranks below b**, that is, when a should come out later than b. The **heap property**:

*for every index i > 0, `comp(v[parent(i)], v[i])` is false.*

In everyday words: no item ranks above its parent. So nothing in the heap ranks above the root, and the root is the item that comes out first.

This lesson's class is `Heap<T, Compare = std::less<T>>`. With `std::less<T>`, `comp(a, b)` is `a < b`, so "a ranks below b" means "a is smaller", and **the largest item is on top**: a max-heap. For a min-heap you pass `std::greater<T>`, where `comp(a, b)` is `a > b`. The standard library chose [[this direction|why-less-means-max]] for `std::priority_queue` too.

### Comparators you can pass

A comparator is any type whose objects can be called with two items and return `bool`. Three common kinds:

- **Library function objects:** `std::less<T>` and `std::greater<T>` from `<functional>`.
- **Your own struct**, when the order is part of your design, such as "the job with the earlier deadline comes first".
- **A lambda.** Every lambda has its own type, which [[has no name you can write|lambda-type]], so you ask the compiler for it with `decltype`:

```cpp fragment
auto shorter_first = [](const std::string& a, const std::string& b) { return a.size() > b.size(); };
Heap<std::string, decltype(shorter_first)> names(shorter_first);
```

`decltype(x)` means "the type of x". A lambda that captures nothing can even be made from its type alone in C++20, so passing the object is optional there. A lambda that captures variables must be passed in.

A comparator must behave like "less than": `comp(a, a)` is always false, and it must never say both `comp(a, b)` and `comp(b, a)`. Writing `<=` instead of `<` breaks that rule, which is called a **strict weak ordering**. The standard library's containers and algorithms assume it, and the balanced-tree lesson shows what goes wrong without it.

### A comparator that counts

A comparator object can hold data. That makes it a precise measuring tool: give it a pointer to a counter, and it counts every comparison the algorithm makes. The checks in this lesson use exactly this to prove the costs.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct CountingLess {
    long long* count;
    bool operator()(int a, int b) const {
        ++*count;
        return a < b;
    }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) v.push_back((i * 7919) % 1000);
    long long comparisons = 0;
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), CountingLess{&comparisons});
    std::cout << std::is_sorted(v.begin(), v.end()) << " " << comparisons << "\n";
}
```

It prints 1 and a number near 10,000, about n log₂ n for n = 1,000. The counter lives outside the comparator because algorithms copy their comparator freely; every copy holds the same pointer, so every copy adds to the same count.

### Moving through a hole instead of swapping

Sift up and sift down move one item along a path, swapping it with a parent or a child at each level. A `std::swap` is **three moves**, so a path of h levels costs 3h moves. For an `int` that is nothing; for an item holding a big struct it is [[real work|move-cost]].

The better way treats the moving item's slot as a **hole**. Take the item out once, slide each item on the path one level into the hole, and put the item down once at the end: h + 2 moves instead of 3h. You have seen this before in insertion sort, which shifts larger items right instead of swapping:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v = {2, 5, 8, 11, 4};   // insert the 4 into the sorted part
    std::size_t hole = v.size() - 1;
    int moving = std::move(v[hole]);         // take it out: the slot is now a hole
    while (hole > 0 && moving < v[hole - 1]) {
        v[hole] = std::move(v[hole - 1]);    // slide a bigger item right, into the hole
        --hole;
    }
    v[hole] = std::move(moving);             // put it down once
    for (int x : v) std::cout << x << " ";   // 2 4 5 8 11
    std::cout << "\n";
}
```

A heap's sift up does the same along the path from a leaf to the root, and sift down along a path of larger children.

### Counting down with an unsigned index

Heapify visits the indexes from the last parent, n/2 − 1, down to 0. With a `std::size_t` index the natural loop is a trap:

```cpp fragment
for (std::size_t i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; --i)   // never ends: i >= 0 is always true
```

An unsigned number is never negative, so after 0 comes the largest `std::size_t`, and the loop runs on (clang and GCC warn that the test is always true). Two other traps hide here: when n is 0 or 1, `n / 2 - 1` itself wraps round to a huge number. A safe form tests *before* taking one away:

```cpp
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::size_t n = 10;
    for (std::size_t i = n / 2; i-- > 0;) {   // test i > 0, then take one away
        std::cout << i << " ";                // 4 3 2 1 0
    }
    std::cout << "\n";
}
```

`i-- > 0` compares the old value with 0 and then lowers it, so the body sees n/2 − 1 down to 0, and nothing at all when n/2 is 0. It is sometimes read as "i [[goes to|goes-to]] 0".

The same care applies going up: the parent of i is (i − 1) / 2 only for i > 0, so sift up loops `while (i > 0)`.

### Pop, top and the empty heap

- `top()` returns a `const T&`: a read-only view of the root. If it handed out a changeable reference, a caller could lower the root's rank and silently break the heap property.
- `pop()` moves the root out, moves the last item into the root, removes the last slot, and sifts the new root down. It returns `std::optional<T>`, so an empty heap is an ordinary answer, not a crash.
- Calling `top()` on an empty heap is undefined behaviour, the same promise `std::vector::front()` makes; callers check `empty()` first.

### Heapify: building from a vector in O(n)

A constructor that takes a `std::vector<T>` by value can **move** it into the heap's storage (no copy of the items), then fix the order bottom-up: sift down every parent, from the last one to the root.

**Why it is correct.** Take the parents in decreasing order of index. When sift down reaches index i, both of i's children are the roots of heaps already: they have bigger indexes, so they were done earlier, or they are leaves. Sifting i down makes the subtree at i a heap. At the end, i = 0, so the whole array is a heap.

**Why it is O(n).** At most n / 2^(h+1) nodes have height h, and sifting one down costs at most 2h comparisons (two per level: pick the larger child, then compare it with the item). So the total is at most the sum over h of 2h · n / 2^(h+1), which is n times the sum of h / 2^h, and [[that sum is 2|height-sum]]. So heapify makes at most 2n comparisons.

### Why push and pop are correct

- **Push** puts the new item at the end, where only the link to its parent can break the heap property. Each step of sift up slides a parent down into the hole only if the new item ranks above it, so the parent now sits above its old children, which it already outranked, and below the new item. When the item is put down, it ranks no higher than its parent. No other link changed.
- **Pop** moves the last item into the root, where only the links to the root's children can break. Sift down picks the child that ranks higher (so that child outranks its sibling) and slides it up if it outranks the moving item. The link from the new root to the other child holds, and the only possibly broken link moves one level down. At a leaf, or when the moving item outranks both children, nothing is broken.

### What it costs

| Operation | Comparisons | Time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `top` | 0 | O(1) |
| `push` | at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ | O(log n), plus amortised O(1) for the vector's growth |
| `pop` | at most 2 ⌊log₂ n⌋ | O(log n) |
| build from n items | at most 2n | O(n) |
| memory | | n items, side by side in one vector |

Pushing items one at a time costs O(n log n) in the worst case (items in increasing order into a max-heap each climb to the root), which is why the O(n) constructor is worth having.

A heap is **not stable**: two items that rank equally may come out in either order. When order of arrival matters, add a sequence number and let the comparator break ties with it.

### Where it is used

- **`std::priority_queue`**, which is a heap on a `std::vector` with `std::less` as the default, exactly as here.
- **Schedulers and [[timer queues|timers]]:** "which task or timer is due next?" in operating systems, event loops and game engines.
- **Graph search:** Dijkstra's shortest paths and A* keep the next vertex to explore in a heap (DSA II).
- **Merging sorted streams:** databases and external sorts merge many sorted runs with a heap of their front items.
- **ORBIT's world:** a ground station's alert queue, where the most severe alert is handled first; and top-k monitoring, keeping the k largest readings with a small heap.

**Watch out:** the direction of the comparator. `Heap<int>` with the default `std::less` gives the **largest** first; people expect the smallest and get the reverse order. The second classic is the unsigned countdown `for (std::size_t i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; --i)`, which never ends and also breaks when n is 0 or 1.

::: context why-less-means-max Why "less" puts the largest on top
The C++ heap tools come from Alexander Stepanov's Standard Template Library of the 1990s, where every ordering algorithm takes a "less than" and sorts into ascending order with it. Heapsort with "less" repeatedly moves the heap's top to the end of the array, so to finish in ascending order the top must be the largest item. `std::priority_queue` reuses those tools, so with `std::less` its top is the largest too. Python made the opposite choice: `heapq` is a min-heap.
:::

::: context lambda-type The type of a lambda
When the compiler meets a lambda, it invents a class for it, with a unique name you cannot type, and an `operator()` holding the lambda's body. The lambda expression makes an object of that class, called a closure. Captured variables become its data members. `decltype(shorter_first)` names that invented class, so it can be passed as a template argument. Two lambdas with identical text still have two different types.
:::

::: context move-cost When moves are not free
Moving a `std::string` or a `std::vector` copies only a few pointers, but moving a struct that holds a `std::array` of telemetry samples copies every sample, because an array has no pointer to hand over. For such items, a heap that swaps does three times the copying of one that slides items through a hole. The standard library's `std::push_heap` and `std::pop_heap` use the hole method for exactly this reason.
:::

::: context goes-to The "goes to" joke
`while (i --> 0)` looks like an arrow meaning "while i goes to 0", and it circulates as a C++ joke. There is no `-->` operator: the compiler reads it as `(i--) > 0`, a post-decrement followed by a greater-than. The same loop written `for (std::size_t i = n; i-- > 0;)` is the standard way to count down over unsigned indexes, and clang's warning `-Wtautological-unsigned-zero-compare` catches the broken `i >= 0` form.
:::

::: context height-sum Why the sum of h over 2^h is 2
Write the sum 1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8 + 4/16 + … as rows: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …, then 1/4 + 1/8 + …, then 1/8 + …, and so on. The first row adds up to 1, the second to 1/2, the third to 1/4, so the rows together make 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 2. In a heap, half the nodes are leaves that never move, a quarter can drop one level, an eighth two levels: the work is dominated by the many short drops, not the few long ones.

::: context timers Timers in real systems
An event loop, such as the one in Node.js (the libuv library) or in the Go runtime, keeps every pending timer in a heap ordered by due time, so finding the next one to fire is O(1) and adding one is O(log n). Go uses a 4-ary heap, where each node has four children: the tree is half as tall, so sift up does fewer steps, and the four children sit next to each other in memory, which suits the cache.
:::
--- task
Write `template <typename T, typename Compare = std::less<T>> class Heap`, a binary heap stored in a `std::vector<T>`, where `comp(a, b)` true means a ranks below b and the top is the item nothing ranks above. No `main`.

- `Heap()`; `explicit Heap(Compare comp)`, which stores the comparator it is given; and `explicit Heap(std::vector<T> items, Compare comp = Compare())`, which moves `items` into the heap and builds it bottom-up in O(n).
- `std::size_t size() const` and `bool empty() const`.
- `const T& top() const`: the top item. Only called when the heap is not empty.
- `void push(T item)`: add an item, moving it into place with sift up.
- `std::optional<T> pop()`: remove the top item and return it (moved out), restoring the heap with sift down; `std::nullopt` if empty.

Sift through a hole, not with swaps: take the moving item out once, slide items into the hole, and put it down once. The checks count comparisons with a counting comparator (building a heap of 65,536 items must take at most 2n comparisons) and count moves with an item type that counts them, and they use a heap of `std::unique_ptr`s, which can only be moved.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, typename Compare = std::less<T>>
class Heap {
public:
    Heap() = default;
    explicit Heap(Compare comp) : comp_(comp) {}
    explicit Heap(std::vector<T> items, Compare comp = Compare()) : comp_(comp) {}

    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    bool empty() const { return true; }
    const T& top() const { return data_.front(); }
    void push(T item) {}
    std::optional<T> pop() { return std::nullopt; }

private:
    std::vector<T> data_;
    Compare comp_{};
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, typename Compare = std::less<T>>
class Heap {
public:
    Heap() = default;
    explicit Heap(Compare comp) : comp_(comp) {}
    explicit Heap(std::vector<T> items, Compare comp = Compare()) : data_(std::move(items)), comp_(comp) {
        for (std::size_t i = data_.size() / 2; i-- > 0;) sift_down(i);
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return data_.size(); }
    bool empty() const { return data_.empty(); }
    const T& top() const { return data_.front(); }

    void push(T item) {
        data_.push_back(std::move(item));
        sift_up(data_.size() - 1);
    }

    std::optional<T> pop() {
        if (data_.empty()) return std::nullopt;
        std::optional<T> out(std::move(data_.front()));
        if (data_.size() > 1) {
            data_.front() = std::move(data_.back());
            data_.pop_back();
            sift_down(0);
        } else {
            data_.pop_back();
        }
        return out;
    }

private:
    void sift_up(std::size_t hole) {
        T moving = std::move(data_[hole]);
        while (hole > 0) {
            std::size_t parent = (hole - 1) / 2;
            if (!comp_(data_[parent], moving)) break;   // the parent does not rank below it
            data_[hole] = std::move(data_[parent]);
            hole = parent;
        }
        data_[hole] = std::move(moving);
    }

    void sift_down(std::size_t hole) {
        const std::size_t n = data_.size();
        T moving = std::move(data_[hole]);
        while (true) {
            std::size_t child = 2 * hole + 1;
            if (child >= n) break;
            if (child + 1 < n && comp_(data_[child], data_[child + 1])) ++child;   // the higher-ranked child
            if (!comp_(moving, data_[child])) break;
            data_[hole] = std::move(data_[child]);
            hole = child;
        }
        data_[hole] = std::move(moving);
    }

    std::vector<T> data_;
    Compare comp_{};
};
--- hint
Keep a `std::vector<T> data_` and a `Compare comp_`. Write two private helpers, `sift_up(i)` and `sift_down(i)`. `push` appends with `push_back(std::move(item))` and sifts the last index up; the vector constructor moves `items` into `data_` and sifts down every parent from `size() / 2 - 1` to 0, counting down with `for (std::size_t i = data_.size() / 2; i-- > 0;)`.
--- hint
In `sift_up`, move the item out into a local, then loop while the hole is above index 0: if `comp_(data_[parent], moving)` is true, the parent ranks below the item, so move the parent down into the hole and go up. Otherwise stop. Finally move the item into the hole.
--- hint
In `sift_down`, pick the child that ranks higher: start with the left child `2 * hole + 1`, and switch to the right one if it exists and `comp_(left, right)` is true. Move that child up into the hole only if `comp_(moving, child)` is true. `pop` moves the root out first, then moves the last item into the root and sifts it down (unless the heap had just one item).
--- check case | The default comparator puts the largest on top
[] { Heap<int> h; for (int x : {5, 1, 9, 3, 7}) h.push(x); std::vector<int> out; while (auto x = h.pop()) out.push_back(*x); return out; }()
=> std::vector<int>{9, 7, 5, 3, 1}
--- check case | std::greater gives the smallest first

=> std::vector<int>{1, 3, 5, 7, 9}
--- check test | top shows the top without removing it, and empty heaps behave

+++ practice | Is it a heap?
--- task
Write a function template that checks the heap property under any comparator. No `main`.

`template <typename T, typename Compare> std::size_t first_violation(const std::vector<T>& v, Compare comp)` returns the smallest index i > 0 where `comp(v[parent], v[i])` is true (the item at i ranks above its parent at (i − 1) / 2), or `v.size()` if there is none, which means `v` is a heap under `comp`. An empty vector and a one-item vector are heaps.

For example, under `std::less<int>()`, `{9, 4, 7, 5}` has its first violation at index 3 (5 ranks above its parent 4), and `{9, 4, 7, 1}` is a heap, so the answer is 4.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, typename Compare>
std::size_t first_violation(const std::vector<T>& v, Compare comp) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, typename Compare>
std::size_t first_violation(const std::vector<T>& v, Compare comp) {
    for (std::size_t i = 1; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        if (comp(v[(i - 1) / 2], v[i])) return i;
    }
    return v.size();
}
--- hint
Every index from 1 up has a parent at `(i - 1) / 2`. Check them in increasing order and return the first index where the comparator says the parent ranks below the child.
--- hint
If the loop finishes, there is no violation: return `v.size()`. The loop starts at 1, so it runs no steps for an empty or one-item vector.
--- check case | The first example from the task
first_violation(std::vector<int>{9, 4, 7, 5}, std::less<int>())
=> 3
--- check case | A max-heap has no violation
first_violation(std::vector<int>{9, 4, 7, 1}, std::less<int>())
=> 4
--- check case | The same vector under std::greater
first_violation(std::vector<int>{9, 4, 7, 1}, std::greater<int>())
=> 1
--- check test | Empty and one item are heaps
first_violation(std::vector<int>{}, std::less<int>()) == 0 && first_violation(std::vector<int>{5}, std::greater<int>()) == 1
--- check test | Equal items do not break the property
first_violation(std::vector<int>{4, 4, 4, 4, 4}, std::less<int>()) == 5 && first_violation(std::vector<int>{1, 1, 2, 1}, std::greater<int>()) == 4
--- check case | A lambda comparator on strings, by length
first_violation(std::vector<std::string>{"a", "bb", "ccc", "dd", "e", "ffff"}, [](const std::string& a, const std::string& b) { return a.size() > b.size(); })
=> 4

+++ practice | Heapsort in place, with any comparator
--- task
Write `template <typename T, typename Compare> void heap_sort(std::vector<T>& v, Compare comp)` that sorts `v` in place into ascending order under `comp`: afterwards no item is followed by one that ranks below it, so `comp(v[i + 1], v[i])` is false for every i. With `std::less` the result is smallest first; with `std::greater`, largest first. No `main`.

Use a heap inside `v` itself, with no second vector: build a heap under `comp` (its top is the item that ranks highest, which belongs at the end), then repeatedly move the top to the end of the unsorted part and sift down the item that took its place, shrinking the heap by one each time.

It must make at most 2·n·log₂ n + 2n comparisons: a check sorts 4,096 items with a counting comparator. It must also work on an empty vector and on one item.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, typename Compare>
void heap_sort(std::vector<T>& v, Compare comp) {
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// Sift the item at `hole` down within v[0, n).
template <typename T, typename Compare>
void sift_down_in(std::vector<T>& v, std::size_t hole, std::size_t n, Compare& comp) {
    T moving = std::move(v[hole]);
    while (true) {
        std::size_t child = 2 * hole + 1;
        if (child >= n) break;
        if (child + 1 < n && comp(v[child], v[child + 1])) ++child;
        if (!comp(moving, v[child])) break;
        v[hole] = std::move(v[child]);
        hole = child;
    }
    v[hole] = std::move(moving);
}

template <typename T, typename Compare>
void heap_sort(std::vector<T>& v, Compare comp) {
    const std::size_t n = v.size();
    for (std::size_t i = n / 2; i-- > 0;) sift_down_in(v, i, n, comp);
    for (std::size_t end = n; end > 1; --end) {
        std::swap(v[0], v[end - 1]);        // the top belongs at the end of the unsorted part
        sift_down_in(v, 0, end - 1, comp);
    }
}
--- hint
Write a helper that sifts down within the first `n` items only, so the sorted tail is left alone. Build the heap by calling it on every parent, counting down with `i-- > 0`.
--- hint
Then, while the heap has more than one item, swap `v[0]` with the last item of the heap part, shrink the heap part by one, and sift the new `v[0]` down within it.
--- check case | Ascending with std::less

=> std::vector<int>{-1, 0, 3, 5, 5, 12}
--- check case | Descending with std::greater
[] { std::vector<int> v = {5, -1, 12, 0, 5, 3}; heap_sort(v, std::greater<int>()); return v; }()
=> std::vector<int>{12, 5, 5, 3, 0, -1}
--- check test | Empty, one item, two items
[] { std::vector<int> a; std::vector<int> b = {7}; std::vector<int> c = {9, 2}; heap_sort(a, std::less<int>()); heap_sort(b, std::less<int>()); heap_sort(c, std::less<int>()); return a.empty() && b == std::vector<int>{7} && c == std::vector<int>{2, 9}; }()
--- check test | Strings by length with a lambda

+++ practice | Merging sorted telemetry streams
--- task
Several ground stations each send a stream of packet timestamps, already sorted from earliest to latest. Write `std::vector<long long> merge_streams(const std::vector<std::vector<long long>>& streams)` that returns every timestamp of every stream in one sorted list. No `main`.

When two timestamps are equal, the one from the stream with the **smaller index** comes first, and timestamps from the same stream keep their order. Some streams may be empty, and there may be no streams at all.

Use a min-heap of each stream's next unused timestamp, as in DSA I: each entry holds the timestamp, the stream's index and the position in that stream. Write a comparator for these entries (with a struct or a lambda) that puts the earliest timestamp on top and breaks ties by stream index. You may write your own small heap or reuse your `Heap` from the lesson. With N timestamps in k streams it must take O(N log k) time.

For example, streams `{1, 4, 9}`, `{2, 4}` and `{}` merge into `{1, 2, 4, 4, 9}`, where the first 4 is stream 0's.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<long long> merge_streams(const std::vector<std::vector<long long>>& streams) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Entry {
    long long time;
    std::size_t stream;
    std::size_t pos;
};

// "a ranks below b": a comes out later, so the earliest time is on top; ties go to the smaller stream.
struct Later {
    bool operator()(const Entry& a, const Entry& b) const {
        if (a.time != b.time) return a.time > b.time;
        return a.stream > b.stream;
    }
};

class EntryHeap {
public:
    bool empty() const { return data_.empty(); }

    void push(Entry e) {
        std::size_t hole = data_.size();
        data_.push_back(e);
        while (hole > 0 && comp_(data_[(hole - 1) / 2], e)) {
            data_[hole] = data_[(hole - 1) / 2];
            hole = (hole - 1) / 2;
        }
        data_[hole] = e;
    }

    Entry pop() {
        Entry top = data_.front();
        Entry moving = data_.back();
        data_.pop_back();
        if (!data_.empty()) {
            std::size_t hole = 0;
            const std::size_t n = data_.size();
            while (true) {
                std::size_t child = 2 * hole + 1;
                if (child >= n) break;
                if (child + 1 < n && comp_(data_[child], data_[child + 1])) ++child;
                if (!comp_(moving, data_[child])) break;
                data_[hole] = data_[child];
                hole = child;
            }
            data_[hole] = moving;
        }
        return top;
    }

private:
    std::vector<Entry> data_;
    Later comp_;
};

std::vector<long long> merge_streams(const std::vector<std::vector<long long>>& streams) {
    EntryHeap heap;
    for (std::size_t s = 0; s < streams.size(); ++s) {
        if (!streams[s].empty()) heap.push({streams[s][0], s, 0});
    }
    std::vector<long long> out;
    while (!heap.empty()) {
        Entry e = heap.pop();
        out.push_back(e.time);
        if (e.pos + 1 < streams[e.stream].size()) heap.push({streams[e.stream][e.pos + 1], e.stream, e.pos + 1});
    }
    return out;
}
--- hint
Start by pushing the first timestamp of every non-empty stream. Then repeat: pop the top entry, append its timestamp, and push the next timestamp from the same stream, if it has one.
--- hint
The comparator says when entry a ranks **below** b, that is, comes out later: a has the later time, or the same time and a bigger stream index. With that, the top is always the earliest time from the lowest-numbered stream.
--- check case | The example from the task
merge_streams({{1, 4, 9}, {2, 4}, {}})
=> std::vector<long long>{1, 2, 4, 4, 9}
--- check case | No streams, and only empty streams
std::vector<std::vector<long long>>{merge_streams({}), merge_streams({{}, {}})}
=> std::vector<std::vector<long long>>{{}, {}}
--- check case | One stream is returned as it is
merge_streams({{-5, 0, 0, 3}})
=> std::vector<long long>{-5, 0, 0, 3}
--- check test | Ties go to the stream with the smaller index
[] { std::vector<std::vector<long long>> st = {{7, 7}, {3, 7}, {7}}; auto out = merge_streams(st); return out == std::vector<long long>{3, 7, 7, 7, 7}; }()
--- check test | 500 streams, 100,000 timestamps, and big values
[] { std::vector<std::vector<long long>> st(500); std::vector<long long> all; unsigned s = 11; for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; long long t = 5000000000LL + static_cast<long long>(s >> 4); st[s % 500].push_back(t); all.push_back(t); } for (auto& v : st) std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()); std::sort(all.begin(), all.end()); return merge_streams(st) == all; }()

+++ practice | A queue that keeps arrival order among equals
--- task
An alert queue must hand out the highest-priority alert first, and among alerts of **equal** priority, the one that arrived first. A heap on its own is not stable, so equal priorities come out in a scrambled order. Fix that with a sequence number. No `main`.

Write `class AlertQueue`:

- `void push(int priority, std::string message)`: higher numbers are more urgent; priorities may be negative.
- `std::optional<std::string> pop()`: remove and return the message of the most urgent alert, the earliest-pushed one among equals; `std::nullopt` when empty.
- `std::size_t size() const`.

Give each alert a sequence number from a counter that goes up with every push (a `std::uint64_t` never runs out), and let the comparator break ties on priority by sequence number. Use a heap, with your own code or your `Heap` from the lesson: a check pushes and pops 200,000 alerts.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class AlertQueue {
public:
    void push(int priority, std::string message) {}
    std::optional<std::string> pop() { return std::nullopt; }
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class AlertQueue {
    struct Alert {
        int priority;
        std::uint64_t seq;
        std::string message;
    };

    // a ranks below b: lower priority, or equal priority and pushed later.
    static bool below(const Alert& a, const Alert& b) {
        if (a.priority != b.priority) return a.priority < b.priority;
        return a.seq > b.seq;
    }

public:
    void push(int priority, std::string message) {
        data_.push_back(Alert{priority, next_seq_++, std::move(message)});
        std::size_t hole = data_.size() - 1;
        Alert moving = std::move(data_[hole]);
        while (hole > 0 && below(data_[(hole - 1) / 2], moving)) {
            data_[hole] = std::move(data_[(hole - 1) / 2]);
            hole = (hole - 1) / 2;
        }
        data_[hole] = std::move(moving);
    }

    std::optional<std::string> pop() {
        if (data_.empty()) return std::nullopt;
        std::string out = std::move(data_.front().message);
        Alert moving = std::move(data_.back());
        data_.pop_back();
        if (!data_.empty()) {
            std::size_t hole = 0;
            const std::size_t n = data_.size();
            while (true) {
                std::size_t child = 2 * hole + 1;
                if (child >= n) break;
                if (child + 1 < n && below(data_[child], data_[child + 1])) ++child;
                if (!below(moving, data_[child])) break;
                data_[hole] = std::move(data_[child]);
                hole = child;
            }
            data_[hole] = std::move(moving);
        }
        return out;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return data_.size(); }

private:
    std::vector<Alert> data_;
    std::uint64_t next_seq_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Store each alert as a struct with its priority, its sequence number and its message. The comparison "a ranks below b" is: a's priority is lower, or the priorities are equal and a's sequence number is bigger (it arrived later).
--- hint
Everything else is an ordinary max-heap on that comparison: push appends and sifts up, pop takes the root's message, moves the last alert into the root and sifts it down.
--- check test | Higher priority first
[] { AlertQueue q; q.push(1, "low"); q.push(5, "high"); q.push(3, "mid"); auto a = q.pop(); auto b = q.pop(); auto c = q.pop(); return a && *a == "high" && b && *b == "mid" && c && *c == "low" && !q.pop(); }()
--- check case | All priorities equal: first in, first out
[] { AlertQueue q; for (std::string m : {"a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g", "h", "i"}) q.push(2, m); std::string out; while (auto m = q.pop()) out += *m; return out; }()
=> "abcdefghi"
?? A heap alone scrambles equal items. Break ties with a sequence number that grows with every push.
--- check case | Negative priorities and interleaved pops
[] { AlertQueue q; q.push(-1, "x1"); q.push(0, "y1"); q.push(-1, "x2"); std::string out = *q.pop(); q.push(0, "y2"); q.push(-5, "z"); while (auto m = q.pop()) out += " " + *m; return out; }()
=> "y1 y2 x1 x2 z"
--- check test | Empty queue
[] { AlertQueue q; bool a = !q.pop() && q.size() == 0; q.push(0, "only"); return a && q.size() == 1 && *q.pop() == "only" && q.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | 200,000 alerts with 10 priority levels come out in order, stable within each level
[] { AlertQueue q; unsigned s = 5; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int p = static_cast<int>((s >> 16) % 10); q.push(p, std::to_string(p) + ":" + std::to_string(i)); } int last_p = 100; int last_i = -1; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { auto m = q.pop(); if (!m) return false; std::size_t colon = m->find(':'); int p = std::stoi(m->substr(0, colon)); int idx = std::stoi(m->substr(colon + 1)); if (p > last_p || (p == last_p && idx < last_i)) return false; if (p != last_p) last_i = -1; last_p = p; last_i = idx; } return !q.pop(); }()

`MaxHeap` should always pop the largest remaining number. It pushes correctly, but it often pops numbers out of order. For example, pushing 1, 9, 5, 8, 7 and popping everything should give 9, 8, 7, 5, 1.

Find the bug and fix it. It is one line.

class MaxHeap {

    void push(int x) {
        data_.push_back(x);
        std::size_t hole = data_.size() - 1;
        while (hole > 0 && data_[(hole - 1) / 2] < x) {
            data_[hole] = data_[(hole - 1) / 2];
            hole = (hole - 1) / 2;
        }
        data_[hole] = x;
    }

    std::optional<int> pop() {
        if (data_.empty()) return std::nullopt;
        int top = data_.front();
        int moving = data_.back();
        data_.pop_back();
        std::size_t n = data_.size();

        if (n > 0) {
            while (true) {

                if (child >= n) break;

                hole = child;

            data_[hole] = moving;

--- hint
