+++ practice | Stretch: the running median of a sensor
--- task
A sensor reports whole-number readings, and the display shows the **median** of all readings so far after each one: the middle value when there is an odd number of readings, and the average of the two middle values when there is an even number. No `main`.

Write `std::vector<double> running_median(const std::vector<int>& readings)` that returns one median per reading, in order. An empty input gives an empty result.

Sorting all readings again for every new one is far too slow: a check uses 200,000 readings. Use **two heaps**: a max-heap `low` holding the smaller half and a min-heap `high` holding the larger half, kept so that `low` has either the same number of readings as `high` or exactly one more. Then the median is `low`'s top, or the average of both tops. Each new reading goes into one heap, and at most one reading moves across to restore the balance, so each step is O(log n). Your `Heap` from the lesson, used with `std::less<int>` and `std::greater<int>`, is exactly the tool; you may paste it in, or write the heaps yourself.

For example, readings 5, 15, 1, 3 give medians 5, 10, 5, 4.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<double> running_median(const std::vector<int>& readings) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename T, typename Compare = std::less<T>>
class Heap {
public:
    std::size_t size() const { return data_.size(); }
    const T& top() const { return data_.front(); }

    void push(T item) {
        std::size_t hole = data_.size();
        data_.push_back(item);
        while (hole > 0 && comp_(data_[(hole - 1) / 2], item)) {
            data_[hole] = data_[(hole - 1) / 2];
            hole = (hole - 1) / 2;
        }
        data_[hole] = item;
    }

    T pop() {
        T out = data_.front();
        T moving = data_.back();
        data_.pop_back();
        const std::size_t n = data_.size();
        if (n > 0) {
            std::size_t hole = 0;
            while (true) {
                std::size_t child = 2 * hole + 1;
                if (child >= n) break;
                if (child + 1 < n && comp_(data_[child], data_[child + 1])) ++child;
                if (!comp_(moving, data_[child])) break;
                data_[hole] = data_[child];
                hole = child;
            }
            data_[hole] = moving;
        }
        return out;
    }

private:
    std::vector<T> data_;
    Compare comp_{};
};

std::vector<double> running_median(const std::vector<int>& readings) {
    Heap<int, std::less<int>> low;       // the smaller half, largest on top
    Heap<int, std::greater<int>> high;   // the larger half, smallest on top
    std::vector<double> medians;
    medians.reserve(readings.size());
    for (int x : readings) {
        if (low.size() == 0 || x <= low.top()) low.push(x);
        else high.push(x);
        if (low.size() > high.size() + 1) high.push(low.pop());
        else if (high.size() > low.size()) low.push(high.pop());
        if (low.size() > high.size()) medians.push_back(low.top());
        else medians.push_back((static_cast<double>(low.top()) + high.top()) / 2.0);
    }
    return medians;
}
--- hint
A new reading at most `low`'s top belongs in the smaller half, `low`; anything bigger goes in `high`. When `low` is empty, put it in `low`.
--- hint
Then rebalance with at most one move: if `low` has two more than `high`, move `low`'s top into `high`; if `high` has more than `low`, move `high`'s top into `low`.
--- hint
After balancing, an odd total means `low` has one extra and its top is the median. An even total means the median is the average of the two tops; convert to `double` before adding, so two big readings cannot overflow an `int`.
--- check case | The example from the task
running_median({5, 15, 1, 3})
=> std::vector<double>{5, 10, 5, 4}
--- check case | Empty and one reading
std::vector<std::vector<double>>{running_median({}), running_median({-7})}
=> std::vector<std::vector<double>>{{}, {-7}}
--- check case | Equal readings and a falling trace
running_median({4, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1})
=> std::vector<double>{4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3.5}
--- check case | Halves and big values
running_median({2000000000, 2000000001, -2000000000})
=> std::vector<double>{2000000000, 2000000000.5, 2000000000}
?? Adding two big ints overflows. Convert to double first.
--- check test | 200,000 readings
[] { std::vector<int> r; unsigned s = 12; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; r.push_back(static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % 1000000)); } auto m = running_median(r); if (m.size() != 200000) return false; double total = 0; for (double x : m) total += x; return total == 98128958443.0 && m[0] == static_cast<double>(r[0]); }()
?? Sorting every prefix is billions of steps. Keep two heaps and move at most one reading across per step.

+++ question | Which heap does std::less give?
--- ask
This lesson's `Heap<int>` uses `std::less<int>` by default, like `std::priority_queue<int>`. You push 3, 8 and 5. What does `top()` return?
--- answer
8
--- why
The comparator says when a ranks **below** b. With `std::less`, a ranks below b when a < b, so smaller numbers rank lower and the largest number, 8, is on top. For the smallest on top, pass `std::greater<int>`.

+++ question | The cost of building a heap
--- ask
Why does building a heap bottom-up from n items take only O(n) comparisons, even though a single sift down can take O(log n)?
--- choice
Because the items are already partly sorted when they arrive.
--- choice correct
Because most nodes are near the bottom: at most n / 2^(h+1) nodes have height h, and the sum of h / 2^h is 2, so the total is at most 2n.
--- choice
Because sift down stops after one level on average, whatever the heap looks like.
--- choice
Because comparisons with leaves are free.
--- why
A node's sift down costs at most twice its height. Half the nodes are leaves (height 0), a quarter have height 1, an eighth height 2, and so on. Adding up 2h · n / 2^(h+1) over all h gives n times the sum of h / 2^h, which is 2. Only the few nodes near the top can drop far.

=== dsacpp-11 | A binary search tree with unique_ptr children
--- teach
Last lesson's heap kept a weak order: it always knew its top, and nothing else. A **binary search tree** keeps the full order, so it can list every key in sorted order and find the nearest key to any value. In DSA I you built one in Python: search, insert, the three cases of delete, and in-order traversal. In C++ the new questions are about the machine. Who owns each node? How do you change a link in the middle of a tree without special cases? What happens when the tree degenerates into a long chain, and your code recurses once per level? This lesson answers them with `std::unique_ptr` children, a pointer to the link, loops instead of recursion, and an in-order iterator that carries its own stack.

### The picture: a family that owns its branches

Think of a tree as a family business where each person owns their share and passes it to at most two heirs, one on the left and one on the right. When someone leaves, everything they own goes with them unless they hand it on first. That is exactly how `unique_ptr` children behave: each node **owns** its two subtrees, and destroying a node destroys everything below it.

### The definition

A **binary search tree** is a binary tree whose nodes hold keys, with the **BST property**: *for every node, every key in its left subtree is less than its key, and every key in its right subtree is greater.* In everyday words: smaller keys go left, larger keys go right, at every level.

This lesson's node:

```cpp fragment
struct Node {
    K key;
    V value;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;    // owns the smaller keys
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;   // owns the larger keys
};
```

The tree itself holds `std::unique_ptr<Node> root_`. Every node has exactly one owner, its parent's `left` or `right` (or `root_`), so there are no leaks and no double frees, whatever the operations do. To *look at* nodes without owning them, use raw pointers from `.get()`, as in lessons 5 and 6: `const Node* n = root_.get();` then `n = n->left.get();` walks down without taking anything from anyone.

### Keys need only `<`

The tree compares keys with `<` and nothing else. Two keys a and b are treated as the same key when neither `a < b` nor `b < a`. That is called **[[equivalence|equivalence]]**, and it is the rule `std::map` and `std::set` use too. So a key type needs only `operator<`, and `find` goes left when `key < n->key`, right when `n->key < key`, and has found it otherwise.

### Changing a link: a pointer to the owning pointer

Inserting and erasing change a link somewhere inside the tree: a `left`, a `right`, or `root_` itself. Code that walks with a `Node*` ends up one step too far: it is standing *on* the node, but needs to change the pointer that points *at* it. The C++ answer is to walk with a **[[pointer to the link|pointer-to-link]]**: a `std::unique_ptr<Node>*`, the address of the owning pointer that points at the current node (or that is empty, where a node would go).

```cpp fragment
std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;       // the address of the root pointer
link = &(*link)->left;                      // now the address of the root's left pointer
```

Read `*link` as "the owning pointer I am standing on", and `(*link)->key` as "the key of the node it points at". When a walk stops at an empty link, that empty `unique_ptr` is exactly where a new node belongs, and assigning to `*link` hangs it there. `root_` needs no special case, because it is just another link.

Here is the idea on a simpler structure, a train of cars kept sorted by number, where a new car may go at the front, in the middle or at the end, all with the same three lines:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>

struct Car {
    int number;
    std::unique_ptr<Car> next;
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr<Car> train;
    for (int n : {30, 10, 20}) {
        std::unique_ptr<Car>* link = &train;
        while (*link && (*link)->number < n) link = &(*link)->next;
        auto car = std::make_unique<Car>(Car{n, nullptr});
        car->next = std::move(*link);   // the rest of the train hangs behind the new car
        *link = std::move(car);         // and the new car hangs on the link
    }
    for (const Car* c = train.get(); c != nullptr; c = c->next.get()) std::cout << c->number << " ";
    std::cout << "\n";                  // prints 10 20 30
}
```

Why not a reference, `std::unique_ptr<Node>& link = root_;`? A reference cannot be re-seated: `link = ...` would not move the reference, it would **assign to the pointer it names**. `link = link->left;` does not compile (a `unique_ptr` cannot be copied), and `link = std::move(link->left);` compiles and hands the root's left subtree to `root_`, destroying the old root and its whole right side. A pointer to the link can be moved along; a reference cannot.

### Detach first, then assign

Erasing a node with one child is a single idea: make the node's link point at the child instead. The tempting line is `*link = std::move((*link)->right);`. Look at what it asks for. The standard says a `unique_ptr` move assignment first takes the pointer out of the source, then **destroys the object it used to own**, and then copies the source's deleter. But the source, `(*link)->right`, is a member of the very node being destroyed, so the last step [[touches a dead object|dead-source]]. With the default deleter nothing is really read, and real libraries survive it; but "which object is still alive?" is the question to ask about every line, and here the honest answer is "not the source". The clean form detaches first:

```cpp fragment
std::unique_ptr<Car> rest = std::move(front->next);   // the rest of the train, now held locally
front = std::move(rest);                              // the old front car is destroyed; rest is alive
```

### Erase: the three cases

With the link to the doomed node in hand:

1. **No left child:** the link takes the node's right child (which may be empty).
2. **No right child:** the link takes the node's left child.
3. **Two children:** find the node's **successor**, the smallest key in its right subtree: go right once, then left as far as possible, keeping a pointer to the link as you go. Move the successor's key and value into the node, then erase the successor, which has no left child, so it is case 1.

**Why case 3 keeps the BST property.** The successor s is the smallest key greater than the node's key. Every key in the node's left subtree is less than the node's key, so less than s. Every other key in the right subtree is greater than s, because s was the smallest there. So s may sit where the node was. And s had no left child (otherwise it would not be the leftmost), so removing it is case 1.

### Recursion follows the height, and the height can be n

A BST's **height** is the number of links on its longest path from the root down (−1 for an empty tree, 0 for a single node). Every operation walks one path, so it costs O(h). With keys inserted in random order, h is [[about 3 log₂ n|random-height]] on average. With keys inserted in sorted order, which happens all the time (timestamps!), every new key goes right, the tree is a chain, and h = n − 1.

That matters twice in C++:

- **Recursive functions** use one stack frame per level. A recursive `find` on a chain of a million nodes needs a million frames, and the [[stack overflows|stack-overflow]]: the program crashes. So `find`, `insert` and `erase` are loops.
- **The default destructor recurses too.** Destroying a node destroys its `left` `unique_ptr`, which destroys that node, which destroys its `left`, and so on down the chain, one frame per level. It is lesson 5's linked-list problem again, in two directions. So the tree's destructor must free the nodes with a loop: repeatedly take a node away from its owner, move its children out onto a to-do list of `unique_ptr`s, and let the node die with no children attached.

### In-order iteration with an explicit stack

Recursive in-order traversal is short, but it cannot stop half way and hand you one key, which is what an iterator must do. So the iterator keeps the recursion's stack itself: a `std::vector<const Node*>`.

- **Begin:** push the root, its left child, its left child's left child, and so on down the left edge. The top is now the smallest key.
- **Dereference:** the node on top of the stack.
- **Step (`++`):** pop the top node, then push its right child and that child's whole left edge.
- **End:** the stack is empty.

**Why it visits every key once, in order.** The invariant has two parts:

1. *The keys not yet visited are exactly the nodes on the stack plus the right subtrees of those nodes.*
2. *Each node on the stack sits in the left subtree of the node just below it.* So, by the BST property, going from the top of the stack down, each node is smaller than the one below it, and each node's right subtree holds keys between it and the node below. The top node is therefore the smallest unvisited key.

At the start, the left edge and the right subtrees hanging off it make up the whole tree, and each node of the left edge is the left child of the one below it: both parts hold. A step visits the top node, the smallest unvisited key, and pops it. Then it pushes the left edge of the popped node's right subtree: those nodes and their right subtrees are exactly that subtree, so part 1 still holds with one key fewer. The first pushed node lies in the left subtree of the node that was below the popped one (the popped node and its right subtree both did), and each later one is the left child of the one before it, so part 2 holds too. Since every step visits the smallest unvisited key, the keys come out in increasing order, each exactly once.

For example, in the tree with root 50, children 30 and 70, and 40 as 30's right child, the stack starts as [50, 30]. Visit 30, pop it, push its right edge: [50, 40]. Visit 40: [50]. Visit 50, push 70: [70]. Visit 70: empty, done.

**What it costs.** Each node is pushed once and popped once over a whole traversal, so iterating over all n keys is O(n), and O(1) per step on average. A single step can cost O(h), when it pushes a long left edge. The stack never holds more than h + 1 nodes, which is far less memory than copying the keys out.

### What it costs

| Operation | Time | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| find, insert, erase | O(h) | h is between ⌊log₂ n⌋ and n − 1 |
| full in-order iteration | O(n) | stack of at most h + 1 pointers |
| destruction | O(n) | with a loop, never recursion |
| memory | n nodes | each a separate heap block, with two pointers |

Nothing here keeps h small. The next lesson turns to `std::map` and `std::set`, which rebalance as they go and guarantee h = O(log n).

### Where it is used

- **`std::map` and `std::set`** are balanced binary search trees with exactly this ownership structure inside.
- **Databases and file systems** use B-trees, which generalise BSTs to nodes with hundreds of keys so that each node fills a disk page.
- **Operating systems:** Linux keeps timers, memory regions and scheduler queues in balanced BSTs.
- **ORBIT's world:** an event log keyed by time, where "the first event at or after 14:03:22" is a walk down one path.

**Watch out:** stepping with a *reference* to a `unique_ptr`. `std::unique_ptr<Node>& cur = root_; cur = std::move(cur->left);` compiles and silently throws away the root and its right subtree. Walk with a pointer to the link, or with an observing `Node*`. And never recurse once per level of a tree you do not control: the one sorted input that turns it into a chain will crash the program.

::: context equivalence Equal, or just equivalent?
For whole numbers, "neither a < b nor b < a" means a == b. For other types it may not. Compare strings case-insensitively, and "Mars" and "MARS" are equivalent without being equal. Compare readings by time only, and two readings at the same second are equivalent even if their values differ. A tree built on `<` treats equivalent keys as one key. That is why the next lesson insists that a comparator behave like a proper "less than", and why `std::map` never calls `==` at all.
:::

::: context pointer-to-link Good taste in linked structures
In a 2016 TED interview, Linus Torvalds, who created Linux, showed two ways to remove an item from a linked list. One walks with a pointer to the current node and needs an `if` for removing the head. The other walks with a pointer to the link that points at the current node, so the head is not special and the `if` disappears. He called the second one "good taste". The pointer to a `unique_ptr` here is the same idea, with ownership built in.

::: context dead-source The order inside a move assignment
The C++ standard describes `p = std::move(q)` for `unique_ptr` as: `reset(q.release())`, then copy q's deleter into p. `release` empties q and hands over its pointer; `reset` stores that pointer and deletes the object p used to own. If q was a member of that object, q is gone before the deleter is copied. `std::default_delete` holds no data, so no real byte is read. A deleter that did hold data would be read from freed memory. Detaching into a local first removes the question entirely.
:::

::: context random-height How tall is a random tree?
Insert n distinct keys in a random order. The average depth of a node is about 1.39 log₂ n, because the tree's shape mirrors quicksort's recursion, whose expected comparisons are about 1.39 n log₂ n. The expected height, the deepest node, is about 4.31 ln n, roughly 3 log₂ n, as Bruce Reed proved in 2003. So for a million random keys, expect a height near 60, against 19 for a perfectly balanced tree and 999,999 for sorted input.
:::

::: context stack-overflow When the stack runs out
Each function call takes a stack frame for its local variables and its return address, often 32 to 100 bytes. A native program's main thread usually gets 8 MB of stack on Linux and macOS; WebAssembly programs, like the ones ORBIT runs in your browser, often get far less. Past the end there is no more memory to use, and the program is killed with a segmentation fault, with no chance to recover. Tail calls can sometimes be turned into loops by the optimiser, but a destructor or an in-order traversal cannot, so the code has to be a loop.
:::
--- task
Write `template <typename K, typename V> class BST`, a binary search tree whose nodes own their children through `std::unique_ptr`. Compare keys with `<` only. No `main`.

- A public `struct Node { K key; V value; std::unique_ptr<Node> left; std::unique_ptr<Node> right; };`.
- `std::size_t size() const`.
- `bool insert(const K& key, const V& value)`: add the pair and return `true`, or return `false` (changing nothing) if the key is there.
- `V* find(const K& key)` and `const V* find(const K& key) const`: a pointer to the value, or `nullptr`.
- `bool erase(const K& key)`: remove the key with the three cases (two children: move the successor's key and value into the node and remove the successor); `false` if missing.
- `int height() const`: −1 for an empty tree, 0 for one node.
- `class const_iterator`: an in-order iterator holding a `std::vector<const Node*>` stack, with the five member types (`std::forward_iterator_tag`, `value_type` = `Node`, `std::ptrdiff_t`, `const Node*`, `const Node&`), `const Node& operator*() const`, `const Node* operator->() const`, prefix and postfix `++`, and `==`. `begin()` and `end()` are `const`, so `for (const auto& node : tree)` visits `node.key` in increasing order.
- A destructor that frees the nodes with a loop, and no recursion anywhere: the checks build chains thousands of nodes deep. Delete the copy constructor and copy assignment.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V>
class BST {
public:
    struct Node {
        K key;
        V value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    };

    class const_iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = Node;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const Node*;
        using reference = const Node&;

        const Node& operator*() const { return *stack_.back(); }
        const Node* operator->() const { return stack_.back(); }
        const_iterator& operator++() { return *this; }
        const_iterator operator++(int) { return *this; }
        bool operator==(const const_iterator& other) const { return true; }

    private:
        std::vector<const Node*> stack_;
    };

    BST() = default;
    BST(const BST&) = delete;
    BST& operator=(const BST&) = delete;

    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) { return false; }
    V* find(const K& key) { return nullptr; }
    const V* find(const K& key) const { return nullptr; }
    bool erase(const K& key) { return false; }
    int height() const { return -1; }
    const_iterator begin() const { return const_iterator(); }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

template <typename K, typename V>
class BST {
public:
    struct Node {
        K key;
        V value;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    };

    class const_iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = Node;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const Node*;
        using reference = const Node&;

        const_iterator() = default;
        explicit const_iterator(const Node* root) { push_left_edge(root); }

        const Node& operator*() const { return *stack_.back(); }
        const Node* operator->() const { return stack_.back(); }

        const_iterator& operator++() {
            const Node* done = stack_.back();
            stack_.pop_back();
            push_left_edge(done->right.get());
            return *this;
        }

        const_iterator operator++(int) {
            const_iterator before = *this;
            ++*this;
            return before;
        }

        bool operator==(const const_iterator& other) const {
            if (stack_.empty() || other.stack_.empty()) return stack_.empty() && other.stack_.empty();
            return stack_.back() == other.stack_.back();
        }

    private:
        void push_left_edge(const Node* n) {
            for (; n != nullptr; n = n->left.get()) stack_.push_back(n);
        }
        std::vector<const Node*> stack_;   // the top is the next node in order
    };

    BST() = default;
    BST(const BST&) = delete;
    BST& operator=(const BST&) = delete;

    ~BST() {
        std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> pending;
        if (root_) pending.push_back(std::move(root_));
        while (!pending.empty()) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> n = std::move(pending.back());
            pending.pop_back();
            if (n->left) pending.push_back(std::move(n->left));
            if (n->right) pending.push_back(std::move(n->right));
        }   // n dies here with no children attached, so nothing recurses
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    bool insert(const K& key, const V& value) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link) {
            if (key < (*link)->key) link = &(*link)->left;
            else if ((*link)->key < key) link = &(*link)->right;
            else return false;
        }
        *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, value, nullptr, nullptr});
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    V* find(const K& key) {
        const V* found = std::as_const(*this).find(key);
        return const_cast<V*>(found);
    }

    const V* find(const K& key) const {
        const Node* n = root_.get();
        while (n != nullptr) {
            if (key < n->key) n = n->left.get();
            else if (n->key < key) n = n->right.get();
            else return &n->value;
        }
        return nullptr;
    }

    bool erase(const K& key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link) {
            if (key < (*link)->key) link = &(*link)->left;
            else if ((*link)->key < key) link = &(*link)->right;
            else break;
        }
        if (!*link) return false;
        Node* doomed = link->get();
        if (!doomed->left) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> child = std::move(doomed->right);   // detach first
            *link = std::move(child);                                 // then the old node dies
        } else if (!doomed->right) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> child = std::move(doomed->left);
            *link = std::move(child);
        } else {
            std::unique_ptr<Node>* succ = &doomed->right;
            while ((*succ)->left) succ = &(*succ)->left;
            doomed->key = std::move((*succ)->key);
            doomed->value = std::move((*succ)->value);
            std::unique_ptr<Node> child = std::move((*succ)->right);  // the successor has no left child
            *succ = std::move(child);
        }
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    int height() const {
        if (!root_) return -1;
        int tallest = 0;
        std::vector<std::pair<const Node*, int>> todo{{root_.get(), 0}};
        while (!todo.empty()) {
            auto [n, depth] = todo.back();
            todo.pop_back();
            if (depth > tallest) tallest = depth;
            if (n->left) todo.push_back({n->left.get(), depth + 1});
            if (n->right) todo.push_back({n->right.get(), depth + 1});
        }
        return tallest;
    }

    const_iterator begin() const { return const_iterator(root_.get()); }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
`insert` and `erase` both start with the same loop: `std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;`, then step with `link = &(*link)->left` or `&(*link)->right` while `*link` is not empty and the key differs. For insert, an empty `*link` is where the new node goes; a match means the key is already there. `find` can walk with a plain `const Node*` from `root_.get()`.
--- hint
In `erase`, with the link to the doomed node: if it has no left child, move its right child into a local `unique_ptr` and then into `*link` (and the mirror case). With two children, walk a second link pointer from `&doomed->right` down the left edge to the successor, move its key and value into the doomed node, then replace the successor's link by its right child, detaching first.
--- hint
The iterator's helper pushes a node and its whole left edge onto the stack. The constructor calls it on the root; `++` pops the top and calls it on the popped node's right child; `end()` is an iterator with an empty stack. For the destructor and `height`, use a loop over a `std::vector` to-do list instead of recursion: for the destructor it holds `std::unique_ptr<Node>`s you have taken away from their parents.

+++ practice | Floor and ceiling by walking one path
--- task
The starter has a `Node` with an `int` key and `unique_ptr` children, and an `insert` helper the checks use to build trees. Write two functions that walk down one path, with a loop. No `main`.

- `const Node* floor_node(const Node* root, int k)`: the node with the largest key that is at most `k`, or `nullptr` if every key is bigger than `k`.
- `const Node* ceiling_node(const Node* root, int k)`: the node with the smallest key that is at least `k`, or `nullptr` if every key is smaller.

An empty tree is `nullptr` and gives `nullptr`. Walk with an observing pointer (`n = n->left.get()`), remembering the best candidate so far: for the floor, every node whose key is at most `k` is a candidate, and a better one can only be in its right subtree.

For example, in a tree of 20, 40, 60 and 80, `floor_node(root, 55)` is the node with 40 and `ceiling_node(root, 55)` is the one with 60.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <memory>

struct Node {
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
};

// Used by the checks to build trees. Keep it.
void insert(std::unique_ptr<Node>& root, int key) {
    std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root;
    while (*link) link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
    *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, nullptr, nullptr});
}

const Node* floor_node(const Node* root, int k) { return nullptr; }
const Node* ceiling_node(const Node* root, int k) { return nullptr; }
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <memory>

struct Node {
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
};

// Used by the checks to build trees. Keep it.
void insert(std::unique_ptr<Node>& root, int key) {
    std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root;
    while (*link) link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
    *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, nullptr, nullptr});
}

const Node* floor_node(const Node* root, int k) {
    const Node* best = nullptr;
    for (const Node* n = root; n != nullptr;) {
        if (n->key == k) return n;
        if (n->key < k) {
            best = n;              // a candidate; anything better is to its right
            n = n->right.get();
        } else {
            n = n->left.get();
        }
    }
    return best;
}

const Node* ceiling_node(const Node* root, int k) {
    const Node* best = nullptr;
    for (const Node* n = root; n != nullptr;) {
        if (n->key == k) return n;
        if (n->key > k) {
            best = n;
            n = n->left.get();
        } else {
            n = n->right.get();
        }
    }
    return best;
}
--- hint
For the floor: at a node with key below `k`, remember it as the best so far and go right, where the only better candidates can be. At a node with key above `k`, go left. A key equal to `k` is the answer at once.
--- hint
The ceiling is the mirror image: remember nodes with keys above `k` and go left from them; go right from keys below `k`. Return the remembered node when you fall off the tree.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { std::unique_ptr<Node> root; for (int k : {40, 20, 80, 60}) insert(root, k); const Node* f = floor_node(root.get(), 55); const Node* c = ceiling_node(root.get(), 55); return f && f->key == 40 && c && c->key == 60; }()

[] { std::unique_ptr<Node> root; for (int k : {40, 20, 80, 60}) insert(root, k); return floor_node(root.get(), 60)->key == 60 && ceiling_node(root.get(), 20)->key == 20; }()
--- check test | Below every key and above every key
[] { std::unique_ptr<Node> root; for (int k : {40, 20, 80, 60}) insert(root, k); return floor_node(root.get(), 5) == nullptr && ceiling_node(root.get(), 5)->key == 20 && floor_node(root.get(), 99)->key == 80 && ceiling_node(root.get(), 99) == nullptr; }()
--- check test | An empty tree
floor_node(nullptr, 3) == nullptr && ceiling_node(nullptr, 3) == nullptr
--- check test | Negative keys and a zigzag shape
[] { std::unique_ptr<Node> root; for (int k : {0, -50, -10, -30, -20}) insert(root, k); return floor_node(root.get(), -25)->key == -30 && ceiling_node(root.get(), -25)->key == -20 && floor_node(root.get(), -11)->key == -20 && ceiling_node(root.get(), -9)->key == 0; }()
--- check test | Every query on a larger tree matches a sorted list
[] { std::unique_ptr<Node> root; std::vector<int> keys; unsigned s = 6; for (int i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int k = static_cast<int>((s >> 12) % 100000); if (std::find(keys.begin(), keys.end(), k) == keys.end()) { keys.push_back(k); insert(root, k); } } std::sort(keys.begin(), keys.end()); for (int q = -5; q < 100005; q += 97) { auto it = std::upper_bound(keys.begin(), keys.end(), q); const Node* f = floor_node(root.get(), q); if (it == keys.begin() ? f != nullptr : (!f || f->key != *(it - 1))) return false; auto jt = std::lower_bound(keys.begin(), keys.end(), q); const Node* c = ceiling_node(root.get(), q); if (jt == keys.end() ? c != nullptr : (!c || c->key != *jt)) return false; } return true; }()

+++ practice | A balanced tree from sorted keys
--- task
When all the keys are known in advance and sorted, you can build a tree of the smallest possible height directly, instead of inserting them one by one (which, for sorted keys, makes a chain). No `main`.

Write `std::unique_ptr<Node> build_balanced(const std::vector<int>& sorted)`. The middle key becomes the root, the keys before it make the left subtree in the same way, and the keys after it the right subtree. Use the middle index `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` of the part you are building, where `hi` is one past its end. An empty vector gives `nullptr`.

The result must hold every key, in a valid BST, with height ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ − 1, the smallest possible. Recursion is fine here, because its depth is only about log₂ n. The starter's two helpers, `height_of` and `keys_in_order`, are used by the checks; keep them.

For example, `{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}` gives root 4, with 2 and 6 below it.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
};

// Used by the checks. Keep both.
int height_of(const Node* root) {
    int tallest = -1;
    std::vector<std::pair<const Node*, int>> todo;
    if (root) todo.push_back({root, 0});
    while (!todo.empty()) {
        auto [n, d] = todo.back();
        todo.pop_back();
        if (d > tallest) tallest = d;
        if (n->left) todo.push_back({n->left.get(), d + 1});
        if (n->right) todo.push_back({n->right.get(), d + 1});
    }
    return tallest;
}

std::vector<int> keys_in_order(const Node* root) {
    std::vector<int> out;
    std::vector<const Node*> stack;
    for (const Node* n = root; n || !stack.empty();) {
        for (; n; n = n->left.get()) stack.push_back(n);
        n = stack.back();
        stack.pop_back();
        out.push_back(n->key);
        n = n->right.get();
    }
    return out;
}

std::unique_ptr<Node> build_balanced(const std::vector<int>& sorted) {
    return nullptr;
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
};

// Used by the checks. Keep both.
int height_of(const Node* root) {
    int tallest = -1;
    std::vector<std::pair<const Node*, int>> todo;
    if (root) todo.push_back({root, 0});
    while (!todo.empty()) {
        auto [n, d] = todo.back();
        todo.pop_back();
        if (d > tallest) tallest = d;
        if (n->left) todo.push_back({n->left.get(), d + 1});
        if (n->right) todo.push_back({n->right.get(), d + 1});
    }
    return tallest;
}

std::vector<int> keys_in_order(const Node* root) {
    std::vector<int> out;
    std::vector<const Node*> stack;
    for (const Node* n = root; n || !stack.empty();) {
        for (; n; n = n->left.get()) stack.push_back(n);
        n = stack.back();
        stack.pop_back();
        out.push_back(n->key);
        n = n->right.get();
    }
    return out;
}

// Builds keys [lo, hi) of the sorted vector.
std::unique_ptr<Node> build_part(const std::vector<int>& sorted, std::size_t lo, std::size_t hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return nullptr;
    std::size_t mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    auto node = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{sorted[mid], nullptr, nullptr});
    node->left = build_part(sorted, lo, mid);
    node->right = build_part(sorted, mid + 1, hi);
    return node;
}

std::unique_ptr<Node> build_balanced(const std::vector<int>& sorted) {
    return build_part(sorted, 0, sorted.size());
}
--- hint
Write a helper that builds the keys from index `lo` up to (not including) `hi`. An empty range, `lo >= hi`, gives `nullptr`.
--- hint
Otherwise make a node for `sorted[mid]`, then set its `left` to the helper's result for `lo` to `mid`, and its `right` to the result for `mid + 1` to `hi`. Return the node: returning a `unique_ptr` hands its ownership to the caller.

+++ practice | Start iterating at the first key at least k
--- task
`IntTree` in the starter is a working BST of `int` keys with an in-order `const_iterator` that keeps a stack, as in the lesson, and `begin()` and `end()`. Add the member function `const_iterator lower_bound(int k) const`: an iterator at the first key that is at least `k`, or `end()` if there is none. No `main`.

It must take O(h) time, by building the iterator's stack while walking down one path from the root. Walking from `begin()` and stepping until the key is big enough is O(n): a check makes 100,000 calls on a tree of 100,000 keys.

The stack must hold exactly the nodes that are still to come, with their right subtrees: walk down from the root; at a node whose key is less than `k`, go right without pushing it (it and its left subtree all come before `k`); at a node whose key is at least `k`, push it and go left. The starter gives the iterator a private constructor taking a finished stack, for you to use.

For example, in a tree of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, iterating from `lower_bound(25)` gives 30, 40, 50.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IntTree {
    struct Node {
        int key;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    };

public:
    class const_iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        const_iterator() = default;
        const int& operator*() const { return stack_.back()->key; }
        const_iterator& operator++() {
            const Node* done = stack_.back();
            stack_.pop_back();
            for (const Node* n = done->right.get(); n; n = n->left.get()) stack_.push_back(n);
            return *this;
        }
        bool operator==(const const_iterator& other) const {
            if (stack_.empty() || other.stack_.empty()) return stack_.empty() && other.stack_.empty();
            return stack_.back() == other.stack_.back();
        }

    private:
        friend class IntTree;
        explicit const_iterator(std::vector<const Node*> stack) : stack_(std::move(stack)) {}
        std::vector<const Node*> stack_;
    };

    bool insert(int key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link) {
            if (key < (*link)->key) link = &(*link)->left;
            else if ((*link)->key < key) link = &(*link)->right;
            else return false;
        }
        *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, nullptr, nullptr});
        return true;
    }

    const_iterator begin() const {
        std::vector<const Node*> stack;
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n; n = n->left.get()) stack.push_back(n);
        return const_iterator(std::move(stack));
    }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(); }

    const_iterator lower_bound(int k) const { return end(); }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IntTree {
    struct Node {
        int key;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    };

public:
    class const_iterator {
    public:
        using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;
        using value_type = int;
        using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;
        using pointer = const int*;
        using reference = const int&;

        const_iterator() = default;
        const int& operator*() const { return stack_.back()->key; }
        const_iterator& operator++() {
            const Node* done = stack_.back();
            stack_.pop_back();
            for (const Node* n = done->right.get(); n; n = n->left.get()) stack_.push_back(n);
            return *this;
        }
        bool operator==(const const_iterator& other) const {
            if (stack_.empty() || other.stack_.empty()) return stack_.empty() && other.stack_.empty();
            return stack_.back() == other.stack_.back();
        }

    private:
        friend class IntTree;
        explicit const_iterator(std::vector<const Node*> stack) : stack_(std::move(stack)) {}
        std::vector<const Node*> stack_;
    };

    bool insert(int key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link) {
            if (key < (*link)->key) link = &(*link)->left;
            else if ((*link)->key < key) link = &(*link)->right;
            else return false;
        }
        *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, nullptr, nullptr});
        return true;
    }

    const_iterator begin() const {
        std::vector<const Node*> stack;
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n; n = n->left.get()) stack.push_back(n);
        return const_iterator(std::move(stack));
    }
    const_iterator end() const { return const_iterator(); }

    const_iterator lower_bound(int k) const {
        std::vector<const Node*> stack;
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n != nullptr;) {
            if (n->key < k) {
                n = n->right.get();       // n and its left subtree all come before k
            } else {
                stack.push_back(n);       // n is still to come; smaller candidates are to its left
                n = n->left.get();
            }
        }
        return const_iterator(std::move(stack));
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root_;
};
--- hint
Walk down from the root with a `const Node*`, building a `std::vector<const Node*>`. Keys less than `k` send you right and are not pushed. Keys at least `k` are pushed, and send you left, to look for a smaller key that is still at least `k`.
--- hint
When the walk falls off the tree, the top of the stack is the smallest key at least `k`, and the nodes below it are exactly the later nodes the iterator would have on its stack anyway. Return `const_iterator(std::move(stack))`; an empty stack is `end()`.

+++ practice | Taking apart a tree a million levels deep
--- task
A tree whose nodes own their children through `unique_ptr` destroys itself recursively: each node's destructor destroys its children first. On a chain a million levels deep that is a million nested calls, and the program crashes. Write the fix. No `main`.

The starter's `Node` counts how many nodes are alive in `Node::live` (its constructor adds one, its destructor takes one away). Write `void dismantle(std::unique_ptr<Node>& root)` that destroys every node of the tree and leaves `root` empty, using a loop and no recursion. The checks build chains of 1,000,000 nodes going left, going right, and zigzagging, then call `dismantle` and expect `Node::live` to be 0.

The idea: never let a node die while it still owns a child. Take nodes away from their owners into a to-do list of `std::unique_ptr<Node>` (a `std::vector` works), and before a node is destroyed, move its children onto the list.
--- starter
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    static inline long long live = 0;
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    explicit Node(int k) : key(k) { ++live; }
    ~Node() { --live; }
};

void dismantle(std::unique_ptr<Node>& root) {
}
--- solution
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    static inline long long live = 0;
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    explicit Node(int k) : key(k) { ++live; }
    ~Node() { --live; }
};

void dismantle(std::unique_ptr<Node>& root) {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> todo;
    if (root) todo.push_back(std::move(root));
    while (!todo.empty()) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node> n = std::move(todo.back());
        todo.pop_back();
        if (n->left) todo.push_back(std::move(n->left));
        if (n->right) todo.push_back(std::move(n->right));
    }   // n is destroyed here, owning no children
}
--- hint
Start by moving `root` itself onto a `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>>`; that also leaves `root` empty, as required.
--- hint
Loop while the vector is not empty: move its last element into a local `unique_ptr`, pop it off, and move that node's `left` and `right` (when they are not empty) onto the vector. When the local goes out of scope at the end of the loop body, the node dies alone.
--- check test | An empty tree and a single node
[] { std::unique_ptr<Node> a; dismantle(a); auto b = std::make_unique<Node>(1); dismantle(b); return !a && !b && Node::live == 0; }()
--- check test | A chain of 1,000,000 nodes going left
[] { auto root = std::make_unique<Node>(0); Node* cur = root.get(); for (int i = 1; i < 1000000; ++i) { cur->left = std::make_unique<Node>(i); cur = cur->left.get(); } bool built = Node::live == 1000000; dismantle(root); return built && !root && Node::live == 0; }()
?? Letting a million-deep chain destroy itself recursively overflows the stack. Move children out before each node dies.
--- check test | A chain of 1,000,000 nodes going right
[] { auto root = std::make_unique<Node>(0); Node* cur = root.get(); for (int i = 1; i < 1000000; ++i) { cur->right = std::make_unique<Node>(i); cur = cur->right.get(); } dismantle(root); return !root && Node::live == 0; }()
--- check test | A zigzag of 1,000,000 nodes, each with an extra leaf
[] { auto root = std::make_unique<Node>(0); Node* cur = root.get(); for (int i = 1; i < 500000; ++i) { auto next = std::make_unique<Node>(i); auto leaf = std::make_unique<Node>(-i); Node* nx = next.get(); if (i % 2) { cur->left = std::move(next); cur->right = std::move(leaf); } else { cur->right = std::move(next); cur->left = std::move(leaf); } cur = nx; } bool built = Node::live == 999999; dismantle(root); return built && !root && Node::live == 0; }()
--- check test | A full tree of 2^18 − 1 nodes
[] { std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> level; for (int i = 0; i < (1 << 17); ++i) level.push_back(std::make_unique<Node>(i)); while (level.size() > 1) { std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> up; for (std::size_t i = 0; i + 1 < level.size(); i += 2) { auto p = std::make_unique<Node>(0); p->left = std::move(level[i]); p->right = std::move(level[i + 1]); up.push_back(std::move(p)); } level = std::move(up); } bool built = Node::live == (1 << 18) - 1; dismantle(level[0]); return built && !level[0] && Node::live == 0; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the erase that loses a branch
--- task
`IntSet` is a BST of `int` keys with `unique_ptr` children. `insert`, `contains`, `size` and `keys()` (all keys in increasing order) work. `erase` should remove one key and keep every other key. It works for keys with zero or one child, but when it erases a key with two children, other keys sometimes vanish too, although `size()` goes down by only one.

For example, after inserting 50, 30, 70, 60, 80, 65 and erasing 50, the keys should be 30, 60, 65, 70, 80. Instead 65 is gone.

Find the bug and fix it. The bug is on one line.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IntSet {
    struct Node {
        int key;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    };

public:
    bool insert(int key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link) {
            if (key < (*link)->key) link = &(*link)->left;
            else if ((*link)->key < key) link = &(*link)->right;
            else return false;
        }
        *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, nullptr, nullptr});
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool contains(int key) const {
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n;) {
            if (key < n->key) n = n->left.get();
            else if (n->key < key) n = n->right.get();
            else return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    bool erase(int key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link && (*link)->key != key) link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
        if (!*link) return false;
        Node* doomed = link->get();
        if (!doomed->left || !doomed->right) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> child = std::move(doomed->left ? doomed->left : doomed->right);
            *link = std::move(child);
        } else {
            std::unique_ptr<Node>* succ = &doomed->right;
            while ((*succ)->left) succ = &(*succ)->left;
            doomed->key = (*succ)->key;
            *succ = nullptr;
        }
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    std::vector<int> keys() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        std::vector<const Node*> stack;
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n || !stack.empty();) {
            for (; n; n = n->left.get()) stack.push_back(n);
            n = stack.back();
            stack.pop_back();
            out.push_back(n->key);
            n = n->right.get();
        }
        return out;
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IntSet {
    struct Node {
        int key;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    };

public:
    bool insert(int key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link) {
            if (key < (*link)->key) link = &(*link)->left;
            else if ((*link)->key < key) link = &(*link)->right;
            else return false;
        }
        *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, nullptr, nullptr});
        ++size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool contains(int key) const {
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n;) {
            if (key < n->key) n = n->left.get();
            else if (n->key < key) n = n->right.get();
            else return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    bool erase(int key) {
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link && (*link)->key != key) link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
        if (!*link) return false;
        Node* doomed = link->get();
        if (!doomed->left || !doomed->right) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> child = std::move(doomed->left ? doomed->left : doomed->right);
            *link = std::move(child);
        } else {
            std::unique_ptr<Node>* succ = &doomed->right;
            while ((*succ)->left) succ = &(*succ)->left;
            doomed->key = (*succ)->key;
            std::unique_ptr<Node> rest = std::move((*succ)->right);   // the successor's right subtree stays
            *succ = std::move(rest);
        }
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }

    std::vector<int> keys() const {
        std::vector<int> out;
        std::vector<const Node*> stack;
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n || !stack.empty();) {
            for (; n; n = n->left.get()) stack.push_back(n);
            n = stack.back();
            stack.pop_back();
            out.push_back(n->key);
            n = n->right.get();
        }
        return out;
    }

private:
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root_;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
};
--- hint
Draw the example. The successor of 50 is 60, the leftmost key of 50's right subtree. It has no left child, but does it have a right child? What does `*succ = nullptr` do to that child?
--- hint
The successor's link must take the successor's right subtree, not nothing. Detach that subtree into a local `unique_ptr` first, then move it into `*succ`.
--- check case | The example from the task

=> std::vector<int>{30, 60, 65, 70, 80}
?? Assigning nullptr to the successor's link destroys the successor's right subtree along with it.
--- check test | size and keys agree after many erases
[] { IntSet s; for (int i = 0; i < 500; ++i) s.insert((i * 7) % 500); for (int i = 0; i < 500; i += 3) s.erase((i * 11) % 500); return s.keys().size() == s.size() && s.size() == 333; }()
--- check test | Erasing leaves and one-child nodes still works
[] { IntSet s; for (int k : {5, 3, 8, 1, 9}) s.insert(k); bool a = s.erase(1) && s.erase(8) && !s.erase(8); return a && s.keys() == std::vector<int>{3, 5, 9}; }()
--- check test | Erasing the root again and again keeps every other key
[] { IntSet s; for (int k : {40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70, 55, 65, 52}) s.insert(k); std::vector<int> left = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 52, 55, 60, 65, 70}; for (int k : {40, 50, 52}) { s.erase(k); left.erase(std::find(left.begin(), left.end(), k)); if (s.keys() != left) return false; } return s.contains(55) && s.contains(65); }()

+++ practice | Stretch: a tree that knows ranks
--- task
A mission log is indexed by event time, and operators ask two kinds of question: "how many events happened before time t?" and "which is the i-th event?". Answer both in O(h) by storing, in every node, the number of nodes in its subtree. No `main`.

Write `class RankTree` for distinct `int` keys:

- `bool insert(int key)`: `false` if the key is there.
- `bool erase(int key)`: `false` if it is missing. Use the lesson's three cases (two children: take the successor's key).
- `std::size_t size() const`.
- `std::size_t rank(int key) const`: how many keys are **less than** `key` (the key itself need not be in the tree).
- `std::optional<int> select(std::size_t i) const`: the i-th smallest key, counting from 0, or `std::nullopt` if `i >= size()`.

Each node keeps `std::size_t count`, the size of its subtree. Every insert and erase must keep all counts right, including along the extra path down to a successor, and must check first whether the key is there, so that it never changes counts for nothing. Then `rank` walks one path: going right past a node adds its left subtree's count plus one. A check runs 200,000 random operations, far too many for anything that visits every node.

For example, with keys 10, 20, 30, 40, `rank(25)` is 2 and `select(3)` is 40.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>

class RankTree {
public:
    bool insert(int key) { return false; }
    bool erase(int key) { return false; }
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t rank(int key) const { return 0; }
    std::optional<int> select(std::size_t i) const { return std::nullopt; }
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <memory>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>

class RankTree {
    struct Node {
        int key;
        std::size_t count;   // nodes in this subtree, this one included
        std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    };

    static std::size_t count_of(const std::unique_ptr<Node>& n) { return n ? n->count : 0; }

public:
    bool insert(int key) {
        if (contains(key)) return false;
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while (*link) {
            ++(*link)->count;   // the new key will be below this node
            link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
        }
        *link = std::make_unique<Node>(Node{key, 1, nullptr, nullptr});
        return true;
    }

    bool erase(int key) {
        if (!contains(key)) return false;
        std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;
        while ((*link)->key != key) {
            --(*link)->count;   // one key below this node is going
            link = key < (*link)->key ? &(*link)->left : &(*link)->right;
        }
        Node* doomed = link->get();
        if (!doomed->left || !doomed->right) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> child = std::move(doomed->left ? doomed->left : doomed->right);
            *link = std::move(child);
        } else {
            --doomed->count;   // it stays, but loses one node below it
            std::unique_ptr<Node>* succ = &doomed->right;
            while ((*succ)->left) {
                --(*succ)->count;
                succ = &(*succ)->left;
            }
            doomed->key = (*succ)->key;
            std::unique_ptr<Node> rest = std::move((*succ)->right);
            *succ = std::move(rest);
        }
        return true;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return count_of(root_); }

    std::size_t rank(int key) const {
        std::size_t less = 0;
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n;) {
            if (n->key < key) {
                less += count_of(n->left) + 1;   // n and its whole left subtree are smaller
                n = n->right.get();
            } else {
                n = n->left.get();
            }
        }
        return less;
    }

    std::optional<int> select(std::size_t i) const {
        if (i >= size()) return std::nullopt;
        const Node* n = root_.get();
        while (true) {
            std::size_t left = count_of(n->left);
            if (i < left) {
                n = n->left.get();
            } else if (i == left) {
                return n->key;
            } else {
                i -= left + 1;
                n = n->right.get();
            }
        }
    }

private:
    bool contains(int key) const {
        for (const Node* n = root_.get(); n;) {
            if (key < n->key) n = n->left.get();
            else if (n->key < key) n = n->right.get();
            else return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    std::unique_ptr<Node> root_;
};
--- hint
Keep a private `contains` and call it first in both `insert` and `erase`. Once you know the operation will happen, walk down with a pointer to the link and add one to (for insert) or take one from (for erase) the count of every node you pass above the change.
--- hint
In erase's two-children case, the node itself stays but loses one node below it, and so does every node on the path down to the successor (not the successor, which is removed). Then splice the successor out, detaching its right subtree first.
--- hint
`select(i)`: at a node with L keys in its left subtree, go left if `i < L`, answer with this node if `i == L`, otherwise take `L + 1` off `i` and go right. `rank(key)` is the same walk, adding `L + 1` each time it goes right past a smaller key.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { RankTree t; for (int k : {20, 10, 40, 30}) t.insert(k); auto s = t.select(3); return t.rank(25) == 2 && s && *s == 40 && t.size() == 4; }()
--- check test | rank at the edges and of keys in the tree
[] { RankTree t; for (int k : {20, 10, 40, 30}) t.insert(k); return t.rank(-5) == 0 && t.rank(10) == 0 && t.rank(11) == 1 && t.rank(40) == 3 && t.rank(99) == 4; }()
--- check test | select every position, and past the end
[] { RankTree t; for (int k : {50, 20, 80, 10, 30, 70, 90, 60}) t.insert(k); std::vector<int> got; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 8; ++i) got.push_back(*t.select(i)); RankTree empty; return got == std::vector<int>{10, 20, 30, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90} && !t.select(8) && !empty.select(0) && empty.rank(3) == 0; }()
--- check test | Duplicates and missing keys change no counts
[] { RankTree t; for (int k : {5, 3, 8}) t.insert(k); bool a = !t.insert(5) && !t.erase(4) && t.size() == 3; return a && t.rank(8) == 2 && *t.select(2) == 8; }()
?? Check whether the key is there before changing any count.
--- check test | Erasing a node with two children keeps every count right
[] { RankTree t; for (int k : {50, 30, 70, 60, 80, 65, 55}) t.insert(k); t.erase(50); t.erase(70); std::vector<int> got; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < t.size(); ++i) got.push_back(*t.select(i)); return t.size() == 5 && got == std::vector<int>{30, 55, 60, 65, 80} && t.rank(62) == 3; }()
--- check test | 200,000 random operations
[] { RankTree t; unsigned s = 21; long long ranks = 0; long long picks = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; unsigned op = (s >> 28) % 4; int key = static_cast<int>((s >> 6) % 1000000); if (op < 2) t.insert(key); else if (op == 2) { t.erase(key); ranks += static_cast<long long>(t.rank(key)); } else if (t.size() > 0) { auto v = t.select(static_cast<std::size_t>(key) % t.size()); if (!v) return false; picks += *v; } } return t.size() == 92845 && ranks == 1182231941LL && picks == 24840408927LL; }()

+++ question | The link that must not be a reference
--- ask
To walk down a tree while keeping hold of the owning pointer, someone writes `std::unique_ptr<Node>& link = root_;` and, to step left, `link = std::move(link->left);`. What does that line do?
--- choice
It makes `link` refer to the root's left child, as intended.
--- choice correct
It assigns to `root_` itself: `root_` takes over the left subtree, and the old root and its right subtree are destroyed.
--- choice
It does not compile, because `unique_ptr` cannot be moved.
--- choice
It copies the left subtree into `root_`, leaving the tree unchanged.
--- why
A reference is another name for the same object, and it can never be re-seated. So `link = ...` is `root_ = ...`: a move assignment into the root pointer, which destroys whatever the root owned before. To walk, use `std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &root_;` and step with `link = &(*link)->left;`, which changes only which pointer you are looking at.

+++ question | Why the successor can be spliced out
--- ask
When erasing a node with two children, the lesson moves the successor's key into the node and then removes the successor by giving its link the successor's **right** child. Why is it safe to ignore the successor's left child?
--- choice
Because the successor is always a leaf.
--- choice correct
Because the successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, so it has no left child.
--- choice
Because the left child is moved into the node along with the key.
--- choice
Because a BST never has a left child below a right child.
--- why
The successor is found by going right once and then left as far as possible; the walk stops exactly at a node with no left child. It may still have a right child, which is why its link must take that right subtree rather than `nullptr`.

=== dsacpp-12 | Balanced trees in the library: std::map and std::set
--- teach
Last lesson's tree was only as good as its insertion order: sorted keys turned it into a chain. The standard library's ordered containers, `std::map` and `std::set`, never degenerate. Every major implementation builds them as **red-black trees**, the balanced trees you met in DSA I, and the standard *guarantees* O(log n) for every lookup, insert and erase. You will not write a red-black tree again. This lesson is about using one well: the exact promises the standard makes, the ordered searches (`lower_bound`, `upper_bound`, `equal_range`) that a hash map cannot do, the rules a comparator must obey, and which iterators survive which operations.

### The picture: a card catalogue

A library's card catalogue keeps one card per book, in alphabetical order, in drawers. You can find one title quickly. But you can also do what a pile of cards sorted by a hash could never do: open the drawer at "the first title starting with *Kep*", and flip forward through every title after it, in order.

### The definition

- `std::set<Key, Compare = std::less<Key>>` holds **unique keys in sorted order**.
- `std::map<Key, T, Compare = std::less<Key>>` holds unique keys in sorted order, **each with a value**. Its elements are `std::pair<const Key, T>`: the key is `const` because changing it in place would put the element in the wrong position.
- `std::multiset` and `std::multimap` are the same, but allow several equivalent keys.

"Sorted" and "unique" are both judged by `Compare`, never by `==`: two keys a and b are the same key when `!comp(a, b) && !comp(b, a)`, the equivalence from last lesson.

### What the standard promises

The standard does not say "red-black tree". It states the costs and the guarantees, and in practice only a balanced tree of separate nodes meets them all:

| Operation | Guarantee |
| --- | --- |
| `find`, `count`, `contains`, `insert`, `erase(key)`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound`, `equal_range` | O(log n) comparisons, worst case |
| iterating from `begin()` to `end()` | in increasing key order; O(n) in total |
| `insert`, `emplace` | never invalidate any iterator, pointer or reference |
| `erase` | invalidates only iterators, pointers and references to the erased elements |

The last two rows are **[[iterator stability|stability]]**, and they are the opposite of lesson 8's vector buckets. Each element lives in its own heap node, and rebalancing only relinks nodes; an element never moves in memory. So a pointer into a `std::map` stays valid until that very element is erased.

### Why the height is below 2 log₂(n + 1)

A red-black tree colours each node red or black. Picture every empty child spot as a black **leaf**. The tree keeps two rules: **a red node has no red child**, and **every path from a node down to a leaf passes the same number of black nodes** (counting the leaf, but not the node itself). For the root, that number is the tree's **black height**, b.

1. A subtree whose root has black height b holds at least 2^b − 1 real nodes. By induction: a leaf has b = 0 and holds 0 real nodes. For a real node, each child has black height b − 1 if the child is black (a leaf counts as black), or b if it is red, so at least b − 1. By induction each child's subtree holds at least 2^(b−1) − 1 real nodes, and the two plus the node itself give at least 2 · (2^(b−1) − 1) + 1 = 2^b − 1.
2. Let h be the height, in links. Follow the path from the root down to a deepest node and on to a leaf below it: under the root it passes h real nodes and then the leaf, h + 1 nodes in all. Every red node on it has a black node right below it (reds never come two in a row, and the path ends at a black leaf), so at least half of those h + 1 nodes are black: b ≥ (h + 1) / 2, so h < 2b.
3. Put these together: n ≥ 2^b − 1 > 2^(h/2) − 1, so h < 2 log₂(n + 1).

For a million keys, that is fewer than 40 levels, whatever order the keys arrived in. Insert and erase restore the two rules with O(1) rotations and O(log n) recolourings, which is where their O(log n) comes from.

### Comparators must be a strict weak ordering

The order comes from `Compare`, and the containers assume it behaves like "less than". Precisely, it must be a **[[strict weak ordering|strict-weak]]**:

- **irreflexive:** `comp(a, a)` is false;
- **transitive:** `comp(a, b)` and `comp(b, c)` give `comp(a, c)`;
- **equivalence is transitive:** if a is equivalent to b, and b to c, then a is equivalent to c.

A comparator on one member of a struct is fine, but it means objects that agree on that member are **the same key**:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <set>
#include <string>

struct Pass {
    std::string station;
    int minute;
};

struct ByMinute {
    bool operator()(const Pass& a, const Pass& b) const { return a.minute < b.minute; }
};

int main() {
    std::set<Pass, ByMinute> passes;
    passes.insert({"Goldstone", 30});
    bool added = passes.insert({"Canberra", 30}).second;   // same minute: same key
    std::cout << added << " " << passes.size() << "\n";     // 0 1
}
```

If both should stay, the comparator must break the tie, for example by station name after the minute. And a comparator written with `<=` is not a strict weak ordering at all: `comp(a, a)` is true, so no two keys are ever equivalent. A set then accepts duplicates, and `find` can never report a match. The standard calls that undefined behaviour, so it may also do worse.

### Searching by order: lower_bound, upper_bound, equal_range

These are the operations a hash map cannot offer:

- `lower_bound(k)`: an iterator to the first element whose key is **not less than** k, that is, the first key ≥ k; `end()` if there is none.
- `upper_bound(k)`: the first element whose key is **greater than** k.
- `equal_range(k)`: both at once, as a `std::pair` of iterators. The elements between them are exactly those equivalent to k: none or one in a set or map, any number in a multiset.

Together with stepping an iterator back, they answer every "nearest" question:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::map<int, std::string> contacts = {{15, "AOS-1"}, {40, "AOS-2"}, {95, "AOS-3"}};
    auto after = contacts.lower_bound(40);     // first key >= 40
    auto later = contacts.upper_bound(40);     // first key > 40
    std::cout << after->second << " " << later->second << "\n";   // AOS-2 AOS-3
    auto it = contacts.lower_bound(10);
    std::cout << (it == contacts.begin()) << "\n";                  // 1: nothing before 10
}
```

The largest key **below** k is one step back from `lower_bound(k)`, and the largest key **at most** k is one step back from `upper_bound(k)`, but only if that iterator is not `begin()`: stepping back from `begin()` is undefined behaviour. `std::prev(it)` from `<iterator>` gives the element before `it` without changing `it`.

### Use the member functions, not the algorithms

`<algorithm>` also has `std::lower_bound`, `std::find` and `std::distance`, and they compile on a map's iterators. They are the wrong tools there:

- A map's iterators are **[[bidirectional|iterator-kinds]]**: they can step forward and back one element at a time, but cannot jump. `std::lower_bound` on them makes only O(log n) comparisons, but moving the iterators to the middle points costs O(n) steps. The member `m.lower_bound(k)` walks down the tree: O(log n).
- `std::find(m.begin(), m.end(), x)` is a linear scan; `m.find(k)` is O(log n).
- `std::distance(first, last)` counts the steps one by one, O(k) for k elements.

### Inserting, reading and erasing

- `insert` and `emplace` return a `std::pair<iterator, bool>`: where the element is, and whether it was new. An existing key is left untouched.
- `try_emplace(k, args...)` builds the value only if k is new; `insert_or_assign(k, v)` overwrites.
- `m[k]` returns a reference to k's value, **inserting** a default value first if k is missing; so it needs a default-constructible `T` and never works on a `const` map. `m.at(k)` does not insert, but a missing key is an error, and with exceptions off the program stops. To only look, use `find`, `contains` or `lower_bound`.
- `erase(k)` removes by key and returns how many elements it removed. `erase(it)` removes one element and **returns the iterator after it**. `erase(first, last)` removes a range in O(log n + k).
- `emplace_hint(pos, ...)` takes a guess at the position. When the guess is right, as with `end()` for keys arriving in increasing order, the insert is amortised O(1), so a map can be built from sorted data in O(n).

To erase while iterating, let `erase` hand you the next position, because the erased element's iterator is dead:

```cpp fragment
for (auto it = logs.begin(); it != logs.end();) {
    if (it->second.empty()) it = logs.erase(it);   // erase returns the next element
    else ++it;
}
```

### What it costs

| | `std::map` / `std::set` | `std::unordered_map` | sorted `std::vector` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| find | O(log n) worst case | O(1) expected, O(n) worst | O(log n), binary search |
| insert, erase | O(log n) | O(1) expected | O(n): shifting |
| in-order iteration, nearest key | yes | no | yes |
| stable iterators and references | yes, across inserts | references yes | no |
| memory per element | the element plus [[a node|node-overhead]] of 3 pointers and a colour | the element plus a node and a bucket | just the element |

A tree pays for its order with memory and cache misses: every step down is a different node somewhere on the heap. For data that is built once and then only read, a sorted vector with `std::lower_bound` is often several times faster, which is why C++23 added `std::flat_map`.

### Where it is used

- **Exchanges' order books** keep the waiting buy orders in a map from price to quantity, sorted high to low, and the sell orders sorted low to high, so the best price is always at `begin()`.
- **Operating systems:** Linux's scheduler for many years kept runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by how much processor time each had received, and took the leftmost one to run next; the kernel also keeps timers and memory regions in red-black trees.
- **Allocators** keep free blocks in a tree by size, so "the smallest block of at least n bytes" is a `lower_bound`.
- **ORBIT's world:** a telemetry timeline from time to reading, where "the value at 14:03:22" means the last reading at or before that time: one `upper_bound` and one step back.

**Watch out:** `std::lower_bound(m.begin(), m.end(), ...)` on a map or set compiles, gives the right answer, and is O(n); use `m.lower_bound(k)`. And in a loop, `m.erase(it); ++it;` steps from a destroyed element; write `it = m.erase(it);`. One more for multisets: `ms.erase(x)` erases **every** copy of x; to remove one copy, write `ms.erase(ms.find(x))` after checking that `find` did not return `end()`.

::: context stability What "stable" buys you
Because elements never move, code can keep a pointer or an iterator to an element for as long as the element exists: an index from one map into another, a list of "watched" entries, a cache that points into a table. With a vector, or with the flat hash tables of lessons 8 and 9, every insert may move everything. The price of stability is one heap allocation per element and a pointer chase per step, which is why the fastest tables give it up.
:::

::: context strict-weak Why these three rules
Sorting and searching need to be able to say "these two are tied" in a consistent way. Irreflexivity means no key comes before itself. Transitivity keeps the order a line, not a loop. Transitive equivalence makes "tied" group keys into clean classes, so every class has one place in the order. A comparison of floating-point numbers breaks the third rule as soon as a NaN appears, because NaN is tied with everything and 1 is not tied with 2. That is why a set of doubles containing NaN can misbehave.
:::

::: context iterator-kinds What an iterator can do
The standard sorts iterators by what they can do. A forward iterator can only move ahead, like a singly linked list's. A bidirectional iterator can also step back, like `std::list` and the tree containers. A random-access iterator can jump by any distance in O(1), like `std::vector`'s and raw pointers. Algorithms adapt: `std::distance` subtracts two random-access iterators, but has to count step by step on a bidirectional one, and `std::sort` refuses to compile on anything below random-access.
:::

::: context node-overhead The size of a tree node
In GCC's library each node of a `std::map` holds a colour, three pointers (parent, left, right) and the element. On a 64-bit machine that is 32 bytes before your data. A `std::map<int, int>` therefore uses about 40 bytes per element, plus the allocator's own bookkeeping, for 8 bytes of real data. A sorted `std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>` uses 8. For a few thousand elements this rarely matters; for tens of millions it decides whether the data fits in memory.
