--- task
Write `class Timeline`, a sensor's readings by time, on top of a `std::map<long long, double>` from a time (in nanoseconds, so it needs `long long`) to a reading. No `main`.

- `void record(long long t, double value)`: store the reading at time `t`, replacing any earlier reading at exactly that time.
- `std::optional<double> value_at(long long t) const`: the reading at the **latest time at or before** `t`, or `std::nullopt` if every reading is later than `t`.
- `std::optional<std::pair<long long, double>> next_after(long long t) const`: the first reading at a time **strictly after** `t`, as a (time, value) pair, or `std::nullopt`.
- `std::vector<std::pair<long long, double>> between(long long lo, long long hi) const`: every reading with `lo <= time <= hi`, in time order; empty if `lo > hi`.
- `std::size_t prune_before(long long t)`: erase every reading at a time before `t`, returning how many it erased, with one range erase.
- `std::size_t size() const`.

Use the map's member functions (`upper_bound`, `lower_bound`, `erase`). A check records 200,000 readings and then asks 200,000 questions, which is far too slow if a question walks through the map.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Timeline {
public:
    void record(long long t, double value) {}
    std::optional<double> value_at(long long t) const { return std::nullopt; }
    std::optional<std::pair<long long, double>> next_after(long long t) const { return std::nullopt; }
    std::vector<std::pair<long long, double>> between(long long lo, long long hi) const { return {}; }
    std::size_t prune_before(long long t) { return 0; }
    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }

private:
    std::map<long long, double> readings_;
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Timeline {
public:
    void record(long long t, double value) { readings_.insert_or_assign(t, value); }

    std::optional<double> value_at(long long t) const {
        auto it = readings_.upper_bound(t);          // first reading after t
        if (it == readings_.begin()) return std::nullopt;
        return std::prev(it)->second;                // the one before it is at or before t
    }

    std::optional<std::pair<long long, double>> next_after(long long t) const {
        auto it = readings_.upper_bound(t);
        if (it == readings_.end()) return std::nullopt;
        return std::make_pair(it->first, it->second);
    }

    std::vector<std::pair<long long, double>> between(long long lo, long long hi) const {
        std::vector<std::pair<long long, double>> out;
        if (lo > hi) return out;
        auto last = readings_.upper_bound(hi);
        for (auto it = readings_.lower_bound(lo); it != last; ++it) out.emplace_back(it->first, it->second);
        return out;
    }

    std::size_t prune_before(long long t) {
        auto first_kept = readings_.lower_bound(t);
        std::size_t gone = static_cast<std::size_t>(std::distance(readings_.begin(), first_kept));
        readings_.erase(readings_.begin(), first_kept);
        return gone;
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return readings_.size(); }

private:
    std::map<long long, double> readings_;
};
--- hint
`upper_bound(t)` is the first reading strictly after `t`, which is exactly `next_after`. The reading at or before `t` is the one just before it: `std::prev(it)`, but only when `it` is not `begin()`.
--- hint
For `between`, walk from `lower_bound(lo)` (the first time at least `lo`) up to, not including, `upper_bound(hi)` (the first time after `hi`). Handle `lo > hi` first, because then those two iterators may be in the wrong order.
--- hint
For `prune_before`, the readings to erase run from `begin()` up to `lower_bound(t)`. Count them with `std::distance` (they are about to be visited by the erase anyway), then erase the whole range with one call.
--- check test | value_at: before, at, between and after the readings

?? The reading at or before t is one step back from upper_bound(t), unless that is begin().

--- check test | next_after is strictly after

?? Walking the map, or calling std::lower_bound on its iterators, is O(n) per question. Use the member functions.

+++ practice | The nearest free channel
--- task
A radio keeps the numbers of its free channels in a `std::set<int>`. Write `std::optional<int> nearest(const std::set<int>& free, int wanted)` that returns the free channel closest to `wanted`. If two are equally close, return the smaller one. If `wanted` itself is free, return it. If the set is empty, return `std::nullopt`. No `main`.

It must take O(log n): use `free.lower_bound(wanted)`, which points at the smallest channel at least `wanted`, and look one step back from it for the largest channel below `wanted`. Remember that you may not step back from `begin()`, nor read `end()`.

For example, with free channels 3, 8 and 20, `nearest(free, 6)` is 8, `nearest(free, 5)` is 3 (2 away, against 3 away for 8), and `nearest(free, 14)` is 8 (a tie at distance 6, so the smaller one).
--- starter
#include <iterator>
#include <optional>
#include <set>

std::optional<int> nearest(const std::set<int>& free, int wanted) {
    return std::nullopt;
}
--- solution
#include <iterator>
#include <optional>
#include <set>

std::optional<int> nearest(const std::set<int>& free, int wanted) {
    if (free.empty()) return std::nullopt;
    auto above = free.lower_bound(wanted);                 // smallest channel >= wanted
    if (above == free.begin()) return *above;              // nothing below
    auto below = std::prev(above);                         // largest channel < wanted
    if (above == free.end()) return *below;                // nothing at or above
    long long up = static_cast<long long>(*above) - wanted;
    long long down = static_cast<long long>(wanted) - *below;
    return up < down ? *above : *below;                    // ties go to the smaller channel
}
--- hint
After `lower_bound`, there are three cases: it is `begin()` (every channel is at least `wanted`), it is `end()` (every channel is below), or there is a channel on each side. Handle the empty set before all of them.
--- hint
With a channel on each side, compare the two distances; only a strictly closer upper channel wins, so a tie picks the lower one. Compute the distances in `long long`, so channels near the limits of `int` cannot overflow.
--- check test | The examples from the task
[] { std::set<int> f = {3, 8, 20}; return *nearest(f, 6) == 8 && *nearest(f, 5) == 3 && *nearest(f, 14) == 8; }()
--- check test | wanted is free, below all, above all
[] { std::set<int> f = {3, 8, 20}; return *nearest(f, 8) == 8 && *nearest(f, -100) == 3 && *nearest(f, 1000) == 20; }()
?? Do not step back from begin(), and do not read end().
--- check test | An empty set and a one-channel set
[] { std::set<int> e; std::set<int> one = {42}; return !nearest(e, 0) && *nearest(one, -5) == 42 && *nearest(one, 99) == 42; }()
--- check test | Extreme values do not overflow
[] { std::set<int> f = {-2147483647 - 1, 2147483647}; return *nearest(f, 0) == 2147483647 && *nearest(f, -1) == -2147483647 - 1; }()
--- check test | Many queries match a brute-force search
[] { std::set<int> f; unsigned s = 4; for (int i = 0; i < 300; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; f.insert(static_cast<int>((s >> 16) % 5000)); } for (int q = -10; q < 5010; q += 7) { int best = *f.begin(); for (int c : f) { long long dc = c > q ? c - q : q - c; long long db = best > q ? best - q : q - best; if (dc < db || (dc == db && c < best)) best = c; } if (*nearest(f, q) != best) return false; } return true; }()

+++ practice | Booking a ground-station antenna
--- task
An antenna's bookings are kept in a `std::map<int, int>` from each booking's start minute to its end minute. A booking covers the half-open interval `[start, end)`: it includes `start` but not `end`, so one booking may end at the minute the next begins. No `main`.

Write `bool book(std::map<int, int>& bookings, int start, int end)`. If `start >= end`, return `false`. If the new interval overlaps any existing booking, return `false` and change nothing. Otherwise add it and return `true`.

Only two existing bookings can overlap the new one, if any does: the first booking starting at or after `start`, which overlaps if it starts before `end`; and the booking just before that, which overlaps if it ends after `start`. Find them with one `lower_bound`, in O(log n).

For example, with a booking `[10, 20)`, booking `[20, 25)` succeeds, but `[15, 30)` and `[5, 11)` fail.
--- starter
#include <utility>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>

bool book(std::map<int, int>& bookings, int start, int end) {
    bookings[start] = end;
    return true;
}
--- solution
#include <utility>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>

bool book(std::map<int, int>& bookings, int start, int end) {
    if (start >= end) return false;
    auto next = bookings.lower_bound(start);                           // first booking starting at or after start
    if (next != bookings.end() && next->first < end) return false;     // it begins before we finish
    if (next != bookings.begin() && std::prev(next)->second > start) return false;   // the one before runs into us
    bookings.emplace_hint(next, start, end);
    return true;
}
--- hint
`lower_bound(start)` gives the first booking that starts at or after `start`. If it exists and starts before `end`, the two overlap.
--- hint
The booking before it (only if `lower_bound` did not return `begin()`) starts before `start`; it overlaps if its end is after `start`. If neither overlaps, insert; `emplace_hint` with the `lower_bound` iterator puts it in place without a second search.
--- check test | The examples from the task
[] { std::map<int, int> b; bool first = book(b, 10, 20); bool touch = book(b, 20, 25); bool over1 = book(b, 15, 30); bool over2 = book(b, 5, 11); return first && touch && !over1 && !over2 && b.size() == 2; }()
--- check test | Ending exactly where a booking starts is fine
[] { std::map<int, int> b; book(b, 50, 60); bool before = book(b, 40, 50); bool inside = book(b, 52, 58); bool around = book(b, 30, 70); return before && !inside && !around && b.size() == 2; }()
--- check test | Empty and backwards intervals are refused
[] { std::map<int, int> b; return !book(b, 5, 5) && !book(b, 9, 3) && b.empty(); }()
?? start >= end is not a booking.
--- check test | A failed booking changes nothing
[] { std::map<int, int> b; book(b, 0, 10); book(b, 20, 30); book(b, 12, 18); bool fits = book(b, 10, 12); bool clash = book(b, 17, 21); return fits && !clash && b.size() == 4 && b.count(17) == 0; }()
--- check test | Two thousand random requests match a brute-force check
[] { std::map<int, int> b; std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> ref; unsigned s = 2; for (int i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int st = static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % 100000); int len = static_cast<int>((s >> 24) % 60); bool ok = len > 0; for (auto [a, e] : ref) if (st < e && a < st + len) ok = false; if (book(b, st, st + len) != ok) return false; if (ok) ref.push_back({st, st + len}); } return b.size() == ref.size(); }()

+++ practice | A set of tasks with a comparator that breaks ties
--- task
A scheduler keeps its tasks in a `std::set` ordered by urgency: higher priority first, and among equal priorities, alphabetical by name. No `main`.

- Write `struct Task { std::string name; int priority; };`.
- Write `struct ByUrgency` whose `bool operator()(const Task& a, const Task& b) const` is a strict weak ordering that puts `a` before `b` when `a` has the higher priority, or the same priority and a name that comes first alphabetically.
- Write `std::vector<std::string> schedule(const std::vector<Task>& tasks)` that puts the tasks into a `std::set<Task, ByUrgency>` and returns their names in the set's order. A task with the same name **and** priority as an earlier one is a duplicate and appears once; two tasks with the same priority but different names are both kept.

For example, tasks `{"ping", 1}`, `{"burn", 5}`, `{"abort", 5}` and `{"ping", 1}` give `{"abort", "burn", "ping"}`.
--- starter
#include <set>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Task {
    std::string name;
    int priority;
};

struct ByUrgency {
    bool operator()(const Task& a, const Task& b) const { return a.priority > b.priority; }
};

std::vector<std::string> schedule(const std::vector<Task>& tasks) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <set>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Task {
    std::string name;
    int priority;
};

struct ByUrgency {
    bool operator()(const Task& a, const Task& b) const {
        if (a.priority != b.priority) return a.priority > b.priority;   // more urgent first
        return a.name < b.name;                                         // then alphabetical
    }
};

std::vector<std::string> schedule(const std::vector<Task>& tasks) {
    std::set<Task, ByUrgency> queue(tasks.begin(), tasks.end());
    std::vector<std::string> names;
    for (const Task& t : queue) names.push_back(t.name);
    return names;
}
--- hint
Comparing priorities alone makes every two tasks with the same priority equivalent, so the set keeps only the first of them. When the priorities differ, decide by priority; only when they are equal, decide by name.
--- hint
The set can be built straight from the vector with its two-iterator constructor, and a range-for over it visits the tasks in comparator order.
--- check case | The example from the task
schedule({{"ping", 1}, {"burn", 5}, {"abort", 5}, {"ping", 1}})
=> std::vector<std::string>{"abort", "burn", "ping"}
?? Two tasks with the same priority and different names must both stay: break ties by name.
--- check case | Same name, different priorities: both kept, in priority order
schedule({{"scan", 2}, {"scan", 9}, {"idle", -1}})
=> std::vector<std::string>{"scan", "scan", "idle"}
--- check case | No tasks
schedule({})
=> std::vector<std::string>{}
--- check test | The comparator is irreflexive and consistent
[] { ByUrgency c; Task a{"x", 3}; Task b{"y", 3}; Task d{"x", 4}; return !c(a, a) && c(a, b) && !c(b, a) && c(d, a) && !c(a, d); }()
--- check test | Lookups use the same order
[] { std::set<Task, ByUrgency> s = {{"b", 1}, {"a", 1}, {"c", 7}}; auto it = s.find(Task{"a", 1}); auto first = s.begin(); return it != s.end() && it->name == "a" && first->name == "c" && s.count(Task{"a", 2}) == 0; }()

+++ practice | Erasing while you walk, and erasing just one copy
--- task
Write two functions. No `main`.

1. `std::size_t purge_below(std::map<std::string, int>& counts, int threshold)` erases every entry whose value is less than `threshold` and returns how many it erased. Walk the map once, using the iterator that `erase` returns; stepping an iterator after its element was erased is undefined behaviour.
2. `bool drop_one(std::multiset<int>& readings, int x)` removes **one** copy of `x` and returns `true`, or returns `false` if there is none. Careful: `readings.erase(x)` removes **every** copy.

The checks try an empty map, a map where every entry goes, where none goes, where the first and last entries go, and where several neighbours go in a row; and multisets with no copy, one copy and several copies.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <map>
#include <set>
#include <string>

std::size_t purge_below(std::map<std::string, int>& counts, int threshold) {
    return 0;
}

bool drop_one(std::multiset<int>& readings, int x) {
    return readings.erase(x) > 0;
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <map>
#include <set>
#include <string>

std::size_t purge_below(std::map<std::string, int>& counts, int threshold) {
    std::size_t gone = 0;
    for (auto it = counts.begin(); it != counts.end();) {
        if (it->second < threshold) {
            it = counts.erase(it);   // the next element, since it is now dead
            ++gone;
        } else {
            ++it;
        }
    }
    return gone;
}

bool drop_one(std::multiset<int>& readings, int x) {
    auto it = readings.find(x);
    if (it == readings.end()) return false;
    readings.erase(it);          // erasing by iterator removes exactly one element
    return true;
}
--- hint
In the loop, do not put `++it` in the `for` header. When the entry goes, set `it` to what `erase(it)` returns; only when it stays, write `++it`.
--- hint
For the multiset, `find(x)` gives an iterator to one copy (or `end()`), and `erase` of an iterator removes just that element.
--- check test | Neighbours, the first and the last entries go
[] { std::map<std::string, int> m = {{"a", 1}, {"b", 1}, {"c", 9}, {"d", 2}, {"e", 0}, {"f", 7}, {"g", 3}}; auto n = purge_below(m, 5); std::string left; for (auto& [k, v] : m) left += k; return n == 5 && left == "cf"; }()
--- check test | Everything goes, nothing goes, and an empty map
[] { std::map<std::string, int> all = {{"x", 1}, {"y", 2}}; std::map<std::string, int> none = {{"x", 10}}; std::map<std::string, int> empty; return purge_below(all, 5) == 2 && all.empty() && purge_below(none, 5) == 0 && none.size() == 1 && purge_below(empty, 5) == 0; }()
--- check test | A value equal to the threshold stays
[] { std::map<std::string, int> m = {{"k", 5}, {"j", 4}}; return purge_below(m, 5) == 1 && m.count("k") == 1; }()
--- check test | drop_one removes exactly one copy
[] { std::multiset<int> r = {4, 7, 7, 7, 9}; bool a = drop_one(r, 7); bool b = !drop_one(r, 5); return a && b && r.count(7) == 2 && r.size() == 4; }()
?? erase(x) removes every copy of x. Erase the iterator that find gives you.
--- check test | Dropping the last copy, then nothing left to drop
[] { std::multiset<int> r = {3}; bool a = drop_one(r, 3); bool b = !drop_one(r, 3); std::multiset<int> e; return a && b && r.empty() && !drop_one(e, 0); }()
--- check test | 20,000 entries, every other one erased
[] { std::map<std::string, int> m; for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) m[std::to_string(i)] = i % 2; auto n = purge_below(m, 1); for (auto& [k, v] : m) if (v != 1) return false; return n == 10000 && m.size() == 10000; }()

+++ practice | Debug: one word per length
--- task
`longest_first(words)` should keep **one word of each length**, the first one seen of that length, and return them from the longest to the shortest. It stores them in a `std::set` with a comparator that orders strings by length. For example, `longest_first({"io", "mars", "ab", "venus", "moon"})` should give `{"venus", "mars", "io"}`: "ab" and "moon" are dropped, because a word of their length came first.

Instead, every word is kept. Find the bug and fix it. It is one line.
--- starter
#include <set>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct LongerFirst {
    bool operator()(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) const { return a.size() >= b.size(); }
};

std::vector<std::string> longest_first(const std::vector<std::string>& words) {
    std::set<std::string, LongerFirst> kept;
    for (const auto& w : words) kept.insert(w);
    return std::vector<std::string>(kept.begin(), kept.end());
}
--- solution
#include <set>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct LongerFirst {
    bool operator()(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) const { return a.size() > b.size(); }
};

std::vector<std::string> longest_first(const std::vector<std::string>& words) {
    std::set<std::string, LongerFirst> kept;
    for (const auto& w : words) kept.insert(w);
    return std::vector<std::string>(kept.begin(), kept.end());
}
--- hint
When are two words the same key for this set? Only when neither comes before the other. With `>=`, is that ever true for two words of the same length? Is `comp(a, a)` false, as a strict weak ordering requires?
--- hint
A comparator must be strict: use `>` for "longer first", so words of equal length are equivalent and the set keeps only the first.
--- check case | The example from the task

=> std::vector<std::string>{"venus", "mars", "io"}
?? With >=, comp(a, a) is true, so no two words are ever equivalent and nothing is dropped.
--- check case | All the same length: only the first stays
longest_first({"sun", "sky", "air"})
=> std::vector<std::string>{"sun"}
--- check case | No words

=> std::vector<std::string>{}

+++ practice | Stretch: a matching engine's order book
--- task
An exchange's order book holds waiting **buy** orders (bids) and **sell** orders (asks), each at a price. When a new order can trade with the waiting orders on the other side, it does; whatever is left waits in the book. No `main`.

Write `BookResult run_book(const std::vector<Order>& orders)`, with these types:

- `struct Order { char side; int price; int qty; };`, where `side` is `'B'` (buy) or `'S'` (sell), and `price` and `qty` are positive;
- `struct BookResult { long long volume; long long notional; std::optional<int> best_bid; std::optional<int> best_ask; std::size_t bid_levels; std::size_t ask_levels; };`.

Keep the book as two maps from price to total waiting quantity: bids in a `std::map<int, int, std::greater<int>>`, so the **highest** bid is at `begin()`, and asks in a `std::map<int, int>`, so the **lowest** ask is at `begin()`. Process the orders in order:

- A buy order trades with the best ask while one exists with price ≤ the buy's price: the traded quantity is the smaller of the two, at the **ask's** price. A price level whose quantity reaches 0 is erased. Any quantity left over is added to the bids at the buy's price.
- A sell order is the mirror image: it trades with the best bid while one exists with price ≥ the sell's price, at the bid's price, and any leftover joins the asks.

`volume` is the total quantity traded, and `notional` the total of quantity × price over all trades. `best_bid` and `best_ask` are the top of each side at the end (`std::nullopt` if that side is empty), and `bid_levels` and `ask_levels` count the prices left on each side.

For example, buy 5 at 100, sell 3 at 101, sell 7 at 99, buy 10 at 102 trades 5 at 100, then 2 at 99 and 3 at 101: volume 10, notional 1001, best bid 102, no asks.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <vector>

struct Order {
    char side;
    int price;
    int qty;
};

struct BookResult {
    long long volume;
    long long notional;
    std::optional<int> best_bid;
    std::optional<int> best_ask;
    std::size_t bid_levels;
    std::size_t ask_levels;
};

BookResult run_book(const std::vector<Order>& orders) {
    return BookResult{0, 0, std::nullopt, std::nullopt, 0, 0};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <vector>

struct Order {
    char side;
    int price;
    int qty;
};

struct BookResult {
    long long volume;
    long long notional;
    std::optional<int> best_bid;
    std::optional<int> best_ask;
    std::size_t bid_levels;
    std::size_t ask_levels;
};

// Trades `qty` against the best levels of `book` while `crosses(level price)` holds.
template <typename Book, typename Crosses>
int match(Book& book, int qty, Crosses crosses, long long& volume, long long& notional) {
    for (auto it = book.begin(); qty > 0 && it != book.end() && crosses(it->first);) {
        int traded = std::min(qty, it->second);
        volume += traded;
        notional += static_cast<long long>(traded) * it->first;
        qty -= traded;
        it->second -= traded;
        if (it->second == 0) it = book.erase(it);   // the level is used up
        else ++it;
    }
    return qty;
}

BookResult run_book(const std::vector<Order>& orders) {
    std::map<int, int, std::greater<int>> bids;   // highest price first
    std::map<int, int> asks;                      // lowest price first
    long long volume = 0;
    long long notional = 0;
    for (const Order& o : orders) {
        if (o.side == 'B') {
            int left = match(asks, o.qty, [&](int ask) { return ask <= o.price; }, volume, notional);
            if (left > 0) bids[o.price] += left;
        } else {
            int left = match(bids, o.qty, [&](int bid) { return bid >= o.price; }, volume, notional);
            if (left > 0) asks[o.price] += left;
        }
    }
    BookResult r{volume, notional, std::nullopt, std::nullopt, bids.size(), asks.size()};
    if (!bids.empty()) r.best_bid = bids.begin()->first;
    if (!asks.empty()) r.best_ask = asks.begin()->first;
    return r;
}
--- hint
Thanks to the comparators, the best price on each side is always `begin()`. A buy walks the asks from `begin()` while the ask's price is at most the buy's; a sell walks the bids from `begin()` while the bid's price is at least the sell's.
--- hint
At each level, trade the smaller of the order's remaining quantity and the level's quantity, at the level's price. If the level is used up, erase it with `it = book.erase(it)`; otherwise the order is used up and the loop ends.
--- hint
Leftover quantity rests at the order's own price: `bids[price] += left` adds to an existing level or creates one. Accumulate `notional` in `long long`, converting before multiplying, because quantity × price can pass two billion.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { auto r = run_book({{'B', 100, 5}, {'S', 101, 3}, {'S', 99, 7}, {'B', 102, 10}}); return r.volume == 10 && r.notional == 1001 && r.best_bid && *r.best_bid == 102 && !r.best_ask && r.bid_levels == 1 && r.ask_levels == 0; }()
--- check test | No trade when the prices do not cross
[] { auto r = run_book({{'B', 99, 4}, {'S', 100, 6}, {'B', 98, 1}}); return r.volume == 0 && r.notional == 0 && *r.best_bid == 99 && *r.best_ask == 100 && r.bid_levels == 2 && r.ask_levels == 1; }()
--- check test | Orders at the same price add up in one level
[] { auto r = run_book({{'S', 50, 2}, {'S', 50, 3}, {'B', 50, 4}}); return r.volume == 4 && r.notional == 200 && !r.best_bid && *r.best_ask == 50 && r.ask_levels == 1; }()
--- check test | A big sell sweeps several bid levels, best price first
[] { auto r = run_book({{'B', 10, 1}, {'B', 12, 2}, {'B', 11, 3}, {'S', 11, 10}}); return r.volume == 5 && r.notional == 12 * 2 + 11 * 3 && *r.best_bid == 10 && *r.best_ask == 11 && r.bid_levels == 1 && r.ask_levels == 1; }()
?? The bids must be in a map with std::greater<int>, so the highest bid is at begin().
--- check test | No orders
[] { auto r = run_book({}); return r.volume == 0 && !r.best_bid && !r.best_ask && r.bid_levels == 0 && r.ask_levels == 0; }()
--- check test | 20,000 random orders
[] { std::vector<Order> orders; unsigned s = 5; for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; char side = ((s >> 31) & 1) ? 'B' : 'S'; int price = 9900 + static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % 200); int qty = 1 + static_cast<int>((s >> 20) % 50); orders.push_back({side, price, qty}); } auto r = run_book(orders); return r.volume == 200680 && r.notional == 2006429954LL && *r.best_bid == 9993 && *r.best_ask == 10002 && r.bid_levels == 48 && r.ask_levels == 61; }()

+++ question | How tall can a red-black tree be?
--- ask
The proof that a red-black tree with n nodes has height below 2 log₂(n + 1) uses the black height b. Which step gives h < 2b?
--- choice
Every subtree with black height b has at least 2^b − 1 nodes.
--- choice correct
A red node never has a red child, so at least half the nodes on any path from the root down to a leaf are black.
--- choice
Rotations keep the tree balanced after every insert.
--- choice
Every path from the root to a leaf has the same length.
--- why
Below the root, a path to a leaf under a deepest node passes h real nodes and then a black leaf. Each red node on it has a black node right below it, so at least half of those h + 1 nodes are black, and the black count is the same b on every path: b ≥ (h + 1)/2, so h < 2b. The other key fact, that such a subtree has at least 2^b − 1 real nodes, then gives n > 2^(h/2) − 1. Paths need not all have the same length: only the same number of black nodes.

+++ question | std::lower_bound on a set
--- ask
`s` is a `std::set<int>` with n elements. What is the running time of `std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), 42)`, the algorithm from `<algorithm>`, compared with `s.lower_bound(42)`?
--- choice
Both are O(log n).
--- choice correct
The algorithm is O(n), because a set's iterators can only step one element at a time; the member function is O(log n).
--- choice
The algorithm is O(log n) and the member function is O(1).
--- choice
The algorithm does not compile on set iterators.
--- why
`std::lower_bound` makes only O(log n) comparisons, but to reach each middle point it must advance a bidirectional iterator step by step, which costs O(n) in total. The member function walks down the tree itself, so it is O(log n) in steps as well as comparisons.

=== dsacpp-13 | unordered_map in depth: buckets, hashes and stability
--- teach
In lessons 8 and 9 you built hash maps by hand, first with chains and then with open addressing, and lesson 8 promised a closer look at `std::unordered_map`. Last lesson opened up `std::map`, the library's balanced tree. This lesson opens up `std::unordered_map`, the library's hash table. You will see what the C++ standard promises about it, what each promise costs, and how to make it work with key types of your own.

### What the standard promises

Picture a post office wall of pigeonholes. A clerk reads a letter's address, works out a pigeonhole number from it, and drops the letter in. To find a letter later, she works out the same number and looks in that one hole only. Several letters can share a hole; she flips through them.

`std::unordered_map<Key, T, Hash, KeyEqual>` is that wall. Precisely, it is a container of (key, value) pairs with **unique keys**, where:

- the pigeonholes are called **buckets**, numbered 0 to `bucket_count() - 1`;
- the object of type `Hash` turns a key into a `std::size_t` number, its **hash**, and the table maps that number to a bucket;
- the object of type `KeyEqual` decides whether two keys are the same key.

`Hash` defaults to `std::hash<Key>` and `KeyEqual` to `std::equal_to<Key>`, which calls `==`. The standard then promises four things:

1. `find`, `insert` and `erase` take O(1) time **on average**, and O(n) in the worst case, where n is `size()`.
2. The order in which you meet the elements when you loop over the map is **unspecified**: it can differ between compilers, and it can change after an insert.
3. The buckets are visible: you can ask how many there are, which bucket a key is in, and how full each bucket is.
4. Pointers and references to elements **stay valid** when the table grows. Iterators do not.

The rest of this lesson is those four promises, one at a time.

### Seeing the buckets

The **bucket interface** lets you look inside. `bucket_count()` is the number of buckets, `bucket(k)` is the bucket a key lives in, and `bucket_size(b)` is how many elements bucket `b` holds:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>

int main() {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, int> passes = {{"Goldstone", 4}, {"Madrid", 3}, {"Canberra", 5}};
    std::cout << "buckets: " << passes.bucket_count() << "\n";
    std::size_t b = passes.bucket("Madrid");
    std::cout << "Madrid is in bucket " << b << ", which holds " << passes.bucket_size(b) << "\n";
    std::cout << "load factor: " << passes.load_factor() << "\n";
}
```

Run it, and the numbers you see belong to your standard library: another compiler may pick a different bucket count, and it will almost surely put "Madrid" in a different bucket. Nothing in a program should depend on them. They are for understanding and for tuning.

### Load factor and rehashing

The **load factor** is the average number of elements per bucket: `size() / bucket_count()`. It is exactly the α of the hashing lessons, and the expected length of a chain when the hash spreads keys evenly.

The map keeps the load factor at or below `max_load_factor()`, which starts at 1.0. When an insert would push it higher, the map **rehashes**: it allocates a bigger bucket array (libraries at least double it, often up to the next prime) and moves every element into the bucket it belongs to under the new count. A rehash touches every element, so it costs Θ(n).

Inserts are still O(1) amortised, by the argument from DSA I's amortised-analysis lesson. Because each rehash at least doubles the bucket count, the rehashes on the way to n elements handled at most n, n/2, n/4, … elements. That sum is below 2n, so the rehash work, spread over n inserts, is at most 2 per insert.

You can move the limit with `max_load_factor(z)`. A lower z means shorter chains and faster lookups, but more buckets, so more memory:

```cpp fragment
std::unordered_map<int, int> m;
m.max_load_factor(0.5f);   // keep chains to half an element on average
```

### reserve: paying for the room once

If you know roughly how many elements are coming, tell the map up front. `m.reserve(n)` sets the bucket count high enough for n elements under the current maximum load factor. It is defined as `rehash(ceil(n / max_load_factor()))`.

The standard adds an exact promise: an insert does **not** rehash as long as the new size is at most `max_load_factor() × bucket_count()`. So after `reserve(n)`, the first n elements go in with no rehash at all:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <unordered_map>

int main() {
    std::unordered_map<int, int> seen;
    seen.reserve(5000);
    std::size_t before = seen.bucket_count();
    for (int i = 0; i < 5000; ++i) seen[i * 7] = i;
    std::cout << (seen.bucket_count() == before ? "no rehash" : "rehashed") << "\n";   // no rehash
}
```

That saves the Θ(n) copies of every rehash, and, as the next step shows, it keeps iterators valid while you insert.

### Why nodes: the stability promise

Inside, `std::unordered_map` is a chained table like your lesson 8 map, with the one difference lesson 8 mentioned: every element lives in its own heap-allocated **node**, and a bucket holds a link into a list of nodes. Rehashing allocates a new bucket array and **relinks** the nodes into it. It never moves or copies an element.

That gives the fourth promise, and here is the argument in plain steps:

- An element's address is the address of its node.
- A node is allocated once, when the element is inserted, and freed only when that element is erased.
- A rehash changes links and the bucket array, never a node's address.
- So a pointer or reference to an element stays valid until that element is erased, however many inserts and rehashes happen in between.

Iterators are a different story. An iterator may record which bucket it is walking, and a rehash changes every bucket. So a rehash invalidates all iterators.

| operation | iterators | pointers and references |
|---|---|---|
| insert, no rehash | stay valid | stay valid |
| insert that rehashes | all invalid | stay valid |
| `erase` | only the erased element's | only the erased element's |
| `clear` | all invalid | all invalid |

Compare the vector of lessons 1 and 2, whose growth moves every element, and your open-addressing table of lesson 9, whose rebuild does too. The price of stability is speed: one allocation per element, and a pointer to follow on every lookup, which is usually a [[cache miss|cache-miss-map]]. Lesson 18 measures that cost, and some libraries [[give up the promise to avoid it|flat-maps]].

### Hashing your own type

Lesson 8 gave you the two things a struct key needs: an `==` (C++20 writes one for you with `= default`) and a hash function object. `std::unordered_map` needs exactly those, with the hash as its third template argument. Leave the hash out, and compilation stops, because the library has `std::hash` for numbers, pointers and strings but cannot guess one for your struct:

```cpp error
#include <unordered_map>

struct Pass {
    int station;
    int orbit;
    bool operator==(const Pass&) const = default;
};

int main() {
    std::unordered_map<Pass, double> signal;   // error: no std::hash<Pass>
    signal[Pass{2, 118}] = -91.5;
}
```

The hash must obey the contract from lesson 8, plus a wish:

1. **Equal keys must give equal hashes.** Required for correctness.
2. **Different keys should rarely give equal hashes.** Required for speed.

**Why rule 1 is required.** `find(k)` computes the hash of `k` and searches that one bucket. Suppose `a == b` but `hash(a) != hash(b)`. Store `a`, then look up `b`: the map searches `b`'s bucket, which is usually not `a`'s, so it misses a key that is there. Worse, `m[b] = 1` then inserts a second entry for what is supposed to be the same key. The map is wrong the moment rule 1 fails.

**Why rule 2 matters.** The expected chain length is α only when keys spread evenly. If every key had the same hash, all n elements would share one bucket, every lookup would scan them all, and n inserts would cost Θ(n²).

### Measure the hash on your keys

Rule 2 is about the keys you will really have, so test it on them. Take small grid cells, pairs (x, y) with both from −100 to 100: 40,401 keys. Count how many **different** hash values each recipe gives:

| recipe | different values |
|---|---|
| `x ^ y` | 256 |
| `x * 31 + y` | 6,401 |
| lesson 8's Boost line, with `std::hash<int>` | 13,187 |
| the mixer below | 40,401 |

The Boost line is fine for strings, whose `std::hash` already scrambles the bits. But the standard libraries of GCC and Clang make `std::hash<int>` return the number itself, so for small integers the line only shifts and adds small numbers, and many pairs land on the same sum. On average about three keys then share each hash value, so every chain is about three times longer than it should be.

A good combiner runs the numbers through a **mixer**: a function where every input bit affects about half of the output bits. This one is the finishing step of a well-known generator called [[splitmix64|splitmix-note]]:

```cpp fragment
std::uint64_t mix(std::uint64_t z) {
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
    return z ^ (z >> 31);
}

std::uint64_t combine(std::uint64_t seed, std::uint64_t h) {
    return mix(seed + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL + h);
}
```

`mix` is a **bijection**: different inputs always give different outputs, since each step (shift-and-xor, and multiplying by an odd number) can be undone. The constant in `combine` is lesson 8's golden-ratio number; it keeps a field of 0 from vanishing.

Here it is hashing `Pass`. Casting to `std::uint32_t` first makes a negative field wrap to a large positive number in the same way on every machine:

```cpp fragment
struct PassHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const Pass& p) const {
        std::uint64_t seed = combine(0, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(p.station));
        seed = combine(seed, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(p.orbit));
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(seed);
    }
};

std::unordered_map<Pass, double, PassHash> signal;   // the hash is the third template argument
```

The last line of `operator()` keeps only the low bits when [[the size type is 32 bits wide|size-t-width]], as it is in ORBIT's browser build. The mixed bits all look random, so the low half is as good as the whole.

### Custom equality

The fourth template argument says when two keys count as the same. Say a radio link between stations 3 and 8 is the same link as between 8 and 3. Write the equality that says so:

```cpp fragment
struct Link {
    int a;
    int b;
};

struct SameLink {
    bool operator()(const Link& x, const Link& y) const {
        return (x.a == y.a && x.b == y.b) || (x.a == y.b && x.b == y.a);
    }
};
```

Now rule 1 has teeth: {3, 8} and {8, 3} are equal, so they **must** hash the same. A hash that combines `a` then `b` breaks the map. Hash the smaller end first and then the larger, and both orders give the same number:

```cpp fragment
struct LinkHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const Link& k) const {
        std::uint64_t seed = combine(0, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(std::min(k.a, k.b)));
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(combine(seed, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(std::max(k.a, k.b))));
    }
};

std::unordered_map<Link, int, LinkHash, SameLink> traffic;
```

### The rest of the interface

- `find(k)` returns an iterator or `end()`; `contains(k)` (C++20) returns `true` or `false`; `count(k)` returns 0 or 1.
- `m[k]` returns a reference to the value, **inserting** a default-made value first when `k` is missing. So it needs a `T` that can be made with no arguments.
- `m.try_emplace(k, args...)` builds the value from `args` only if `k` is missing, and returns a pair: an iterator, and `true` if it inserted.
- `m.insert_or_assign(k, v)` inserts or overwrites.
- `m.erase(k)` returns how many it erased, 0 or 1. `m.erase(it)` returns an iterator to the next element, so this loop removes entries safely while walking:

```cpp fragment
for (auto it = fuel.begin(); it != fuel.end(); ) {
    if (it->second == 0) it = fuel.erase(it);   // erase hands back the next position
    else ++it;
}
```

C++20 also offers `std::erase_if(fuel, predicate)`, which does the same in one call.

In ORBIT, C++ runs without exceptions, so `m.at(k)` on a missing key stops the whole program. Use `find` when a key may be missing.

### What it costs

| operation | average | worst case |
|---|---|---|
| `find`, `contains`, `count`, `m[k]` | O(1) | O(n) |
| `insert`, `try_emplace`, `erase(k)` | O(1) amortised | O(n) |
| `rehash`, `reserve` | Θ(n + buckets) | Θ(n + buckets) |
| looping over all elements | Θ(n + buckets) | Θ(n + buckets) |
| memory | one node per element, plus the bucket array | |

The averages assume the hash spreads your keys well. The worst case is every key in one bucket, which a careless hash can cause by accident and an attacker who knows your hash can cause on purpose: lesson 8's hash flooding.

### Where it is used

- **Symbol tables** in compilers and interpreters, and caches keyed by request, file or query.
- **Deduplicating** telemetry packets by (spacecraft, sequence number), a two-field key exactly like `Pass`.
- **Graph algorithms** on sparse grids, where the vertices are (x, y) cells and only the visited ones are stored.
- **Indexes that hand out pointers**: because of the stability promise, a registry can store objects in an `unordered_map` and give out raw pointers to them that survive growth.

**Watch out:** five classic mistakes.

- **Inserting while iterating.** An insert that rehashes invalidates the loop's iterator, and the loop then reads freed memory. Either `reserve` first, or collect the new keys in a vector and insert them after the loop.
- **Relying on the order.** A test that prints an `unordered_map` can pass on your laptop and fail in ORBIT's browser build, because the two libraries order buckets differently. Copy the pairs into a vector and sort them before printing.
- **A hash that disagrees with equality**, like hashing a string exactly while comparing it ignoring case. Lookups then miss keys that are present.
- **Testing membership with `m[k]`.** It inserts `k`, so `size()` grows and the map fills with zeros. Use `contains` or `find`.
- **Changing a key.** Keys are `const` inside the map, because a new key would belong in a different bucket. To re-key an element, erase and insert again, or move its node with `extract`.

::: context cache-miss-map Why a pointer hop is slow
Memory is fast only when the processor finds what it needs in its small caches, which fetch 64 bytes at a time. Nodes allocated one by one end up scattered around the heap, so following a link usually lands on memory that is not in the cache. That is a cache miss, and it costs on the order of 100 nanoseconds: long enough to do hundreds of additions. A table that keeps its elements side by side, like your open-addressing map, avoids most of them. Lesson 18 measures the difference.
:::

::: context flat-maps Hash maps that give up stability
Google's Abseil library has `absl::flat_hash_map`, and Boost has `boost::unordered_flat_map`. Both store elements directly in one array with open addressing, like your lesson 9 table, and scan small groups of slots at once with vector instructions. They are often much faster than `std::unordered_map` and use less memory. The price is exactly the promise this lesson is about: a rehash moves elements, so pointers and references to them dangle. Code that needs stable addresses either keeps `std::unordered_map` or stores pointers to separately allocated objects.
:::

::: context splitmix-note Where the mixer comes from
Sebastiano Vigna published splitmix64 in 2014 as a fast random number generator. Each output is a counter pushed through the three lines of `mix`. Those lines were tuned by computer search so that flipping any single input bit flips each output bit with probability close to one half, a property called avalanche. The same finisher appears in Java's `SplittableRandom` and in many hash tables. It is not cryptographic: someone who wants collisions can still find them, so it is a good hash for data you trust.
:::

::: context size-t-width How wide is std::size_t?
`std::size_t` is the unsigned type the language uses for sizes and hashes, and its width follows the machine's addresses. On a 64-bit laptop it is 8 bytes; in ORBIT's browser build, which compiles C++ to 32-bit WebAssembly, it is 4 bytes. A hash computed in `std::uint64_t` and cast to `std::size_t` keeps all 64 bits on one and the low 32 on the other. So never print hash values or bucket numbers as expected answers: they legitimately differ between the two.
:::

--- task
A rover starts at cell (0, 0) of an endless grid and follows a path of moves: `'N'` adds 1 to `y`, `'S'` subtracts 1 from `y`, `'E'` adds 1 to `x` and `'W'` subtracts 1 from `x`. The starter defines `struct Cell` with a defaulted `==`. Write, with no `main`:

- `struct CellHash` with `std::size_t operator()(const Cell& c) const`. It must obey both rules: equal cells give equal hashes, and different cells rarely collide. A check hashes every cell with `x` and `y` from −100 to 100 (40,401 cells) and needs at least 40,000 different values, so `x ^ y` and `x * 31 + y` fail. Use the lesson's mixer.
- `std::unordered_map<Cell, int, CellHash> visit_counts(const std::string& path)`: how many times the rover is on each cell. The start counts as one visit to (0, 0), and each move is one visit to the cell it lands on. Call `reserve(path.size() + 1)` before filling the map: a check makes sure the returned map has room for that many cells.
- `int first_revisit(const std::string& path)`: the number of the first move (counting moves from 1) that lands on a cell the rover has already been on, or `-1` if it never does.

For example, on the path `"NESW"` the rover visits (0,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,0) and (0,0) again, so `(0,0)` has 2 visits, every other cell 1, and `first_revisit("NESW")` is 4.

--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <unordered_set>

struct Cell {
    int x;
    int y;
    bool operator==(const Cell&) const = default;
};

std::uint64_t mix(std::uint64_t z) {
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
    return z ^ (z >> 31);
}

std::uint64_t combine(std::uint64_t seed, std::uint64_t h) {
    return mix(seed + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL + h);
}

struct CellHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const Cell& c) const {
        std::uint64_t seed = combine(0, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(c.x));
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(combine(seed, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(c.y)));
    }
};

Cell step(Cell c, char move) {
    if (move == 'N') ++c.y;
    else if (move == 'S') --c.y;
    else if (move == 'E') ++c.x;
    else if (move == 'W') --c.x;
    return c;
}

std::unordered_map<Cell, int, CellHash> visit_counts(const std::string& path) {
    std::unordered_map<Cell, int, CellHash> counts;
    counts.reserve(path.size() + 1);
    Cell here{0, 0};
    counts[here] = 1;
    for (char move : path) {
        here = step(here, move);
        ++counts[here];
    }
    return counts;
}

int first_revisit(const std::string& path) {
    std::unordered_set<Cell, CellHash> seen;
    seen.reserve(path.size() + 1);
    Cell here{0, 0};
    seen.insert(here);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < path.size(); ++i) {
        here = step(here, path[i]);
        if (!seen.insert(here).second) return static_cast<int>(i) + 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
--- hint
For `CellHash`, copy the lesson's `mix` and `combine` above it. Combine a seed of 0 with `x` (cast to `std::uint32_t`), then combine the result with `y`, and cast the final value to `std::size_t`.
--- hint
Write a small helper that takes a `Cell` and a move and returns the next cell. In `visit_counts`, reserve first, set the start's count to 1, then for each move step and add one to the new cell's count with `++counts[here]`.
--- hint
For `first_revisit`, keep an `std::unordered_set<Cell, CellHash>` of cells seen so far, starting with (0, 0). `insert` returns a pair whose `.second` is `false` when the cell was already there: that move's number (index + 1) is the answer.

+++ practice | Call signs in any case
--- task
Radio operators write call signs in any mix of upper and lower case: `"ORB1"`, `"orb1"` and `"Orb1"` are the same call sign. Write, with no `main`:

- `struct NoCaseHash` with `std::size_t operator()(const std::string& s) const`: hash the lowercase version of `s` with `std::hash<std::string>`.
- `struct NoCaseEqual` with `bool operator()(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) const`: `true` when the two strings have the same length and the same letters ignoring case.
- `int distinct_callsigns(const std::vector<std::string>& log)`: how many different call signs the log holds, ignoring case.
- `int mentions(const std::vector<std::string>& log, const std::string& sign)`: how many entries of the log are `sign`, ignoring case.

Use an `std::unordered_map<std::string, int, NoCaseHash, NoCaseEqual>` for the counting. For example, in `{"ORB1", "orb1", "Vega", "VEGA", "vega", "Io"}` there are 3 call signs, and `mentions` of `"VeGa"` is 3. An empty log gives 0 for both.
--- starter

    std::size_t operator()(const std::string& s) const {
        return std::hash<std::string>{}(s);
    }
};

    bool operator()(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) const {
        return a == b;
    }
};

    return 0;
}

    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <cctype>
#include <cstddef>
#include <functional>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

std::string lowered(const std::string& s) {
    std::string out = s;
    for (char& c : out) c = static_cast<char>(std::tolower(static_cast<unsigned char>(c)));
    return out;
}

struct NoCaseHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const std::string& s) const {
        return std::hash<std::string>{}(lowered(s));
    }
};

struct NoCaseEqual {
    bool operator()(const std::string& a, const std::string& b) const {
        if (a.size() != b.size()) return false;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i) {
            if (std::tolower(static_cast<unsigned char>(a[i])) != std::tolower(static_cast<unsigned char>(b[i]))) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
};

using NoCaseCounts = std::unordered_map<std::string, int, NoCaseHash, NoCaseEqual>;

NoCaseCounts count_all(const std::vector<std::string>& log) {
    NoCaseCounts counts;
    counts.reserve(log.size());
    for (const auto& s : log) ++counts[s];
    return counts;
}

int distinct_callsigns(const std::vector<std::string>& log) {
    return static_cast<int>(count_all(log).size());
}

int mentions(const std::vector<std::string>& log, const std::string& sign) {
    NoCaseCounts counts = count_all(log);
    auto it = counts.find(sign);
    return it == counts.end() ? 0 : it->second;
}
--- hint
Write a helper that returns a lowercase copy of a string, using `std::tolower` on each character (cast it to `unsigned char` first). The hash is `std::hash<std::string>{}` of that copy. Then the hash agrees with the equality: strings equal ignoring case have the same lowercase copy.
--- hint
Count with `++counts[s]` into the map with both custom types. Its `size()` is the number of different call signs. For `mentions`, use `find`, not `[ ]`, so that looking up an absent sign returns 0 without adding it.
--- check test | Equal ignoring case: same hash, and equal
NoCaseHash{}("OrB1") == NoCaseHash{}("orb1") && NoCaseEqual{}("OrB1", "oRb1") && !NoCaseEqual{}("orb1", "orb12") && !NoCaseEqual{}("orb1", "orb2")
--- check case | The example from the task
distinct_callsigns({"ORB1", "orb1", "Vega", "VEGA", "vega", "Io"}) * 10 + mentions({"ORB1", "orb1", "Vega", "VEGA", "vega", "Io"}, "VeGa")
=> 33
--- check case | An empty log
distinct_callsigns({}) + mentions({}, "x")
=> 0
--- check case | A sign that is not in the log

=> 0
--- check case | Digits and punctuation are compared exactly
distinct_callsigns({"k-9", "K-9", "k_9", "K9", "k9"})
=> 3
--- check test | Many spellings of one sign

+++ practice | Buckets, observed
--- task
The standard promises that an insert does not rehash while the new size is at most `max_load_factor() × bucket_count()`. See it for yourself. Write, with no `main`:

- `int rehashes(int n, float max_load, bool reserve_first)`: make an empty `std::unordered_map<int, int>`, set its `max_load_factor` to `max_load`, and, if `reserve_first` is `true`, call `reserve(n)` **after** setting the load factor. Then insert the keys 0, 1, …, n − 1 (any values). Return how many of those inserts changed `bucket_count()`.
- `float load_after(int n, float max_load)`: the same map without reserving; return its `load_factor()` after the n inserts.

The exact counts without reserving depend on your library, so the checks only test what the standard promises: with `reserve_first`, the answer is 0; without it, a map that grows from empty to 1,000 keys rehashes at least once; and the final load factor never exceeds `max_load`. For `n` of 0, `rehashes` returns 0.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <unordered_map>

int rehashes(int n, float max_load, bool reserve_first) {
    return -1;
}

float load_after(int n, float max_load) {
    return 99.0f;
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <unordered_map>

int rehashes(int n, float max_load, bool reserve_first) {
    std::unordered_map<int, int> m;
    m.max_load_factor(max_load);
    if (reserve_first) m.reserve(n);
    int changes = 0;
    std::size_t buckets = m.bucket_count();
    for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k) {
        m[k] = k;
        if (m.bucket_count() != buckets) {
            ++changes;
            buckets = m.bucket_count();
        }
    }
    return changes;
}

float load_after(int n, float max_load) {
    std::unordered_map<int, int> m;
    m.max_load_factor(max_load);
    for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k) m[k] = k;
    return m.load_factor();
}
--- hint
Remember `bucket_count()` before the loop. After each insert, compare the new count with the remembered one; when it differs, add one and remember the new count.
--- hint
Set the load factor with `m.max_load_factor(max_load)` first, and only then `m.reserve(n)`: reserve works out the bucket count from the current maximum load factor.
--- check case | Reserved: no rehash for 10, 1,000 or 100,000 keys
rehashes(10, 1.0f, true) + rehashes(1000, 1.0f, true) + rehashes(100000, 1.0f, true)
=> 0
--- check case | Reserved with a low load factor: still no rehash
rehashes(50000, 0.25f, true) + rehashes(777, 0.5f, true)
=> 0
--- check test | Not reserved: growing to 1,000 keys rehashes
rehashes(1000, 1.0f, false) >= 1 && rehashes(1000, 0.5f, false) >= 1
--- check case | No keys, no rehash
rehashes(0, 1.0f, false) + rehashes(0, 1.0f, true)
=> 0
--- check test | The load factor stays at or under the maximum
load_after(1000, 1.0f) <= 1.0f && load_after(4097, 0.5f) <= 0.5f && load_after(30000, 0.75f) <= 0.75f && load_after(1000, 1.0f) > 0.0f

+++ practice | Forget the stale sensors
--- task
A ground station keeps `std::unordered_map<std::string, int> last_seen`: for each sensor, the time of its last packet. Write, with no `main`:

`int drop_stale(std::unordered_map<std::string, int>& last_seen, int now, int max_age)`

It removes every sensor whose age `now - last_seen[sensor]` is **greater than** `max_age`, keeps the rest untouched, and returns how many it removed. Walk the map once with an iterator and erase as you go, using the iterator that `erase` returns. (A sensor whose age is exactly `max_age` stays.)

For example, with `{{"imu", 90}, {"gps", 40}, {"sun", 100}}`, `now` 100 and `max_age` 30, only `"gps"` (age 60) goes, and the function returns 1.
--- starter
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>

int drop_stale(std::unordered_map<std::string, int>& last_seen, int now, int max_age) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>

int drop_stale(std::unordered_map<std::string, int>& last_seen, int now, int max_age) {
    int removed = 0;
    for (auto it = last_seen.begin(); it != last_seen.end(); ) {
        if (now - it->second > max_age) {
            it = last_seen.erase(it);
            ++removed;
        } else {
            ++it;
        }
    }
    return removed;
}
--- hint
Write the `for` loop with no increment in its header. In the body, either erase (and take the iterator `erase` returns) or move on with `++it`, never both.
--- hint
`it->first` is the sensor and `it->second` its time. The test for removing is `now - it->second > max_age`.
--- check test | The example from the task

+++ practice | Stations on one line of sight
--- task
From a spacecraft, every ground station lies in some direction `(dx, dy)`, whole numbers with absolute values up to 1,000,000,000. Two stations are on the same **line** through the spacecraft when their directions are multiples of each other, positive or negative: (2, 4), (−1, −2) and (3, 6) are all on one line.

Write `int most_on_one_line(const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& dirs)`, with no `main`: the largest number of directions that lie on one line. A direction of (0, 0) is the spacecraft itself: skip it. Return 0 when there is nothing else.

Turn each direction into one key per line: divide both numbers by their greatest common divisor (`std::gcd` from `<numeric>`, which works on negative numbers), then flip both signs if `dx` is negative, or if `dx` is 0 and `dy` is negative. Count the keys in an `unordered_map` with a hash for the pair that you write yourself. Duplicate directions count separately.

For example, `{{2, 4}, {-1, -2}, {3, 6}, {0, 5}, {0, -1}, {1, 0}}` gives 3.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <numeric>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int most_on_one_line(const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& dirs) {
    return static_cast<int>(dirs.size());
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <numeric>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::uint64_t mix(std::uint64_t z) {
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
    return z ^ (z >> 31);
}

struct PairHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const std::pair<int, int>& p) const {
        std::uint64_t packed = (static_cast<std::uint64_t>(static_cast<std::uint32_t>(p.first)) << 32) | static_cast<std::uint32_t>(p.second);
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(mix(packed));
    }
};

std::pair<int, int> line_key(int dx, int dy) {
    int g = std::gcd(dx, dy);
    dx /= g;
    dy /= g;
    if (dx < 0 || (dx == 0 && dy < 0)) {
        dx = -dx;
        dy = -dy;
    }
    return {dx, dy};
}

int most_on_one_line(const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& dirs) {
    std::unordered_map<std::pair<int, int>, int, PairHash> counts;
    counts.reserve(dirs.size());
    int best = 0;
    for (const auto& [dx, dy] : dirs) {
        if (dx == 0 && dy == 0) continue;
        int c = ++counts[line_key(dx, dy)];
        if (c > best) best = c;
    }
    return best;
}
--- hint
Write `line_key(dx, dy)`: divide by `std::gcd(dx, dy)` (never 0 once you have skipped (0, 0)), then fix the sign so that each line has exactly one key. (0, 5) and (0, −1) must both become (0, 1).
--- hint
`std::pair<int, int>` has no `std::hash`. Write a hash struct: pack the two numbers into one `std::uint64_t` (the first, cast to `std::uint32_t`, shifted left 32 bits, OR the second, cast the same way) and return `mix` of it.
--- check case | The example from the task
most_on_one_line({{2, 4}, {-1, -2}, {3, 6}, {0, 5}, {0, -1}, {1, 0}})
=> 3
--- check case | Only the spacecraft, or nothing at all
most_on_one_line({{0, 0}, {0, 0}}) + most_on_one_line({})
=> 0
--- check case | Vertical and horizontal lines, both directions
most_on_one_line({{0, 7}, {0, -3}, {0, 1}, {-4, 0}, {9, 0}})
=> 3
--- check case | Duplicates count separately
most_on_one_line({{5, 5}, {5, 5}, {-1, -1}, {2, 3}})
=> 3
--- check case | Huge values and the other diagonal
most_on_one_line({{1000000000, -1000000000}, {-999999999, 999999999}, {7, -7}, {1000000000, 999999999}, {-1000000000, -999999999}})
=> 3
--- check test | Fifty thousand directions on 100 lines
[] { std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> d; for (int i = 1; i <= 50000; ++i) { int k = i % 101; int m = (i % 7) - 3; if (m == 0) m = 5; d.push_back({m * (k + 1), m * (k * k + 3)}); } return most_on_one_line(d) == 991; }()
?? Every line must turn into exactly one key: check the sign rule when both numbers are negative.

+++ practice | Debug: the lookup that adds
--- task
`Catalog` maps component names to part numbers. `add(name, part)` stores a part number, `part_of(name)` should return the part number, or `-1` when the name is unknown, and `size()` should be the number of names **added**.

It passes its first tests, but after a few lookups of unknown names, `size()` is too big, and `part_of` returns 0 instead of `-1` for names that were never added. Find the bug and fix it, keeping the class's interface.
--- starter
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>

class Catalog {
public:
    void add(const std::string& name, int part) { parts_[name] = part; }

    int part_of(const std::string& name) {
        if (parts_[name] == 0) return -1;
        return parts_[name];
    }

    int size() const { return static_cast<int>(parts_.size()); }

private:
    std::unordered_map<std::string, int> parts_;
};
--- solution
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>

class Catalog {
public:
    void add(const std::string& name, int part) { parts_[name] = part; }

    int part_of(const std::string& name) {
        auto it = parts_.find(name);
        if (it == parts_.end()) return -1;
        return it->second;
    }

    int size() const { return static_cast<int>(parts_.size()); }

private:
    std::unordered_map<std::string, int> parts_;
};
--- hint
What does `parts_[name]` do when `name` is not a key yet? Count the elements before and after one call.
--- hint
Look the name up with `find`, which never inserts, and compare the result with `end()`. That also fixes a second problem: a real part number of 0 is not the same as "unknown".
--- check case | A known part
[] { Catalog c; c.add("valve", 17); return c.part_of("valve"); }()
=> 17
--- check case | An unknown name gives -1
[] { Catalog c; c.add("valve", 17); return c.part_of("pump"); }()
=> -1
--- check case | Lookups do not add names
[] { Catalog c; c.add("valve", 17); c.part_of("pump"); c.part_of("tank"); c.part_of("pump"); return c.size(); }()
=> 1
--- check case | A real part number of 0 is found
[] { Catalog c; c.add("seal", 0); return c.part_of("seal"); }()
=> 0
--- check case | Adding again overwrites
[] { Catalog c; c.add("valve", 17); c.add("valve", 23); return c.part_of("valve") * 10 + c.size(); }()
=> 231

+++ practice | A simulator that repeats itself
--- task
A simple orbit simulator keeps its state in four whole numbers, `struct State { int x; int y; int vx; int vy; }` (given in the starter, with a defaulted `==`). The world is m cells wide and m cells tall, and wraps around at the edges. One step turns a state into the next:

1. `x` becomes `x + vx` mod m, and `y` becomes `y + vy` mod m. Here "mod m" means the remainder from 0 to m − 1, even when `x + vx` is negative. (C++'s `%` gives a negative remainder for a negative number, so use `((a % m) + m) % m`.)
2. Then, using the **new** x and y: `vx` becomes `(x * y + vx * vx) % 7 - 3`, and `vy` becomes `(x + 2 * y + vy * vy) % 7 - 3`.

There are finitely many states, so the run s₀ (the start), s₁, s₂, … must eventually repeat, and from then on it goes round a cycle forever. Write `std::pair<int, int> find_cycle(State start, int m)`, with no `main`. It returns `{mu, lambda}`: `mu` is the index of the first state that comes back later (the first state on the cycle), and `lambda` is the length of the cycle.

Remember each state's index in an `std::unordered_map<State, int, StateHash>`, with a `StateHash` you write that mixes all four numbers. The first time a step produces a state already in the map, at index j, with the stored index i, the answer is `{i, j - i}`. Runs in the checks visit up to 160,000 states, so searching a list of past states is too slow.

For example, with m = 1 every position is 0, and from (0, 0, 1, −2) the states are (0, 0, 1, −2), (0, 0, −2, 1), (0, 0, 1, −2), …: the answer is {0, 2}.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

struct State {
    int x;
    int y;
    int vx;
    int vy;
    bool operator==(const State&) const = default;
};

std::pair<int, int> find_cycle(State start, int m) {
    return {0, 0};
}
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>

struct State {
    int x;
    int y;
    int vx;
    int vy;
    bool operator==(const State&) const = default;
};

std::uint64_t mix(std::uint64_t z) {
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
    return z ^ (z >> 31);
}

std::uint64_t combine(std::uint64_t seed, std::uint64_t h) {
    return mix(seed + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL + h);
}

struct StateHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const State& s) const {
        std::uint64_t h = combine(0, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(s.x));
        h = combine(h, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(s.y));
        h = combine(h, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(s.vx));
        h = combine(h, static_cast<std::uint32_t>(s.vy));
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(h);
    }
};

State next_state(State s, int m) {
    s.x = ((s.x + s.vx) % m + m) % m;
    s.y = ((s.y + s.vy) % m + m) % m;
    s.vx = (s.x * s.y + s.vx * s.vx) % 7 - 3;
    s.vy = (s.x + 2 * s.y + s.vy * s.vy) % 7 - 3;
    return s;
}

std::pair<int, int> find_cycle(State start, int m) {
    std::unordered_map<State, int, StateHash> first_seen;
    State s = start;
    int index = 0;
    while (true) {
        auto [it, inserted] = first_seen.try_emplace(s, index);
        if (!inserted) return {it->second, index - it->second};
        s = next_state(s, m);
        ++index;
    }
}
--- hint
Write `next_state(State s, int m)` first, straight from the two rules. The velocity rule needs no extra care: `x * y + vx * vx` is never negative, so `%` behaves.
--- hint
The hash combines the four numbers one after another with the lesson's `combine`, casting each to `std::uint32_t` first. Then loop: `try_emplace(s, index)` stores the index only if `s` is new; if it was already there, the iterator it returns holds the old index.
--- check case | The example from the task
find_cycle(State{0, 0, 1, -2}, 1)
=> std::pair<int, int>{0, 2}
--- check case | A small world with a tail before the cycle
find_cycle(State{0, 0, 1, -2}, 7)
=> std::pair<int, int>{35, 54}
--- check case | Starting with negative velocities
find_cycle(State{5, 3, -3, 3}, 10)
=> std::pair<int, int>{18, 60}
--- check case | A 50 by 50 world
find_cycle(State{25, 16, -3, 3}, 50)
=> std::pair<int, int>{591, 495}
--- check case | A 300 by 300 world: about 90,000 states
find_cycle(State{0, 0, 1, -2}, 300)
=> std::pair<int, int>{87933, 2330}
--- check case | A 10,000 by 10,000 world: about 150,000 states
find_cycle(State{5000, 3333, -3, 3}, 10000)
=> std::pair<int, int>{77708, 74540}

+++ practice | A sensor registry with pointers that last
--- task
A flight computer registers sensors by name while it boots, and hands out raw pointers to them so that drivers can update their readings directly. More sensors keep arriving after pointers have been handed out, so **every pointer must stay valid however many sensors are added later**.

The starter defines `struct Sensor` (a name, a reading count and a running total). Write `class Registry`, with no `main`:

- `Sensor* add(const std::string& name)`: returns a pointer to the sensor with that name, creating it (with `readings` 0 and `total` 0.0) if it is new. Adding an existing name returns the same pointer as before and changes nothing.
- `Sensor* find(const std::string& name)`: the pointer, or `nullptr` if there is no such sensor.
- `int size() const`: how many sensors there are.

Choose the container so that the promise holds. A `std::vector<Sensor>` would break it: growing the vector moves every sensor.
--- starter
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>

struct Sensor {
    std::string name;
    int readings = 0;
    double total = 0.0;
};

class Registry {
public:
    Sensor* add(const std::string& name) { return nullptr; }
    Sensor* find(const std::string& name) { return nullptr; }
    int size() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>

struct Sensor {
    std::string name;
    int readings = 0;
    double total = 0.0;
};

class Registry {
public:
    Sensor* add(const std::string& name) {
        auto [it, inserted] = sensors_.try_emplace(name);
        if (inserted) it->second.name = name;
        return &it->second;
    }

    Sensor* find(const std::string& name) {
        auto it = sensors_.find(name);
        return it == sensors_.end() ? nullptr : &it->second;
    }

    int size() const { return static_cast<int>(sensors_.size()); }

private:
    std::unordered_map<std::string, Sensor> sensors_;
};
--- hint
An `std::unordered_map<std::string, Sensor>` keeps each element in its own node, and rehashing only relinks nodes. So `&it->second` stays valid until that sensor is erased.
--- hint
In `add`, `try_emplace(name)` inserts a default `Sensor` only when the name is new, and returns a pair: an iterator and whether it inserted. Set the new sensor's `name` when it did, then return `&it->second`.
--- check test | add then find give the same sensor
[] { Registry r; Sensor* a = r.add("gyro-x"); return a != nullptr && a->name == "gyro-x" && a->readings == 0 && r.find("gyro-x") == a && r.size() == 1; }()
--- check test | Adding twice returns the same pointer and keeps the data
[] { Registry r; Sensor* a = r.add("sun"); if (!a) return false; a->readings = 4; Sensor* b = r.add("sun"); return b == a && b->readings == 4 && r.size() == 1; }()
--- check test | An unknown name is nullptr
[] { Registry r; r.add("a"); return r.find("b") == nullptr && r.size() == 1; }()
--- check test | Early pointers survive 50,000 more sensors
[] { Registry r; Sensor* first = r.add("imu"); Sensor* second = r.add("gps"); if (!first || !second) return false; first->readings = 3; first->total = 1.5; for (int i = 0; i < 50000; ++i) { Sensor* s = r.add("probe-" + std::to_string(i)); if (!s) return false; s->readings = i; } first->readings += 1; second->total = 9.0; return r.size() == 50002 && r.find("imu") == first && first->name == "imu" && r.find("imu")->readings == 4 && r.find("gps")->total == 9.0 && r.find("probe-49999")->readings == 49999; }()
?? A vector moves its elements when it grows. Store the sensors in a container whose elements never move.
--- check test | Pointers to many sensors all stay valid
