+++ question | Which pointers survive
--- ask
`double* p = &m["imu"];` points into an `std::unordered_map<std::string, double>`. Which of these, done next, can leave `p` dangling?
--- choice
Inserting 100,000 new keys, which rehashes the table several times.
--- choice
Calling `m.reserve(1000000)`.
--- choice correct
Calling `m.erase("imu")`.
--- choice
Erasing every key except `"imu"`.
--- why
Each element lives in its own node, allocated when it is inserted and freed only when it is erased. Rehashing, whether caused by inserts or by `reserve`, relinks nodes without moving them, so pointers and references stay valid (iterators do not). Erasing other keys frees other nodes. Only erasing `"imu"` itself, or `clear()`, frees the node `p` points into.

+++ question | The hash that ignores case, and the equality that does not
--- ask
A map uses `std::hash<std::string>` on the lowercased key as its hash, and ordinary `==` as its equality. Keys `"Vega"` and `"vega"` are both inserted. What happens?
--- choice
The map is broken: rule 1 fails, so lookups can miss keys that are there.
--- choice correct
Nothing breaks: the two keys are different under `==`, so they are two entries that happen to share a hash, which rule 1 allows.
--- choice
The second insert overwrites the first, because the hashes are equal.
--- choice
It does not compile, because the hash and the equality disagree.
--- why
Rule 1 says equal keys must have equal hashes; it says nothing against unequal keys sharing a hash. Here equality is stricter than the hash, so every pair of equal keys does hash the same. The two spellings are simply a collision: correct, a little slower. The dangerous direction is the opposite one, a loose equality (ignoring case) with a strict hash (exact bytes).

+++ question | What reserve promises
--- ask
After `m.max_load_factor(0.5f); m.reserve(1000);` on an empty `std::unordered_map`, what is guaranteed?
--- choice
`m.bucket_count()` is exactly 1,000.
--- choice
`m.bucket_count()` is exactly 2,000.
--- choice correct
The next 1,000 inserts of new keys cause no rehash, so iterators taken in between stay valid.
--- choice
No insert will ever rehash the map again.
--- why
`reserve(n)` is `rehash(ceil(n / max_load_factor()))`, which asks for at least 2,000 buckets here; the library may choose more, often the next prime. The standard then promises that inserts do not invalidate iterators while the size stays at most `max_load_factor() × bucket_count()`, which covers at least 1,000 elements. Past that, the map grows as usual.

=== dsacpp-14 | priority_queue and the container adapters
--- teach
Last lesson took `std::unordered_map` apart. In lesson 10 you built `Heap<T, Compare>` on a vector and learned why `std::less` puts the largest item on top; in lesson 7 you built a fixed-size queue in a ring buffer. This lesson meets the library's stack, queue and priority queue. None of the three is a container of its own: each is a thin wrapper around one, and choosing what is inside is part of using them well. It ends with the trick that makes a priority queue handle changes it was never designed for: lazy deletion.

### Adapters: a narrow door onto a container

Think of a ticket counter in front of a storeroom. The storeroom holds everything, but the counter lets you do only three things: hand a box in, see the box at the window, take that box away. You cannot wander along the shelves.

A **container adapter** is that counter. It holds a real container inside (a vector, a deque or a list) and offers only a few operations on it. The three adapters are class templates whose second parameter is the container they wrap:

```cpp fragment
template <class T, class Container = std::deque<T>> class stack;
template <class T, class Container = std::deque<T>> class queue;
template <class T, class Container = std::vector<T>,
          class Compare = std::less<typename Container::value_type>> class priority_queue;
```

Why wrap at all, when a vector could do the job? Because a narrow interface is a promise. Code that takes a `std::stack` cannot reach into the middle, so whoever reads it knows it is last in, first out.

### std::stack and what it needs

A `std::stack` has `push`, `pop`, `top`, `empty` and `size`. `push(x)` calls the container's `push_back(x)`, `top()` returns its `back()`, and `pop()` calls its `pop_back()`. So any container with those three works, and you pick it with the second template argument:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <stack>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::stack<int, std::vector<int>> altitudes;   // a stack stored in a vector
    altitudes.push(120);
    altitudes.push(340);
    altitudes.push(95);
    std::cout << altitudes.top() << "\n";   // 95, the last one in
    altitudes.pop();
    std::cout << altitudes.top() << " " << altitudes.size() << "\n";   // 340 2
}
```

Notice that `pop()` returns nothing. You read the top with `top()` first, then remove it with `pop()`. The reason is [[old but still good|pop-void]].

### std::queue and what it needs

A `std::queue` has `push` (at the back), `front`, `back`, `pop` (from the front), `empty` and `size`. It uses the container's `push_back`, `front`, `back` and `pop_front`. A vector has no `pop_front`, because removing its first element would shift all the others, so a queue on a vector is refused. The error appears only where `pop` is used, because, as lesson 3 showed, the compiler builds each member of a class template only when something calls it:

```cpp error
#include <queue>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::queue<int, std::vector<int>> q;
    q.push(1);   // fine: vector has push_back
    q.pop();     // error: no member named 'pop_front' in 'std::vector<int>'
}
```

A `std::list` works, and so does the default, `std::deque`.

### Why the default is a deque

A **`std::deque`** ("deck", short for double-ended queue) is a sequence you can grow and shrink at both ends in O(1) time (amortised: now and then its small pointer array must grow), and index in O(1) time. It is not one array. It keeps [[fixed-size blocks|deque-blocks]] of elements plus a small array of pointers to those blocks. Pushing at either end fills the end block, or adds a new block when that one is full. Finding element i takes a division to pick the block and a remainder to pick the slot.

Two things make it the right default for `stack` and `queue`:

- **No big copies.** When a vector grows it moves every element into a new array. A deque adds one block and leaves the old elements where they are.
- **Stable references at the ends.** Pushing or popping at either end never moves the other elements, so a reference to an element stays valid until that element is removed. (Iterators are invalidated by a push, as with `std::unordered_map`'s rehash, because the pointer array may be replaced.)

Unlike your ring buffer of lesson 7, a deque never runs out of room. A vector is still a fine choice for a stack, and often a little faster, because all its elements sit in one array.

### std::priority_queue over a container

A **`std::priority_queue`** is your lesson 10 heap: `push` appends and sifts up, `top()` reads index 0, and `pop()` moves the last element to the root and sifts down. The comparator means what it meant in lesson 10: `comp(a, b)` is true when **a comes out after b**. So `std::less<T>` gives the largest first and `std::greater<T>` the smallest first:

```cpp
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::priority_queue<int> loudest;                                          // largest on top
    std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>> quietest;   // smallest on top
    for (int db : {62, 88, 71, 90, 55}) {
        loudest.push(db);
        quietest.push(db);
    }
    std::cout << loudest.top() << " " << quietest.top() << "\n";   // 90 55
}
```

To give a comparator you must also name the container, because template arguments can only be left out from the right. The container needs random-access iterators plus `front`, `push_back` and `pop_back`: a vector or a deque, not a list. A vector is the default because a heap jumps between index i and 2i + 1, and one contiguous array is kind to the cache.

For a struct, the comparator is a function object, exactly as for your `Heap`. Here an event simulator wants the **earliest** event first, so a later event counts as lower priority:

```cpp fragment
struct Event {
    double time;
    std::string what;
};

struct LaterFirst {   // true when a comes out after b: a happens later
    bool operator()(const Event& a, const Event& b) const { return a.time > b.time; }
};

std::priority_queue<Event, std::vector<Event>, LaterFirst> timeline;
```

It keeps every promise of your heap: `push` and `pop` in O(log n), `top` in O(1), equal priorities in no particular order (add a sequence number when order matters, as in lesson 10), and a range constructor that builds the heap in O(n) with `std::make_heap`:

```cpp fragment
std::vector<int> readings = {7, 3, 9, 1, 8};
std::priority_queue<int> pq(readings.begin(), readings.end());   // O(n), top() is 9
```

### What it will not do

A `std::priority_queue` offers no loop over its elements, no search, no way to remove an element that is not on top, and no way to change an element's priority in place (the **decrease-key** of textbook Dijkstra). Its `top()` returns a `const` reference, so you cannot edit the top either. Real problems want those things all the time: an alert is cancelled, a task's deadline moves, a route gets cheaper.

There are three ways out:

1. **Lazy deletion:** leave old entries in the heap and throw them away when they surface. The next step shows it.
2. **A balanced tree as the queue:** `std::set` keeps elements sorted, so `*s.begin()` is the smallest and `*s.rbegin()` the largest, and it can `erase` any element in O(log n). Changing a priority is erase plus insert. Every operation costs more than a heap's (a node allocation, pointer chasing), but nothing is ever stale.
3. **The heap algorithms on your own vector:** `std::make_heap`, `std::push_heap` (after a `push_back`), `std::pop_heap` (before a `pop_back`) and `std::sort_heap` take the same comparator with the same meaning, and leave the array in your hands to read or scan.

### Lazy deletion

Keep, next to the heap, the **true current state** of every item: a map from each item to its current priority, or a flag saying it was cancelled. Then:

- **To change** an item's priority, record the new priority and push a new entry. Leave the old entry in the heap.
- **To cancel** an item, record that it is cancelled. Leave its entries in the heap.
- **Before reading the top**, throw away entries that disagree with the current state: they are **stale**. Only a top that agrees is real.

Here is the cleaning step for a heap of (price, depot) pairs, where `price` is a map holding every open depot's current price:

```cpp fragment
while (!cheapest.empty()) {
    auto [p, depot] = cheapest.top();
    auto it = price.find(depot);
    if (it != price.end() && it->second == p) break;   // agrees with the current state: real
    cheapest.pop();                                      // closed, or re-priced since: stale
}
```

**Why it is correct.** Two facts hold after every operation. First, every live item has an entry in the heap carrying its current priority, because every change pushed one. Second, an entry either agrees with the current state or is stale. The cleaning step removes only stale entries, and only from the top, so the heap order is never disturbed. When it stops, the top agrees with the current state, and it is the best of all entries still in the heap. Every live item's current entry is among those, so the top is the best live item. (Two identical entries for one item, from changing a priority away and back, both agree with the state, which is harmless: whichever surfaces first stands for the item.)

**What it costs.** Every entry is pushed once and popped at most once. So over a whole run, each operation costs O(log H) amortised, where H is the number of entries ever pushed: at most one per change. The price is memory: stale entries sit in the heap until they surface. If changes vastly outnumber the live items, rebuild the heap from the live items now and then.

Lesson 16 uses exactly this for Dijkstra's algorithm.

### What it costs

| operation | stack (deque) | queue (deque) | priority_queue (vector) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `push` | O(1) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| `pop` | O(1) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| `top` / `front` | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) |
| build from n elements | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) with the range constructor |
| change or remove one element | not offered | not offered | lazy: O(log H) amortised |

For the vector underneath, `push_back` is O(1) amortised, so the heap's O(log n) is too.

### Where it is used

- **Schedulers:** operating systems and flight software pick the highest-priority ready task, and lazy deletion handles tasks that finish or change priority early.
- **[[Discrete-event simulation|event-sim]]**, where the next event to process is the earliest one, and cancelled events are skipped when they surface.
- **Graph algorithms:** Dijkstra and Prim (lesson 16 and DSA II), and A* route planning.
- **Stacks and queues** everywhere: undo histories, parsers, breadth-first search, message buffers between two parts of a program.

**Watch out:** `std::priority_queue<int>` gives the **largest** first, and a comparator `a.time < b.time` gives the **latest** event first; lesson 10's rule still holds, "true means a comes out after b". Calling `top()` or `pop()` on an empty queue is undefined behaviour, so test `empty()` first. And a loop like `for (std::size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); ++i) q.pop();` stops halfway, because `size()` shrinks while `i` grows; drain a queue with `while (!q.empty())`.

::: context pop-void Why pop returns nothing
In the 1990s, when the library was designed, copying an element could throw an exception. If `pop()` removed the element and then returned a copy, and that copy failed, the element would be lost forever. Splitting the job in two, `top()` to read and `pop()` to remove, means nothing is removed until you have safely taken what you need. It also saves a copy when you only want to look. Your lesson 10 heap returned `std::optional<T>` instead, which is a fine modern choice when moves cannot fail.
:::

::: context deque-blocks How a deque is laid out
A deque keeps its elements in blocks of the same size, with a small array of pointers to the blocks in order. libstdc++ uses 512-byte blocks and libc++ 4,096-byte blocks. Pushing at the front fills the first block backwards, pushing at the back fills the last block forwards, and a full end block gets a new neighbour. Element i is found with one division and one remainder, so indexing is O(1), a little slower than a vector's.


::: context event-sim Simulating by jumping from event to event
A discrete-event simulation does not tick a clock every millisecond. It keeps a priority queue of future events, each with a time: "packet arrives at 3.20 s", "antenna finishes slewing at 3.75 s". It pops the earliest, updates the world, and pushes whatever new events that causes. Nothing happens between events, so the simulation skips straight over quiet stretches. Network simulators, factory models and mission-planning tools that check whether a satellite's passes over its ground stations leave enough downlink time all work this way, and they cancel events lazily: a "timeout" event whose reply already arrived is simply ignored when it surfaces.
:::
--- task
A ground station's alert board shows the most severe open alert. Alerts are raised, their severity can be changed, and they can be cancelled. Write `class AlertBoard`, with no `main`, on a `std::priority_queue` with **lazy deletion**:

- `void raise(int id, int severity)`: opens alert `id` with that severity, or, if `id` is already open, changes its severity.
- `bool cancel(int id)`: closes alert `id` and returns `true`, or returns `false` if it is not open.
- `int peek()`: the id of the most severe open alert, the **smaller id** among equal severities, or −1 if none is open. It may throw away stale entries, so it is not `const`.
- `int pop()`: closes that alert and returns its id, or returns −1 if none is open.
- `int size() const`: how many alerts are open.

Keep an `std::unordered_map<int, int>` from each open id to its current severity, and a priority queue of (severity, id) entries arranged so the top is the most severe, smallest id first. Never search or rebuild the heap: a check makes 300,000 calls, so every call must be O(log n) amortised.

For example: raise(7, 2), raise(3, 5), raise(9, 5), then peek() is 3; raise(3, 1), then peek() is 9; cancel(9), then pop() is 7, then pop() is 3, then pop() is −1.
--- starter
#include <map>
#include <queue>
#include <set>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class AlertBoard {
public:
    void raise(int id, int severity) {}
    bool cancel(int id) { return false; }
    int peek() { return -1; }
    int pop() { return -1; }
    int size() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <map>
#include <queue>
#include <set>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class AlertBoard {
public:
    void raise(int id, int severity) {
        open_[id] = severity;
        heap_.push({severity, -id});
    }

    bool cancel(int id) { return open_.erase(id) == 1; }

    int peek() {
        while (!heap_.empty()) {
            auto [severity, neg_id] = heap_.top();
            auto it = open_.find(-neg_id);
            if (it != open_.end() && it->second == severity) return -neg_id;
            heap_.pop();
        }
        return -1;
    }

    int pop() {
        int id = peek();
        if (id != -1) {
            open_.erase(id);
            heap_.pop();
        }
        return id;
    }

    int size() const { return static_cast<int>(open_.size()); }

private:
    std::unordered_map<int, int> open_;              // id -> current severity
    std::priority_queue<std::pair<int, int>> heap_;  // (severity, -id): largest first
};
--- hint
Store heap entries as `(severity, -id)` in a plain `std::priority_queue<std::pair<int, int>>`. Pairs compare the first member, then the second, and `std::less` puts the largest on top: the highest severity, and among equals the largest `-id`, which is the smallest id.
--- hint
`raise` records `open_[id] = severity` and pushes a new entry; `cancel` only erases from the map (`erase` returns how many it removed). Neither touches old entries.
--- hint
`peek` loops: look at the top entry; if the map has that id with that severity, it is real, so return the id; otherwise pop it and look again. `pop` calls `peek`, and if it found an alert, erases it from the map and pops its entry.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { AlertBoard b; b.raise(7, 2); b.raise(3, 5); b.raise(9, 5); int a = b.peek(); b.raise(3, 1); int c = b.peek(); bool x = b.cancel(9); int d = b.pop(); int e = b.pop(); int f = b.pop(); return a == 3 && c == 9 && x && d == 7 && e == 3 && f == -1 && b.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | An empty board
[] { AlertBoard b; return b.peek() == -1 && b.pop() == -1 && b.size() == 0 && !b.cancel(4); }()
--- check test | Cancelling twice, and cancelling what was never raised
[] { AlertBoard b; b.raise(1, 10); bool first = b.cancel(1); bool second = b.cancel(1); bool never = b.cancel(2); return first && !second && !never && b.peek() == -1 && b.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Raising an open alert changes it rather than adding one
[] { AlertBoard b; b.raise(5, 1); b.raise(5, 9); b.raise(6, 4); int s = b.size(); int p1 = b.pop(); int p2 = b.pop(); return s == 2 && p1 == 5 && p2 == 6 && b.pop() == -1; }()
--- check test | A severity changed away and back
[] { AlertBoard b; b.raise(4, 3); b.raise(4, 8); b.raise(4, 3); b.raise(2, 5); int p1 = b.pop(); int p2 = b.pop(); return p1 == 2 && p2 == 4 && b.pop() == -1 && b.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Popped alerts can be raised again
[] { AlertBoard b; b.raise(1, 5); b.pop(); b.raise(1, 2); b.raise(2, 3); return b.pop() == 2 && b.pop() == 1 && b.size() == 0; }()
--- check test | Equal severities: smaller id first, negative severities too

--- check test | 300,000 mixed calls agree with a sorted set
[] { AlertBoard b; std::map<int, int> sev; std::set<std::pair<int, int>> ref; unsigned s = 77; for (int i = 0; i < 300000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int op = static_cast<int>((s >> 16) % 4); s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int id = static_cast<int>((s >> 12) % 5000); s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int sv = static_cast<int>((s >> 12) % 100); if (op <= 1) { auto it = sev.find(id); if (it != sev.end()) ref.erase({-it->second, id}); sev[id] = sv; ref.insert({-sv, id}); b.raise(id, sv); } else if (op == 2) { auto it = sev.find(id); bool had = it != sev.end(); if (had) { ref.erase({-it->second, id}); sev.erase(it); } if (b.cancel(id) != had) return false; } else { int want = ref.empty() ? -1 : ref.begin()->second; if (!ref.empty()) { sev.erase(want); ref.erase(ref.begin()); } if (b.pop() != want) return false; } if (b.size() != static_cast<int>(sev.size())) return false; } return true; }()
?? Searching the heap or rebuilding it on every cancel is too slow here. Leave stale entries in and skip them when they reach the top.

+++ practice | The k loudest readings
--- task
Write `std::vector<int> k_largest(const std::vector<int>& readings, int k)`, with no `main`. It returns the k largest readings, largest first, keeping repeats (if 9 appears twice among the k largest, it appears twice). If `k` is 0 or less, return an empty vector; if `k` is at least the number of readings, return all of them, largest first.

Use a **min-heap of size at most k**: `std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>>`. Push each reading, and pop whenever the heap holds more than k, so the heap always holds the k largest seen so far and its top is the smallest of them. That is O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, which matters when there are millions of readings and k is 10.

For example, `k_largest({4, 9, 1, 9, 7, 3}, 3)` is `{9, 9, 7}`.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> k_largest(const std::vector<int>& readings, int k) {
    return readings;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> k_largest(const std::vector<int>& readings, int k) {
    if (k <= 0) return {};
    std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>> kept;
    for (int r : readings) {
        kept.push(r);
        if (static_cast<int>(kept.size()) > k) kept.pop();
    }
    std::vector<int> out;
    while (!kept.empty()) {
        out.push_back(kept.top());
        kept.pop();
    }
    std::reverse(out.begin(), out.end());
    return out;
}
--- hint
With `std::greater<int>` the top is the smallest element in the heap. After each push, if the heap has more than k elements, pop: that throws away the smallest, which cannot be among the k largest.
--- hint
Popping the heap at the end gives the kept readings smallest first. Collect them into a vector and reverse it (`std::reverse` from `<algorithm>`).
--- check case | The example from the task
k_largest({4, 9, 1, 9, 7, 3}, 3)
=> std::vector<int>{9, 9, 7}
--- check case | k of zero or less
k_largest({5, 6}, 0).size() + k_largest({5, 6}, -2).size()
=> 0
--- check case | k larger than the input
k_largest({2, -8, 5}, 10)
=> std::vector<int>{5, 2, -8}
--- check case | Empty input
k_largest({}, 4)
=> std::vector<int>{}
--- check case | All equal
k_largest({3, 3, 3, 3}, 2)
=> std::vector<int>{3, 3}
--- check test | A million readings, the top 5
[] { std::vector<int> v; unsigned s = 7; for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) { s = s * 1664525u + 1013904223u; v.push_back(static_cast<int>(s >> 8)); } std::vector<int> want = v; std::sort(want.begin(), want.end(), std::greater<int>()); want.resize(5); return k_largest(v, 5) == want; }()

+++ practice | Round robin on a queue of lists
--- task
A flight computer shares its processor between jobs in **round robin**: it takes the job at the front of a queue, runs it for up to `quantum` milliseconds, and if the job still has work left, puts it at the back of the queue. A job that finishes leaves the queue.

Write `std::vector<std::string> finish_order(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>& jobs, int quantum)`, with no `main`. Each job is a name and the milliseconds of work it needs (at least 1). The jobs start in the queue in the order given. Return the names in the order the jobs finish.

Use `std::queue` with a `std::list` as its container: `std::queue<std::pair<std::string, int>, std::list<std::pair<std::string, int>>>`. For example, with jobs `{{"nav", 5}, {"cam", 2}, {"log", 3}}` and a quantum of 2, the order is `{"cam", "log", "nav"}`: nav runs 2 (3 left), cam runs 2 and finishes, log runs 2 (1 left), nav runs 2 (1 left), log runs 1 and finishes, nav runs 1 and finishes. An empty list of jobs gives an empty result.
--- starter
#include <list>
#include <queue>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<std::string> finish_order(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>& jobs, int quantum) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <list>
#include <queue>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<std::string> finish_order(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>& jobs, int quantum) {
    std::queue<std::pair<std::string, int>, std::list<std::pair<std::string, int>>> ready;
    for (const auto& job : jobs) ready.push(job);
    std::vector<std::string> done;
    while (!ready.empty()) {
        auto job = ready.front();
        ready.pop();
        job.second -= quantum;
        if (job.second > 0) ready.push(job);
        else done.push_back(job.first);
    }
    return done;
}
--- hint
Push every job into the queue first. Then loop while it is not empty: copy the front, pop it, and take `quantum` off its remaining work.
--- hint
If the job has work left (more than 0), push it back; otherwise its name goes on the result.
--- check case | The example from the task
finish_order({{"nav", 5}, {"cam", 2}, {"log", 3}}, 2)
=> std::vector<std::string>{"cam", "log", "nav"}
--- check case | No jobs
finish_order({}, 3)
=> std::vector<std::string>{}
--- check case | A big quantum: everything finishes in order
finish_order({{"a", 4}, {"b", 1}, {"c", 9}}, 100)
=> std::vector<std::string>{"a", "b", "c"}
--- check case | A quantum of 1
finish_order({{"a", 3}, {"b", 1}, {"c", 2}}, 1)
=> std::vector<std::string>{"b", "c", "a"}
--- check case | Work that is an exact multiple of the quantum
finish_order({{"x", 4}, {"y", 2}}, 2)
=> std::vector<std::string>{"y", "x"}
--- check source | Uses a queue stored in a list
std::queue<[^;]*std::list

+++ practice | The loudest reading in every window
--- task
A microphone logs one loudness reading per millisecond. For a display, write `std::vector<int> window_max(const std::vector<int>& readings, int k)`, with no `main`: for every window of `k` consecutive readings, from the window starting at index 0 to the one ending at the last reading, the largest reading in it. There are `n - k + 1` windows for n readings. If `k` is less than 1 or more than n, return an empty vector.

Use a `std::priority_queue` of (reading, index) pairs and lazy deletion: push each reading as the window reaches it, and before reading the top, pop entries whose index has fallen out of the window (index at most i − k when the window ends at i). Entries that left the window but are not on top can stay; they are harmless until they surface. That is O(n log n); a check uses 500,000 readings with windows of 5,000, where rescanning every window is far too slow.

For example, `window_max({4, 2, 12, 3, 8, 1}, 3)` is `{12, 12, 12, 8}`.
--- starter
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> window_max(const std::vector<int>& readings, int k) {
    std::vector<int> out;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i + k <= readings.size(); ++i) out.push_back(readings[i]);
    return out;
}
--- solution
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> window_max(const std::vector<int>& readings, int k) {
    int n = static_cast<int>(readings.size());
    std::vector<int> out;
    if (k < 1 || k > n) return out;
    std::priority_queue<std::pair<int, int>> heap;   // (reading, index)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        heap.push({readings[i], i});
        if (i < k - 1) continue;
        while (heap.top().second <= i - k) heap.pop();
        out.push_back(heap.top().first);
    }
    return out;
}
--- hint
Walk `i` over every index and push `(readings[i], i)`. The first full window ends at `i = k - 1`; from there on, each `i` produces one answer.
--- hint
Before answering for the window ending at `i`, pop while the top's index is `<= i - k`. The heap is never empty at that point, because the entry just pushed is inside the window.
--- check case | The example from the task
window_max({4, 2, 12, 3, 8, 1}, 3)
=> std::vector<int>{12, 12, 12, 8}
--- check case | A window of 1 is the readings themselves
window_max({5, -1, 7}, 1)
=> std::vector<int>{5, -1, 7}
--- check case | A window as long as the log
window_max({3, 9, 2}, 3)
=> std::vector<int>{9}
--- check case | Windows too long, or not positive
window_max({1, 2}, 3).size() + window_max({1, 2}, 0).size() + window_max({}, 1).size()
=> 0
--- check case | Repeated maxima and a falling log
window_max({6, 6, 5, 4, 3, 6}, 2)
=> std::vector<int>{6, 6, 5, 4, 6}
--- check case | 500,000 readings, windows of 5,000
[] { std::vector<int> v; unsigned s = 21; for (int i = 0; i < 500000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; v.push_back(static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % 1000000)); } auto m = window_max(v, 5000); long long sum = 0; for (int x : m) sum += x; return static_cast<long long>(m.size()) * 1000000000000LL + sum; }()
=> 495001494887669526LL

+++ practice | The cheapest pairs
--- task
A mission buys one launch and one payload adapter. `a` holds the launch prices and `b` the adapter prices, each sorted from cheapest to dearest; prices are between −2,000,000,000 and 2,000,000,000 (a negative price is a rebate). Write `std::vector<long long> cheapest_pairs(const std::vector<int>& a, const std::vector<int>& b, int k)`, with no `main`: the k smallest totals `a[i] + b[j]` over all pairs (i, j), in increasing order.

Edge cases: if `k` is 0 or less, or either list is empty, return an empty vector; if `k` is more than the number of pairs, return all the totals. Totals can pass 2,100,000,000, so add in `long long`.

Do not build all the pairs: there can be ten billion. Use a min-heap of (total, i, j). Start with (a[0] + b[j], 0, j) for every j below k (and below the size of b). Each time you pop (total, i, j), record the total and push (a[i + 1] + b[j], i + 1, j) if `i + 1` is inside `a`. Every pair enters the heap only after the pair just above it in its column was taken, so the heap always holds the next candidate of each column, and the work is O(k log k).

For example, with `a` = {1, 7, 11} and `b` = {2, 4, 6}, `cheapest_pairs(a, b, 4)` is {3, 5, 7, 9}.
--- starter
#include <functional>
#include <queue>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

std::vector<long long> cheapest_pairs(const std::vector<int>& a, const std::vector<int>& b, int k) {
    std::vector<long long> out;
    for (int i = 0; i < k && i < static_cast<int>(a.size()) && i < static_cast<int>(b.size()); ++i) out.push_back(a[i] + b[i]);
    return out;
}
--- solution
#include <functional>
#include <queue>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

std::vector<long long> cheapest_pairs(const std::vector<int>& a, const std::vector<int>& b, int k) {
    std::vector<long long> out;
    if (k <= 0 || a.empty() || b.empty()) return out;
    using Entry = std::tuple<long long, int, int>;   // total, i, j
    std::priority_queue<Entry, std::vector<Entry>, std::greater<Entry>> heap;
    for (int j = 0; j < static_cast<int>(b.size()) && j < k; ++j) heap.push({static_cast<long long>(a[0]) + b[j], 0, j});
    while (!heap.empty() && static_cast<int>(out.size()) < k) {
        auto [total, i, j] = heap.top();
        heap.pop();
        out.push_back(total);
        if (i + 1 < static_cast<int>(a.size())) heap.push({static_cast<long long>(a[i + 1]) + b[j], i + 1, j});
    }
    return out;
}
--- hint
The starter adds `a[i] + b[i]` as `int`s, which overflows, and it only ever looks at matching positions. The cheapest total is `a[0] + b[0]`, but the second cheapest could be `a[1] + b[0]` or `a[0] + b[1]`.
--- hint
Use `std::priority_queue<std::tuple<long long, int, int>, std::vector<std::tuple<long long, int, int>>, std::greater<std::tuple<long long, int, int>>>`. Convert `a[i]` to `long long` before adding. Stop when you have k totals or the heap is empty.
--- check case | The example from the task
cheapest_pairs({1, 7, 11}, {2, 4, 6}, 4)
=> std::vector<long long>{3, 5, 7, 9}
--- check case | k of 0, and an empty list
cheapest_pairs({1}, {1}, 0).size() + cheapest_pairs({}, {5, 6}, 3).size() + cheapest_pairs({5, 6}, {}, 3).size()
=> 0
--- check case | k past the number of pairs gives all of them
cheapest_pairs({1, 2}, {10, 20}, 9)
=> std::vector<long long>{11, 12, 21, 22}
--- check case | Totals past two billion, and rebates
cheapest_pairs({-2000000000, 2000000000}, {-2000000000, 2000000000}, 4)
=> std::vector<long long>{-4000000000LL, 0, 0, 4000000000LL}
--- check case | Equal prices
cheapest_pairs({1, 1, 1}, {0, 0}, 5)
=> std::vector<long long>{1, 1, 1, 1, 1}
--- check case | 100,000 prices each, the 100,000 cheapest totals
[] { std::vector<int> a, b; for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) { a.push_back(i * 3); b.push_back(i * 5 + 1); } auto r = cheapest_pairs(a, b, 100000); long long sum = 0; for (long long x : r) sum += x; return static_cast<long long>(r.size()) * 1000000000000LL + sum; }()
=> 100000000115170227LL

--- task

#include <queue>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> loudest_first(const std::vector<int>& readings) {
    std::priority_queue<int> q(readings.begin(), readings.end());
    std::vector<int> out;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        out.push_back(q.top());
        q.pop();
    }
    return out;
}
--- hint
Trace the loop on four readings. After two passes, what are `i` and `q.size()`?
--- hint
The loop compares a growing counter with a shrinking size, so they meet in the middle. Loop on the queue itself: `while (!q.empty())`.

+++ practice | Assigning downloads to antennas
--- task
A ground station has `m` antennas, numbered 0 to m − 1, all free at time 0. Download jobs arrive in order: job i arrives at `arrive[i]` (never earlier than the job before it) and needs `length[i]` minutes. Each job, in order, goes to the antenna that becomes free the **earliest**; if several are free equally early, the lowest-numbered one. The job starts at its arrival time or when that antenna frees up, whichever is later, and keeps the antenna busy for its length.

Write `std::vector<long long> start_times(int m, const std::vector<int>& arrive, const std::vector<int>& length)`, with no `main`, returning each job's start time. Keep a min-heap of (free time, antenna number) pairs as `long long` and `int`: pop the top, start the job, push the antenna back with its new free time. Times can pass 2,000,000,000, hence `long long`.

For example, with m = 2, arrivals {0, 0, 1, 10} and lengths {5, 3, 4, 1}: job 0 takes antenna 0 at 0 (free at 5), job 1 takes antenna 1 at 0 (free at 3), job 2 waits for antenna 1 and starts at 3 (free at 7), job 3 takes antenna 0 at 10. The answer is {0, 0, 3, 10}.
--- starter
#include <functional>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<long long> start_times(int m, const std::vector<int>& arrive, const std::vector<int>& length) {
    return std::vector<long long>(arrive.size(), 0);
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<long long> start_times(int m, const std::vector<int>& arrive, const std::vector<int>& length) {
    using Slot = std::pair<long long, int>;   // free time, antenna
    std::priority_queue<Slot, std::vector<Slot>, std::greater<Slot>> antennas;
    for (int a = 0; a < m; ++a) antennas.push({0, a});
    std::vector<long long> starts;
    starts.reserve(arrive.size());
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < arrive.size(); ++i) {
        auto [free_at, a] = antennas.top();
        antennas.pop();
        long long start = std::max(free_at, static_cast<long long>(arrive[i]));
        starts.push_back(start);
        antennas.push({start + length[i], a});
    }
    return starts;
}
--- hint
With `std::greater<std::pair<long long, int>>`, the top is the smallest pair: the earliest free time, and the lowest antenna number among equal times.
--- hint
For each job: pop the top (free_at, a); the start is `std::max(free_at, arrive[i])` as a `long long`; record it; push (start + length[i], a).
--- check case | The example from the task
start_times(2, {0, 0, 1, 10}, {5, 3, 4, 1})
=> std::vector<long long>{0, 0, 3, 10}
--- check case | No jobs
start_times(3, {}, {}).size()
=> 0
--- check case | One antenna: jobs queue up
start_times(1, {0, 1, 2}, {10, 10, 10})
=> std::vector<long long>{0, 10, 20}
--- check case | Ties on free time go to the lowest antenna

=> std::vector<long long>{0, 0, 0, 4, 4, 4}
--- check case | Times past two billion
start_times(1, {2000000000, 2000000000}, {2000000000, 5})
=> std::vector<long long>{2000000000, 4000000000}
--- check case | 200,000 jobs on 1,000 antennas: the sum of the start times
[] { std::vector<int> ar, len; unsigned s = 5; int t = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; t += (s >> 16) % 3; ar.push_back(t); len.push_back(1 + static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % 5000)); } auto st = start_times(1000, ar, len); long long sum = 0; for (long long x : st) sum += x; return st.size() == 200000 ? sum : -1LL; }()
=> 49755213051LL

+++ practice | Undo and redo
--- task
A command console keeps an undo history. Write `class Console`, with no `main`, using two stacks stored in vectors, `std::stack<std::string, std::vector<std::string>>`: one of commands that can be undone, and one of commands that can be redone.

- `void run(const std::string& cmd)`: the command runs. It becomes the newest command that can be undone, and the redo history is **cleared** (a new command makes the old redo history meaningless).
- `std::string undo()`: undoes the newest command that can be undone, moves it onto the redo history, and returns it; returns `""` if there is nothing to undo.
- `std::string redo()`: redoes the command that was undone most recently, moves it back onto the undo history, and returns it; returns `""` if there is nothing to redo.
- `int undo_depth() const` and `int redo_depth() const`: how many commands each history holds.

For example: run "a", run "b", undo gives "b", undo gives "a", redo gives "a", run "c" (redo history cleared), redo gives "".
--- starter
#include <stack>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class Console {
public:
    void run(const std::string& cmd) {}
    std::string undo() { return ""; }
    std::string redo() { return ""; }
    int undo_depth() const { return 0; }
    int redo_depth() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <stack>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class Console {
public:
    void run(const std::string& cmd) {
        done_.push(cmd);
        undone_ = {};
    }

    std::string undo() { return shift(done_, undone_); }
    std::string redo() { return shift(undone_, done_); }
    int undo_depth() const { return static_cast<int>(done_.size()); }
    int redo_depth() const { return static_cast<int>(undone_.size()); }

private:
    using History = std::stack<std::string, std::vector<std::string>>;

    static std::string shift(History& from, History& to) {
        if (from.empty()) return "";
        std::string cmd = from.top();
        from.pop();
        to.push(cmd);
        return cmd;
    }

    History done_;
    History undone_;
};
--- hint
Undo and redo are the same move in opposite directions: take the top of one stack, pop it, push it onto the other, return it. A small helper taking both stacks by reference does both.
--- hint
A stack has no `clear()`. Assigning an empty stack, `undone_ = {};`, empties it.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { Console c; c.run("a"); c.run("b"); std::string u1 = c.undo(); std::string u2 = c.undo(); std::string r1 = c.redo(); c.run("c"); std::string r2 = c.redo(); return u1 == "b" && u2 == "a" && r1 == "a" && r2 == "" && c.undo_depth() == 2 && c.redo_depth() == 0; }()
--- check test | Nothing to undo or redo
[] { Console c; return c.undo() == "" && c.redo() == "" && c.undo_depth() == 0 && c.redo_depth() == 0; }()
--- check test | Undo everything, then redo everything, in the right orders

--- check test | A new command clears only the redo history
[] { Console c; c.run("x"); c.run("y"); c.run("z"); c.undo(); c.undo(); c.run("w"); return c.redo_depth() == 0 && c.undo_depth() == 2 && c.undo() == "w" && c.undo() == "x"; }()

+++ question | What a queue can sit on
--- ask
Which containers can `std::queue<int, Container>` use, if your code calls `push`, `front` and `pop`?
--- choice
Any standard sequence: `std::vector`, `std::deque` or `std::list`.
--- choice correct
`std::deque` or `std::list`, but not `std::vector`.
--- choice
Only `std::deque`, the default.
--- choice
Only `std::vector`, because a queue needs one contiguous array.
--- why
`pop()` calls the container's `pop_front()`. `std::deque` and `std::list` have it; `std::vector` does not, because removing its first element would shift every other one. The error appears at the first call to `pop()`, since members of a class template are only built when used.

+++ question | Why lazy deletion never loses a live alert
--- ask
In `AlertBoard`, `peek` pops entries from the top until one agrees with the map of open alerts. Why can it never throw away the entry that carries an open alert's current severity?
--- choice
The heap keeps entries sorted, so current entries always sit above stale ones.
--- choice correct
That entry has the alert's id and its current severity, so it agrees with the map, and the loop only pops entries that disagree.
--- choice
`raise` removes the alert's old entry before pushing the new one.
--- choice
`peek` pushes every popped entry back before it returns.
--- why
The proof rests on two facts: every change pushes an entry with the new state, and the cleaning loop removes only entries that disagree with the current state. A stale entry can sit above a current one (a cancelled alert with a high severity, say), which is exactly why the loop exists; the heap is never searched or rebuilt.

+++ question | The most one peek can pop
--- ask
An `AlertBoard` holds 10 open alerts. Then `raise` is called 1,000 times, each call changing the severity of one of those 10 alerts (no alert opens or closes). Before the next `peek`, the heap holds its old entries plus 1,000 new ones. At most how many of the new entries can that one `peek` pop?
--- answer
990
--- why
Each alert's latest entry agrees with the map, so 10 of the 1,000 new entries are live and 990 are stale. In the worst case all 990 stale ones have higher severities and surface first, so one `peek` pops them all. That is why the cost is amortised: every entry is popped at most once over the whole run, so the 990 pops are paid for by the 990 raises that pushed them.

=== dsacpp-15 | The algorithms: sort, stable_sort, partial_sort, nth_element, partition
--- teach
Last lesson's priority queue gave you the largest element again and again. Often you want something in between "the largest" and "everything sorted": the ten largest, the median, the failed readings moved to the back. In DSA I you wrote merge sort, quicksort and quickselect yourself. This lesson is about the library's versions in `<algorithm>`: what each one promises, what it costs, and how to pick the cheapest one that does the job.

### Five jobs, five tools

Picture a pile of exam papers. You might need them all in mark order; or in mark order with papers of equal mark kept in the order they were handed in; or only the top ten, in order; or only the paper in the middle; or just the passes on one side and the fails on the other. Each job is less work than the one before it, and each has its own tool:

| job | algorithm | comparisons | stable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| everything in order | `std::sort` | O(n log n), worst case | no |
| in order, ties keep their order | `std::stable_sort` | O(n log n) with spare memory | yes |
| the smallest k, in order | `std::partial_sort` | O(n log k) | no |
| the element at position k | `std::nth_element` | O(n) on average | no |
| split by a yes/no test | `std::partition` | exactly n tests | no |

All of them work **in place** on a range given by two iterators, and all of them except `partition` take an optional comparator, the same kind of strict weak ordering as last lesson's priority queue. Here `comp(a, b)` has its everyday meaning: "a goes before b".

### std::sort

`std::sort(first, last, comp)` sorts the range. Since C++11 the standard requires O(n log n) comparisons **in the worst case**, which rules out plain quicksort. Libraries use **[[introsort|introsort-note]]**: quicksort, switching to heapsort if the recursion gets too deep, and insertion sort for small pieces.

It needs **random-access iterators**, because quicksort jumps around the range. A vector, an array or a deque works; a `std::list` does not, and has its own member function `lst.sort()`, a merge sort that relinks nodes.

`std::sort` is **not stable**: equal elements can come out in any order. Here is a comparator on a struct, sorting crew members by age:

```cpp fragment
struct Crew {
    std::string name;
    int age;
};

std::sort(crew.begin(), crew.end(), [](const Crew& a, const Crew& b) { return a.age < b.age; });
```

Two crew members of the same age may swap places. Whether they do depends on the library and the input.

### Several keys in one comparator

To sort by age and then by name, compare the ages first and the names only on a tie. `std::tie`, from `<tuple>`, packs references to fields into a tuple, and tuples compare field by field, left to right:

```cpp fragment
std::sort(crew.begin(), crew.end(), [](const Crew& a, const Crew& b) {
    return std::tie(a.age, a.name) < std::tie(b.age, b.name);
});
```

To make one key go the other way, swap `a` and `b` for that field only. `std::tie(b.age, a.name) < std::tie(a.age, b.name)` sorts by age from oldest to youngest, and by name A to Z within an age.

### std::stable_sort

`std::stable_sort(first, last, comp)` sorts and keeps equal elements in their original order. It is a merge sort. With a spare buffer (libraries ask for up to n elements) it makes O(n log n) comparisons; if that memory cannot be had, it falls back to merging in place, with O(n log² n).

Stability gives you multi-key sorting [[in passes|stable-picture]], the way a spreadsheet does when you click one column header and then another. **Claim:** sort by the second key, then `stable_sort` by the first key, and the result is ordered by the first key, with ties ordered by the second key.

**Why:** after the second pass the first keys are in order, because it is a correct sort. Take any two elements with the same first key. The second pass is stable, so they keep the order they had after the first pass, and the first pass put them in order of the second key. So every group of equal first keys is ordered by the second key. ∎

The same argument shows why the passes go from the **least** important key to the most important. Do them the other way round and the last pass, on the minor key, scrambles the major one.

### std::partial_sort

`std::partial_sort(first, middle, last, comp)` puts the smallest `middle - first` elements, in sorted order, into `[first, middle)`. The rest of the range ends up in no particular order.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> lap_times = {71, 64, 90, 58, 77, 62, 85};
    std::partial_sort(lap_times.begin(), lap_times.begin() + 3, lap_times.end());
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) std::cout << lap_times[i] << " ";   // 58 62 64
    std::cout << "\n";
}
```

**Why it costs O(n log k)**, with k = `middle - first`: it makes a max-heap of the first k elements (O(k)). Then for each of the other n − k elements it compares with the heap's top, the largest of the k kept so far. If the new element is smaller, it replaces the top and sifts down, O(log k). At the end the heap holds the k smallest, and `sort_heap` puts them in order, O(k log k). That is at most O(n log k) in total. For the top 10 of a million, that is about a million comparisons instead of the twenty million of a full sort.

### std::nth_element

`std::nth_element(first, nth, last, comp)` rearranges the range so that:

- the element at `nth` is the one that would be there if the range were sorted;
- no element before `nth` is greater than it, and no element after `nth` is smaller.

Nothing else is promised: the two sides are not sorted. It is quickselect from DSA I, as introselect, and it costs O(n) **on average**.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> depths = {40, 12, 33, 7, 25, 50, 18};
    auto mid = depths.begin() + depths.size() / 2;
    std::nth_element(depths.begin(), mid, depths.end());
    std::cout << *mid << "\n";   // 25, the median of 7 values
}
```

Its promise is also a **partition**, and that is useful: after `nth_element` at index i, everything you might want at an index greater than i is already to its right. A second `nth_element` can then work on `[nth + 1, last)` only.

For a list with an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values. After `nth_element` at index n/2, the other middle value, at index n/2 − 1, is the **largest** element of the left part, so `std::max_element(first, nth)` finds it in O(n) without a second selection.

### std::partition

`std::partition(first, last, pred)` moves every element for which `pred` returns `true` in front of every element for which it returns `false`. It returns an iterator to the first element of the second group. It applies `pred` exactly once per element, and it is not stable.

```cpp fragment
auto split = std::partition(ids.begin(), ids.end(), [](int id) { return id % 2 == 0; });
// [ids.begin(), split) are the even ids, [split, ids.end()) the odd ones
```

`std::stable_partition` keeps the original order inside both groups, for O(n) with a spare buffer or O(n log n) without one.

On a range that is **already** partitioned, `std::partition_point(first, last, pred)` finds the boundary by binary search, in O(log n): the same idea as `lower_bound`, which is the special case of a sorted range and the test "less than the value".

### Removing duplicates: sort, unique, erase

`std::unique(first, last)` removes **neighbouring** duplicates: it slides the elements it keeps to the front and returns an iterator to the new end. It cannot change the vector's size, since it only sees iterators, so the leftovers after the new end are still there, holding unspecified values. The idiom is three steps:

```cpp fragment
std::sort(tags.begin(), tags.end());                          // duplicates become neighbours
auto new_end = std::unique(tags.begin(), tags.end());         // keep one of each, at the front
tags.erase(new_end, tags.end());                              // cut off the leftovers
```

### Counting what they cost

Lesson 10 measured your heap with a comparator that counts through a pointer. A lambda does the same job more briefly: capture the counter **by reference** with `[&count]`. By reference matters for the same reason the pointer did: the algorithm copies the comparator, and every copy must add to the same counter.

```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) v.push_back((i * 7919) % 100003);
    long long count = 0;
    auto counting_less = [&count](int a, int b) { ++count; return a < b; };
    std::vector<int> w = v;
    std::sort(w.begin(), w.end(), counting_less);
    std::cout << "sort: " << count << "\n";
    count = 0;
    w = v;
    std::nth_element(w.begin(), w.begin() + 50000, w.end(), counting_less);
    std::cout << "nth_element: " << count << "\n";
}
```

The exact counts depend on your library, but the shape does not. With libstdc++ the sort makes about 2.0 million comparisons (n log₂ n is 1.66 million), and `nth_element` about 0.28 million, under 3n.

### Choosing

Ask for the least you need:

- All of it in order? `sort`. Ties must keep their order? `stable_sort`.
- The top k, in order? `partial_sort`. The top k, any order, or one element by rank (a median, a percentile)? `nth_element`.
- Two groups by a yes/no test? `partition`, or `stable_partition` to keep the order.

### Where it is used

- **Databases** run `ORDER BY … LIMIT 10` as a partial sort, and spreadsheet column sorts are stable.
- **Monitoring** reports median and [[99th-percentile latency|tail-latency]] with selection, not full sorts.
- **Quicksort itself** is `partition` applied recursively, and `nth_element` is the same with one side dropped.
- **Telemetry cleanup**: `stable_partition` moves failed packets out of the way while keeping the good ones in time order.

**Watch out:** the comparator must be a strict weak ordering. `[](int a, int b) { return a <= b; }` compiles, and it may run fine for months, but it is undefined behaviour: with many equal elements, some library versions of `std::sort` [[walk off the end of the array|sort-crash]]. Two more classics: `nth_element` does not sort either side, so do not read the first k elements after it as if they were in order; and `v.erase(std::unique(v.begin(), v.end()))` with one argument erases a single element, not the leftovers.

::: context introsort-note Introsort: quicksort with a safety net
David Musser described introsort in 1997. It runs quicksort, but counts how deep the recursion has gone. If the depth passes about 2 log₂ n, the pivots must have been bad, so it sorts that piece with heapsort instead, which is O(n log n) whatever the input. Pieces smaller than a threshold (16 elements in libstdc++) are left for one final insertion sort pass, which is faster than quicksort on tiny ranges. The result is quicksort's speed on typical data with heapsort's worst-case guarantee.
:::

::: context stable-picture Two passes, pictured
Sorting by the minor key first and then stably by the major key, on (team, name) pairs:

::: context tail-latency Why the 99th percentile
If a web page makes 100 requests to a service, and 1 in 100 requests is slow, then most page loads include at least one slow request. So engineers watch the slowest responses, not the average: p99 is the time that 99% of requests beat. An average hides a few terrible cases among many good ones; a percentile does not. Monitoring systems compute these over millions of samples a minute, which is why selection in O(n), or approximate sketches, matter more there than full sorts.
:::

::: context sort-crash Why a bad comparator can crash sort
To save a bounds check in its innermost loop, libstdc++'s insertion sort step moves left while `comp(value, previous)` is true, trusting that an element no greater than the value sits at the front of the range. With `<=`, an element equal to the value also returns true, so if the front element equals it, the loop does not stop there and reads memory before the array. The same trust appears in the quicksort partition loop. The algorithm is correct for every strict weak ordering; it is your comparator that broke the contract.
:::
--- task
A telemetry report works on readings. The starter defines `struct Reading { std::string sensor; int time; double value; };`. Write three functions, with no `main`:

- `void order_for_report(std::vector<Reading>& v)`: sort by `sensor` name, A to Z. Readings of the same sensor must stay in the order they are in now, whatever their times (the report shows arrival order).
- `double median_value(std::vector<Reading> v)`: the median of the `value`s: the middle one for an odd count, the mean of the two middle ones for an even count, and `0.0` for no readings. Use `std::nth_element`, not a full sort.
- `std::vector<Reading> hottest(std::vector<Reading> v, int k)`: the k readings with the largest `value`, largest first; among equal values, the smaller `time` first. If `k` is 0 or less, return an empty vector; if it is more than the number of readings, return them all in that order. Use `std::partial_sort`.

For example, with readings (sensor, time, value) `{"b", 1, 2.0}`, `{"a", 5, 9.0}`, `{"b", 0, 7.0}`, `{"a", 2, 9.0}`: `order_for_report` gives a@5, a@2, b@1, b@0; `median_value` is 8.0; and `hottest(…, 2)` gives a@2 then a@5 (equal values, smaller time first).
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

struct Reading {
    std::string sensor;
    int time;
    double value;
};

void order_for_report(std::vector<Reading>& v) {}

double median_value(std::vector<Reading> v) {
    return 0.0;
}

std::vector<Reading> hottest(std::vector<Reading> v, int k) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

struct Reading {
    std::string sensor;
    int time;
    double value;
};

void order_for_report(std::vector<Reading>& v) {
    std::stable_sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const Reading& a, const Reading& b) { return a.sensor < b.sensor; });
}

double median_value(std::vector<Reading> v) {
    if (v.empty()) return 0.0;
    auto by_value = [](const Reading& a, const Reading& b) { return a.value < b.value; };
    auto mid = v.begin() + v.size() / 2;
    std::nth_element(v.begin(), mid, v.end(), by_value);
    if (v.size() % 2 == 1) return mid->value;
    double lower = std::max_element(v.begin(), mid, by_value)->value;
    return (lower + mid->value) / 2.0;
}

std::vector<Reading> hottest(std::vector<Reading> v, int k) {
    if (k <= 0) return {};
    std::size_t keep = std::min(v.size(), static_cast<std::size_t>(k));
    std::partial_sort(v.begin(), v.begin() + keep, v.end(), [](const Reading& a, const Reading& b) {
        return std::tie(b.value, a.time) < std::tie(a.value, b.time);
    });
    v.resize(keep);
    return v;
}
--- hint
Only one of the three sorts must keep equal elements in their original order. That one needs `std::stable_sort` with a comparator on `sensor` alone.
--- hint
For the median, `nth_element` at `v.begin() + v.size() / 2` places the upper middle value. For an even count, the lower middle value is the largest element before it: `std::max_element` over `[v.begin(), mid)` with the same comparator.
--- hint

+++ practice | The fastest three laps
--- task
Write `std::vector<int> smallest_k_sorted(std::vector<int> v, int k)`, with no `main`: the k smallest values of `v`, smallest first, keeping repeats. Use `std::partial_sort`, then shrink the vector to k elements. If `k` is 0 or less, return an empty vector; if `k` is larger than the size, return all the values sorted.

For example, `smallest_k_sorted({71, 64, 90, 58, 77, 62}, 3)` is `{58, 62, 64}`.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> smallest_k_sorted(std::vector<int> v, int k) {
    return v;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> smallest_k_sorted(std::vector<int> v, int k) {
    if (k <= 0) return {};
    std::size_t keep = std::min(v.size(), static_cast<std::size_t>(k));
    std::partial_sort(v.begin(), v.begin() + keep, v.end());
    v.resize(keep);
    return v;
}
--- hint
Clamp `k` to the size before using it as an offset: `v.begin() + k` past `v.end()` is undefined behaviour.
--- hint
`std::partial_sort(v.begin(), v.begin() + keep, v.end())` puts the `keep` smallest in order at the front; `v.resize(keep)` drops the rest.
--- check case | The example from the task

=> std::vector<int>{58, 62, 64}

=> 0
--- check case | k larger than the size

=> std::vector<int>{-1, 2, 3}
--- check case | Repeats are kept

=> std::vector<int>{1, 1, 5, 5}

+++ practice | Bad packets to the back, in order
--- task
The starter defines `struct Packet { int seq; int payload; int checksum; };`. A packet is **valid** when `payload % 256 == checksum`. Write `int keep_valid(std::vector<Packet>& packets)`, with no `main`. It rearranges `packets` so that all valid packets come first and all invalid ones after, with **both** groups keeping their original order, and returns the number of valid packets.

Use `std::stable_partition`. For example, packets with seq 1 (valid), 2 (invalid), 3 (valid), 4 (invalid) end up in the order 1, 3, 2, 4, and the function returns 2.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

struct Packet {
    int seq;
    int payload;
    int checksum;
};

int keep_valid(std::vector<Packet>& packets) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

struct Packet {
    int seq;
    int payload;
    int checksum;
};

int keep_valid(std::vector<Packet>& packets) {
    auto split = std::stable_partition(packets.begin(), packets.end(), [](const Packet& p) { return p.payload % 256 == p.checksum; });
    return static_cast<int>(split - packets.begin());
}
--- hint
`std::stable_partition(first, last, pred)` puts the elements for which `pred` is true first, keeping order in both groups, and returns an iterator to the first element of the second group.
--- hint
The number of valid packets is the distance from `packets.begin()` to that iterator: subtract the two iterators.

+++ practice | Ranking without moving the data
--- task
A leaderboard shows crew members by score. Write `std::vector<int> ranking(const std::vector<std::string>& names, const std::vector<int>& scores)`, with no `main`: the **indexes** 0 to n − 1, ordered by score from highest to lowest, then by name from A to Z, then by index from low to high. The two vectors have the same length. Do not copy or reorder the names.

Make the index vector with `std::iota` (from `<numeric>`: it fills a range with 0, 1, 2, …), then sort it with a lambda that captures both vectors by reference and compares what the indexes point at.

For example, names `{"lin", "ada", "sam", "ada"}` with scores `{7, 9, 7, 9}` give `{1, 3, 0, 2}`: the two adas scored 9 (index 1 before index 3), then lin and sam scored 7 (lin first).
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> ranking(const std::vector<std::string>& names, const std::vector<int>& scores) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> ranking(const std::vector<std::string>& names, const std::vector<int>& scores) {
    std::vector<int> order(names.size());
    std::iota(order.begin(), order.end(), 0);
    std::sort(order.begin(), order.end(), [&names, &scores](int a, int b) {
        return std::tie(scores[b], names[a], a) < std::tie(scores[a], names[b], b);
    });
    return order;
}
--- hint
`std::vector<int> order(names.size());` then `std::iota(order.begin(), order.end(), 0);` gives 0, 1, 2, …. The lambda compares two indexes `a` and `b` by looking up `scores[a]`, `names[a]` and so on.
--- hint
Three keys, one of them reversed: with `std::tie`, put `b` on the left for the score only: `std::tie(scores[b], names[a], a) < std::tie(scores[a], names[b], b)`. Because the last key is the index, no two elements tie, so `std::sort` is enough.
--- check case | The example from the task

=> std::vector<int>{1, 3, 0, 2}
--- check case | Nobody on the board

=> 0
--- check case | Negative scores and one name repeated
ranking({"kim", "kim", "al"}, {-5, -5, -9})
=> std::vector<int>{0, 1, 2}
--- check case | Names break ties, then indexes
ranking({"zed", "amy", "zed", "amy", "bo"}, {3, 3, 3, 3, 4})
=> std::vector<int>{4, 1, 3, 0, 2}
--- check test | 30,000 entries with many ties
[] { std::vector<std::string> n; std::vector<int> s; for (int i = 0; i < 30000; ++i) { n.push_back(std::string(1, static_cast<char>('a' + i % 5))); s.push_back((i * 37) % 11); } auto r = ranking(n, s); if (r.size() != 30000) return false; for (std::size_t k = 1; k < r.size(); ++k) { int a = r[k - 1], b = r[k]; if (s[a] < s[b]) return false; if (s[a] == s[b] && n[a] > n[b]) return false; if (s[a] == s[b] && n[a] == n[b] && a > b) return false; } return true; }()

+++ practice | The median, with every edge case
--- task
Write `double median(std::vector<int> v)`, with no `main`, using `std::nth_element`: the middle value for an odd count, the mean of the two middle values for an even count, and `0.0` for an empty vector.

The values can be as large as 2,100,000,000 in size, so two middle values do not always add up to something that fits in an `int`: add them as `double` or `long long`. For example, `median({4, 1, 3, 2})` is 2.5, and `median({2000000000, 2100000000})` is 2,050,000,000.0.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

double median(std::vector<int> v) {
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    return (v[v.size() / 2] + v[(v.size() - 1) / 2]) / 2;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

double median(std::vector<int> v) {
    if (v.empty()) return 0.0;
    auto mid = v.begin() + v.size() / 2;
    std::nth_element(v.begin(), mid, v.end());
    if (v.size() % 2 == 1) return *mid;
    int lower = *std::max_element(v.begin(), mid);
    return (static_cast<double>(lower) + static_cast<double>(*mid)) / 2.0;
}
--- hint
The starter has three bugs: it reads `v[0]` of an empty vector, it adds two `int`s that can overflow, and it divides by the integer 2, which throws away the half. Handle the empty case first.
--- hint
After `nth_element` at `v.begin() + v.size() / 2`, the lower middle value (for an even count) is the largest element before that position. Convert both to `double` before adding, and divide by `2.0`.
--- check case | Even count

=> 2.5
--- check case | Odd count

=> 7.0
--- check case | Empty

=> 0.0
--- check case | One value
median({-17})
=> -17.0
--- check case | Two huge values do not overflow
median({2000000000, 2100000000})
=> 2050000000.0
--- check case | Two huge negative values

=> -2050000000.0
--- check case | Duplicates in the middle

std::vector<int> distinct_ids(std::vector<int> ids) {
