+++ practice | Percentiles of a latency log
--- task
A monitoring page shows percentiles of the last million response times. The **p-th percentile** of n values (n at least 1, p from 0 to 100) is the value at index `p * (n - 1) / 100` (integer division, computed in `long long`) of the values in sorted order. So p = 0 is the smallest, p = 100 the largest, and p = 50 a median.

Write `std::vector<int> percentiles(std::vector<int> v, const std::vector<int>& ps)`, with no `main`. `ps` is sorted from smallest to largest and may repeat. Return one value per entry of `ps`, in the same order; for an empty `v`, return an empty vector.

Do not sort all of `v`. Call `std::nth_element` once per percentile, and use its promise: after placing index i, every index after i is in `[v.begin() + i + 1, v.end())`, so the next call only needs to search from `v.begin() + i` onwards. That makes the later calls work on smaller and smaller ranges.

For example, with `v` = {50, 10, 40, 20, 30} and `ps` = {0, 50, 90, 100}: the indexes are 0, 2, 3 and 4, so the result is {10, 30, 40, 50}.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> percentiles(std::vector<int> v, const std::vector<int>& ps) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> percentiles(std::vector<int> v, const std::vector<int>& ps) {
    std::vector<int> out;
    if (v.empty()) return out;
    long long n = static_cast<long long>(v.size());
    auto from = v.begin();
    for (int p : ps) {
        auto at = v.begin() + static_cast<long long>(p) * (n - 1) / 100;
        std::nth_element(from, at, v.end());
        out.push_back(*at);
        from = at;
    }
    return out;
}
--- hint
Keep an iterator `from` that starts at `v.begin()`. For each p, compute the target position `at`, call `std::nth_element(from, at, v.end())`, and record `*at`.
--- hint
After the call, set `from = at`. The next target is at or after `at`, and everything that belongs at or after `at` is already in `[at, v.end())`, so the next search can start there. Using `at` rather than `at + 1` handles repeated percentiles.
--- check case | The example from the task
percentiles({50, 10, 40, 20, 30}, {0, 50, 90, 100})
=> std::vector<int>{10, 30, 40, 50}
--- check case | Empty log
percentiles({}, {50}).size()
=> 0
--- check case | One value answers every percentile
percentiles({7}, {0, 50, 100})
=> std::vector<int>{7, 7, 7}
--- check case | Repeated percentiles and repeated values
percentiles({3, 3, 1, 9, 3, 1}, {20, 20, 60, 100})
=> std::vector<int>{1, 1, 3, 9}
--- check test | A million latencies: p50, p90, p99, p99 again, p100
[] { std::vector<int> v; unsigned s = 17; for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; v.push_back(static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % 1000000)); } std::vector<int> w = v; std::sort(w.begin(), w.end()); std::vector<int> ps = {50, 90, 99, 99, 100}; std::vector<int> want; for (int p : ps) want.push_back(w[static_cast<long long>(p) * 999999 / 100]); return percentiles(v, ps) == want; }()
--- check source | Uses nth_element
nth_element

+++ practice | Counting what the algorithms cost
--- task
Measure the algorithms by counting comparisons. Write three functions, with no `main`, each of which runs one algorithm on its own copy of `v` with a comparator that counts its calls, and returns the count as a `long long`:

- `long long sort_comparisons(std::vector<int> v)`: `std::sort` on the whole vector.
- `long long partial_sort_comparisons(std::vector<int> v, int k)`: `std::partial_sort` of the smallest `k` (assume 0 ≤ k ≤ size).
- `long long nth_element_comparisons(std::vector<int> v, int k)`: `std::nth_element` at index `k` (assume 0 ≤ k < size).

The comparator must still compare correctly, `a < b`. Capture the counter by reference, because the algorithms copy the comparator.

The checks run all three on the same 100,000 mixed values. The exact counts depend on the library, so the checks test the shape: a full sort needs more than 1,400,000 comparisons (no comparison sort can average fewer than about n log₂ n − 1.44 n, which is 1.52 million here), the top 10 by `partial_sort` fewer than 300,000, and the median by `nth_element` fewer than 800,000.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

long long sort_comparisons(std::vector<int> v) {
    return 0;
}

long long partial_sort_comparisons(std::vector<int> v, int k) {
    return 0;
}

long long nth_element_comparisons(std::vector<int> v, int k) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

long long sort_comparisons(std::vector<int> v) {
    long long count = 0;
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [&count](int a, int b) { ++count; return a < b; });
    return count;
}

long long partial_sort_comparisons(std::vector<int> v, int k) {
    long long count = 0;
    std::partial_sort(v.begin(), v.begin() + k, v.end(), [&count](int a, int b) { ++count; return a < b; });
    return count;
}

long long nth_element_comparisons(std::vector<int> v, int k) {
    long long count = 0;
    std::nth_element(v.begin(), v.begin() + k, v.end(), [&count](int a, int b) { ++count; return a < b; });
    return count;
}
--- hint
The comparator is a lambda that adds one to a counter and then returns `a < b`. Declare `long long count = 0;` in the function and capture it with `[&count]`.
--- hint
If you capture by value (`[count]`), the lambda cannot change it; with `mutable` it changes only its own copy, and the algorithm's copies count separately. By reference, every copy adds to the same variable.
--- check test | A full sort of 100,000 values needs over 1,400,000 comparisons
[] { std::vector<int> v; for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) v.push_back(static_cast<int>((static_cast<long long>(i) * 7919) % 100003)); return sort_comparisons(v) > 1400000; }()
--- check test | The 10 smallest by partial_sort: fewer than 300,000
[] { std::vector<int> v; for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) v.push_back(static_cast<int>((static_cast<long long>(i) * 7919) % 100003)); long long c = partial_sort_comparisons(v, 10); return c > 99000 && c < 300000; }()
--- check test | The median by nth_element: fewer than 800,000
[] { std::vector<int> v; for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) v.push_back(static_cast<int>((static_cast<long long>(i) * 7919) % 100003)); long long c = nth_element_comparisons(v, 50000); return c > 99000 && c < 800000; }()
--- check test | Tiny inputs: one value needs no comparison, two need at least one
sort_comparisons({5}) == 0 && sort_comparisons({2, 1}) >= 1 && partial_sort_comparisons({3, 1, 2}, 0) >= 0

+++ question | Which pass goes first
--- ask
Crew records must end up ordered by team, and by name within each team. You will do it in two passes, each a sort on one key. Which is right?
--- choice
`std::sort` by team, then `std::stable_sort` by name.
--- choice correct
Any correct sort by name, then `std::stable_sort` by team.
--- choice
`std::stable_sort` by team, then `std::stable_sort` by name.
--- choice
Either order works, as long as both passes are stable.
--- why
The last pass decides the major order, so it must be the team pass, and it must be stable so that it keeps, inside each team, the order the earlier pass produced: by name. Sorting by name last would scramble the teams, stable or not.

+++ question | What nth_element leaves behind
--- ask
After `std::nth_element(v.begin(), v.begin() + 3, v.end())` on `v = {9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 3, 6}`, which statement is guaranteed?
--- choice
`v` is `{1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9}`.
--- choice
`v[0]` to `v[2]` are `1, 2, 3` in that order.
--- choice correct
`v[3]` is 6, the elements before it are 1, 2 and 3 in some order, and the elements after it are 7, 8 and 9 in some order.
--- choice
Only `v[3] == 6`; the other elements may be anywhere.
--- why
`nth_element` promises the element that sorting would put at position 3, and a partition around it: nothing before it is greater, nothing after it is smaller. It promises no order inside the two sides, which is exactly why it can run in O(n) on average.

+++ question | The cost of the top ten
--- ask
You need the 10 smallest of n = 1,000,000 values, in order. About how many comparisons does `std::partial_sort` make, compared with sorting everything?
--- choice
About the same as `std::sort`: n log₂ n, about 20 million.
--- choice correct
About n plus a little: each value past the first 10 is compared with the top of a 10-element heap, and only the rare smaller ones cost log₂ 10 more.
--- choice
About 10 log₂ 10, around 33, since only 10 values are sorted.
--- choice
About n², since every value is compared with every other.
--- why
`partial_sort` keeps a max-heap of the k best so far. Every one of the n − k other values needs at least the one comparison with the heap's top, so the cost is O(n log k), and on typical data close to n: about a million comparisons instead of twenty million.

=== dsacpp-16 | Graphs in C++: adjacency lists, BFS and Dijkstra
--- teach
In DSA I you stored graphs as lists of lists and searched them breadth first and depth first. Lesson 14 gave you `std::priority_queue`, and lesson 15 the algorithms. This lesson puts them together: a graph stored the C++ way, breadth-first search with a queue, and **Dijkstra's algorithm**, which finds the cheapest routes when edges have costs, using a priority queue and a trick called lazy deletion.

### Storing a graph: vector<vector<int>>

Number the vertices 0 to n − 1. Each vertex keeps a list of its neighbours, like each ground station keeping a contact list of the stations it can reach. In C++ that is a vector of vectors, one inner vector per vertex:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    int n = 4;
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n);   // 4 empty neighbour lists
    int links[][2] = {{0, 1}, {0, 2}, {2, 3}};
    for (auto& link : links) {
        adj[link[0]].push_back(link[1]);   // a link works both ways,
        adj[link[1]].push_back(link[0]);   // so store it in both lists
    }
    for (int v = 0; v < n; ++v) {
        std::cout << v << ":";
        for (int w : adj[v]) std::cout << " " << w;
        std::cout << "\n";
    }
}
```

This prints `0: 1 2`, `1: 0`, `2: 0 3` and `3: 2`. `adj(n)` with round brackets makes n empty inner vectors. For a **directed** graph, store each edge once, in the list of the vertex it leaves.

**Memory.** The outer vector holds n inner vector objects (three pointers each: 24 bytes on a 64-bit machine, 12 in ORBIT's browser build), and each non-empty inner vector owns its own block on the heap. The neighbours themselves take one `int` per directed edge. So the space is Θ(n + m) for n vertices and m edges, but with n separate heap blocks.

### Weighted edges

When edges have costs (signal delay, fuel, distance), store the cost next to the neighbour:

```cpp fragment
struct Arc {
    int to;
    int cost;
};

std::vector<std::vector<Arc>> out(n);
out[3].push_back({7, 120});   // an edge from 3 to 7 costing 120
```

### A compact layout: offsets and targets

Those n heap blocks are scattered in memory, so walking from one vertex's list to the next jumps around, which caches dislike (lesson 18 measures how much). Large graph libraries use a **[[compressed layout|csr-note]]** instead: one array `targets` holding every vertex's neighbours back to back, and one array `offset` of n + 1 numbers, where vertex v's neighbours are `targets[offset[v]]` up to, but not including, `targets[offset[v + 1]]`. Two allocations in total, and every list sits next to the one before it. You will build one in the practice.

### Breadth-first search with a queue

Breadth-first search finds the fewest edges from a source to every vertex. You proved in DSA I why it works: the queue holds vertices in order of distance, and never more than two distances at once, d and d + 1. In C++ the pieces are a `std::queue<int>` (a deque inside) and a vector of distances where −1 means "not reached yet":

```cpp fragment
std::vector<int> dist(n, -1);
std::queue<int> frontier;
dist[source] = 0;
frontier.push(source);
while (!frontier.empty()) {
    int v = frontier.front();
    frontier.pop();
    for (int w : adj[v]) {
        if (dist[w] == -1) {        // first time we see w:
            dist[w] = dist[v] + 1;  // set its distance now,
            frontier.push(w);       // and queue it exactly once
        }
    }
}
```

Setting `dist[w]` at the moment `w` is **pushed**, not when it is popped, means every vertex enters the queue at most once. Each vertex is popped once and each of its edges looked at once, so BFS costs Θ(n + m) time, and the queue never holds more than n vertices.

### Shortest paths with costs

Now every edge has a cost of zero or more, and the length of a path is the sum of its costs. The **single-source shortest path** problem asks for the smallest length from a source s to every vertex. BFS no longer works: a route with three cheap edges can beat one expensive edge.

**Dijkstra's algorithm**, [[published by Edsger Dijkstra in 1959|dijkstra-story]], grows a set S of **settled** vertices whose distances are final. Every other vertex v has a **tentative** distance `dist[v]`: the length of the best path found so far, which uses only settled vertices before its last edge.

1. Set `dist[s] = 0` and every other `dist[v] = ∞`. S is empty.
2. Pick the unsettled vertex u with the smallest `dist[u]`, and add it to S.
3. **Relax** every edge (u, v) with cost c: if `dist[u] + c < dist[v]`, set `dist[v] = dist[u] + c`.
4. Repeat from step 2 until no unsettled vertex has a finite distance.

Everyday picture: pour water in at s. It spreads along the pipes at a constant speed, and the order in which the junctions get wet is the order Dijkstra settles them.

### Why Dijkstra is correct

**Claim:** when u is picked in step 2, `dist[u]` is the true shortest distance from s to u.

**Proof,** by induction on the number of settled vertices. Suppose every vertex settled so far has its true distance, and u is picked next. Take any path P from s to u. It starts inside S (at s) and ends outside S (at u), so it has a first edge (x, y) that leaves S: x is settled, y is not.

- By the induction assumption, `dist[x]` is x's true distance, so the part of P from s to x is at least `dist[x]` long, and the part up to y is at least `dist[x] + cost(x, y)`. When x was settled, the edge (x, y) was relaxed, so `dist[y] ≤ dist[x] + cost(x, y)`. Together: the part of P up to y is at least `dist[y]`.
- u was picked as the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, so `dist[y] ≥ dist[u]`.
- The rest of P, from y to u, has no negative costs, so it adds zero or more.

Putting the three together, the length of P is at least `dist[u]`. Every path to u is at least `dist[u]` long, and `dist[u]` is the length of a real path, so it is the shortest. ∎

The third step is where **negative costs** break the algorithm. With edges s→a costing 1, s→b costing 2 and b→a costing −2, Dijkstra settles a at distance 1, but the path s→b→a costs 0.

### Lazy deletion: Dijkstra with std::priority_queue

Step 2 needs "the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance", which is a min-priority queue of (distance, vertex) pairs. But step 3 *lowers* distances, and `std::priority_queue` cannot change an element that is already inside it.

**Lazy deletion** gets around that. Whenever a distance improves, push a **new** pair with the new distance, and leave the old pair where it is. When a pair (d, v) comes to the top and `d > dist[v]`, it is **stale**: a better pair for v was pushed after it. Skip it.

```cpp fragment
using Item = std::pair<long long, int>;   // (distance, vertex): pairs compare distance first
std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item>, std::greater<Item>> pending;   // smallest on top

auto [d, v] = pending.top();
pending.pop();
if (d > dist[v]) {
    // stale: v was already settled with a smaller distance, so skip this pair
}
```

**Why lazy deletion is still Dijkstra.** A pair is pushed only when a distance strictly drops, so for every unsettled vertex w with a finite distance, exactly one pair in the queue carries its current `dist[w]`, and all its other pairs carry larger, stale values. Now suppose (d, v) reaches the top and is not stale, so d = `dist[v]`. Every unsettled w has its current pair somewhere below, so `dist[v] ≤ dist[w]`: v is a vertex step 2 could pick. It is settled, and its edges relaxed, exactly as in the plain algorithm. After that `dist[v]` never changes (it is final, by the proof), so every pair for v still in the queue is stale and is skipped when it surfaces.

**What it costs.** A pair is pushed only when an edge relaxation succeeds, and each edge is relaxed once, when its start vertex is settled. So there are at most m + 1 pushes and m + 1 pops, each O(log m). The total is O((n + m) log m), and since m ≤ n², log m ≤ 2 log n, so it is O((n + m) log n). The price, compared with a heap that supports decrease-key, is memory: the queue can hold up to m + 1 pairs instead of n.

### Distances in long long

Costs in the millions along paths of thousands of edges pass the 2.1 billion an `int` can hold. Use `long long` for distances. For "unreached", `std::numeric_limits<long long>::max()` works only if you never add a cost to it: `max() + 5` overflows, which is undefined behaviour. Dijkstra only relaxes edges out of vertices it pops, whose distances are finite, so the addition is safe there. When in doubt, use a smaller sentinel such as `max() / 4`, which leaves room.

### Recovering the route

Distances say how far, not which way. Keep a `parent` vector: when relaxing (u, v) succeeds, set `parent[v] = u`. After the search, walk back from the target through the parents to the source, then reverse the list with `std::reverse`. The parents form a **shortest-path tree**: every vertex's parent was its predecessor on a shortest path at the moment it was settled.

### Deep recursion is fragile here

A recursive depth-first search goes one call deeper for every vertex on the current path, and a path can be as long as the graph. In ORBIT's browser build the call stack is [[much smaller than on a laptop|wasm-stack]], so a recursive DFS on a 100,000-vertex chain crashes. Graph code in C++ uses explicit stacks and queues, as BFS and Dijkstra do, whenever the depth could be large.

### What it costs

| task | time | extra memory |
|---|---|---|
| build adjacency lists from m edges | Θ(n + m) | Θ(n + m) |
| BFS | Θ(n + m) | Θ(n) |
| Dijkstra, lazy deletion | O((n + m) log n) | Θ(n + m) |
| recover one route | O(n) | O(n) |

### Where it is used

- **Route planning:** map apps and rover path planners run Dijkstra or its heuristic cousin A*.
- **Networks:** internet routers running the OSPF protocol compute shortest paths with Dijkstra over the network map, and a relay network of ground stations picks the lowest-latency chain of links the same way.
- **BFS** everywhere a step counts as one: fewest hops in a network, moves in a puzzle, degrees of separation.
- **Graph libraries** like the Boost Graph Library and many analytics engines store graphs in the compressed layout.

**Watch out:** the most common Dijkstra bug in C++ is the queue's direction. `std::priority_queue<std::pair<long long, int>>` with no comparator is a **max**-heap, so it pops the farthest vertex first. The code still ends with correct distances, because a later, better pair keeps correcting them, but the running time can blow up. Always write `std::greater<Item>`. And in BFS, set a vertex's distance when you push it, not when you pop it; the debug practice shows what goes wrong otherwise.

::: context dijkstra-story Twenty minutes in a café
Dijkstra said he designed the algorithm in about twenty minutes, in 1956, sitting at a café terrace in Amsterdam with his fiancée, without pencil and paper. He wanted a problem that non-computer people could understand to show off a new computer, the ARMAC, and chose the shortest route between two Dutch cities on a map of 64 towns. Not having paper, he said, forced him to avoid all avoidable complexity. It was published three years later in a three-page paper.
:::

::: context wasm-stack Why the browser's stack is small
Every function call takes a frame on the call stack: its local variables, its arguments and where to return. A program on a Linux desktop usually gets 8 MB of stack, enough for a recursion about a hundred thousand calls deep. WebAssembly programs built with the usual tools reserve far less, often 64 KB to 1 MB, so a few thousand deep calls can already run out, and the program stops with a stack overflow. Replacing recursion with a `std::vector` used as a stack moves the storage onto the heap, which can grow to hundreds of megabytes.
:::
--- task
The starter defines `struct Edge { int from; int to; int weight; };`, a **directed** edge. Vertices are numbered 0 to n − 1. Write two functions, with no `main`:

- `std::vector<int> bfs_hops(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int source)`: for every vertex, the fewest edges on a path from `source` to it, ignoring weights, or −1 if it cannot be reached.
- `std::vector<long long> shortest_delays(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int source)`: for every vertex, the smallest total weight of a path from `source`, or −1 if it cannot be reached. Weights are between 0 and 1,000,000,000. Use Dijkstra with `std::priority_queue` and lazy deletion.

Both first build adjacency lists from `edges`. Edges may repeat, and an edge may go from a vertex to itself. The checks include graphs with 100,000 vertices and 400,000 edges, so both must be O((n + m) log n) or better.

For example, with n = 4 and edges 0→1 (weight 5), 0→2 (weight 1) and 2→1 (weight 2), `bfs_hops` from 0 is {0, 1, 1, −1} and `shortest_delays` from 0 is {0, 3, 1, −1}.
--- starter
#include <functional>
#include <limits>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Edge {
    int from;
    int to;
    int weight;
};

std::vector<int> bfs_hops(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int source) {
    return std::vector<int>(n, -1);
}

std::vector<long long> shortest_delays(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int source) {
    return std::vector<long long>(n, -1);
}
--- solution
#include <functional>
#include <limits>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Edge {
    int from;
    int to;
    int weight;
};

std::vector<int> bfs_hops(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int source) {
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (const Edge& e : edges) adj[e.from].push_back(e.to);
    std::vector<int> hops(n, -1);
    std::queue<int> frontier;
    hops[source] = 0;
    frontier.push(source);
    while (!frontier.empty()) {
        int v = frontier.front();
        frontier.pop();
        for (int w : adj[v]) {
            if (hops[w] == -1) {
                hops[w] = hops[v] + 1;
                frontier.push(w);
            }
        }
    }
    return hops;
}

std::vector<long long> shortest_delays(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int source) {
    std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>> adj(n);   // (to, weight)
    for (const Edge& e : edges) adj[e.from].push_back({e.to, e.weight});
    const long long unreached = std::numeric_limits<long long>::max();
    std::vector<long long> dist(n, unreached);
    using Item = std::pair<long long, int>;
    std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item>, std::greater<Item>> pending;
    dist[source] = 0;
    pending.push({0, source});
    while (!pending.empty()) {
        auto [d, u] = pending.top();
        pending.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;
        for (auto [v, w] : adj[u]) {
            if (d + w < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = d + w;
                pending.push({dist[v], v});
            }
        }
    }
    for (long long& x : dist) if (x == unreached) x = -1;
    return dist;
}
--- hint
Build `std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n)` for BFS and `std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>>` holding (to, weight) for Dijkstra, pushing each edge into the list of `e.from` only: the edges are directed.
--- hint
BFS is the lesson's loop with `hops` in place of `dist`. For Dijkstra, keep `dist` as `long long` starting at a huge value, push `{0, source}` into a min-queue of (distance, vertex), and loop: pop, skip the pair if `d > dist[u]`, otherwise relax every edge out of `u`.
--- hint
Relaxing (u, v, w): if `d + w < dist[v]`, set `dist[v] = d + w` and push `{dist[v], v}`. At the end, turn every distance still at the huge value into −1.
--- check case | bfs_hops on the example
bfs_hops(4, {{0, 1, 5}, {0, 2, 1}, {2, 1, 2}}, 0)
=> std::vector<int>{0, 1, 1, -1}
--- check case | shortest_delays on the example
shortest_delays(4, {{0, 1, 5}, {0, 2, 1}, {2, 1, 2}}, 0)
=> std::vector<long long>{0, 3, 1, -1}
--- check case | Edges are directed
bfs_hops(3, {{1, 0, 1}, {1, 2, 1}}, 0)
=> std::vector<int>{0, -1, -1}
--- check case | A single vertex with a self-loop
shortest_delays(1, {{0, 0, 7}}, 0)
=> std::vector<long long>{0}
--- check case | Parallel edges: the cheapest one counts
shortest_delays(2, {{0, 1, 9}, {0, 1, 4}, {0, 1, 6}}, 0)
=> std::vector<long long>{0, 4}
--- check case | Zero-weight edges
shortest_delays(4, {{0, 1, 0}, {1, 2, 0}, {0, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 0}}, 0)
=> std::vector<long long>{0, 0, 0, 0}
--- check case | More edges can be cheaper than fewer
shortest_delays(5, {{0, 4, 100}, {0, 1, 10}, {1, 2, 10}, {2, 3, 10}, {3, 4, 10}}, 0)
=> std::vector<long long>{0, 10, 20, 30, 40}
--- check case | A source in the middle
bfs_hops(5, {{0, 1, 1}, {1, 2, 1}, {2, 3, 1}, {3, 4, 1}, {4, 0, 1}}, 2)
=> std::vector<int>{3, 4, 0, 1, 2}

[] { std::vector<Edge> e; for (int i = 0; i + 1 < 100000; ++i) e.push_back({i, i + 1, 1000000000}); auto d = shortest_delays(100000, e, 0); return d[99999]; }()

+++ practice | Reading a network from input
--- task
Write a whole program, with `main`, that reads an undirected network from standard input and prints each station's neighbours.

The first line holds `n` and `m`: the number of stations (numbered 0 to n − 1) and the number of links. Each of the next `m` lines holds two station numbers `u v`, a link between them. No link appears twice and no link joins a station to itself.

Store the network as `std::vector<std::vector<int>>`, then print one line per station, in order: the station number, its degree (number of neighbours) in brackets, a colon, and its neighbours from smallest to largest, each after one space. A station with no neighbours prints just its number, degree and colon. For example, a station 2 linked to 4, 0 and 1 prints `2 (3): 0 1 4`.
--- stdin
6 5
0 1
0 4
4 1
2 4
1 3
--- starter
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    int n, m;
    std::cin >> n >> m;
    std::cout << n << " stations\n";
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    int n, m;
    std::cin >> n >> m;
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int u, v;
        std::cin >> u >> v;
        adj[u].push_back(v);
        adj[v].push_back(u);
    }
    for (int v = 0; v < n; ++v) {
        std::sort(adj[v].begin(), adj[v].end());
        std::cout << v << " (" << adj[v].size() << "):";
        for (int w : adj[v]) std::cout << " " << w;
        std::cout << "\n";
    }
}
--- hint
Make `adj(n)` with round brackets, then for each link push each end into the other's list: the network is undirected.
--- hint
Before printing a station's line, sort its list with `std::sort`. Print the number, then `" ("`, the size, `"):"`, and then `" "` before each neighbour.
--- check output | Six stations, one of them alone
0 (2): 1 4
1 (3): 0 3 4
2 (1): 4
3 (1): 1
4 (3): 0 1 2
5 (0):

+++ practice | Fewest steps across a grid
--- task
A rover's map is a grid of strings: `'.'` is open ground, `'#'` is rock, `'S'` is the start and `'T'` the target (both open). Each step moves one cell up, down, left or right, never onto rock or off the grid. Write `int fewest_steps(const std::vector<std::string>& grid)`, with no `main`: the fewest steps from `S` to `T`, or −1 if `T` cannot be reached. Every grid has exactly one `S` and one `T`, and all rows have the same length.

The grid is a graph whose vertices are cells and whose edges join neighbouring open cells. Do not build adjacency lists: number cell (r, c) as `r * width + c`, and let BFS work out the neighbours as it goes. A check uses a 999 by 1,000 grid, so the search must be Θ(cells).

For example, in `{"S.#", ".##", "..T"}` the answer is 4.
--- starter
#include <queue>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int fewest_steps(const std::vector<std::string>& grid) {
    return -1;
}
--- solution
#include <queue>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int fewest_steps(const std::vector<std::string>& grid) {
    int h = static_cast<int>(grid.size());
    int w = static_cast<int>(grid[0].size());
    int start = -1;
    for (int r = 0; r < h; ++r)
        for (int c = 0; c < w; ++c)
            if (grid[r][c] == 'S') start = r * w + c;
    std::vector<int> dist(h * w, -1);
    std::queue<int> frontier;
    dist[start] = 0;
    frontier.push(start);
    const int dr[] = {1, -1, 0, 0};
    const int dc[] = {0, 0, 1, -1};
    while (!frontier.empty()) {
        int cell = frontier.front();
        frontier.pop();
        int r = cell / w;
        int c = cell % w;
        if (grid[r][c] == 'T') return dist[cell];
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k) {
            int nr = r + dr[k];
            int nc = c + dc[k];
            if (nr < 0 || nr >= h || nc < 0 || nc >= w || grid[nr][nc] == '#') continue;
            int next = nr * w + nc;
            if (dist[next] == -1) {
                dist[next] = dist[cell] + 1;
                frontier.push(next);
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
--- hint
Find `S` first and turn it into one number, `r * w + c`. A cell number turns back into its row and column with `cell / w` and `cell % w`.
--- hint
Two small arrays of row and column changes, `{1, -1, 0, 0}` and `{0, 0, 1, -1}`, give the four neighbours in a loop. Skip a neighbour that is off the grid or rock; otherwise treat it exactly like a neighbour in the lesson's BFS.
--- hint
Stop as soon as you pop the `T` cell and return its distance; if the queue empties first, return −1.

+++ practice | The route, not just its cost
--- task
Distances are not enough for a rover: it needs the route. Using the lesson's directed `struct Edge { int from; int to; int weight; };` (weights from 0 to 1,000,000), write `std::vector<int> cheapest_route(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int from, int to)`, with no `main`. It returns the vertices of a cheapest path from `from` to `to`, starting with `from` and ending with `to`. If `to` cannot be reached, return an empty vector; if `from == to`, return just `{from}`.

Run Dijkstra with lazy deletion, keeping a `parent` vector: when relaxing the edge (u, v) lowers `dist[v]`, set `parent[v] = u`. Then walk back from `to` along the parents and reverse. The checks use graphs whose cheapest paths are unique, except the large one, which checks that your route is a real path with the cheapest cost.

For example, with edges 0→1 (4), 0→2 (1), 2→1 (1), 1→3 (1) and 2→3 (5), the route from 0 to 3 is `{0, 2, 1, 3}`, costing 3.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <limits>
#include <map>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Edge {
    int from;
    int to;
    int weight;
};

std::vector<int> cheapest_route(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int from, int to) {
    return {from, to};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <limits>
#include <map>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Edge {
    int from;
    int to;
    int weight;
};

std::vector<int> cheapest_route(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int from, int to) {
    std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>> adj(n);
    for (const Edge& e : edges) adj[e.from].push_back({e.to, e.weight});
    const long long unreached = std::numeric_limits<long long>::max();
    std::vector<long long> dist(n, unreached);
    std::vector<int> parent(n, -1);
    using Item = std::pair<long long, int>;
    std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item>, std::greater<Item>> pending;
    dist[from] = 0;
    pending.push({0, from});
    while (!pending.empty()) {
        auto [d, u] = pending.top();
        pending.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;
        if (u == to) break;
        for (auto [v, w] : adj[u]) {
            if (d + w < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = d + w;
                parent[v] = u;
                pending.push({dist[v], v});
            }
        }
    }
    if (dist[to] == unreached) return {};
    std::vector<int> route;
    for (int v = to; v != -1; v = parent[v]) route.push_back(v);
    std::reverse(route.begin(), route.end());
    return route;
}
--- hint
Start `parent` at −1 for every vertex. In the relaxation, whenever `dist[v]` goes down, record `parent[v] = u` at the same moment.
--- hint
Once `to` is popped and not stale, its distance is final, so you may stop the search early. Then follow `parent` from `to` until you reach −1 (the source has no parent), collecting vertices, and reverse the collection.
--- check case | The example from the task
cheapest_route(4, {{0, 1, 4}, {0, 2, 1}, {2, 1, 1}, {1, 3, 1}, {2, 3, 5}}, 0, 3)
=> std::vector<int>{0, 2, 1, 3}
--- check case | Unreachable target
cheapest_route(3, {{0, 1, 2}, {2, 1, 2}}, 0, 2).size()
=> 0
--- check case | From a vertex to itself
cheapest_route(6, {{5, 0, 1}}, 5, 5)
=> std::vector<int>{5}
--- check case | A cheap long way round
cheapest_route(6, {{0, 5, 50}, {0, 1, 5}, {1, 2, 5}, {2, 3, 5}, {3, 4, 5}, {4, 5, 5}, {2, 5, 40}}, 0, 5)
=> std::vector<int>{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
--- check case | 3,000 vertices and 15,000 edges: a real path with the cheapest cost
[] { int n = 3000; std::vector<Edge> e; std::map<std::pair<int, int>, int> cheapest; unsigned s = 77; for (int i = 0; i < 15000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int a = static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % n); s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int b = static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % n); s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int w = 1 + static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % 100000); e.push_back({a, b, w}); auto it = cheapest.find({a, b}); if (it == cheapest.end() || w < it->second) cheapest[{a, b}] = w; } auto r = cheapest_route(n, e, 0, n - 1); if (r.empty() || r.front() != 0 || r.back() != n - 1) return -1LL; long long cost = 0; for (std::size_t i = 1; i < r.size(); ++i) { auto it = cheapest.find({r[i - 1], r[i]}); if (it == cheapest.end()) return -2LL; cost += it->second; } return cost; }()

+++ practice | The nearest ground station
--- task
A relay network has `n` nodes (0 to n − 1) joined by undirected links, and some nodes are ground stations. Write `std::vector<int> nearest_station(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links, const std::vector<int>& stations)`, with no `main`: for every node, the fewest links to **any** station (0 for a station itself), or −1 if no station can be reached.

Run **one** BFS that starts from all the stations at once: give every station distance 0 and put them all in the queue before the loop. The queue then still holds vertices in order of distance, so the first time a node is reached is from its nearest station. That is Θ(n + m), however many stations there are.

Edge cases the checks use: no stations at all (every node gets −1), a station listed twice, links listed twice, a link from a node to itself, and nodes with no links. For example, with n = 6, links {0–1, 1–2, 3–4} and stations {2, 4, 4}, the answer is {2, 1, 0, 1, 0, −1}.
--- starter
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> nearest_station(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links, const std::vector<int>& stations) {
    return std::vector<int>(n, 0);
}
--- solution
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> nearest_station(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links, const std::vector<int>& stations) {
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [a, b] : links) {
        adj[a].push_back(b);
        adj[b].push_back(a);
    }
    std::vector<int> dist(n, -1);
    std::queue<int> frontier;
    for (int s : stations) {
        if (dist[s] == -1) {
            dist[s] = 0;
            frontier.push(s);
        }
    }
    while (!frontier.empty()) {
        int v = frontier.front();
        frontier.pop();
        for (int w : adj[v]) {
            if (dist[w] == -1) {
                dist[w] = dist[v] + 1;
                frontier.push(w);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}
--- hint
Before the loop, set every station's distance to 0 and push it, but only if its distance is still −1, so a station listed twice is pushed once.
--- hint
The loop itself is the lesson's BFS unchanged. A self-loop or a repeated link does no harm, because a vertex whose distance is already set is never pushed again.
--- check case | The example from the task

=> std::vector<int>{2, 1, 0, 1, 0, -1}
--- check case | No stations at all

=> std::vector<int>{-1, -1, -1}
--- check case | Repeated links and a self-loop
nearest_station(4, {{0, 1}, {1, 0}, {1, 1}, {1, 2}, {2, 3}, {2, 3}}, {3})
=> std::vector<int>{3, 2, 1, 0}
--- check case | Every node is a station
nearest_station(3, {{0, 1}}, {0, 1, 2})
=> std::vector<int>{0, 0, 0}
--- check case | Nodes and no links
nearest_station(2, {}, {1})
=> std::vector<int>{-1, 0}
--- check case | A chain of 200,000 with three stations
[] { int n = 200000; std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> l; for (int i = 0; i + 1 < n; ++i) l.push_back({i, i + 1}); auto d = nearest_station(n, l, {0, n - 1, 150000, 150000}); long long sum = 0; int far = 0; for (int x : d) { sum += x; if (x > far) far = x; } return sum * 1000000 + far; }()
=> 6249975000075000LL

+++ practice | Debug: distances that grow
--- task
`hops_from(n, links, source)` should return, for every node of an undirected network, the fewest links from `source`, or −1 if it cannot be reached. On a triangle of nodes 0, 1 and 2 it returns {0, 1, 2} from node 0, but node 2 is one link away. Find the bug and fix it.
--- starter
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> hops_from(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links, int source) {
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [a, b] : links) {
        adj[a].push_back(b);
        adj[b].push_back(a);
    }
    std::vector<int> dist(n, -1);
    std::vector<bool> seen(n, false);
    std::queue<int> frontier;
    dist[source] = 0;
    frontier.push(source);
    while (!frontier.empty()) {
        int v = frontier.front();
        frontier.pop();
        if (seen[v]) continue;
        seen[v] = true;
        for (int w : adj[v]) {
            if (!seen[w]) {
                dist[w] = dist[v] + 1;
                frontier.push(w);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}
--- solution
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> hops_from(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links, int source) {
    std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto [a, b] : links) {
        adj[a].push_back(b);
        adj[b].push_back(a);
    }
    std::vector<int> dist(n, -1);
    std::queue<int> frontier;
    dist[source] = 0;
    frontier.push(source);
    while (!frontier.empty()) {
        int v = frontier.front();
        frontier.pop();
        for (int w : adj[v]) {
            if (dist[w] == -1) {
                dist[w] = dist[v] + 1;
                frontier.push(w);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}
--- hint
Trace the triangle. Node 0 is popped and sets both neighbours to 1. Then node 1 is popped. Is node 2 marked `seen` yet? What does the loop do to `dist[2]`?
--- hint
A node is only marked when it is popped, but its distance is written every time it is pushed, so a later, longer route overwrites the first. Decide a node's distance once, when it is first reached: push `w` only if `dist[w] == -1`. Then `seen` is not needed at all.

+++ practice | One free burn
--- task
A spacecraft plans a trip through a network of orbits. Each directed edge (using the lesson's `struct Edge { int from; int to; int weight; };`) is a manoeuvre costing `weight` kilograms of fuel, from 0 to 1,000,000. Mission control has one **free burn**: on at most one edge of the trip, the fuel cost is 0.

Write `long long cheapest_with_one_free(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int from, int to)`, with no `main`: the least fuel for a trip from `from` to `to` using the free burn at most once, or −1 if `to` cannot be reached.

Run Dijkstra on a bigger graph whose vertices are pairs (orbit, used), where `used` is 0 before the free burn and 1 after it. From (u, 0), an edge (u, v, w) leads to (v, 0) at cost w, and to (v, 1) at cost 0. From (u, 1), it leads only to (v, 1) at cost w. Number the pair (v, used) as `2 * v + used`, so the new graph has 2n vertices and at most 3m edges, and all the costs are still non-negative. The answer is the smaller of the distances to (to, 0) and (to, 1).

For example, with edges 0→1 (10), 1→2 (100), 0→3 (30) and 3→2 (40), the cheapest trip from 0 to 2 without the free burn costs 70 (through 3), but with it the answer is 10: fly 0→1 for 10, then use the free burn on 1→2.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <limits>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Edge {
    int from;
    int to;
    int weight;
};

long long cheapest_with_one_free(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int from, int to) {
    return -1;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <limits>
#include <queue>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Edge {
    int from;
    int to;
    int weight;
};

long long cheapest_with_one_free(int n, const std::vector<Edge>& edges, int from, int to) {
    std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>> adj(2 * n);   // state 2v + used
    for (const Edge& e : edges) {
        adj[2 * e.from].push_back({2 * e.to, e.weight});
        adj[2 * e.from].push_back({2 * e.to + 1, 0});
        adj[2 * e.from + 1].push_back({2 * e.to + 1, e.weight});
    }
    const long long unreached = std::numeric_limits<long long>::max();
    std::vector<long long> dist(2 * n, unreached);
    using Item = std::pair<long long, int>;
    std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item>, std::greater<Item>> pending;
    dist[2 * from] = 0;
    pending.push({0, 2 * from});
    while (!pending.empty()) {
        auto [d, u] = pending.top();
        pending.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;
        for (auto [v, w] : adj[u]) {
            if (d + w < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = d + w;
                pending.push({dist[v], v});
            }
        }
    }
    long long best = std::min(dist[2 * to], dist[2 * to + 1]);
    return best == unreached ? -1 : best;
}
--- hint
Build adjacency lists for 2n states. For each edge (u, v, w), add three arcs: `2u → 2v` costing w, `2u → 2v + 1` costing 0, and `2u + 1 → 2v + 1` costing w.
--- hint
Then run the lesson's Dijkstra from state `2 * from` unchanged. The answer is the smaller of `dist[2 * to]` and `dist[2 * to + 1]`, or −1 if both are still unreached.
--- check case | The example from the task

=> 10LL
--- check case | A single edge becomes free

=> 0LL
--- check case | Unreachable stays unreachable
cheapest_with_one_free(3, {{0, 1, 5}, {2, 1, 5}}, 0, 2)
=> -1LL
--- check case | Already there
cheapest_with_one_free(2, {{0, 1, 5}}, 1, 1)
=> 0LL
--- check case | The free burn makes a costly shortcut the best route
cheapest_with_one_free(4, {{0, 1, 3}, {1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 3}, {0, 2, 20}}, 0, 3)
=> 3LL
--- check case | 5,000 orbits and 30,000 manoeuvres, four targets

=> std::vector<long long>{1097444, 711403, 796663, -1}

+++ practice | A graph in two arrays
--- task
Build the compressed layout from the lesson. The starter defines `struct Csr { std::vector<int> offset; std::vector<int> targets; };`. Write, with no `main`:

- `Csr build_csr(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& edges)`: the directed edges (from, to) of a graph with vertices 0 to n − 1, stored so that vertex v's targets are `targets[offset[v]]` up to but not including `targets[offset[v + 1]]`, in the order the edges appear in the input. `offset` has n + 1 entries, starting at 0 and ending at the number of edges.
- `int count_reachable(const Csr& g, int source)`: how many vertices can be reached from `source`, counting `source` itself.

Build it in Θ(n + m) with counting: first count each vertex's out-degree into `offset[v + 1]`, then add up the counts from left to right (a running sum), then place each edge at the next free spot of its vertex, using a copy of `offset` as the list of next free spots. For `count_reachable`, use an explicit stack or queue, not recursion: a check uses a chain of 200,000 vertices.

For example, the edges 0→1, 0→2, 2→0, 2→3 and 3→1 with n = 4 give `offset` {0, 2, 2, 4, 5} and `targets` {1, 2, 0, 3, 1}; from vertex 1 only 1 vertex is reachable, and from vertex 0 all 4.
--- starter
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Csr {
    std::vector<int> offset;
    std::vector<int> targets;
};

Csr build_csr(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& edges) {
    return {};
}

int count_reachable(const Csr& g, int source) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Csr {
    std::vector<int> offset;
    std::vector<int> targets;
};

Csr build_csr(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& edges) {
    Csr g;
    g.offset.assign(n + 1, 0);
    for (auto [from, to] : edges) ++g.offset[from + 1];
    for (int v = 0; v < n; ++v) g.offset[v + 1] += g.offset[v];
    g.targets.resize(edges.size());
    std::vector<int> next_free(g.offset.begin(), g.offset.end() - 1);
    for (auto [from, to] : edges) g.targets[next_free[from]++] = to;
    return g;
}

int count_reachable(const Csr& g, int source) {
    int n = static_cast<int>(g.offset.size()) - 1;
    std::vector<bool> seen(n, false);
    std::vector<int> stack = {source};
    seen[source] = true;
    int count = 0;
    while (!stack.empty()) {
        int v = stack.back();
        stack.pop_back();
        ++count;
        for (int i = g.offset[v]; i < g.offset[v + 1]; ++i) {
            int w = g.targets[i];
            if (!seen[w]) {
                seen[w] = true;
                stack.push_back(w);
            }
        }
    }
    return count;
}
--- hint
After counting, `offset[v + 1]` holds v's out-degree. The running sum `offset[v + 1] += offset[v]`, for v from 0 upwards, turns the counts into starting positions.
--- hint
Copy the first n entries of `offset` into `next_free`. For each edge (from, to), in input order, write `to` at `targets[next_free[from]]` and move `next_free[from]` on by one. That keeps each vertex's targets in input order.
--- hint
For `count_reachable`, a `std::vector<int>` used as a stack works: mark a vertex when you push it, count it when you pop it, and loop over its stretch of `targets`.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { Csr g = build_csr(4, {{0, 1}, {0, 2}, {2, 0}, {2, 3}, {3, 1}}); return g.offset == std::vector<int>{0, 2, 2, 4, 5} && g.targets == std::vector<int>{1, 2, 0, 3, 1}; }()
--- check case | Reachable counts on the example
[] { Csr g = build_csr(4, {{0, 1}, {0, 2}, {2, 0}, {2, 3}, {3, 1}}); return count_reachable(g, 1) * 10 + count_reachable(g, 0); }()
=> 14
--- check test | No edges
[] { Csr g = build_csr(3, {}); return g.offset == std::vector<int>{0, 0, 0, 0} && g.targets.empty() && count_reachable(g, 2) == 1; }()
--- check test | Input order kept inside each vertex, edges out of order overall
[] { Csr g = build_csr(3, {{2, 0}, {0, 2}, {2, 1}, {0, 1}, {2, 2}}); return g.offset == std::vector<int>{0, 2, 2, 5} && g.targets == std::vector<int>{2, 1, 0, 1, 2}; }()
--- check case | A chain of 200,000 vertices
[] { int n = 200000; std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> e; for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; --i) e.push_back({i - 1, i}); Csr g = build_csr(n, e); return count_reachable(g, 0) + count_reachable(g, n - 1); }()
=> 200001
?? A recursive search 200,000 calls deep overflows the stack. Use a vector as an explicit stack.

+++ question | Where the proof needs non-negative costs
--- ask
The proof that Dijkstra settles u at its true distance takes any path P from s to u, with first edge (x, y) leaving the settled set, and argues P is at least `dist[u]` long. Which step fails when some edge costs are negative?
--- choice
`dist[y] ≤ dist[x] + cost(x, y)`, because x's edges were relaxed when x was settled.
--- choice
`dist[y] ≥ dist[u]`, because u had the smallest tentative distance.
--- choice correct
The rest of P, from y to u, adds zero or more to the length.
--- choice
The induction assumption that x's distance was already correct.
--- why
The first two steps come from what the algorithm did, whatever the costs. The third needs every edge on the rest of the path to cost at least 0; a negative edge after y can make P shorter than `dist[u]`, which is exactly what happens with s→b→a costing 2 − 2 = 0 while a was settled at 1.

+++ question | How big the lazy queue gets
--- ask
Dijkstra with lazy deletion runs on a graph with n vertices and m edges. What bounds the number of pairs ever pushed onto the priority queue?
--- choice
n, because each vertex is settled once.
--- choice correct
m + 1: the source's pair, plus at most one pair per edge, pushed when relaxing it succeeds.
--- choice
n × m, because each vertex can be improved once per edge.
--- choice
There is no bound; stale pairs can be pushed again and again.
--- why
Each edge (u, v) is relaxed exactly once, when u is popped and not stale, and a push happens only when that relaxation lowers `dist[v]`. So there are at most m pushes plus the first one. That bounds both the time, O((n + m) log n), and the queue's memory, Θ(n + m) in the worst case, against Θ(n) for a heap with decrease-key.

=== dsacpp-17 | Union-find and tries in C++: flat arrays and index links
--- teach
Last lesson stored graphs in vectors of vectors. In DSA I you built union-find and tries in Python, where every node was an object or a dictionary. This lesson builds both again the way C++ programs do: as flat arrays of integers, with links stored as **indexes** rather than pointers. You will see why that layout is small and fast, why indexes are safer than pointers into a vector, and how to put a number on the memory.

### Union-find as two vectors

A **union-find** structure (also called **disjoint sets**) keeps the numbers 0 to n − 1 split into groups, and supports two operations:

- `find(x)`: the **representative** of x's group, one member that stands for the whole group. Two items are in the same group exactly when they have the same representative.
- `unite(a, b)`: merge the groups of a and b into one.

Everyday picture: every club has a president, and every member knows someone closer to the president. To find your club, follow "who do you know" until you reach someone who knows only themselves.

In C++ that is one vector, `parent`, where `parent[x] == x` marks a representative (a **root**). `std::iota` from `<numeric>` fills it with 0, 1, 2, …, so at the start every item is its own group:

```cpp fragment
std::vector<int> parent(n);
std::iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0);   // parent[i] == i: n groups of one
```

Each item is one `int`: 4 bytes. Ten million items take 40 MB. The same structure as a Python dictionary of objects takes many times that.

### find without recursion

Following parents up to the root is a loop. **Path halving** shortens the path while it walks: every node on the way is pointed at its grandparent, so the next search from there takes about half as many steps.

```cpp fragment
while (parent[x] != x) {
    parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];   // skip a level
    x = parent[x];
}
// x is now the root
```

A recursive `find` is shorter to write, but its recursion is as deep as the tree is tall. Without the rule in the next step, a tree can be a chain of n items, and a recursion 200,000 deep crashes on ORBIT's small browser stack (lesson 16). The loop needs no stack at all.

### Union by size, and why trees stay short

Merging two groups means pointing one root at the other. Which one? **Union by size** keeps a second vector, `size`, where `size[r]` is the number of items in root r's group, and always points the **smaller** group's root at the larger one's, then adds the sizes.

**Claim:** with union by size, no item is ever more than log₂ n links below its root.

**Why:** an item's depth grows by one only when its root is pointed at another root, and that only happens to the smaller group. The group it then belongs to is at least as big again as its old group, so its group size at least doubles. A group can double at most log₂ n times before it holds all n items. So every item's depth is at most log₂ n, and `find` costs O(log n) even without path halving. ∎

The classic alternative is **union by rank**: keep `rank[r]`, an upper bound on the height of r's tree, point the root of lower rank at the other, and add one to the rank only when two equal ranks meet. The same doubling argument works (a root of rank k has at least 2ᵏ items). Size is the handier choice, because it also answers "how big is this group?".

With both union by size and path halving (or full path compression), a sequence of m operations on n items costs O(m α(n)), where α is the [[inverse Ackermann function|ackermann-note]]. For any n you could store, α(n) is at most 4: in practice, constant time.

### A trie over fixed-size child arrays

Now tries. A **trie** stores strings as paths from a root: each node has one child per possible next letter. For lowercase words that is 26 children, and C++ can store them in a fixed-size array inside the node:

```cpp fragment
struct TrieNode {
    std::array<int, 26> child{};   // index of the child for 'a' + i, or 0 for none
    int ends = 0;                  // how many inserted words end here
    int passes = 0;                // how many inserted words pass through or end here
};

std::vector<TrieNode> nodes(1);    // nodes[0] is the root
```

The children are **indexes into the `nodes` vector**, not pointers. Index 0 is the root, and the root is never anyone's child, so 0 can safely mean "no child". The `{}` after `child` fills the array with zeros. `std::array<int, 26>` (from `<array>`) is a plain block of 26 ints with a size that is part of the type: no heap allocation, and the node is one contiguous 112-byte record.

Letter c goes to slot `c - 'a'`: `'a'` is 0, `'b'` is 1, …, `'z'` is 25, because the letters are consecutive in ASCII.

### Why indexes, not pointers

Adding a node means `nodes.push_back(TrieNode{})`. When the vector is full, that moves every node to a bigger array, exactly as your own vector did in lessons 1 and 2. A pointer or reference to a node taken **before** the push then points at freed memory. An index still works, because `nodes[i]` looks the node up again in the new array.

So the one rule for index-linked structures in a vector: never hold a reference to an element across a `push_back`. Here is the pattern that breaks it, next to one that is safe:

```cpp fragment
// broken: 'here' may dangle after push_back moves the nodes
TrieNode& here = nodes[at];
nodes.push_back(TrieNode{});
here.child[slot] = static_cast<int>(nodes.size()) - 1;

// safe: push first, then look the parent up again by its index
nodes.push_back(TrieNode{});
nodes[at].child[slot] = static_cast<int>(nodes.size()) - 1;
```

The broken version may even pass small tests: while the vector still has spare capacity nothing moves. It fails the first time the vector grows at the wrong moment, which makes it a nasty bug to find.

### What a trie costs

- **Time:** inserting or searching a string of length L visits L + 1 nodes and does O(1) work at each, so O(L), however many words are stored.
- **Memory:** one node per distinct prefix. Here each node is 26 × 4 + 4 + 4 = 112 bytes. A dictionary of 100,000 words with 800,000 letters in total has at most 800,001 nodes, about 90 MB in the worst case, and shared prefixes usually make it much less.

When 112 bytes a node is too much, the alternatives trade speed for space: a `std::map<char, int>` of children (small but O(log σ) per step, for an alphabet of σ letters), a sorted vector of (letter, index) pairs, or a **radix trie** that stores a whole chain of single-child nodes as one edge labelled with a string.

### What it costs, side by side

| operation | union-find (size + halving) | trie (array children) |
|---|---|---|
| build for n items | Θ(n) | Θ(total letters) |
| `find` / `unite` | O(α(n)) amortised, O(log n) worst | |
| insert / search / count a prefix of length L | | O(L) |
| memory | 8 bytes per item | 112 bytes per node |

### Where it is used

- **Union-find:** Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (DSA II), checking whether a network stays connected as links fail or come up, grouping pixels into regions in images, and physics simulations of [[percolation|percolation-note]].
- **Tries:** autocomplete and spell checkers, word games, and **longest-prefix match** in internet routers, which store address prefixes in a binary trie (two children per node, one per bit).

**Watch out:** three classic bugs. Comparing `parent[a] == parent[b]` to test whether a and b are together: only their **roots** say that, so compare `find(a) == find(b)`. Uniting the items instead of their roots: `parent[a] = b` detaches a from its own group. And holding a reference into the node vector across a `push_back`, as above. One more for tries: `c - 'a'` is only a valid slot for `'a'` to `'z'`. An uppercase letter or a digit gives a slot outside the array, which is [[undefined behaviour|ub-slot]].

::: context ackermann-note A function that grows absurdly fast
The Ackermann function A(m, n) grows faster than any tower of exponents you could write down: A(4, 2) already has 19,729 digits. Its inverse, α(n), is the number of steps it takes to climb back down, so it grows absurdly slowly: α(n) ≤ 4 for every n up to a number far larger than the count of atoms in the universe. Robert Tarjan proved in 1975 that union-find with both union by rank and path compression costs O(α(n)) per operation, amortised, and later work showed no structure of this kind can do better.
:::

::: context percolation-note Does water get through?
Take a grid where each cell is open with probability p. Does an open path connect the top row to the bottom row? Physicists ask this about porous rock, forest fires and electrical networks. Simulations open cells one at a time and use union-find to merge each new cell with its open neighbours, plus two extra items standing for "the top" and "the bottom". The system percolates the moment those two are in one group. For large square grids that happens at p ≈ 0.593, a number known only from such simulations.

::: context ub-slot Why an out-of-range slot is so dangerous
`std::array` does not check its index with `[ ]`. For `'A'`, `'A' - 'a'` is −32, so `child[-32]` reads or writes memory 128 bytes before the array: some other node's fields, or the vector's bookkeeping. The program keeps running with quietly corrupted data, and the crash, if one comes, happens far away from the bug. Check that every character is between `'a'` and `'z'` before using it, or map other characters explicitly, or use `child.at(i)` while debugging, which stops the program on a bad index.
:::
--- task
Write two classes, with no `main`.

`class DisjointSets` over the items 0 to n − 1:

- `explicit DisjointSets(int n)`: n groups of one.
- `int find(int x)`: the representative of x's group. Use a loop with path halving, not recursion.
- `bool unite(int a, int b)`: merge the two groups using union by size, returning `true`, or return `false` if a and b were already together.
- `int size_of(int x)`: how many items are in x's group.
- `int components() const`: how many groups there are.

`class Trie` of lowercase words (letters `'a'` to `'z'` only), with nodes in a `std::vector` and children as `std::array<int, 26>` of indexes:

- `void insert(const std::string& word)`: adds the word. Inserting a word twice counts it twice.
- `bool contains(const std::string& word) const`: whether the word was inserted at least once. A prefix of an inserted word is not contained unless it was inserted itself.
- `int count_prefix(const std::string& prefix) const`: how many inserted words (repeats included) start with `prefix`. Every word starts with the empty prefix `""`.

Checks unite 200,000 items into one chain and then call `find` 200,000 times, so a `find` that walks the whole chain every time is too slow.

For example: in `DisjointSets d(5)`, after `unite(0, 1)` and `unite(3, 4)`, `components()` is 3 and `size_of(4)` is 2. After inserting `"orbit"`, `"orbiter"` and `"orbit"`, `count_prefix("orb")` is 3, `count_prefix("orbite")` is 1, and `contains("orbite")` is `false`.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class DisjointSets {
public:
    explicit DisjointSets(int n) {}
    int find(int x) { return x; }
    bool unite(int a, int b) { return false; }
    int size_of(int x) { return 1; }
    int components() const { return 0; }
};

class Trie {
public:
    void insert(const std::string& word) {}
    bool contains(const std::string& word) const { return false; }
    int count_prefix(const std::string& prefix) const { return 0; }

--- solution
#include <array>
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class DisjointSets {
public:
    explicit DisjointSets(int n) : parent_(n), size_(n, 1), groups_(n) {
        std::iota(parent_.begin(), parent_.end(), 0);
    }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent_[x] != x) {
            parent_[x] = parent_[parent_[x]];
            x = parent_[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    bool unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a);
        b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return false;
        if (size_[a] < size_[b]) std::swap(a, b);
        parent_[b] = a;
        size_[a] += size_[b];
        --groups_;
        return true;
    }

    int size_of(int x) { return size_[find(x)]; }
    int components() const { return groups_; }

private:
    std::vector<int> parent_;
    std::vector<int> size_;
    int groups_;
};

class Trie {
public:
    Trie() : nodes_(1) {}

    void insert(const std::string& word) {
        int at = 0;
        ++nodes_[0].passes;
        for (char c : word) {
            int slot = c - 'a';
            if (nodes_[at].child[slot] == 0) {
                nodes_.push_back(Node{});
                nodes_[at].child[slot] = static_cast<int>(nodes_.size()) - 1;
            }
            at = nodes_[at].child[slot];
            ++nodes_[at].passes;
        }
        ++nodes_[at].ends;
    }

    bool contains(const std::string& word) const {
        int at = walk(word);
        return at >= 0 && nodes_[at].ends > 0;
    }

    int count_prefix(const std::string& prefix) const {
        int at = walk(prefix);
        return at >= 0 ? nodes_[at].passes : 0;
    }

private:
    struct Node {
        std::array<int, 26> child{};
        int ends = 0;
        int passes = 0;
    };

    int walk(const std::string& s) const {   // the node for s, or -1
        int at = 0;
        for (char c : s) {
            at = nodes_[at].child[c - 'a'];
            if (at == 0) return -1;
        }
        return at;
    }

    std::vector<Node> nodes_;
};
--- hint
For `DisjointSets`, keep `parent` (filled with `std::iota`), `size` (all 1) and a count of groups. `unite` must work on the two **roots**: call `find` on both first, and if they are equal return `false`.
--- hint
Point the smaller root at the larger (`std::swap` them if needed so that `a` is the larger), add the sizes into the new root, and take one off the group count. `size_of(x)` is the size stored at `find(x)`.
--- hint
For `Trie`, start `nodes_` with one root node. `insert` walks from index 0, counting `passes` on every node it visits (the root too), and creates a missing child by pushing a node and then setting the parent's slot through its index. `count_prefix` walks the prefix and returns that node's `passes`, or 0 if the walk falls off.

+++ practice | Counting ice fields
--- task
A satellite image of a polar region is a grid of strings: `'#'` is ice and `'.'` is water. Two ice cells belong to the same **field** when they touch up, down, left or right (not diagonally), directly or through other ice cells. Write `int count_fields(const std::vector<std::string>& grid)`, with no `main`: the number of ice fields. The grid has at least one row, and all rows have the same length.

Use union-find over the cells, numbering cell (r, c) as `r * width + c`: unite each ice cell with the ice cell to its right and the one below it, then count the ice cells that are their own representative. A check uses a 1,000 by 1,000 image.

For example, `{"##.", ".#.", "..#"}` has 2 fields: the three cells at the top left touch, and the bottom-right cell touches none of them.
--- starter
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int count_fields(const std::vector<std::string>& grid) {
    return 0;
}
--- solution
#include <numeric>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Groups {
    std::vector<int> parent;
    std::vector<int> size;

    explicit Groups(int n) : parent(n), size(n, 1) { std::iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0); }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    void unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a);
        b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return;
        if (size[a] < size[b]) std::swap(a, b);
        parent[b] = a;
        size[a] += size[b];
    }
};

int count_fields(const std::vector<std::string>& grid) {
    int h = static_cast<int>(grid.size());
    int w = static_cast<int>(grid[0].size());
    Groups g(h * w);
    for (int r = 0; r < h; ++r) {
        for (int c = 0; c < w; ++c) {
            if (grid[r][c] != '#') continue;
            if (c + 1 < w && grid[r][c + 1] == '#') g.unite(r * w + c, r * w + c + 1);
            if (r + 1 < h && grid[r + 1][c] == '#') g.unite(r * w + c, (r + 1) * w + c);
        }
    }
    int fields = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < h; ++r)
        for (int c = 0; c < w; ++c)
            if (grid[r][c] == '#' && g.find(r * w + c) == r * w + c) ++fields;
    return fields;
}
--- hint
Write a small union-find (parent and size vectors, `find` with path halving, `unite` by size) for `height * width` items. Water cells are simply never united with anything.
--- hint
Looking only right and down is enough: every touching pair of cells is the right or lower neighbour of one of the two. At the end, a field is counted once, at its root: count ice cells `x` with `find(x) == x`.
--- check case | The example from the task
count_fields({"##.", ".#.", "..#"})
=> 2
--- check case | All water
count_fields({"...", "..."})
=> 0
--- check case | One cell of ice
count_fields({"#"})
=> 1
--- check case | Diagonal cells do not touch
count_fields({"#.#", ".#.", "#.#"})
=> 5
--- check case | A ring around a lake is one field
count_fields({"#####", "#...#", "#.#.#", "#...#", "#####"})
=> 2
--- check case | A 1,000 by 1,000 image of stripes and blocks

=> 83750

+++ practice | The biggest group after each link
--- task
Relay satellites come online one link at a time. Write `std::vector<int> largest_after_each(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links)`, with no `main`: after each link (a, b) joins satellites a and b, record the number of satellites in the **largest** connected group. Satellites are numbered 0 to n − 1, and a link may join two satellites that are already connected, or a satellite to itself.

Use union-find with union by size, and keep the largest size seen so far: a group only grows, so the maximum can only go up, and it changes only when a merge produces a bigger group. For example, with n = 5 and links (0, 1), (2, 3), (1, 0), (1, 3), (4, 4), the answer is {2, 2, 2, 4, 4}.
--- starter
#include <numeric>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> largest_after_each(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links) {
    return std::vector<int>(links.size(), 1);
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <numeric>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> largest_after_each(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& links) {
    std::vector<int> parent(n);
    std::vector<int> size(n, 1);
    std::iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0);
    auto find = [&parent](int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };
    int largest = n > 0 ? 1 : 0;
    std::vector<int> out;
    out.reserve(links.size());
    for (auto [a, b] : links) {
        a = find(a);
        b = find(b);
        if (a != b) {
            if (size[a] < size[b]) std::swap(a, b);
            parent[b] = a;
            size[a] += size[b];
            largest = std::max(largest, size[a]);
        }
        out.push_back(largest);
    }
    return out;
}
--- hint
Before any link, the largest group has 1 satellite. A link between two satellites already in one group changes nothing, so record the same maximum again.
--- hint
After a real merge, the new group's size is stored at the new root: compare it with the largest so far.
--- check case | The example from the task
largest_after_each(5, {{0, 1}, {2, 3}, {1, 0}, {1, 3}, {4, 4}})
=> std::vector<int>{2, 2, 2, 4, 4}
--- check case | No links
largest_after_each(3, {}).size()
=> 0
--- check case | Only self-links
largest_after_each(2, {{0, 0}, {1, 1}})
=> std::vector<int>{1, 1}
--- check case | Two groups merging late
largest_after_each(6, {{0, 1}, {1, 2}, {3, 4}, {4, 5}, {2, 5}})
=> std::vector<int>{2, 3, 3, 3, 6}

+++ practice | Sorting with a trie
--- task
A trie visits words in dictionary order if you walk it the right way. Write `std::vector<std::string> sorted_by_trie(const std::vector<std::string>& words)`, with no `main`. Words use only the letters `'a'` to `'z'` and may repeat, and the empty word may appear.

Insert every word into a trie whose nodes live in a `std::vector` with `std::array<int, 26>` children, counting at each node how many words end there. Then walk the trie **depth first**, visiting a node before its children and the children in order `'a'` to `'z'`, and output a node's word once for each time it was inserted. Keep the current word as a string: add a letter when you go down to a child, and remove it when you come back.

That order is exactly sorted order, because a word comes before every longer word that starts with it, and two words that differ first at some letter are ordered by that letter. The result must equal what `std::sort` gives. For example, `{"bat", "b", "ant", "bat", ""}` gives `{"", "ant", "b", "bat", "bat"}`.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

std::vector<std::string> sorted_by_trie(const std::vector<std::string>& words) {
    return words;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    std::array<int, 26> child{};
    int ends = 0;
};

void collect(const std::vector<Node>& nodes, int at, std::string& word, std::vector<std::string>& out) {
    for (int k = 0; k < nodes[at].ends; ++k) out.push_back(word);
    for (int slot = 0; slot < 26; ++slot) {
        int next = nodes[at].child[slot];
        if (next == 0) continue;
        word.push_back(static_cast<char>('a' + slot));
        collect(nodes, next, word, out);
        word.pop_back();
    }
}

std::vector<std::string> sorted_by_trie(const std::vector<std::string>& words) {
    std::vector<Node> nodes(1);
    for (const auto& w : words) {
        int at = 0;
        for (char c : w) {
            int slot = c - 'a';
            if (nodes[at].child[slot] == 0) {
                nodes.push_back(Node{});
                nodes[at].child[slot] = static_cast<int>(nodes.size()) - 1;
            }
            at = nodes[at].child[slot];
        }
        ++nodes[at].ends;
    }
    std::vector<std::string> out;
    out.reserve(words.size());
    std::string word;
    collect(nodes, 0, word, out);
    return out;
}
--- hint
Insertion is the lesson's insert with only an `ends` count. Remember to push the new node first and only then set the parent's slot through its index.
--- hint
Write a recursive helper `collect(nodes, at, word, out)`: first output `word` `nodes[at].ends` times, then for each slot from 0 to 25 that has a child, append the letter, recurse, and pop the letter off again. The recursion is only as deep as the longest word, so it is safe here.
--- check case | The example from the task
sorted_by_trie({"bat", "b", "ant", "bat", ""})
=> std::vector<std::string>{"", "ant", "b", "bat", "bat"}
--- check case | No words
sorted_by_trie({}).size()
=> 0
--- check case | Prefixes come first
sorted_by_trie({"orbiter", "orbit", "orb", "or"})
=> std::vector<std::string>{"or", "orb", "orbit", "orbiter"}
--- check case | One letter decides
sorted_by_trie({"zz", "za", "az", "aa", "m"})
=> std::vector<std::string>{"aa", "az", "m", "za", "zz"}
--- check test | 20,000 random words match std::sort
[] { std::vector<std::string> w; unsigned s = 8; for (int i = 0; i < 20000; ++i) { std::string x; s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int len = static_cast<int>((s >> 16) % 7); for (int j = 0; j < len; ++j) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; x += static_cast<char>('a' + (s >> 16) % 5); } w.push_back(x); } std::vector<std::string> want = w; std::sort(want.begin(), want.end()); return sorted_by_trie(w) == want; }()

+++ practice | A trie that forgets
--- task
Extend a trie with removal. Write `class CountingTrie`, with no `main`, for words of lowercase letters (the empty word allowed), using a `std::vector` of nodes with `std::array<int, 26>` children:

- `void insert(const std::string& w)`: adds one copy of `w`.
- `bool erase(const std::string& w)`: removes one copy of `w` and returns `true`; if `w` is not stored, it returns `false` and **changes nothing**.
- `int count(const std::string& w) const`: how many copies of `w` are stored.
- `int count_prefix(const std::string& p) const`: how many stored words (with copies) start with `p`.

Nodes are never freed: `erase` only lowers the counts along the word's path. The edge cases are where sloppy code fails: erasing a word that was never inserted, erasing a prefix of a stored word that was not itself inserted, erasing more copies than there are, the empty word, and prefix counts after erasing. For example, after inserting `"sat"` twice and `"satellite"` once, `erase("sa")` is `false`, `erase("sat")` is `true`, and then `count("sat")` is 1 and `count_prefix("sat")` is 2.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class CountingTrie {
public:
    void insert(const std::string& w) {}
    bool erase(const std::string& w) { return true; }
    int count(const std::string& w) const { return 0; }
    int count_prefix(const std::string& p) const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class CountingTrie {
public:
    CountingTrie() : nodes_(1) {}

    void insert(const std::string& w) {
        int at = 0;
        ++nodes_[0].passes;
        for (char c : w) {
            int slot = c - 'a';
            if (nodes_[at].child[slot] == 0) {
                nodes_.push_back(Node{});
                nodes_[at].child[slot] = static_cast<int>(nodes_.size()) - 1;
            }
            at = nodes_[at].child[slot];
            ++nodes_[at].passes;
        }
        ++nodes_[at].ends;
    }

    bool erase(const std::string& w) {
        if (count(w) == 0) return false;
        int at = 0;
        --nodes_[0].passes;
        for (char c : w) {
            at = nodes_[at].child[c - 'a'];
            --nodes_[at].passes;
        }
        --nodes_[at].ends;
        return true;
    }

    int count(const std::string& w) const {
        int at = walk(w);
        return at < 0 ? 0 : nodes_[at].ends;
    }

    int count_prefix(const std::string& p) const {
        int at = walk(p);
        return at < 0 ? 0 : nodes_[at].passes;
    }

private:
    struct Node {
        std::array<int, 26> child{};
        int ends = 0;
        int passes = 0;
    };

    int walk(const std::string& s) const {
        int at = 0;
        for (char c : s) {
            at = nodes_[at].child[c - 'a'];
            if (at == 0) return -1;
        }
        return at;
    }

    std::vector<Node> nodes_;
};
--- hint
Keep two counts per node, as in the lesson: `ends` (copies that end here) and `passes` (copies that pass through or end here, the root included).
--- hint
In `erase`, check first, change second: if `count(w)` is 0, return `false` before touching anything. Only then walk the path again, taking one off `passes` at every node (the root too) and one off `ends` at the last.
--- check test | The example from the task

--- check test | Erasing a word that was never inserted changes nothing
[] { CountingTrie t; t.insert("moon"); bool a = t.erase("mars"); bool b = t.erase("moons"); bool c = t.erase("mo"); return !a && !b && !c && t.count("moon") == 1 && t.count_prefix("") == 1 && t.count_prefix("mo") == 1; }()
--- check test | More erases than copies

--- check test | The empty word
[] { CountingTrie t; bool before = t.erase(""); t.insert(""); t.insert("a"); bool a = t.erase(""); return !before && a && t.count("") == 0 && t.count_prefix("") == 1 && t.count("a") == 1; }()

+++ practice | Debug: the link that breaks a group
--- task
`Network` tracks which stations can reach each other as links are added. `link(a, b)` should join the two stations' groups and return `true`, or return `false` if they were already in one group; `connected(a, b)` says whether they are in one group; `groups()` counts the groups.

After `link(0, 1)` and `link(0, 2)`, stations 1 and 2 should be connected, but `connected(1, 2)` returns `false`. Find the bug and fix it. It is one line.
--- starter
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

class Network {
public:
    explicit Network(int n) : parent_(n), groups_(n) { std::iota(parent_.begin(), parent_.end(), 0); }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent_[x] != x) x = parent_[x];
        return x;
    }

    bool link(int a, int b) {
        if (find(a) == find(b)) return false;
        parent_[a] = b;
        --groups_;
        return true;
    }

    bool connected(int a, int b) { return find(a) == find(b); }
    int groups() const { return groups_; }

    std::vector<int> parent_;
    int groups_;

--- solution
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

class Network {
public:
    explicit Network(int n) : parent_(n), groups_(n) { std::iota(parent_.begin(), parent_.end(), 0); }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent_[x] != x) x = parent_[x];
        return x;
    }

    bool link(int a, int b) {
        if (find(a) == find(b)) return false;
        parent_[find(a)] = find(b);
        --groups_;
        return true;
    }

    bool connected(int a, int b) { return find(a) == find(b); }
    int groups() const { return groups_; }

private:
    std::vector<int> parent_;
    int groups_;
};
--- hint

--- hint
Only a root may be pointed somewhere else. Point the root of a's group at the root of b's group: `parent_[find(a)] = find(b)`.
