+++ practice | When does it percolate?
--- task
An n by n grid starts with every cell blocked. Cells are opened one at a time, in the order given by `openings`, a list of (row, column) pairs with rows and columns from 0 to n − 1. The grid **percolates** when some path of open cells, moving up, down, left or right, joins a cell in the top row to a cell in the bottom row.

Write `int percolates_after(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& openings)`, with no `main`: the number of openings (counting from 1) after which the grid first percolates, or −1 if it never does. Opening a cell that is already open changes nothing, but still counts as one opening.

Use union-find with two extra items: `n * n` stands for the top and `n * n + 1` for the bottom. When a cell opens, unite it with each open neighbour, with the top if it is in row 0, and with the bottom if it is in row n − 1. The grid percolates exactly when the top and the bottom have the same representative. For n = 1, the first opening percolates at once. A check opens all 250,000 cells of a 500 by 500 grid in a scrambled order.

For example, in a 3 by 3 grid, opening (0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 0), (2, 1) percolates after the 4th opening.
--- starter
#include <numeric>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int percolates_after(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& openings) {
    return -1;
}
--- solution
#include <numeric>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Groups {
public:
    explicit Groups(int n) : parent_(n), size_(n, 1) { std::iota(parent_.begin(), parent_.end(), 0); }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent_[x] != x) {
            parent_[x] = parent_[parent_[x]];
            x = parent_[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    void unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a);
        b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return;
        if (size_[a] < size_[b]) std::swap(a, b);
        parent_[b] = a;
        size_[a] += size_[b];
    }

private:
    std::vector<int> parent_;
    std::vector<int> size_;
};

int percolates_after(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& openings) {
    const int top = n * n;
    const int bottom = n * n + 1;
    Groups g(n * n + 2);
    std::vector<bool> open(n * n, false);
    const int dr[] = {1, -1, 0, 0};
    const int dc[] = {0, 0, 1, -1};
    for (std::size_t k = 0; k < openings.size(); ++k) {
        auto [r, c] = openings[k];
        int cell = r * n + c;
        if (!open[cell]) {
            open[cell] = true;
            if (r == 0) g.unite(cell, top);
            if (r == n - 1) g.unite(cell, bottom);
            for (int d = 0; d < 4; ++d) {
                int nr = r + dr[d];
                int nc = c + dc[d];
                if (nr >= 0 && nr < n && nc >= 0 && nc < n && open[nr * n + nc]) g.unite(cell, nr * n + nc);
            }
        }
        if (g.find(top) == g.find(bottom)) return static_cast<int>(k) + 1;
    }
    return -1;
}
--- hint
Make a union-find of `n * n + 2` items and a `std::vector<bool>` of which cells are open. Number cell (r, c) as `r * n + c`.
--- hint
When a cell opens: unite it with `n * n` if `r == 0`, with `n * n + 1` if `r == n - 1` (for n = 1 both happen), and with each of its four neighbours that is inside the grid and already open. After every opening, compare the representatives of the two extra items.
--- check case | The example from the task
percolates_after(3, {{0, 1}, {1, 1}, {2, 0}, {2, 1}})
=> 4
--- check case | A one-cell grid
percolates_after(1, {{0, 0}})
=> 1
--- check case | Never percolates
percolates_after(3, {{0, 0}, {1, 0}, {1, 2}, {2, 2}})
=> -1
--- check case | No openings
percolates_after(2, {})
=> -1
--- check case | Opening the same cell twice still counts
percolates_after(2, {{0, 0}, {0, 0}, {1, 0}})
=> 3
--- check case | Diagonal cells do not connect
percolates_after(2, {{0, 0}, {1, 1}, {0, 1}})
=> 3
--- check case | 500 by 500, all cells in a scrambled order
[] { int n = 500; std::vector<int> cells(n * n); std::iota(cells.begin(), cells.end(), 0); unsigned s = 2718; for (int i = n * n - 1; i > 0; --i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int j = static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % static_cast<unsigned>(i + 1)); std::swap(cells[i], cells[j]); } std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> op; for (int c : cells) op.push_back({c / n, c % n}); return percolates_after(n, op); }()
=> 151083

+++ practice | Routing by longest prefix
--- task
An internet router forwards each packet by its destination address. Its table holds **prefixes**, like `10.1.0.0/16`: every address whose first 16 bits equal those of 10.1.0.0 matches. When several prefixes match, the **longest** wins. Write `class RouteTable`, with no `main`:

- `void add(const std::string& address, int length, int port)`: add the prefix made of the first `length` bits (0 to 32) of `address`, a dotted address like `"10.1.0.0"`, sending matches to `port`. Bits after the first `length` are ignored. Adding the same prefix again replaces its port. Length 0 matches every address.
- `int lookup(const std::string& address) const`: the port of the longest prefix matching the address, or −1 if none matches.

Store the prefixes in a **binary trie**: nodes in a `std::vector`, each with `std::array<int, 2> child` (indexes, 0 for none) and a port (−1 for none). Bit 31 of the address, its highest bit, decides the first step, bit 30 the second, and so on. `lookup` walks down as far as the address's bits allow and remembers the last port it passed. Turn the dotted text into a `std::uint32_t` yourself: four numbers from 0 to 255, the first one highest.

For example, after `add("10.0.0.0", 8, 1)` and `add("10.1.0.0", 16, 2)`, the address `"10.1.7.9"` goes to port 2, `"10.200.0.1"` to port 1, and `"11.0.0.1"` to −1.
--- starter
#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

class RouteTable {
public:
    void add(const std::string& address, int length, int port) {}
    int lookup(const std::string& address) const { return -1; }
};
--- solution
#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

std::uint32_t parse_address(const std::string& text) {
    std::uint32_t value = 0;
    std::uint32_t part = 0;
    for (char c : text) {
        if (c == '.') {
            value = (value << 8) | part;
            part = 0;
        } else {
            part = part * 10 + static_cast<std::uint32_t>(c - '0');
        }
    }
    return (value << 8) | part;
}

class RouteTable {
public:
    RouteTable() : nodes_(1) {}

    void add(const std::string& address, int length, int port) {
        std::uint32_t bits = parse_address(address);
        int at = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < length; ++i) {
            int b = static_cast<int>((bits >> (31 - i)) & 1u);
            if (nodes_[at].child[b] == 0) {
                nodes_.push_back(Node{});
                nodes_[at].child[b] = static_cast<int>(nodes_.size()) - 1;
            }
            at = nodes_[at].child[b];
        }
        nodes_[at].port = port;
    }

    int lookup(const std::string& address) const {
        std::uint32_t bits = parse_address(address);
        int at = 0;
        int best = nodes_[0].port;
        for (int i = 0; i < 32; ++i) {
            at = nodes_[at].child[(bits >> (31 - i)) & 1u];
            if (at == 0) break;
            if (nodes_[at].port != -1) best = nodes_[at].port;
        }
        return best;
    }

private:
    struct Node {
        std::array<int, 2> child{};
        int port = -1;
    };

    std::vector<Node> nodes_;
};
--- hint
Parsing: keep a running `value` and the current number `part`. On each digit, `part = part * 10 + digit`; on each dot, shift `value` left 8 bits and OR in `part`, then reset `part`. Do the same once more at the end.
--- hint
Bit i of the prefix, counting from the top, is `(bits >> (31 - i)) & 1`. `add` walks `length` steps, creating children as needed (push first, then set the slot through the parent's index), and stores the port at the node it ends on. The root is the node for length 0.
--- hint
`lookup` starts with the root's port as the best so far, then follows up to 32 bits, stopping when a child is missing, and updates the best at every node that has a port.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { RouteTable t; t.add("10.0.0.0", 8, 1); t.add("10.1.0.0", 16, 2); return t.lookup("10.1.7.9") == 2 && t.lookup("10.200.0.1") == 1 && t.lookup("11.0.0.1") == -1; }()
--- check test | An empty table
[] { RouteTable t; return t.lookup("1.2.3.4") == -1 && t.lookup("0.0.0.0") == -1; }()
--- check test | A default route of length 0

--- check test | Bits past the length are ignored, and re-adding replaces

--- check test | Full 32-bit routes and 255s
[] { RouteTable t; t.add("255.255.255.255", 32, 7); t.add("255.255.255.254", 31, 6); return t.lookup("255.255.255.255") == 7 && t.lookup("255.255.255.254") == 6 && t.lookup("255.255.255.253") == -1; }()

=> 46268604936LL

+++ question | What union by size guarantees
--- ask
Union-find uses union by size but no path halving. After any sequence of `unite` calls on n = 1,024 items, how many links can an item be below its root, at most?
--- answer
10
--- why
An item sinks one level only when its group is the smaller one in a merge, and the merged group is then at least twice as big. Starting from a group of 1, it can double at most log₂ 1,024 = 10 times before the group holds all 1,024 items. So no item is more than 10 links from its root, and `find` takes at most 10 steps.

+++ question | Why the trie links by index
--- ask
A trie keeps its nodes in a `std::vector<Node>` and links children by index. Why not store `Node*` pointers to the children instead?
--- choice
Pointers take more memory than `int` indexes, and that is the only difference.
--- choice correct
`push_back` may move every node to a bigger array, which leaves every stored pointer dangling; an index still finds the node in the new array.
--- choice
A `std::vector` cannot hold objects that point at each other.
--- choice
Indexes let the trie be searched in O(1) instead of O(L).
--- why
When the vector's capacity runs out, `push_back` moves all elements into a new block and frees the old one, as your own vector did in lessons 1 and 2. Pointers into the old block then point at freed memory. `nodes[i]` looks the node up again in whatever block the vector now uses. (An index is also 4 bytes against a pointer's 8 on a 64-bit machine, a pleasant bonus.)

=== dsacpp-18 | Measuring: std::chrono, cache misses and big-O against real time
--- teach
All course long, costs have been big-O bounds and exact counts: comparisons, probes, allocations. Last lesson's union-find was "near-constant time", and a std::list insert is "O(1)". Those statements are true, and they leave out two things: the constant in front, and the machine. This lesson measures real time with `std::chrono`, shows the biggest hidden constant, which is memory, and ends with how to read a big-O bound against a stopwatch.

### A stopwatch in C++: std::chrono

The header `<chrono>` has three kinds of things: **clocks**, which tell the time; **time points**, a moment on one clock; and **durations**, a length of time. Subtract two time points and you get a duration.

Everyday picture: a kitchen wall clock and a stopwatch. The wall clock shows the time of day, and someone may set it forward or back. The stopwatch only ever moves forward, which is the one property you need to time an egg.

C++ has both:

- `std::chrono::system_clock` is the wall clock. It can jump when the computer [[corrects its time|clock-jumps]], so it is wrong for timing.
- `std::chrono::steady_clock` is the stopwatch: it never goes backwards. **Always time code with `steady_clock`.**

```cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    long long total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10000000; ++i) total += i % 7;
    auto stop = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto us = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(stop - start);
    std::cout << "total " << total << " in " << us.count() << " us\n";
}
```

`stop - start` is a duration in the clock's own unit (often nanoseconds). `duration_cast` converts it to microseconds, and `.count()` gives the plain number.

### Durations and their units

A **duration** is a count plus a unit fixed in its type: `std::chrono::milliseconds` is a whole number of thousandths of a second, `std::chrono::seconds` of seconds, and so on. Converting to a **finer** unit loses nothing, so it happens by itself. Converting to a **coarser** one could lose a fraction, so you must ask with `duration_cast`, and it [[drops the fraction|truncation-note]], rounding towards zero:

```cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::chrono::seconds burn(90);
    std::chrono::milliseconds ms = burn;                                    // fine: 90000
    auto whole_minutes = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::minutes>(burn);   // 1, the 30 s are dropped
    std::chrono::duration<double, std::ratio<60>> exact_minutes = burn;     // 1.5: a double count keeps fractions
    std::cout << ms.count() << " " << whole_minutes.count() << " " << exact_minutes.count() << "\n";
}
```

The unit is written as a `std::ratio`: `std::ratio<60>` means 60 seconds, and `std::milli` means 1/1000 of a second. A duration with a `double` count, like `std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>`, holds fractional milliseconds, which is what you want for averages.

### Measuring well

A single timing is almost worthless. Five rules make a measurement mean something:

1. **Use `steady_clock`.**
2. **Keep the work alive.** An optimising compiler removes work whose result is never used, and then you time nothing. Use the result: print it, or add it to a total you print.
3. **Warm up.** The first run pays extra: memory is touched for the first time, and the caches are cold. Throw that run away.
4. **Time enough work.** A clock has a resolution, and in a browser it is [[deliberately coarse|browser-timer]]. Time a batch that takes at least a few milliseconds, and divide.
5. **Repeat, and keep the minimum.** A measured time is the true cost plus noise: other programs, interrupts, the operating system. That noise only ever **adds** time. So the smallest of several runs is the closest to the true cost, and more runs can only bring it closer.

Rule 5 is worth a function, and a function worth testing. But you cannot test timing code against a real clock: the answers change every run. The trick is to make the **clock a template parameter**. Real code passes `std::chrono::steady_clock`; a test passes a pretend clock whose `now()` returns times from a script. Any type with a `duration`, a `time_point` and a static `now()` works, which is what the standard calls a clock.

### The memory hierarchy

Here is the hidden constant. A processor does an addition in well under a nanosecond, but fetching a value from main memory takes about [[100 nanoseconds|latency-numbers]]. To hide that, it keeps small, fast copies of recently used memory in **caches**:

| where the data is | about how long |
|---|---|
| a register | under 1 ns |
| L1 cache (tens of KB) | 1 ns |
| L2 cache (about a MB) | 4 ns |
| L3 cache (several MB) | 10–20 ns |
| main memory | 80–100 ns |

Two facts decide whether your data structure is fast:

- Memory moves in **cache lines** of 64 bytes. Read one `int`, and its 15 neighbours come along for free.
- The processor watches your reads, and when they march forward in order it **prefetches** the next lines before you ask.

So reading an array from start to end costs about one miss per 16 `int`s, and the prefetcher hides most of those. Jumping to scattered addresses costs a full miss almost every time.

### Vector against list: same big-O, different speed

Summing n numbers is Θ(n) in a `std::vector` and in a `std::list`. But the list keeps every element in its own node (the value plus two pointers, 24 bytes or more), and after nodes have been inserted, removed or relinked, consecutive nodes sit at unrelated addresses. Walking the list is **pointer chasing**: each step waits for a miss before it even knows where the next node is.

This program makes the list scattered on purpose: it sorts the list by random keys, which relinks the nodes without moving them, and then times both sums:

```cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <list>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const int n = 1000000;
    std::vector<int> vec;
    std::list<std::pair<unsigned, int>> lst;
    unsigned s = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u;
        vec.push_back(i % 100);
        lst.push_back({s, i % 100});
    }
    lst.sort();   // relinks nodes into random-key order: memory order is now scrambled

    auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    long long a = 0;
    for (int x : vec) a += x;
    auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    long long b = 0;
    for (const auto& node : lst) b += node.second;
    auto t2 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    using ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>;
    std::cout << "vector: " << a << " in " << ms(t1 - t0).count() << " ms\n";
    std::cout << "list:   " << b << " in " << ms(t2 - t1).count() << " ms\n";
}
```

Both sums print 49,500,000. On a typical laptop the vector takes well under a millisecond and the scattered list tens of milliseconds: the same Θ(n), with a constant [[fifty times larger or more|list-vs-vector]].

The same effect decides the famous "insert into the middle" question. Inserting into a sorted sequence at a random position means first finding the position, O(n) for both, and then inserting: O(1) for a list, O(n) shifting for a vector. On paper the list wins. In practice the vector wins at every size people have tried, because its search and its shift both stream through contiguous memory, while the list's search chases a pointer per step.

### Big-O against real time

Big-O describes how the cost **grows**; it says nothing about the cost at one size. Real programs use that:

- `std::sort` switches to insertion sort, Θ(n²), for pieces under about 16 elements, because on tiny ranges its tight loop beats quicksort's overhead.
- A linear scan of a small sorted array can beat binary search: no unpredictable branches, and the whole array is one or two cache lines.
- A sorted vector with binary search often beats `std::map` for lookups up to many thousands of keys, for the vector-against-list reason.

To see the growth in real times, use the **doubling experiment**. Time the same code at n, 2n, 4n, … If T(n) ≈ c·nᵇ, then T(2n) / T(n) ≈ 2ᵇ, so b ≈ log₂ of the ratio. A ratio near 2 means linear, near 4 quadratic, near 8 cubic, and a little above 2 fits n log n (at a million elements, 2 × 21 / 20 = 2.1). Between two sizes n₁ and n₂ in general:

b ≈ log(t₂ / t₁) / log(n₂ / n₁)

With more than two sizes, fit a straight line through the points (log n, log t): its slope is b. Expect surprises where n crosses a cache size: when the data stops fitting in L2 or L3, the time per element jumps, and the ratio for that one doubling looks worse than the algorithm really is.

### Counting or timing?

Every check in this course counts operations instead of timing them, and that is deliberate. A count is exact, the same on every machine, and the same every run, so it can prove a bound. A time is noisy and machine-dependent, but it is the only thing that sees the memory hierarchy. Engineers use both: counts to check the algorithm, times to check the program.

### What it costs

| structure, walked from start to end | work | cache misses, roughly |
|---|---|---|
| `std::vector<int>` of n | Θ(n) | n / 16, mostly hidden by prefetching |
| `std::list<int>` of n, scattered nodes | Θ(n) | about n, none hidden |
| `std::deque<int>` of n | Θ(n) | about n / 16, plus one per block |
| tree or hash chain of n nodes, one path | Θ(depth) | about one per node on the path |

### Where it is used

- **Profilers and benchmark libraries** (such as Google Benchmark) repeat, warm up and report minimums or medians, exactly as the rules above say.
- **Performance tests in continuous integration** fail a change that makes a hot path measurably slower.
- **Flight software** has timing budgets: a control loop must finish within its [[worst-case execution time|wcet]], so engineers measure the slowest run, not the average, and prefer contiguous, preallocated data.
- **Databases** lay out rows in pages and columns in arrays for the same cache reasons, and choose B-trees over binary trees because one node fills whole cache lines.

**Watch out:** the classic benchmarking mistakes. Timing work the compiler has removed (the time comes out near zero; use the result). Timing once, or timing the first, cold run. Using `system_clock`. And dividing after a `duration_cast`: `duration_cast<milliseconds>(total) / runs` truncates the total to whole milliseconds first, so 999 microseconds becomes 0. Convert to a `double` duration, then divide.

::: context clock-jumps Why the wall clock can go backwards
Computers keep their clocks right by asking time servers on the internet, using the Network Time Protocol, and adjusting. If a clock was fast, it may be set back. Daylight saving time, a user changing the time, and leap-second handling can all move `system_clock`. A duration measured across such a jump can come out wrong, even negative. `steady_clock` counts from an arbitrary starting point, such as when the computer booted, and only moves forward at a steady rate.
:::

::: context truncation-note Truncating is not rounding
`duration_cast` to a coarser unit throws away the remainder, like integer division: 1,999 milliseconds cast to seconds is 1 second, and −1,999 ms is −1 s. C++17 added `std::chrono::round`, `floor` and `ceil` for durations, which round to nearest, down or up. Or keep a `double` count, as in `std::chrono::duration<double>`, and nothing is lost until you print it.
:::

::: context browser-timer Why browser clocks are coarse
In 2018 the Spectre attacks showed that a web page could read memory it should not by timing cache hits and misses very precisely. Browsers answered by making their clocks coarse and slightly random: `performance.now()` is rounded to somewhere between 5 microseconds and 1 millisecond, depending on the browser and page settings. ORBIT's C++ runs in the browser, so `steady_clock` there is only as fine as the browser allows. Time batches of work that take milliseconds, never single operations.
:::

::: context latency-numbers Numbers every programmer should know
A list with this name, popularised by Jeff Dean at Google from figures Peter Norvig had published, gives rough costs from around 2010: an L1 cache reference about 0.5 ns, a branch mispredict about 5 ns, an L2 reference about 7 ns, a main-memory reference about 100 ns, a round trip within a data centre about 500 µs, and a packet from California to the Netherlands and back about 150 ms. The exact values drift with hardware, but the ratios between the levels have stayed roughly the same for decades.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 140" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Inter, Arial, sans-serif">
  <text x="10" y="22" font-size="11" fill="#1f2a44">L1 1 ns</text>
  <rect x="100" y="12" width="3" height="14" fill="#1d6fd1"/>
  <text x="10" y="50" font-size="11" fill="#1f2a44">L2 4 ns</text>
  <rect x="100" y="40" width="10" height="14" fill="#1d6fd1"/>
  <text x="10" y="78" font-size="11" fill="#1f2a44">L3 15 ns</text>
  <rect x="100" y="68" width="37" height="14" fill="#1d6fd1"/>
  <text x="10" y="106" font-size="11" fill="#1f2a44">memory 100 ns</text>
  <rect x="100" y="96" width="250" height="14" fill="#b4232c"/>
  <text x="180" y="132" font-size="10" fill="#6c7a93">bar length: time for one read</text>

```
:::

::: context list-vs-vector How much slower, exactly?
It depends on the machine, the list's size and how scattered its nodes are. If a list is built by `push_back` and never changed, a simple allocator may hand out its nodes one after another, and walking it is only a few times slower than a vector. Once the nodes are scattered, as after sorting or many inserts and erases, every step is a cache miss, and ratios of 50 to 100 are common for lists much bigger than the caches. In ORBIT's browser build the numbers differ again, but the vector still wins clearly.
:::

::: context wcet Worst-case execution time
A spacecraft's attitude controller might run every 10 milliseconds and must always finish in time: a late answer is a wrong answer. Engineers therefore bound the worst-case execution time, by measurement under stress and by static analysis tools that model the processor's caches and pipeline. Data structures that allocate while running, or whose speed depends on how scattered their nodes are, make that bound hard to trust, which is one reason flight software favours fixed arrays and ring buffers allocated at start-up.
:::
--- task
Write a tiny benchmarking toolkit, with no `main`:

- `template <class Clock, class F> typename Clock::duration best_of(int runs, F work)`: calls `work()` exactly `runs` times (runs is at least 1), timing each call on its own with `Clock::now()` just before and just after it, and returns the **smallest** of the `runs` durations.
- `double growth_exponent(double n1, double t1, double n2, double t2)`: the exponent b for which t is proportional to nᵇ, estimated from two measurements, time `t1` at size `n1` and time `t2` at size `n2`: b = log(t2 / t1) / log(n2 / n1). Use `std::log` from `<cmath>`.

The starter defines `ScriptedClock`, a pretend clock for testing: each call to its `now()` returns the next number from `ScriptedClock::script`, in nanoseconds. Do not change it. A check sets the script to 0, 50, 100, 130, 200, 290: three runs that took 50, 30 and 90 nanoseconds, so `best_of<ScriptedClock>(3, work)` must return 30 nanoseconds. Other checks use the real `std::chrono::steady_clock`.

For example, `growth_exponent(1000, 2.0, 2000, 8.0)` is 2.0: doubling n multiplied the time by 4.
--- starter
#include <chrono>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstddef>
#include <vector>

// A pretend clock for tests: now() returns the next scripted time, in nanoseconds. Leave it as it is.
struct ScriptedClock {
    using rep = long long;
    using period = std::nano;
    using duration = std::chrono::nanoseconds;
    using time_point = std::chrono::time_point<ScriptedClock, duration>;
    static constexpr bool is_steady = true;
    static inline std::vector<long long> script;
    static inline std::size_t next = 0;
    static time_point now() { return time_point(duration(script[next++])); }
};

template <class Clock, class F>
typename Clock::duration best_of(int runs, F work) {
    return typename Clock::duration(0);
}

double growth_exponent(double n1, double t1, double n2, double t2) {
    return 0.0;
}
--- solution
#include <chrono>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstddef>
#include <vector>

// A pretend clock for tests: now() returns the next scripted time, in nanoseconds. Leave it as it is.
struct ScriptedClock {
    using rep = long long;
    using period = std::nano;
    using duration = std::chrono::nanoseconds;
    using time_point = std::chrono::time_point<ScriptedClock, duration>;
    static constexpr bool is_steady = true;
    static inline std::vector<long long> script;
    static inline std::size_t next = 0;
    static time_point now() { return time_point(duration(script[next++])); }
};

template <class Clock, class F>
typename Clock::duration best_of(int runs, F work) {
    typename Clock::duration best = Clock::duration::max();
    for (int i = 0; i < runs; ++i) {
        auto start = Clock::now();
        work();
        auto stop = Clock::now();
        if (stop - start < best) best = stop - start;
    }
    return best;
}

double growth_exponent(double n1, double t1, double n2, double t2) {
    return std::log(t2 / t1) / std::log(n2 / n1);
}
--- hint
Start `best` at the largest duration the clock can hold, `Clock::duration::max()`, so that the first run always replaces it. To declare the variable, write its type as `typename Clock::duration`: the word `typename` tells the compiler that this name, which depends on the template parameter, is a type.
--- hint
In the loop, take `Clock::now()` right before `work()` and right after it; the difference is one run's duration. Durations compare with `<` like numbers.
--- hint
`growth_exponent` is one line: `std::log(t2 / t1) / std::log(n2 / n1)`. Any base of logarithm works, as long as both use the same one.
--- check test | The scripted runs: 50, 30 and 90 ns give 30 ns
[] { ScriptedClock::script = {0, 50, 100, 130, 200, 290}; ScriptedClock::next = 0; int calls = 0; auto d = best_of<ScriptedClock>(3, [&calls] { ++calls; }); return d == std::chrono::nanoseconds(30) && calls == 3 && ScriptedClock::next == 6; }()
?? Call now() once before and once after each run, and keep the smallest difference.
--- check test | One run: its duration is the answer
[] { ScriptedClock::script = {1000, 1777}; ScriptedClock::next = 0; int calls = 0; auto d = best_of<ScriptedClock>(1, [&calls] { ++calls; }); return d == std::chrono::nanoseconds(777) && calls == 1 && ScriptedClock::next == 2; }()
--- check test | The fastest run is the last one
[] { ScriptedClock::script = {0, 500, 600, 1000, 1000, 1010}; ScriptedClock::next = 0; auto d = best_of<ScriptedClock>(3, [] {}); return d == std::chrono::nanoseconds(10); }()
--- check test | The fastest run is the first one, with gaps between runs
[] { ScriptedClock::script = {10, 12, 5000, 5100, 9000, 9400}; ScriptedClock::next = 0; auto d = best_of<ScriptedClock>(3, [] {}); return d == std::chrono::nanoseconds(2); }()
--- check test | With the real steady_clock: work runs 5 times, and the time is not negative
[] { int calls = 0; long long sink = 0; auto d = best_of<std::chrono::steady_clock>(5, [&] { ++calls; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) sink += i; }); return calls == 5 && d.count() >= 0 && sink == 5 * 499500LL; }()
--- check test | Quadratic, linear and cubic growth
std::fabs(growth_exponent(1000, 2.0, 2000, 8.0) - 2.0) < 1e-9 && std::fabs(growth_exponent(1e6, 10.0, 4e6, 40.0) - 1.0) < 1e-9 && std::fabs(growth_exponent(100, 1.0, 1000, 1000.0) - 3.0) < 1e-9
--- check test | Constant time, and n log n between 1 and 1.1
[] { double c = growth_exponent(1000, 5.0, 8000, 5.0); double nlogn = growth_exponent(1 << 20, (1 << 20) * 20.0, 1 << 21, (1 << 21) * 21.0); return std::fabs(c) < 1e-9 && nlogn > 1.0 && nlogn < 1.1; }()

+++ practice | Mission elapsed time
--- task
Mission control shows elapsed time as `HH:MM:SS.mmm`: hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds, with at least two digits for the hours (more when there are 100 hours or more), exactly two for minutes and seconds, and exactly three for milliseconds. Write `std::string format_duration(std::chrono::milliseconds d)`, with no `main`. `d` is never negative.

Split the duration with `std::chrono::duration_cast`: take the whole hours, subtract them, take the whole minutes of what is left, and so on. For example, 3,723,004 ms is `"01:02:03.004"`, 0 ms is `"00:00:00.000"`, and 100 hours is `"100:00:00.000"`.
--- starter
#include <chrono>
#include <string>

std::string format_duration(std::chrono::milliseconds d) {
    return std::to_string(d.count());
}
--- solution
#include <chrono>
#include <string>

std::string two_digits(long long v, int width) {
    std::string s = std::to_string(v);
    while (static_cast<int>(s.size()) < width) s = "0" + s;
    return s;
}

std::string format_duration(std::chrono::milliseconds d) {
    auto h = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::hours>(d);
    d -= h;
    auto m = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::minutes>(d);
    d -= m;
    auto s = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::seconds>(d);
    d -= s;
    return two_digits(h.count(), 2) + ":" + two_digits(m.count(), 2) + ":" + two_digits(s.count(), 2) + "." + two_digits(d.count(), 3);
}
--- hint
`auto h = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::hours>(d);` gives the whole hours. `d -= h;` removes them: subtracting hours from milliseconds converts them automatically, because that loses nothing.
--- hint
Pad each number with zeros on the left until it has the width it needs: 2 for hours, minutes and seconds, 3 for milliseconds. A small helper taking the number and the width keeps it short.
--- check case | The example from the task
format_duration(std::chrono::milliseconds(3723004))
=> std::string("01:02:03.004")
--- check case | Zero
format_duration(std::chrono::milliseconds(0))
=> std::string("00:00:00.000")
--- check case | A hundred hours
format_duration(std::chrono::hours(100))
=> std::string("100:00:00.000")
--- check case | Just under a day
format_duration(std::chrono::milliseconds(86399999))
=> std::string("23:59:59.999")
--- check case | Minutes and seconds only
format_duration(std::chrono::minutes(7) + std::chrono::seconds(5) + std::chrono::milliseconds(60))
=> std::string("00:07:05.060")

+++ practice | Summarising timing samples
--- task
A benchmark collected one timing per run, in nanoseconds. The first few runs were warm-up and must be ignored. Write, with no `main`:

- `struct Summary { long long min_ns; long long median_ns; };`
- `Summary summarize(std::vector<long long> samples, int warmup)`: drop the first `warmup` samples, then return the smallest remaining sample and the **lower median** of the remaining samples: the one at index (k − 1) / 2, rounded down, when the k remaining samples are sorted. If no samples remain (or `warmup` is at least the number of samples), return {0, 0}.

Use `std::min_element` for the minimum and `std::nth_element` for the median, not a full sort. For example, samples {900, 120, 100, 130, 125, 400} with a warm-up of 1 leave {120, 100, 130, 125, 400}: the minimum is 100 and the lower median is 125.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

struct Summary {
    long long min_ns;
    long long median_ns;
};

Summary summarize(std::vector<long long> samples, int warmup) {
    return {samples[0], samples[0]};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

struct Summary {
    long long min_ns;
    long long median_ns;
};

Summary summarize(std::vector<long long> samples, int warmup) {
    if (warmup < 0) warmup = 0;
    if (static_cast<std::size_t>(warmup) >= samples.size()) return {0, 0};
    samples.erase(samples.begin(), samples.begin() + warmup);
    long long lowest = *std::min_element(samples.begin(), samples.end());
    auto mid = samples.begin() + (samples.size() - 1) / 2;
    std::nth_element(samples.begin(), mid, samples.end());
    return {lowest, *mid};
}
--- hint
Handle "nothing left" first, before touching `samples[0]`. Then `samples.erase(samples.begin(), samples.begin() + warmup)` removes the warm-up runs.
--- hint
The lower median sits at `samples.begin() + (samples.size() - 1) / 2` after `std::nth_element` places it.
--- check test | The example from the task
[] { Summary s = summarize({900, 120, 100, 130, 125, 400}, 1); return s.min_ns == 100 && s.median_ns == 125; }()
--- check test | No warm-up, odd count
[] { Summary s = summarize({7, 3, 5}, 0); return s.min_ns == 3 && s.median_ns == 5; }()
--- check test | Even count takes the lower middle
[] { Summary s = summarize({40, 10, 30, 20}, 0); return s.min_ns == 10 && s.median_ns == 20; }()
--- check test | Everything was warm-up, or no samples at all
[] { Summary a = summarize({5, 6}, 2); Summary b = summarize({5, 6}, 9); Summary c = summarize({}, 0); return a.min_ns == 0 && a.median_ns == 0 && b.min_ns == 0 && c.median_ns == 0; }()
--- check test | One sample left
[] { Summary s = summarize({999, 999, 42}, 2); return s.min_ns == 42 && s.median_ns == 42; }()
--- check test | 100,001 samples after a slow first run
[] { std::vector<long long> v = {1000000000LL}; for (int i = 0; i < 100001; ++i) v.push_back(1000 + (static_cast<long long>(i) * 7919) % 100001); Summary s = summarize(v, 1); return s.min_ns == 1000 && s.median_ns == 51000; }()

+++ practice | Reading growth from a table of timings
--- task
A doubling experiment gives a table of (n, seconds) pairs. With more than two rows, the best estimate of the exponent b in t ≈ c·nᵇ is the slope of the straight line fitted through the points (log n, log t) by **least squares**:

b = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ (xᵢ − x̄)², where xᵢ = log nᵢ, yᵢ = log tᵢ, and x̄, ȳ are their averages.

Write, with no `main`:

- `double fitted_exponent(const std::vector<std::pair<double, double>>& runs)`: that slope. There are at least two rows, with at least two different values of n, and every time is positive.
- `std::string growth_class(const std::vector<std::pair<double, double>>& runs)`: round the slope to the nearest whole number and return `"constant"` for 0, `"linear"` for 1, `"quadratic"` for 2, `"cubic"` for 3, and `"other"` for anything else. (An n log n algorithm has a slope a little above 1, so it reads as linear here.)

For example, the rows (1000, 0.5), (2000, 2.0), (4000, 8.0) have slope exactly 2: `"quadratic"`.
--- starter
#include <cmath>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

double fitted_exponent(const std::vector<std::pair<double, double>>& runs) {
    return std::log(runs.back().second / runs.front().second) / std::log(runs.back().first / runs.front().first) + 0.3;
}

std::string growth_class(const std::vector<std::pair<double, double>>& runs) {
    return "other";
}
--- solution
#include <cmath>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

double fitted_exponent(const std::vector<std::pair<double, double>>& runs) {
    double mean_x = 0.0;
    double mean_y = 0.0;
    for (auto [n, t] : runs) {
        mean_x += std::log(n);
        mean_y += std::log(t);
    }
    mean_x /= runs.size();
    mean_y /= runs.size();
    double top = 0.0;
    double bottom = 0.0;
    for (auto [n, t] : runs) {
        double dx = std::log(n) - mean_x;
        top += dx * (std::log(t) - mean_y);
        bottom += dx * dx;
    }
    return top / bottom;
}

std::string growth_class(const std::vector<std::pair<double, double>>& runs) {
    long long k = std::llround(fitted_exponent(runs));
    if (k == 0) return "constant";
    if (k == 1) return "linear";
    if (k == 2) return "quadratic";
    if (k == 3) return "cubic";
    return "other";
}
--- hint
Make two passes over the rows. The first adds up log n and log t to get the two averages. The second adds up `dx * dy` and `dx * dx`, where `dx` and `dy` are the distances from the averages.
--- hint
For `growth_class`, `std::llround` from `<cmath>` rounds to the nearest whole number as a `long long`.
--- check test | The example from the task
std::fabs(fitted_exponent({{1000, 0.5}, {2000, 2.0}, {4000, 8.0}}) - 2.0) < 1e-9 && growth_class({{1000, 0.5}, {2000, 2.0}, {4000, 8.0}}) == "quadratic"
--- check test | Two rows are just the two-point formula
std::fabs(fitted_exponent({{100, 3.0}, {800, 24.0}}) - 1.0) < 1e-9 && growth_class({{100, 3.0}, {800, 24.0}}) == "linear"
--- check test | Noisy cubic data
[] { std::vector<std::pair<double, double>> r; double noise[] = {1.04, 0.97, 1.02, 0.99, 1.03}; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) { double n = 100.0 * (1 << i); r.push_back({n, 1e-9 * n * n * n * noise[i]}); } double b = fitted_exponent(r); return b > 2.95 && b < 3.05 && growth_class(r) == "cubic"; }()
--- check test | n log n reads as linear, flat as constant
[] { std::vector<std::pair<double, double>> r, c; for (int i = 10; i <= 20; ++i) { double n = 1 << i; r.push_back({n, n * i * 1e-8}); c.push_back({n, 0.002}); } double b = fitted_exponent(r); return b > 1.05 && b < 1.2 && growth_class(r) == "linear" && growth_class(c) == "constant"; }()
--- check test | A jump the rounding calls other
growth_class({{10, 1.0}, {100, 100000.0}}) == "other" && growth_class({{10, 1.0}, {100, 0.001}}) == "other"

+++ practice | A direct-mapped cache, edge cases included
--- task
Model a **direct-mapped cache**: it has `lines` slots, each holding one block of `line_bytes` bytes. An address a belongs to block L = a / line_bytes (integer division); the block can only go in slot L % lines, and the slot remembers which block it holds by the **tag** L / lines. An access is a **hit** if the slot already holds that block's tag, and a **miss** otherwise, after which the slot holds it.

Write `long long count_misses(const std::vector<long long>& addresses, int line_bytes, int lines)`, with no `main`: the number of misses for the accesses in order, starting from an empty cache (every slot empty, so the first access to any slot misses). Addresses are non-negative and can be as large as 10¹⁵, so keep them in `long long`.

The edge cases the checks use: no accesses at all, a cache of one slot, blocks of one byte, the same address again and again, two addresses that fight over one slot, and huge addresses. For example, with 64-byte blocks and 2 slots, the accesses 0, 8, 16, 64, 0, 128, 0 give 4 misses: 0 misses, 8 and 16 hit (same block), 64 misses (slot 1), 0 hits, 128 misses (block 2 takes slot 0), and 0 misses again.
--- starter
#include <vector>

long long count_misses(const std::vector<long long>& addresses, int line_bytes, int lines) {
    return static_cast<long long>(addresses.size());
}
--- solution
#include <vector>

long long count_misses(const std::vector<long long>& addresses, int line_bytes, int lines) {
    std::vector<long long> tag(lines, -1);   // -1: the slot is empty
    long long misses = 0;
    for (long long a : addresses) {
        long long block = a / line_bytes;
        long long slot = block % lines;
        long long t = block / lines;
        if (tag[slot] != t) {
            tag[slot] = t;
            ++misses;
        }
    }
    return misses;
}
--- hint
Keep one `long long` tag per slot, starting at −1 to mean "empty": no real tag is negative, so the first access to every slot misses.
--- hint
For each address, work out the block, the slot and the tag, all in `long long`. A miss is a tag that differs from the one stored; store the new tag and count it.
--- check case | The example from the task
count_misses({0, 8, 16, 64, 0, 128, 0}, 64, 2)
=> 4LL
--- check case | No accesses
count_misses({}, 64, 4)
=> 0LL
--- check case | The same address again and again
count_misses({5, 5, 5, 5}, 1, 1)
=> 1LL
--- check case | Two blocks fighting over a one-slot cache
count_misses({0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1}, 1, 1)
=> 6LL
--- check case | The first access to slot 0 misses, even for block 0
count_misses({0}, 64, 8)
=> 1LL
--- check case | Huge addresses
count_misses({1000000000000000LL, 1000000000000063LL, 1000000000000064LL, 1000000000000000LL}, 64, 8)
=> 2LL
--- check case | 200,000 mixed accesses
[] { std::vector<long long> tr; unsigned s = 7; for (int i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; tr.push_back(i % 3 ? static_cast<long long>((s >> 4) % (1u << 20)) : static_cast<long long>(i) * 4); } return count_misses(tr, 64, 256); }()
=> 143987LL

+++ practice | Debug: the average that lost its fractions
--- task
`average_ms(samples)` should return the mean of timing samples, given in microseconds, as a number of milliseconds with its fraction: samples of 400 µs and 700 µs average 0.55 ms. It returns 0.5 instead. An empty list should give 0.0, which already works. Find the bug and fix it.
--- starter
#include <chrono>
#include <vector>

double average_ms(const std::vector<std::chrono::microseconds>& samples) {
    if (samples.empty()) return 0.0;
    std::chrono::microseconds total(0);
    for (auto s : samples) total += s;
    return std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(total).count() / static_cast<double>(samples.size());
}
--- solution
#include <chrono>
#include <vector>

double average_ms(const std::vector<std::chrono::microseconds>& samples) {
    if (samples.empty()) return 0.0;
    std::chrono::microseconds total(0);
    for (auto s : samples) total += s;
    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(total).count() / static_cast<double>(samples.size());
}
--- hint
Work out the total for 400 µs and 700 µs, then what `duration_cast<milliseconds>` does to it.
--- hint
`duration_cast` to milliseconds drops the fraction: 1,100 µs becomes 1 ms. Convert to a duration with a `double` count instead, `std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(total)`, which keeps 1.1 ms.
--- check test | The example from the task

--- check test | Under a millisecond in total
std::fabs(average_ms({std::chrono::microseconds(999)}) - 0.999) < 1e-12
--- check test | Whole milliseconds still work
std::fabs(average_ms({std::chrono::microseconds(2000), std::chrono::microseconds(4000)}) - 3.0) < 1e-12
--- check test | No samples

+++ practice | Why the list is slower: a cache model
--- task
Explain the vector-against-list gap by counting cache misses in a model. Use a direct-mapped cache as in the earlier problem (`lines` slots of `line_bytes`-byte blocks; block L = a / line_bytes goes in slot L % lines with tag L / lines; the cache starts empty).

- Summing a `std::vector<int>` of n values reads the addresses 0, 4, 8, …, 4(n − 1), in that order.
- Summing a list of n values reads one 16-byte node per value. The node for the k-th value in the list is stored at address 2³⁰ + 16 × `order[k]`, where `order` is a permutation of 0 to n − 1 describing where the allocator happened to put each node.

Write `std::pair<long long, long long> sum_misses(int n, const std::vector<int>& order, int line_bytes, int lines)`, with no `main`, returning the misses of the vector sum and of the list sum, in that order, each counted from an empty cache.

For example, with n = 8, `order` = {3, 1, 0, 2, 7, 5, 4, 6}, 64-byte blocks and 2 slots, the answer is {1, 2}: the whole vector fits in one block, and the list's nodes fill two blocks, each missed once. The checks then run 100,000 values with 64-byte blocks and 512 slots: with nodes in order the list misses 25,000 times (four nodes per block) against the vector's 6,250 (sixteen ints per block), and with nodes scattered by a shuffle it misses almost every time.
--- starter
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::pair<long long, long long> sum_misses(int n, const std::vector<int>& order, int line_bytes, int lines) {
    return {n, n};
}
--- solution
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

long long misses_of(const std::vector<long long>& addresses, int line_bytes, int lines) {
    std::vector<long long> tag(lines, -1);
    long long misses = 0;
    for (long long a : addresses) {
        long long block = a / line_bytes;
        long long slot = block % lines;
        long long t = block / lines;
        if (tag[slot] != t) {
            tag[slot] = t;
            ++misses;
        }
    }
    return misses;
}

std::pair<long long, long long> sum_misses(int n, const std::vector<int>& order, int line_bytes, int lines) {
    std::vector<long long> vec_addresses;
    std::vector<long long> list_addresses;
    vec_addresses.reserve(n);
    list_addresses.reserve(n);
    const long long list_base = 1LL << 30;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        vec_addresses.push_back(4LL * i);
        list_addresses.push_back(list_base + 16LL * order[i]);
    }
    return {misses_of(vec_addresses, line_bytes, lines), misses_of(list_addresses, line_bytes, lines)};
}
--- hint
Build the two address traces as vectors of `long long`, then run the same miss counter on each. The counter is the direct-mapped model from the earlier problem, with a fresh, empty cache per trace.
--- hint
The k-th list access is at `(1LL << 30) + 16LL * order[k]`. Compute in `long long` so nothing overflows.
--- check case | The example from the task
sum_misses(8, {3, 1, 0, 2, 7, 5, 4, 6}, 64, 2)
=> std::pair<long long, long long>{1, 2}
--- check case | Nodes in memory order: 100,000 values
[] { std::vector<int> order(100000); for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) order[i] = i; return sum_misses(100000, order, 64, 512); }()
=> std::pair<long long, long long>{6250, 25000}
--- check case | Nodes scattered by a shuffle: 100,000 values
[] { std::vector<int> order(100000); for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) order[i] = i; unsigned s = 4242; for (int i = 99999; i > 0; --i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int j = static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % static_cast<unsigned>(i + 1)); std::swap(order[i], order[j]); } return sum_misses(100000, order, 64, 512); }()
=> std::pair<long long, long long>{6250, 98473}
--- check case | No values
sum_misses(0, {}, 64, 4)
=> std::pair<long long, long long>{0, 0}

+++ question | Why keep the fastest run
--- ask
You time the same function 20 times. Why is the **minimum** usually a better estimate of its cost than the average?
--- choice
The minimum is always exactly the true cost.
--- choice correct
Noise from other programs, interrupts and cold caches only ever adds time, so the smallest run is the one least disturbed.
--- choice
The average is skewed by the clock's rounding, and the minimum is not.
--- choice
The compiler optimises the later runs, and the minimum picks the optimised one.
--- why
A measured time is the true cost plus a disturbance that is never negative. The average includes every disturbance; the minimum includes the smallest one, and it only gets closer to the true cost as you add runs. (For a latency budget you would look at the maximum instead: there the question is how slow it can get.)

+++ question | What duration_cast prints
--- ask
What does this print?

```cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::chrono::milliseconds total(2999);
    std::cout << std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::seconds>(total).count() << "\n";
}
```
--- answer
2
--- why
`duration_cast` to a coarser unit drops the remainder, like integer division: 2,999 ms is 2 whole seconds and 999 ms, and the 999 ms are thrown away. For 3, use `std::chrono::round<std::chrono::seconds>`; for 2.999, cast to `std::chrono::duration<double>`.

+++ question | Reading a doubling experiment
--- ask
A function takes 0.20 s at n = 100,000, 0.81 s at n = 200,000 and 3.18 s at n = 400,000. What growth does that suggest?
--- choice
Linear: the time grows with n.
--- choice
n log n: the ratios are a little above 2.
--- choice correct
Quadratic: each doubling of n multiplies the time by about 4.
--- choice
Exponential: the time more than doubles each step.
--- why
The ratios are 0.81 / 0.20 ≈ 4.05 and 3.18 / 0.81 ≈ 3.93, so b ≈ log₂ 4 = 2. n log n would give ratios near 2.1, linear near 2. Exponential growth in n would multiply the time by a huge factor for each extra 100,000, not by a steady 4.

+++ problem | A vector with room inside
--- task
Many small vectors never grow past a handful of elements, and allocating heap memory for each is wasteful. Write `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class SmallVector`: a vector that keeps up to `N` elements in a buffer **inside the object**, and moves to heap memory only when it grows past that. No `main`.

The starter gives the heap ledger (`heap::live` counts blocks from `operator new` not yet given back), the counting element `Probe` (no default constructor), and the inline buffer: `alignas(T) unsigned char inline_[N * sizeof(T)]`, with `inline_data()` returning it as a `T*`. Keep them as they are. Build elements with `std::construct_at`, destroy them with `std::destroy_at`, and get heap memory from `std::allocator<T>`, as in lesson 3.

- A new `SmallVector` has size 0, capacity `N`, and allocates nothing.
- `push_back(const T&)` and `push_back(T&&)`. When the vector is full, allocate twice the capacity, **move** the elements across, destroy the old ones, and free the old block if it was on the heap.
- `pop_back()` destroys the last element (nothing if empty); `size()`, `capacity()`, `operator[]` (both versions), and `begin()`/`end()` returning `T*`, so range-for and `std::sort` work.
- The destructor destroys every element and frees heap memory.
- The copy constructor makes a deep copy: inline if it fits in `N`, otherwise on the heap with capacity equal to the size.
- The move constructor: if the source is on the heap, take its block without allocating or moving any element, and leave the source empty and inline (size 0, capacity `N`). If the source is inline, move-construct each element into this object's buffer, destroy the source's elements, and leave the source empty.
- Copy and move **assignment** are deleted.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: blocks from operator new not yet given back. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// An element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class SmallVector {
public:
    SmallVector() {}
    SmallVector(const SmallVector& other) {}
    SmallVector(SmallVector&& other) noexcept {}
    SmallVector& operator=(const SmallVector&) = delete;
    SmallVector& operator=(SmallVector&&) = delete;
    ~SmallVector() {}

    void push_back(const T& x) {}
    void push_back(T&& x) {}
    void pop_back() {}

    std::size_t size() const { return 0; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return 0; }
    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    T* begin() { return data_; }
    T* end() { return data_; }

private:
    T* inline_data() { return reinterpret_cast<T*>(inline_); }

    alignas(T) unsigned char inline_[N * sizeof(T)];
    T* data_ = nullptr;
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

// The heap ledger: blocks from operator new not yet given back. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

// An element with no default constructor that counts itself. Leave it as it is.
struct Probe {
    static inline int live = 0;
    static inline int copies = 0;
    static inline int moves = 0;
    int id;
    explicit Probe(int i) : id(i) { ++live; }
    Probe(const Probe& o) : id(o.id) { ++live; ++copies; }
    Probe(Probe&& o) noexcept : id(o.id) { ++live; ++moves; }
    Probe& operator=(const Probe& o) { id = o.id; ++copies; return *this; }
    Probe& operator=(Probe&& o) noexcept { id = o.id; ++moves; return *this; }
    ~Probe() { --live; }
};

template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class SmallVector {
public:
    SmallVector() : data_(inline_data()), size_(0), cap_(N) {}

    SmallVector(const SmallVector& other) : data_(inline_data()), size_(0), cap_(N) {
        if (other.size_ > N) {
            data_ = std::allocator<T>().allocate(other.size_);
            cap_ = other.size_;
        }
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < other.size_; ++i) std::construct_at(data_ + i, other.data_[i]);
        size_ = other.size_;
    }

    SmallVector(SmallVector&& other) noexcept : data_(inline_data()), size_(0), cap_(N) {
        if (other.on_heap()) {
            data_ = other.data_;
            size_ = other.size_;
            cap_ = other.cap_;
        } else {
            for (std::size_t i = 0; i < other.size_; ++i) {
                std::construct_at(data_ + i, std::move(other.data_[i]));
                std::destroy_at(other.data_ + i);
            }
            size_ = other.size_;
        }
        other.data_ = other.inline_data();
        other.size_ = 0;
        other.cap_ = N;
    }

    SmallVector& operator=(const SmallVector&) = delete;
    SmallVector& operator=(SmallVector&&) = delete;

    ~SmallVector() {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
        if (on_heap()) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
    }

    void push_back(const T& x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) grow();
        std::construct_at(data_ + size_, x);
        ++size_;
    }

    void push_back(T&& x) {
        if (size_ == cap_) grow();
        std::construct_at(data_ + size_, std::move(x));
        ++size_;
    }

    void pop_back() {
        if (size_ == 0) return;
        --size_;
        std::destroy_at(data_ + size_);
    }

    std::size_t size() const { return size_; }
    std::size_t capacity() const { return cap_; }
    T& operator[](std::size_t i) { return data_[i]; }
    const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const { return data_[i]; }
    T* begin() { return data_; }
    T* end() { return data_ + size_; }

private:
    T* inline_data() { return reinterpret_cast<T*>(inline_); }
    bool on_heap() const { return data_ != reinterpret_cast<const T*>(inline_); }

    void grow() {
        std::size_t new_cap = cap_ * 2;
        T* fresh = std::allocator<T>().allocate(new_cap);
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < size_; ++i) {
            std::construct_at(fresh + i, std::move(data_[i]));
            std::destroy_at(data_ + i);
        }
        if (on_heap()) std::allocator<T>().deallocate(data_, cap_);
        data_ = fresh;
        cap_ = new_cap;
    }

    alignas(T) unsigned char inline_[N * sizeof(T)];
    T* data_ = nullptr;
    std::size_t size_ = 0;
    std::size_t cap_ = 0;
};
--- check test | Up to N elements live inside: no heap memory
[] { long long before = heap::live; SmallVector<int, 4> v; for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) v.push_back(i * 10); return heap::live == before && v.size() == 4 && v.capacity() == 4 && v[3] == 30; }()
--- check test | The fifth element moves everything to one heap block of capacity 8
[] { long long before = heap::live; SmallVector<int, 4> v; for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) v.push_back(i); bool ok = heap::live == before + 1 && v.capacity() == 8 && v[0] == 0 && v[4] == 4; return ok; }()
--- check test | Growth moves Probes and never copies them

+++ problem | A text buffer with a cursor
--- task
A command console edits one line of text with a cursor between characters. Write `class TextBuffer`, with no `main`, as a **doubly linked list of characters with a sentinel node**: each node owns the next one through a `std::unique_ptr<Node>`, and points back at the previous one with a plain `Node*` that owns nothing. Do not use `std::list`, `std::string` or `std::vector` to hold the text.

The cursor sits just before some node; when it sits before the sentinel, it is at the end of the text.

- `void insert(char c)`: puts `c` just before the cursor (the cursor stays after it).
- `bool backspace()`: deletes the character just before the cursor and returns `true`, or returns `false` at the start.
- `bool left()` and `bool right()`: move the cursor one character, or return `false` at the start or end.
- `std::string text() const`: the whole text; `int size() const`.
- The destructor must free every node **without recursion**: a check builds a line of a million characters, and a chain of `unique_ptr` destructors a million calls deep overflows the stack.

Every operation except `text()` must be O(1). The starter gives the heap ledger, `heap::live`; the checks use it to catch leaks.

For example: insert a, b, c; left; left; insert X; the text is `"aXbc"`. Then backspace; right; right; backspace: the text is `"ab"`.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: blocks from operator new not yet given back. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class TextBuffer {
public:
    void insert(char c) {}
    bool backspace() { return false; }
    bool left() { return false; }
    bool right() { return false; }
    std::string text() const { return ""; }
    int size() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <memory>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

// The heap ledger: blocks from operator new not yet given back. Leave it as it is.
namespace heap { inline long long live = 0; }
void* operator new(std::size_t bytes) { ++heap::live; return std::malloc(bytes ? bytes : 1); }
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { if (p) { --heap::live; std::free(p); } }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { operator delete(p); }

class TextBuffer {
public:
    TextBuffer() : cursor_(&end_) {}

    TextBuffer(const TextBuffer&) = delete;
    TextBuffer& operator=(const TextBuffer&) = delete;

    ~TextBuffer() {
        std::unique_ptr<Node> p = std::move(first_);
        while (p) p = std::move(p->next);   // each step frees one node; its next was moved out first
    }

    void insert(char c) {
        auto node = std::make_unique<Node>();
        node->ch = c;
        Node* before = cursor_->prev;
        std::unique_ptr<Node>& slot = before ? before->next : first_;   // owns the cursor node, or is empty at the end
        node->prev = before;
        node->next = std::move(slot);
        cursor_->prev = node.get();
        slot = std::move(node);
        ++size_;
    }

    bool backspace() {
        Node* victim = cursor_->prev;
        if (!victim) return false;
        Node* before = victim->prev;
        std::unique_ptr<Node>& slot = before ? before->next : first_;   // owns victim
        cursor_->prev = before;
        slot = std::move(victim->next);   // takes victim's successor, which frees victim
        --size_;
        return true;
    }

    bool left() {
        if (!cursor_->prev) return false;
        cursor_ = cursor_->prev;
        return true;
    }

    bool right() {
        if (cursor_ == &end_) return false;
        cursor_ = cursor_->next ? cursor_->next.get() : &end_;
        return true;
    }

    std::string text() const {
        std::string out;
        out.reserve(size_);
        for (const Node* p = first_.get(); p; p = p->next.get()) out += p->ch;
        return out;
    }

    int size() const { return size_; }

private:
    struct Node {
        char ch = 0;
        std::unique_ptr<Node> next;   // owns the node after this one
        Node* prev = nullptr;         // observes the node before this one
    };

    std::unique_ptr<Node> first_;   // owns the first character's node
    Node end_;                      // the sentinel: never owned, never freed; end_.prev is the last character
    Node* cursor_;                  // the node the cursor sits before
    int size_ = 0;
};

+++ problem | Duplicate packets in a sliding window
--- task
Radio links resend packets, so a ground station sees duplicates. A packet is identified by `struct PacketId { int craft; long long seq; }` (given in the starter, with a defaulted `==`). The station remembers only the last `window` packets it **accepted**. Write, with no `main`:

- `struct PacketIdHash`, a hash for `PacketId` that mixes both fields (the lesson 13 mixer works).
- `class DupFilter` with `explicit DupFilter(int window)` (window at least 1):
  - `bool accept(const PacketId& p)`: if `p` is among the remembered packets, return `false` and change nothing. Otherwise accept it: it becomes the newest remembered packet, the oldest is forgotten if `window` packets were already remembered, and return `true`.
  - `int remembered() const`: how many packets are remembered now.

Keep the remembered packets in a **ring buffer**, a `std::vector<PacketId>` of size `window` allocated once, with the index of the oldest and a count, as in lesson 7; and keep an `std::unordered_set<PacketId, PacketIdHash>` of the same packets for O(1) lookups. A check feeds 500,000 packets through a window of 50,000, so scanning the window for every packet is too slow.

For example, with a window of 2: accept (1, 5) → true, (1, 5) → false, (2, 5) → true, (1, 6) → true (so (1, 5) is forgotten), (1, 5) → true.
--- starter
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <deque>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>

struct PacketId {
    int craft;
    long long seq;
    bool operator==(const PacketId&) const = default;
};

struct PacketIdHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const PacketId& p) const { return 0; }
};

class DupFilter {
public:
    explicit DupFilter(int window) {}
    bool accept(const PacketId& p) { return true; }
    int remembered() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <deque>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>

struct PacketId {
    int craft;
    long long seq;
    bool operator==(const PacketId&) const = default;
};

std::uint64_t mix(std::uint64_t z) {
    z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
    z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
    return z ^ (z >> 31);
}

struct PacketIdHash {
    std::size_t operator()(const PacketId& p) const {
        std::uint64_t h = mix(0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL + static_cast<std::uint32_t>(p.craft));
        h = mix(h + 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL + static_cast<std::uint64_t>(p.seq));
        return static_cast<std::size_t>(h);
    }
};

class DupFilter {
public:
    explicit DupFilter(int window) : ring_(window, PacketId{0, 0}) { seen_.reserve(window); }

    bool accept(const PacketId& p) {
        if (seen_.contains(p)) return false;
        int cap = static_cast<int>(ring_.size());
        if (count_ == cap) {
            seen_.erase(ring_[oldest_]);
            ring_[oldest_] = p;
            oldest_ = (oldest_ + 1) % cap;
        } else {
            ring_[(oldest_ + count_) % cap] = p;
            ++count_;
        }
        seen_.insert(p);
        return true;
    }

    int remembered() const { return count_; }

private:
    std::vector<PacketId> ring_;
    int oldest_ = 0;
    int count_ = 0;
    std::unordered_set<PacketId, PacketIdHash> seen_;
};

+++ problem | Median per sensor
--- task
A ground station receives readings as (sensor name, value) pairs, all sensors mixed together. Write `std::vector<std::pair<std::string, double>> sensor_medians(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, double>>& readings)`, with no `main`. It returns one pair per sensor: the sensor's name and the **median** of its values (the middle value for an odd count, the mean of the two middle values for an even count), sorted by name from A to Z. No readings give an empty result.

Group the values with an `std::unordered_map<std::string, std::vector<double>>`, find each group's median with `std::nth_element` (the lower middle, for an even count, is the largest element before the upper middle), and sort the result by name at the end. With n readings in total that is O(n) expected for the medians plus O(s log s) to sort the s sensor names.

For example, readings ("gyro", 3), ("sun", 10), ("gyro", 1), ("gyro", 2), ("sun", 20) give {("gyro", 2.0), ("sun", 15.0)}.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

std::vector<std::pair<std::string, double>> sensor_medians(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, double>>& readings) {
    return {};
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

double median_of(std::vector<double>& v) {
    auto mid = v.begin() + v.size() / 2;
    std::nth_element(v.begin(), mid, v.end());
    if (v.size() % 2 == 1) return *mid;
    return (*std::max_element(v.begin(), mid) + *mid) / 2.0;
}

std::vector<std::pair<std::string, double>> sensor_medians(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, double>>& readings) {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::vector<double>> groups;
    for (const auto& [name, value] : readings) groups[name].push_back(value);
    std::vector<std::pair<std::string, double>> out;
    out.reserve(groups.size());
    for (auto& [name, values] : groups) out.push_back({name, median_of(values)});
    std::sort(out.begin(), out.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) { return a.first < b.first; });
    return out;
}

+++ problem | A heap that can lower a key
--- task
Textbook Dijkstra needs a priority queue that can **lower** an item's key in place. Write `class IndexedMinHeap`, with no `main`, for items numbered 0 to n − 1, as a binary heap in a `std::vector<int>` of item numbers, plus a `std::vector<int>` giving each item's position in that heap (−1 when absent) and a `std::vector<long long>` of keys:

- `explicit IndexedMinHeap(int n)`: an empty heap for items 0 to n − 1.
- `void push_or_lower(int item, long long key)`: if the item is absent, insert it with that key; if it is present with a **larger** key, lower its key to `key`; otherwise do nothing.
- `int pop_min()`: remove and return the item with the smallest key, the smaller item number among equal keys, or −1 if empty.
- `bool contains(int item) const`, `long long key_of(int item) const` (only called for items present), and `int size() const`.

Every operation must be O(log n): lowering a key sifts the item up from where it is, which is why the position vector exists. Keep the position vector correct on every swap. A check makes 300,000 calls.

For example: push_or_lower(3, 50), push_or_lower(1, 20), push_or_lower(4, 30), push_or_lower(3, 10), push_or_lower(1, 25) (ignored: 25 is larger); then pop_min gives 3, then 1, then 4, then −1.
--- starter
#include <map>
#include <set>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IndexedMinHeap {
public:
    explicit IndexedMinHeap(int n) {}
    void push_or_lower(int item, long long key) {}
    int pop_min() { return -1; }
    bool contains(int item) const { return false; }
    long long key_of(int item) const { return 0; }
    int size() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <map>
#include <set>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class IndexedMinHeap {
public:
    explicit IndexedMinHeap(int n) : pos_(n, -1), key_(n, 0) {}

    void push_or_lower(int item, long long key) {
        if (pos_[item] == -1) {
            key_[item] = key;
            pos_[item] = static_cast<int>(heap_.size());
            heap_.push_back(item);
            sift_up(pos_[item]);
        } else if (key < key_[item]) {
            key_[item] = key;
            sift_up(pos_[item]);
        }
    }

    int pop_min() {
        if (heap_.empty()) return -1;
        int top = heap_[0];
        place(0, heap_.back());
        heap_.pop_back();
        pos_[top] = -1;
        if (!heap_.empty()) sift_down(0);
        return top;
    }

    bool contains(int item) const { return pos_[item] != -1; }
    long long key_of(int item) const { return key_[item]; }
    int size() const { return static_cast<int>(heap_.size()); }

private:
    bool before(int a, int b) const { return key_[a] != key_[b] ? key_[a] < key_[b] : a < b; }

    void place(int i, int item) {
        heap_[i] = item;
        pos_[item] = i;
    }

    void sift_up(int i) {
        int item = heap_[i];
        while (i > 0) {
            int parent = (i - 1) / 2;
            if (!before(item, heap_[parent])) break;
            place(i, heap_[parent]);
            i = parent;
        }
        place(i, item);
    }

    void sift_down(int i) {
        int n = static_cast<int>(heap_.size());
        int item = heap_[i];
        while (true) {
            int child = 2 * i + 1;
            if (child >= n) break;
            if (child + 1 < n && before(heap_[child + 1], heap_[child])) ++child;
            if (!before(heap_[child], item)) break;
            place(i, heap_[child]);
            i = child;
        }
        place(i, item);
    }

    std::vector<int> heap_;
    std::vector<int> pos_;
    std::vector<long long> key_;
};
--- check test | The example from the task

+++ problem | Two keys swapped in a search tree
--- task
A binary search tree had two of its keys swapped by a memory fault: the shape is untouched, but two nodes now hold each other's keys, so an in-order walk is no longer sorted. The starter gives `struct Node` (a key, and `unique_ptr` children) and `struct Tree`, whose destructor takes the tree apart without recursion; keep both. All keys are different. Write, with no `main`:

- `std::vector<int> in_order(const Node* root)`: the keys in in-order (left subtree, node, right subtree), using an **explicit stack** of `const Node*`, not recursion. Trees in the checks are up to 200,000 levels deep.
- `void repair(Node* root)`: find the two nodes whose keys were swapped and swap their keys back, so the tree is a valid search tree again. It must also be iterative.

In the in-order sequence of the damaged tree, look for places where a key is bigger than the next one. If the two swapped nodes were next to each other in in-order, there is one such place, and the two nodes are its two sides. Otherwise there are two places: the first node of the first place and the second node of the second place were swapped. Remember **nodes** (pointers) during the walk, not just keys, so you can fix them.

For example, the tree with root 2, left child 3 and right child 1 walks in in-order as 3, 2, 1; `repair` swaps the 3 and the 1, and the walk becomes 1, 2, 3.
--- starter
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    explicit Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

// Owns a tree and takes it apart without recursion. Leave it as it is.
struct Tree {
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root;
    ~Tree() {
        std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> pending;
        if (root) pending.push_back(std::move(root));
        while (!pending.empty()) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> n = std::move(pending.back());
            pending.pop_back();
            if (n->left) pending.push_back(std::move(n->left));
            if (n->right) pending.push_back(std::move(n->right));
        }
    }
};

std::vector<int> in_order(const Node* root) {
    return {};
}

void repair(Node* root) {}
--- solution
#include <memory>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Node {
    int key;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> left;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> right;
    explicit Node(int k) : key(k) {}
};

// Owns a tree and takes it apart without recursion. Leave it as it is.
struct Tree {
    std::unique_ptr<Node> root;
    ~Tree() {
        std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Node>> pending;
        if (root) pending.push_back(std::move(root));
        while (!pending.empty()) {
            std::unique_ptr<Node> n = std::move(pending.back());
            pending.pop_back();
            if (n->left) pending.push_back(std::move(n->left));
            if (n->right) pending.push_back(std::move(n->right));
        }
    }
};

std::vector<int> in_order(const Node* root) {
    std::vector<int> keys;
    std::vector<const Node*> stack;
    const Node* at = root;
    while (at || !stack.empty()) {
        while (at) {
            stack.push_back(at);
            at = at->left.get();
        }
        at = stack.back();
        stack.pop_back();
        keys.push_back(at->key);
        at = at->right.get();
    }
    return keys;
}

void repair(Node* root) {
    Node* first = nullptr;
    Node* second = nullptr;
    Node* previous = nullptr;
    std::vector<Node*> stack;
    Node* at = root;
    while (at || !stack.empty()) {
        while (at) {
            stack.push_back(at);
            at = at->left.get();
        }
        at = stack.back();
        stack.pop_back();
        if (previous && previous->key > at->key) {
            if (!first) first = previous;
            second = at;
        }
        previous = at;
        at = at->right.get();
    }
    if (first && second) std::swap(first->key, second->key);
}

+++ problem | Coverage of a sky survey
--- task
A telescope survey records which stretches of a long strip of sky it has covered, as half-open intervals [lo, hi) of whole numbers (lo < hi, values up to 2,000,000,000). Write `class Coverage`, with no `main`:

- `void add(long long lo, long long hi)`: records [lo, hi). Stored intervals never overlap or touch: an interval that overlaps or touches others (like [1, 3) and [3, 5)) is merged with them into one.
- `long long covered() const`: the total length covered, counting overlaps once.
- `bool contains(long long x) const`: whether some stored interval has lo ≤ x < hi.
- `int pieces() const`: how many separate intervals are stored.

Store the intervals in an `std::map<long long, long long>` from start to end, and keep the covered total as you go. In `add`, `upper_bound(lo)` finds the first interval starting after `lo`; the one just before it (if any) may reach `lo`; then absorb every following interval that starts at or before `hi`. Each interval is inserted once and erased at most once, so a long run of adds costs O(log n) amortised per add. A check makes 200,000 adds.

For example: add [10, 20), add [30, 40), add [15, 30); then there is 1 piece, [10, 40), covering 30, and `contains(40)` is `false`.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>
#include <vector>

class Coverage {
public:
    void add(long long lo, long long hi) {}
    long long covered() const { return 0; }
    bool contains(long long x) const { return false; }
    int pieces() const { return 0; }
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <iterator>
#include <map>
#include <vector>

class Coverage {
public:
    void add(long long lo, long long hi) {
        auto it = spans_.upper_bound(lo);
        if (it != spans_.begin()) {
            auto before = std::prev(it);
            if (before->second >= lo) {
                lo = before->first;
                hi = std::max(hi, before->second);
                total_ -= before->second - before->first;
                it = spans_.erase(before);
            }
        }
        while (it != spans_.end() && it->first <= hi) {
            hi = std::max(hi, it->second);
            total_ -= it->second - it->first;
            it = spans_.erase(it);
        }
        spans_[lo] = hi;
        total_ += hi - lo;
    }

    long long covered() const { return total_; }

    bool contains(long long x) const {
        auto it = spans_.upper_bound(x);
        if (it == spans_.begin()) return false;
        return x < std::prev(it)->second;
    }

    int pieces() const { return static_cast<int>(spans_.size()); }

private:
    std::map<long long, long long> spans_;   // start -> end, disjoint and not touching
    long long total_ = 0;
};
