+++ problem | Autocomplete from a trie
--- task
A command console suggests completions as the operator types. Write `class Autocomplete`, with no `main`, on a trie whose nodes live in a `std::vector` with `std::array<int, 26>` children (indexes, 0 for none), as in lesson 17:

- `void add(const std::string& word, int times)`: the word (lowercase letters only, at least one letter) was typed `times` more times (at least 1). Counts add up over calls.
- `std::vector<std::string> top3(const std::string& prefix) const`: up to three words that start with `prefix` (a word counts as starting with itself), the most-typed first; words typed equally often in alphabetical order. The empty prefix matches every word. No match gives an empty vector.

Walk to the prefix's node, collect every (count, word) pair in the subtree below it, then keep the best three with `std::partial_sort` (lesson 15) and a comparator you write: higher count first, then smaller word.

For example, after add("burn", 5), add("bus", 2), add("bursts", 5), add("busy", 9), add("arm", 1): `top3("bu")` is {"busy", "burn", "bursts"}, `top3("bur")` is {"burn", "bursts"}, and `top3("c")` is empty.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Autocomplete {
public:
    void add(const std::string& word, int times) {}
    std::vector<std::string> top3(const std::string& prefix) const { return {}; }
};
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

class Autocomplete {
public:
    Autocomplete() : nodes_(1) {}

    void add(const std::string& word, int times) {
        int at = 0;
        for (char c : word) {
            int slot = c - 'a';
            if (nodes_[at].child[slot] == 0) {
                nodes_.push_back(Node{});
                nodes_[at].child[slot] = static_cast<int>(nodes_.size()) - 1;
            }
            at = nodes_[at].child[slot];
        }
        nodes_[at].count += times;
    }

    std::vector<std::string> top3(const std::string& prefix) const {
        int at = 0;
        for (char c : prefix) {
            at = nodes_[at].child[c - 'a'];
            if (at == 0) return {};
        }
        std::vector<std::pair<long long, std::string>> found;
        std::vector<std::pair<int, std::string>> stack = {{at, prefix}};
        while (!stack.empty()) {
            auto [node, word] = std::move(stack.back());
            stack.pop_back();
            if (nodes_[node].count > 0) found.push_back({nodes_[node].count, word});
            for (int slot = 0; slot < 26; ++slot) {
                int next = nodes_[node].child[slot];
                if (next != 0) stack.push_back({next, word + static_cast<char>('a' + slot)});
            }
        }
        std::size_t keep = std::min<std::size_t>(3, found.size());
        std::partial_sort(found.begin(), found.begin() + keep, found.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) {
            return a.first != b.first ? a.first > b.first : a.second < b.second;
        });
        std::vector<std::string> out;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < keep; ++i) out.push_back(found[i].second);
        return out;
    }

private:
    struct Node {
        std::array<int, 26> child{};
        long long count = 0;
    };

    std::vector<Node> nodes_;
};

+++ problem | Drilling the fewest rocks
--- task
A mining rover crosses a grid of strings from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, moving up, down, left or right. `'.'` is open ground and `'#'` is rock. Entering an open cell costs nothing; entering a rock cell costs one drilling. The start cell counts too: if it is rock, that is one drilling before the first move. Write `int fewest_drills(const std::vector<std::string>& grid)`, with no `main`: the fewest drillings needed to reach the bottom-right cell. The grid has at least one cell, and all rows have the same length.

This is a shortest path with edge costs 0 and 1. Dijkstra works, but **0-1 BFS** is simpler and O(cells): keep a `std::deque` of cells; when you reach a neighbour more cheaply through a cost-0 step, push it at the **front**, and through a cost-1 step, push it at the **back**. The deque then always holds cells in order of distance, with at most two distances in it at once, as in BFS. (A cell may be pushed more than once; skip it if you pop it after a better distance was found.) A check uses a 600 by 800 grid.

For example, `{"..#", "#..", "##."}` needs 0 drillings: the path right, down, right, down avoids every rock. `{".#", "#."}` needs 1.
--- starter
#include <deque>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int fewest_drills(const std::vector<std::string>& grid) {
    int count = 0;
    for (const auto& row : grid)
        for (char c : row)
            if (c == '#') ++count;
    return count;
}
--- solution
#include <deque>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int fewest_drills(const std::vector<std::string>& grid) {
    int h = static_cast<int>(grid.size());
    int w = static_cast<int>(grid[0].size());
    const int unreached = 1 << 30;
    std::vector<int> dist(h * w, unreached);
    std::deque<int> cells;
    dist[0] = grid[0][0] == '#' ? 1 : 0;
    cells.push_back(0);
    const int dr[] = {1, -1, 0, 0};
    const int dc[] = {0, 0, 1, -1};
    while (!cells.empty()) {
        int cell = cells.front();
        cells.pop_front();
        int r = cell / w;
        int c = cell % w;
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k) {
            int nr = r + dr[k];
            int nc = c + dc[k];
            if (nr < 0 || nr >= h || nc < 0 || nc >= w) continue;
            int next = nr * w + nc;
            int cost = grid[nr][nc] == '#' ? 1 : 0;
            if (dist[cell] + cost < dist[next]) {
                dist[next] = dist[cell] + cost;
                if (cost == 0) cells.push_front(next);
                else cells.push_back(next);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist[h * w - 1];
}
--- check case | Around the rocks for free

=> 0
--- check case | One rock in every path

=> 1
--- check case | A single cell, open or rock
fewest_drills({"."}) * 10 + fewest_drills({"#"})
=> 1
--- check case | The start and the end are rock
fewest_drills({"#..", "...", "..#"})
=> 2
--- check case | A wall with a long way round
fewest_drills({"......", "#####.", "......", ".#####", "......"})
=> 0
--- check case | Drilling beats the long way when there is none
fewest_drills({"..#..", "..#..", "..#..", "..#.."})
=> 1
--- check case | A 600 by 800 grid, 45% rock
[] { std::vector<std::string> g; unsigned s = 99; for (int r = 0; r < 600; ++r) { std::string row; for (int c = 0; c < 800; ++c) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; row += (s >> 16) % 100 < 45 ? '#' : '.'; } g.push_back(row); } return fewest_drills(g); }()
=> 43

+++ problem | The cheapest cable network
--- task
Ground stations 0 to n − 1 must all be connected by fibre, directly or through other stations. `links` lists the possible cables as (a, b, cost) tuples: a cable between stations a and b costing `cost` (0 to 1,000,000,000). Write `long long min_cable(int n, const std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, int>>& links)`, with no `main`: the smallest total cost of a set of cables that connects every station, or −1 if even all the cables together cannot connect them. One station needs no cable (cost 0).

Use **Kruskal's algorithm**: sort the cables by cost with `std::sort`, then take each cable in that order if its two stations are not yet connected, which a union-find with union by size and path halving answers (lesson 17). Kruskal's choice is optimal by the cut property: the cheapest cable joining two separate groups is always part of some cheapest network. Totals can reach 10¹⁴, so add in `long long`. A check uses 100,000 stations and about 400,000 cables.

For example, with n = 4 and cables (0, 1, 5), (1, 2, 3), (0, 2, 4), (2, 3, 8), (1, 3, 9), the answer is 3 + 4 + 8 = 15.
--- starter
#include <algorithm>
#include <numeric>
#include <tuple>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

long long min_cable(int n, const std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, int>>& links) {
    long long total = 0;
    for (const auto& [a, b, cost] : links) total += cost;
    return total;
}
--- solution
#include <algorithm>
#include <numeric>
#include <tuple>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

long long min_cable(int n, const std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, int>>& links) {
    std::vector<int> parent(n);
    std::vector<int> size(n, 1);
    std::iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0);
    auto find = [&parent](int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };
    std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, int>> by_cost = links;
    std::sort(by_cost.begin(), by_cost.end(), [](const auto& x, const auto& y) { return std::get<2>(x) < std::get<2>(y); });
    long long total = 0;
    int joined = 0;
    for (const auto& [a, b, cost] : by_cost) {
        int ra = find(a);
        int rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) continue;
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) std::swap(ra, rb);
        parent[rb] = ra;
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        total += cost;
        ++joined;
    }
    return joined == n - 1 ? total : -1;
}
--- check case | The example from the task
min_cable(4, {{0, 1, 5}, {1, 2, 3}, {0, 2, 4}, {2, 3, 8}, {1, 3, 9}})
=> 15LL
--- check case | One station, no cables
min_cable(1, {})
=> 0LL
--- check case | Two groups that cannot meet
min_cable(4, {{0, 1, 1}, {2, 3, 1}})
=> -1LL
--- check case | Parallel cables and a cable from a station to itself
min_cable(3, {{0, 0, 1}, {0, 1, 7}, {0, 1, 2}, {1, 2, 5}, {2, 1, 4}})
=> 6LL
--- check case | Costs that pass two billion in total
min_cable(4, {{0, 1, 1000000000}, {1, 2, 1000000000}, {2, 3, 1000000000}})
=> 3000000000LL
--- check case | 100,000 stations, 300,000 random cables plus a costly chain
[] { int n = 100000; std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, int>> e; unsigned s = 31; for (int i = 0; i < 300000; ++i) { s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int a = static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % n); s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; int b = static_cast<int>((s >> 8) % n); s = s * 1103515245u + 12345u; e.push_back({a, b, static_cast<int>((s >> 2) % 1000000000u)}); } long long apart = min_cable(n, e); for (int i = 0; i + 1 < n; ++i) e.push_back({i, i + 1, 999999999}); return apart == -1 ? min_cable(n, e) : -2; }()

+++ question | The pointer after push_back
--- ask
```cpp fragment
std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3};
int* p = &v[0];
v.push_back(4);
```

What can you say about `p` afterwards?
--- choice
It still points at the 1: vector elements never move.
--- choice correct
It dangles if the push needed more capacity, because growing moves every element to a new block and frees the old one; it is safe only if `v.capacity()` was already at least 4.
--- choice
It now points at the 4, the newest element.
--- choice
It is always invalid after any `push_back`.
--- why
A vector keeps its elements in one block. When `size() == capacity()`, `push_back` allocates a bigger block, moves the elements across and frees the old one, so every pointer, reference and iterator into the old block dangles. If there was spare capacity, nothing moves and `p` stays valid, which is why `reserve` in advance is the standard way to keep pointers stable while filling a vector.

+++ question | Why the list's destructor crashed
--- ask
A singly linked list holds each node's successor in a `std::unique_ptr<Node> next`, and has no destructor of its own. Destroying a list of a million nodes crashes. Why?
--- choice
`unique_ptr` cannot free more than a few thousand objects.
--- choice correct
Destroying the head destroys its `next`, which destroys its `next`, and so on: a chain of nested destructor calls a million deep, which overflows the call stack.
--- choice
The nodes are freed twice, once by the list and once by `unique_ptr`.
--- choice
Moving `unique_ptr`s during destruction is undefined behaviour.
--- why
Each node's destructor runs its members' destructors, so freeing node 1 must first finish freeing node 2, and so on: the recursion is as deep as the list is long. The fix is a destructor that detaches one node at a time in a loop, moving each `next` out before its owner is freed, so no call ever nests.

+++ question | Owning next, observing prev
--- ask
In a doubly linked list where `next` is a `std::unique_ptr<Node>`, why is `prev` a plain `Node*` rather than another `std::unique_ptr<Node>`?
--- choice
Plain pointers are faster to follow than smart pointers.
--- choice correct
Each node must have exactly one owner; if `prev` also owned, every node would have two owners and would be freed twice.
--- choice
`unique_ptr` cannot point backwards.
--- choice
So that `prev` can be `nullptr` at the head; a `unique_ptr` cannot be empty.
--- why
`unique_ptr` means sole ownership. With `next` owning, each node is owned by the node before it (or the list). A second owning pointer from the node after would make two owners, and both would delete it. `prev` only observes: it may be followed while the node lives, and it never frees anything.

+++ question | Full or empty
--- ask
A ring buffer stores up to 8 items in an array of 8, with `head` (the index of the oldest item) and `tail` (the index where the next item goes), both wrapping modulo 8, and nothing else. After 8 pushes, `head == tail`. What is the problem?
--- choice
None: `head == tail` always means the buffer is full.
--- choice correct
`head == tail` also describes the empty buffer, so the two states cannot be told apart; keep a count as well, or leave one slot unused.
--- choice
The modulo makes `tail` negative after 8 pushes.
--- choice
The 8th push overwrites the oldest item.
--- why
Both "no items" and "8 items" leave the two indexes equal. The usual fixes are to store the number of items (so full is `count == 8`), or to call the buffer full at 7 items so that `head == tail` only ever means empty.

+++ question | Why probing is fast
--- ask
Linear probing suffers from clustering, yet on real hardware it often beats a chained hash table at the same load factor. What is the main reason?
--- choice
Linear probing never has collisions.
--- choice correct
The probes for one lookup read neighbouring slots of one array, usually in the same cache line or the next, while a chain follows pointers to nodes scattered around memory.
--- choice
Linear probing uses a better hash function.
--- choice
Chaining needs to rehash on every insert.
--- why
Clustering adds probes, but each extra probe is a step to the next slot, which the cache and the prefetcher have usually loaded already. A chain step is a pointer dereference to a separately allocated node, often a cache miss of around 100 ns. Counting probes favours chaining; timing often favours probing, which is lesson 18's point about big-O and real time.

+++ question | What the queue prints
--- ask
What does this print?

```cpp
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>> q;
    for (int x : {5, 1, 8, 3}) q.push(x);
    q.pop();
    std::cout << q.top() << "\n";
}
```
--- answer
3
--- why
With `std::greater<int>` the comparator says "a comes out after b" when a > b, so the smallest is on top: a min-heap. The first `pop` removes 1, leaving 3, 5 and 8, and the top is 3.

+++ question | Which iterators an erase breaks
--- ask
You hold iterators to three different elements of a `std::map`. You erase the element that the first iterator points to. Which iterators are now invalid?
--- choice
All three: erasing rebalances the tree and moves nodes.
--- choice correct
Only the first one; the other two still point at their elements.
--- choice
The first one and every iterator to a larger key.
--- choice
None, as long as you do not use `end()`.
--- why
`std::map` is a node-based red-black tree. Rebalancing after an erase changes colours and links, but never moves an element to another node, so only iterators to the erased element are invalidated. That is why erasing inside a loop with `it = m.erase(it)` is safe.

+++ question | Inserting while walking an unordered_map
--- ask
A loop walks an `std::unordered_map<int, int>` with an iterator, and for some elements inserts a new key into the same map. What is wrong?
--- choice
Nothing, since pointers to elements survive a rehash.
--- choice correct
An insert that triggers a rehash invalidates every iterator, including the loop's, so the next `++it` is undefined behaviour.
--- choice
The new keys are always visited twice.
--- choice
Inserting into an `unordered_map` is not allowed while it has iterators.
--- why
References and pointers to elements survive a rehash, but iterators do not, because the bucket structure they walk is rebuilt. Either `reserve` enough room first (then no insert rehashes), or collect the new keys and insert them after the loop. Even without a rehash, a new key may land before or after the iterator, so the loop may or may not visit it.

+++ question | The fastest median
--- ask
Which call finds the median of ten million `double`s fastest, on average?
--- choice
`std::sort`, then read the middle element.
--- choice
`std::stable_sort`, then read the middle element.
--- choice correct
`std::nth_element` at the middle position, then read that element.
--- choice
`std::partial_sort` of the smallest half, then read the last element of that half.
--- why
`nth_element` is selection: expected O(n), a few comparisons per element. Both sorts cost O(n log n), about 23 comparisons per element here. `partial_sort` of half the range still costs O(n log n) with k = n / 2.

+++ question | Dijkstra with the wrong heap
--- ask
A Dijkstra implementation with lazy deletion accidentally uses `std::priority_queue<std::pair<long long, int>>`, a **max**-heap, so it always pops the farthest pending vertex. All edge costs are non-negative. What happens?
--- choice
It returns wrong distances on most graphs.
--- choice
It never terminates.
--- choice correct
It still ends with correct distances, because every improvement is pushed and processed later, but it can re-process vertices many times and run far slower.
--- choice
It does not compile, because the pair has no `>`.
--- why
Whenever a distance drops, the vertex is pushed again, and when that entry is popped (not stale) its edges are relaxed with the new distance. When the queue empties, no edge can improve any distance, which is exactly the condition for shortest distances. What is lost is the order: popping the smallest first is what guarantees each vertex is settled once, so the wrong heap turns an O((n + m) log n) algorithm into one that can take exponential time on bad graphs.

+++ question | Testing whether two stations are connected
--- ask
In a union-find, a programmer tests whether a and b are in the same group with `parent[a] == parent[b]`. Why is that wrong?
--- choice
It is right, but slower than calling `find`.
--- choice correct
Two items of one group can have different parents: only their roots are guaranteed equal, so the test must be `find(a) == find(b)`.
--- choice
`parent[a]` is undefined until `a` has been united with something.
--- choice
It fails only when a or b is itself a root.
--- why
A group is a tree, and `parent` holds just one step towards the root. Items at different depths, or in different branches, have different parents but the same root. Only `find`, which follows the parents to the top, gives the representative.

+++ question | Same big-O, different speed
--- ask
Summing a million `int`s takes well under a millisecond in a `std::vector` and tens of milliseconds in a `std::list` whose nodes have been shuffled in memory. Both loops are Θ(n). Why the difference?
--- choice
The list's loop does more additions.
--- choice
Iterating a list needs a function call per element.
--- choice correct
The vector's elements sit side by side, so each 64-byte cache line brings 16 of them and the prefetcher streams ahead; each list node is somewhere else in memory, so nearly every step is a cache miss that must finish before the next address is even known.
--- choice
The vector is sorted and the list is not.
--- why
Big-O counts operations and hides the cost of each one. Here the operations are the same, but a vector read usually hits the cache (about 1 ns) and a scattered list step usually misses it (about 100 ns). That is why contiguous structures win so often in practice, even against better big-O on paper.
